en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Division Concerning the Aggregate of Virtue in the Dīgha Nikāya.
I pay homage to the Sugata,
who is free from the cycle of rebirths, revered by the world of humans and devas,
whose heart is cooled by compassion, and whose darkness of delusion is dispelled by the lamp of wisdom.
I pay homage to that unsurpassed Dhamma which the Buddha— having developed and realized the state of Buddhahood— has attained,
being one whose taints have departed. To the sons of the Sugata, the destroyers of Māra’s army...
I pay homage with my head to the Noble Saṅgha, the assembly of these eight [types of noble ones].
Thus, may the merit arising from this homage to the Triple Gem by me,
whose mind is serene— by the power of that merit— may all obstacles be thoroughly dispelled.
For the purpose of elucidating the meaning of this long *Āgama*, which is marked by long suttas,
subtle, excellent, praised by those awakened after the Buddha, and possessing qualities that inspire faith—
the *Aṭṭhakathā* was composed at the beginning by the six hundred *Vasīs*.
That which was chanted at the five councils, and subsequently recited again—
this was brought to the Island of Siṃhala by the venerable Mahinda and established in the Sinhalese language for the benefit of the inhabitants of the island.
Then, having set aside the delightful Sinhalese language,
I composed this work in a faultless style appropriate to the method of the discourses (Tanti),
not transgressing the tradition of the Elders who are lamps of the lineage of the Theras.
Having abandoned the matter that has been repeatedly approached by those dwelling in the Mahāvihāra who possess subtle discernment,
I shall clarify the meaning for the satisfaction of virtuous people and for the long endurance of the Dhamma.
The discourse on virtue, the ascetic practices, all the meditation subjects,
the detailed exposition of the jhānas and attainments together with the methods of conduct,
all the higher knowledges, and the compendium of the calculation of wisdom;
The aggregates, elements, sense bases, and faculties; the four Noble Truths;
the teaching on the mode of conditions with its perfectly pure and subtle methods;
the paths to liberation; and the development of insight.
Since all this has been very thoroughly explained by me in the *Visuddhimagga*, I shall not further analyze it here. Indeed,
this *Visuddhimagga* stands in the midst of the four *Āgamas*.
"Having stood [there], he will reveal the meaning as it was spoken therein.
For this reason, having taken that [text] together with this commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*),
you should understand the meaning based on the *Dīgha-aṭṭhakathā*.
In that regard, the Dīgha Āgama consists of three sections by way of its divisions: the Sīlakkhandha-vagga, the Mahā-vagga, and the Pāṭika-vagga.
By way of its discourses, it comprises a collection of thirty-four suttas. Among its sections, the Sīlakkhandha-vagga is the first; among its suttas—
The *Brahmajāla*. For the *Brahmajāla* as well, the introduction beginning with "Thus have I heard" was spoken by the Venerable Ānanda at the time of the First Great Council (*paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti*).
Regarding the account of the First Great Council:
although this so-called First Great Council is included in the sequence of the Vinaya Piṭaka, for the sake of proficiency regarding the introductory narratives (*nidāna*), [it is discussed here].

However, here too it should be understood in this way. For when the Blessed One, the Lord of the World, had performed his Buddha-activities— beginning from the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma up until the conversion of the wanderer Subhadda—

and having attained final Nibbāna through the element of Nibbāna without residue at the time of dawn on the full moon of Visākha, between the twin Sāla trees in the Upavattana of the Mallas near Kusinārā, [the following occurred] regarding the Blessed One...

On the day of the distribution of the relics, when seven hundred thousand bhikkhus had assembled, the Elder of the Saṅgha, the Venerable Mahākassapa, said to Subhadda, who had gone forth in old age: "Enough, friends;
do not grieve, do not lament. We are well rid of that great ascetic, for we were oppressed by him."
Recalling the words spoken [by the Teacher]: "This is permissible for you;
this is not permissible for you," and considering how difficult it will be to find another such assembly of the Saṅgha again, thinking:
"It is indeed possible that wicked bhikkhus, [thinking] 'the Teacher has passed away'..."
Thinking, "This is the Teacher's word," and having gained a faction, they would cause the true Dhamma to disappear before long.
As long as the Dhamma and Vinaya remain, the Teacher's word remains as if the Teacher has not passed away. For this was said by the Blessed One:
"Ānanda, the Dhamma and Vinaya taught and laid down by me to you shall be your teacher after my passing."
‘What if I were now to recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya, so that this Teaching might endure for a long time and remain stable?
And because the Blessed One,
having said to me, ‘Kassapa, you shall wear my hempen rag-robes that have been washed,’ [entrusted me] with the common use of his robes.
“Monks, as much as I wish, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, I enter and dwell in the first jhāna,

which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. And Kassapa too, monks, as much as he wishes, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, [enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought].”
"Having attained and dwelling in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied thought (savicāra), born of seclusion, and filled with rapture and happiness"— in this manner,

he was assisted by being established as his equal in the superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) distinguished by the nine successive dwellings (navānupubbavihāra) and the six direct knowledges (chaḷabhiññā);
likewise, by waving his hand in the air, through the state of a mind unattached...
And since he was praised for his practice that is like the moon, what other debtlessness could there be for him? Did not the Blessed One,

regarding me as one who would establish his own lineage of true Dhamma— just as a king, by bestowing his own armor and sovereignty, regards a son who will establish his royal dynasty— favor me with this extraordinary favor, thinking,
"This one shall be the establisher of my lineage of true Dhamma," and with this [practice]...?
Reflecting that he was being praised with lofty praise, he inspired the bhikkhus to undertake the recitation of the Dhamma and Vinaya.
As it is said: “Then the Venerable Mahākassapa addressed the bhikkhus:
‘Friends, on one occasion I was traveling along the highway from Pāvā to Kusinārā together with a great Saṅgha of bhikkhus, numbering about five hundred bhikkhus.’”
The entire Subhadda chapter should be understood in detail. However, its meaning we shall explain at the very point where it occurs at the conclusion of the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta.
Following that, he said:
“Come, friends, let us recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya before un-Dhamma shines forth and the Dhamma is suppressed;
before non-Vinaya shines forth and the Vinaya is suppressed;

before those who speak what is not Dhamma become powerful and those who speak the Dhamma become weak; before those who speak what is not Vinaya become powerful and those who speak the Vinaya become weak.”
The bhikkhus said, "In that case, venerable sir, let the Elder select the bhikkhus. But the Elder,
having set aside many hundreds and thousands of bhikkhus— both worldlings, stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, dry-insight practitioners, and those whose taints were exhausted—

who maintained the learning of the Teacher’s entire ninefold dispensation, selected those of great power who had attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) and mastered every classification of the Three Pitakas.

For the most part, when the Blessed One’s supreme status was being established, he selected four hundred and ninety-nine bhikkhus who were arahants with taints destroyed, distinguished by their mastery of the three knowledges (*tevijjā*) and so forth.
It was with reference to them that this was said: “Then the Venerable Mahākassapa chose four hundred and ninety-nine arahants.”
But why did the Elder leave one [discourse] out? It was for the sake of making way for the Venerable Ānanda.

For it would have been impossible to hold the Dhamma Saṅgīti either with him or without him. That Venerable One was still a trainee (sekha) who had duties yet to perform; therefore, it would have been impossible even with him.
However, as for certain discourses, verses, and so forth taught by the One of Ten Powers that were not within his direct experience—
There is no such thing. As it is said:
“I received eighty-two thousand [teachings] from the Buddha, two thousand from the monks, and eighty-four thousand are those doctrines that have been transmitted to me.”
Therefore, it was not possible even without him.
If this were so, then since he too was a trainee (*sekha*), why was he not selected by the Elder for the recitation of the Dhamma (*dhammasaṅgīti*) because of his great usefulness?
[The answer is: Because of his avoidance of censure from others. For the Elder was exceedingly confident in the Venerable Ānanda.
For even though grey hairs had grown upon his head, he would still address him as "boy," advising him with the words, "This boy has not yet reached his full measure.
Furthermore, the Venerable One was born into the Sakyan clan; he was the Tathāgata’s brother, the son of his younger paternal uncle.
Thereupon, some monks, suspecting it might be a case of acting out of favoritism, [said]: "Many have attained the analytical knowledges of one beyond training..."
They might criticize him, saying, "The Elder excluded Ānanda, who was a trainee (sekha) yet had attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
Avoiding such criticism from others, he thought, "It is not possible to hold the Dhamma Council without Ānanda;
I shall include him with the consent of the monks themselves," and so he did not exclude him.
Then the monks themselves requested the Elder on behalf of Ānanda. As it is said:

“The monks said this to the Venerable Mahākassapa: ‘Venerable sir, although this Venerable Ānanda is still a trainee (sekha), he is incapable of going astray through desire, hatred, delusion, or fear; moreover, he has spent much time in the presence of the Blessed One.’”
“The Dhamma and the Vinaya have been mastered; therefore, venerable sir, let the Elder choose Venerable Ānanda as well.
Then Venerable Mahākassapa chose Venerable Ānanda as well.
Thus, together with that Venerable who had been chosen by the consent of the monks, there were five hundred elders.
Then it occurred to the elder bhikkhus: "Where indeed should we recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya?
Then it occurred to the elder bhikkhus: "Rājagaha has a vast alms-resort and many dwellings;
what if we were to spend the rains retreat at Rājagaha and recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya there?"
“Let no other bhikkhus enter the rains residence at Rājagaha.

Why, then, did this thought occur to them? “This is our secure undertaking; perhaps some person of a different disposition might enter the midst of the Saṅgha and reopen the matter. Then the Venerable Mahākassapa made the announcement by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and a second resolution:
“Let the venerable Saṅgha hear me. If it is agreeable to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha [authorize] these five hundred bhikkhus...”
“Let the Saṅgha appoint these five hundred bhikkhus to dwell for the rains at Rājagaha in order to recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya;
no other bhikkhus should dwell for the rains at Rājagaha. This is the motion.
“Let the venerable Saṅgha hear me: the Saṅgha appoints these five hundred bhikkhus [to dwell] for the rains at Rājagaha...”
"In order to recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya during the rains retreat, it is not for other monks to dwell in the rains retreat at Rājagaha.
To whichever venerable one it is agreeable that these five hundred monks be authorized to dwell in the rains retreat at Rājagaha to recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya,
and that no other monks dwell in the rains retreat at Rājagaha— [speak up]."
Therefore, he who is silent approves; he who does not approve should speak.

“The Saṅgha has authorized these five hundred bhikkhus, dwelling for the rains at Rājagaha, to recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya, and that no other bhikkhus should dwell for the rains at Rājagaha. This is pleasing to the Saṅgha.”
"Therefore, be silent; thus do I decree this.
This formal proclamation (*kammavācā*) was made on the twenty-first day after the Tathāgata’s final *parinibbāna*.
For the Blessed One had attained *parinibbāna* at dawn on the full moon of the month of Visākha; thereafter, his body remained for seven days with a golden hue.
They honored [the remains] with perfumes, garlands, and so forth. Thus, there were seven days known as the "days of joyful celebration.
Then, for seven days, they cremated [the body] with fire on the funeral pyre; for seven days, having constructed a cage of spears, they performed the worship of the relics in the Hall of Truth.
In this way, twenty-one days passed. On the very fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jeṭṭhamūla, they divided the relics.

On this day of the assembly of the great Saṅgha of bhikkhus at the Dhātubhājana festival, after Subhadda—who had gone forth in old age—had reported the misconduct he had committed and, in the manner already described, selected the bhikkhus, this formal act (kammavācā) was performed.
Having performed this formal act, the Elder addressed the bhikkhus: "Friends, now for you there are forty..."
An opportunity has been granted for [only] these many days; beyond that, it is not permitted to say, "We have such-and-such an obstacle.

Therefore, during this interval, whoever has an obstacle such as illness, or an obstacle regarding a teacher or preceptor, or an obstacle regarding mother or father, or who must cook a bowl, or must make a robe—such a person, having severed that obstacle, [may go].
"Let him perform what is to be done.
Having spoken thus, the Elder departed for Rājagaha, surrounded by his own retinue of five hundred.
Other great elders as well, taking their respective followers with them, desired to comfort the great multitude who were pierced by the arrow of grief.

They departed in various directions. But the Elder Puṇṇa, accompanied by a retinue of seven hundred bhikkhus, remained right there at Kusinārā, thinking, "I shall comfort the great multitude of people who have come one after another to the place of the Tathāgata’s final Nibbāna.
The Venerable Ānanda acted for the Blessed One who had attained final Nibbāna exactly as he had done previously when the Blessed One was not yet finally extinguished.
Taking his bowl and robe, he set out on a walking tour toward Sāvatthī together with five hundred bhikkhus.
As he traveled, however, the number of bhikkhus in his retinue exceeded all calculation. Wherever the Venerable One went, there was great lamentation.
Eventually, when the Elder had gradually arrived at Sāvatthī, the people living in Sāvatthī—
Hearing that "the Elder has arrived," they went out to meet him with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings in their hands, weeping as they said such things as:
"Venerable Ānanda, formerly you used to come together with the Blessed One; today, having left the Blessed One behind, where have you come from?
There was a great lamentation, just like on the day of the Parinibbāna of the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda, having instructed that great multitude with a discourse on the Dhamma connected with impermanence and other such themes,
entered the Jeta Grove. He paid homage to the Perfumed Chamber where the One of Ten Powers had dwelt,
opened the door, removed the bed and chair, shook them out, swept the Perfumed Chamber, and discarded the withered garlands and refuse.
Having carried the bed and chair back and placed them again in their original positions, he performed every duty that ought to be done while the Blessed One was present.
While performing these tasks—at times such as sweeping the bathhouse or preparing the water for bathing—he would pay homage to the Fragrant Chamber and say:
"Is it not so, Blessed One? This is your time for bathing; this is your time for teaching the Dhamma; this is the time for the bhikkhus..."
He performed these acts while lamenting in this manner: “This is the time for giving exhortation; this is the time for making the lion’s posture;

this is the time for washing the face,” and so forth. This was because his affection was established through a deep remembrance of the nectar-like qualities of the Blessed One, and because his taints were not yet exhausted, and because his heart was softened by the sense of mutual service rendered over many hundreds of thousands of births. Thus he—
A certain deity exhorted him, saying, "Venerable Ānanda, while you are lamenting in this way, how will you console others?
Stirred by these words, his heart filled with agitation, he steadied himself;

and because he had spent much time standing and sitting since the Tathāgata’s final nibbāna, his body was afflicted by an excess of humors. To restore his health, on the following day he took a purgative of milk.
Having drunk it, he sat down right there in the monastery. With reference to this, he said to the young man whom Subha the Māṇava had sent:
"It is not the right time, young man; I have taken a dose of medicine today. Perhaps we might come again tomorrow.
On the following day, having gone with the Elder Cetaka as his attendant monk, he was questioned by Subha the Māṇava and spoke the tenth discourse in this Dīgha Nikāya, known as the Subha Sutta.

Then the Elder Ānanda, having overseen the restoration of what was broken and dilapidated in the Great Monastery of Jetavana, departed for Rājagaha with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus when the time for the commencement of the rains retreat had approached; others who were compilers of the Dhamma did likewise.
It was with reference to them, having thus departed, that this was said: "Then the elder bhikkhus [went] to Rājagaha..."
"...and to recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya. Having observed the Uposatha on the full moon day of Āsāḷhī, they assembled on the first day of the fortnight (pāṭipada) and entered the rains retreat.
At that time, there were eighteen great monasteries surrounding Rājagaha, and all of them—
They became discarded, fallen, and ruined. Indeed, at the Parinibbāna of the Blessed One, all the bhikkhus took their own bowls and robes and departed, leaving behind the monasteries and the cells.

There, the elders who were performing the established duties, for the sake of honoring the word of the Blessed One and for the sake of avoiding the doctrines of the non-Buddhist sects, [said]: "During the first month..."

They thought, "We shall repair what is broken and dilapidated. For the followers of other sects might say, "The disciples of the ascetic Gotama looked after the monasteries only while the Teacher was still alive;
now that he has attained Parinibbāna, they have abandoned them, and thus the great wealth given by the families is being wasted. It is said that they thought this in order to refute such arguments.
Having reflected thus, they made a formal agreement, with reference to which it was said:
"Then it occurred to the elder bhikkhus: 'Friends, the Blessed One has praised the repair of what is broken and dilapidated;
come, friends, let us perform the repair of what is broken and dilapidated during the first month.'"
“Having assembled for the middle month, we shall recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya.
On the following day, they went and stood at the king’s gate. The king came out, paid homage, and asked, “What is it, venerable sirs, that you have come for?
He then inquired about the task he himself was to perform. The elders [requested] manual labor for the purpose of repairing the eighteen great monasteries.

They informed [the king]. The king provided men for manual labor. After the elders had completed the repairs throughout the entire monastery during the first month, they reported to the king: "Great King, the restoration of the monastery is finished;
now let us perform the compilation of the Dhamma and Vinaya. "Very well, venerable sirs, carry it out with confidence; this is my royal command."
"And may the Wheel of Dhamma be yours as well; give your command, venerable sir, what shall I do?
"A place for the monks who are gathering together to sit in assembly, Great King. "Where shall I build it, venerable sir?
"It would be appropriate, Great King, to build it on the slope of Mount Vebhāra at the entrance to the Sattapaṇṇi Cave. "Very well, venerable sir," said King Ajātasattu.
With its walls, pillars, and stairways so well-proportioned as to resemble the work of Vissakamma himself;
variegated with various kinds of floral and creeper designs; surpassing, as it were, the splendor of royal palaces; mocking, as it were, the glory of the celestial mansions of the gods;
like a dwelling-place of majesty and like a bathing-ghat for the birds that are the eyes of gods and men; it was like the collective essence of all the world’s loveliness.
Having had a pavilion constructed— the very essence of all that is worthy of being seen—
with beautiful canopies hanging down from garlands of various flowers, its floor appearing like a mosaic of diverse gems and jewels,

and its ground-work perfectly finished and variegated with offerings of many kinds of blossoms so that it resembled the celestial palace of Brahmā; therein, for five hundred bhikkhus, [he prepared] priceless...

Having prepared five hundred lawful rugs, he arranged the seat for the Elder facing north against the southern side, and in the center of the pavilion, he prepared the Dharma-seat worthy of the Blessed Buddha facing east;
having placed a fan inlaid with ivory there, he announced to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus: "It is finished."
“Venerable sir, this is my duty.
On that very day, some bhikkhus, referring to the Venerable Ānanda, said:
“In this Saṅgha of bhikkhus, there is one bhikkhu who wanders about emitting a foul odor. When the Elder heard this, he [thought]: “In this...”
"There is no other monk in the Saṅgha who wanders about emitting such a foul odor;
surely they are speaking of me," he thought, and he was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*). Some said to him: "Friend Ānanda, there is a gathering tomorrow.
Since you are still a trainee (*sekha*) with work yet to be done, it is not fitting for you to go to the assembly; be diligent."
Then the Venerable Ānanda thought: "The assembly is tomorrow; it would not be fitting for me, being still a trainee (sekha), to go to the assembly.

Having spent much of the night with mindfulness directed to the body, at the time of dawn he descended from his walking path, entered his dwelling, and as he was about to lie down, he directed his mind toward his body; [then] his two feet left the ground.
When his head was released from the hair and reached the pillow, in that interval his mind was liberated from the taints through non-clinging.
For this venerable one, having spent much time outside walking back and forth and being unable to produce further distinction, thought:
"Did not the Blessed One say this to me: 'Ānanda, you have performed merit; apply yourself to striving, for quickly...'"
“You shall become one free from taints. Now, there is no fault in the speech of the Buddhas;
however, my energy was excessive, and because of that, my mind tended toward agitation. “Come now, I shall apply myself to evenness of energy.
Having descended from his walking path, he stood at the place for washing his feet, washed his feet, entered the dwelling, sat down on the couch, and [thought]: “A little...”
"I shall rest," he said, and shifted his body onto the couch. Two feet were lifted from the ground, yet his head had not reached the pillow;
in that interval, his mind was liberated from the taints without further clinging—the Elder’s attainment of Arahantship, which transcends the four postures.
Therefore, [the Buddha asked]: "In this teaching, what monk has not lain down, not sat, not stood, and not walked?"
When it was said, "He has attained Arahatship," it was appropriate to say, "The Elder Ānanda.
Then, on the second day, the fifth of the dark fortnight, the elder monks, having finished their meal and put away their bowls and robes, assembled in the Dhamma Hall.
Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda, being an Arahat, [joined] the assembly.
He went. How did he go? With a heart joyful and elated, thinking, "Now I am worthy to enter the midst of the assembly," he arranged his robe over one shoulder;

like a palmyra fruit released from its stalk, like a natural gem placed upon a yellowish-white woolen cloth, like the full moon risen in a cloudless sky, [he appeared] with a body as golden as the pollen of a flower opened by the touch of the morning sun.

And like a lotus, he went along with his face so pure, bright, radiant, and beautiful that it was as if he were announcing his own attainment of Arahantship. Then, seeing him, it occurred to the Venerable Mahākassapa:
"Truly, the venerable Ānanda shines forth having attained Arahantship; had the Teacher still been living, [he would surely have...]"
“Let us give our applause to the Venerable Ānanda; come, let me give the applause that should be given by the Teacher.
And so he gave his applause three times.
However, the reciters of the Majjhima Nikāya say: “The Elder Ānanda, desiring to make known his own attainment of Arahatship, [said] to the monks...”
The monks arrived together and sat down on their respective seats according to seniority;
however, they left the seat for the Elder Ānanda vacant and sat down. There, some asked, “Whose seat is this?
“It is Ānanda’s. “But where has Ānanda gone? At that moment, the Elder thought, “Now it is time for me to depart.”
Then, displaying his own supernatural power, he submerged into the earth and showed himself right at his own seat;

some say that he went through the air and sat down. Whether it was one way or the other, in every respect, it was entirely appropriate for the Venerable Mahākassapa to give his approval upon seeing him.
When the Venerable Mahākassapa Thera had thus arrived, he addressed the bhikkhus:
"Friends, what shall we recite first: the Dhamma or the Vinaya? The bhikkhus replied:
"Venerable Mahākassapa, the Vinaya is indeed the life-span of the Buddha’s Dispensation. When the Vinaya stands, the Dispensation is said to stand. Therefore, let us first [recite the Vinaya]."
“Let us chant the Vinaya together. “Upon whom shall we rely as our authority? “Upon the Venerable Upāli. “Is it that Ānanda is not capable?

“It is not that he is not capable; however, while the Perfectly Enlightened One was still living, he established the Venerable Upāli in this foremost position based on his mastery of the Vinaya, saying:
‘Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my disciples, the bhikkhus, in regard to the mastery of the Vinaya.’”
"Among those who uphold the Vinaya, this one is Upāli. "Therefore, let us recite the Vinaya after consulting the Elder Upāli.

Thereupon, the Elder himself appointed himself for the purpose of questioning on the Vinaya; and the Elder Upāli was appointed for the purpose of answering. Herein is the Pāḷi: Then the Venerable Mahākassapa made a motion to the Saṅgha:
"Let the venerable Saṅgha listen to me. If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha..."
“I shall question the Venerable Upāli regarding the Vinaya.
The Venerable Upāli then informed the Saṅgha:
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, [let it authorize me].”
“If asked about the Vinaya by the Venerable Mahākassapa, I shall answer.

Having thus appointed himself, the Venerable Upāli rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, paid homage to the elder bhikkhus, and sat down on the Dhamma-seat, taking up a fan inlaid with ivory. Then the Elder Mahākassapa—
Having sat down on the elder’s seat, he questioned the Venerable Upāli regarding the Vinaya: "Friend Upāli, where was the first *pārājika* offense laid down?
"At Vesālī, Bhante. "With reference to whom? "With reference to Sudinna, the son of Kalandaka.
"On what matter? "On sexual intercourse."
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa questioned the Venerable Upāli regarding the basis of the first *pārājika* offense:
he questioned him about the origin, the individual, the formal rule, the supplementary rule, the offense, and the non-offense.
Being questioned again and again, the Venerable Upāli answered.
But here, in this first *pārājika*, is there anything that ought to be removed or added?
There is nothing to be removed. For in what was spoken by the Blessed Buddha, there is indeed nothing to be removed;
for the Tathāgatas do not utter even a single syllable in vain. However, [this may differ] in what was spoken by disciples or deities.
There was also material that ought to be removed, which the Elders who compiled the Dhamma removed.
However, there was also material that ought to be included everywhere; therefore, they simply inserted whatever was appropriate to be inserted wherever it belonged.
What, then, is this material? It is such expressions as “at that time,” or “now at that time,” or “then indeed,” or “thus it was said.”
Or, "He said this," or such like words merely expressing the connection. Having thus inserted what was appropriate to be inserted, they established it with the words:

"This is the first *pārājika*. When the first *pārājika* had been included in the collection, five hundred *arahants* performed the communal recitation (*gaṇasajjhāya*) according to the very method by which the collection had been compiled: "At that time..."
“The Buddha, the Blessed One, is dwelling at Verañjā. At the very moment they began their recitation, the great earth, bounded by the waters, shook as if giving its approval.
In this same manner, they compiled the remaining three *pārājika* rules and established them as the “Pārājika Section.”
They established thirteen rules as the "Thirteen" (terasa-saṅghādisesa). They established two training rules as the "Undetermined" (aniyata).
They established thirty training rules as the "Forfeiture and Expiation" (nissaggiya-pācittiya). They established ninety-two training rules as the "Expiation" (pācittiya).
They established four training rules as the "Confession" (pāṭidesanīya). Seventy-five...
They established the training rules as "the Sekhiyas. They established the seven principles as "the Settling of Litigations.
Thus, having proclaimed two hundred and twenty-seven training rules as the "Mahāvibhaṅga," they established them.
At the conclusion of the Mahāvibhaṅga, the great earth shook once more in the same manner as before.
Then, in the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga, they established eight training rules as "the Pārājika section";
seventeen training rules as "the Seventeen"; thirty training rules as "the Nissaggiya Pācittiya rules";
and one hundred and sixty-six training rules as "the Pācittiya rules. Eight...
They established the training rules as "those to be confessed" (pāṭidesanīya). They established seventy-five training rules as "the trainings" (sekhiya).
They established seven principles as "the settling of legal issues" (adhikaraṇasamatha).
Having thus proclaimed three hundred and four training rules as the "Bhikkhunī-vibhaṅga," [it was said]: "This is called the 'Analysis for Both' (Ubhatovibhaṅga)."
They established [the text] with the words, "The sixty-fourth section. At the conclusion of both the *Vibhaṅgas*, there was likewise a great earthquake in the manner already described.
By this same method, having compiled the *Khandhaka* measuring eighty sections and the *Parivāra* measuring twenty-five sections, they established it, saying, "This is called the Vinaya Piṭaka.
At the conclusion of the Vinaya Piṭaka, too, in the manner already described...
A great earthquake occurred. They entrusted that Venerable Upāli to him, saying, "Friend, teach this to those who depend on you.

At the conclusion of the compilation of the Vinaya Piṭaka, the Elder Upāli set down his ivory-inlaid fan, descended from the Dhamma throne, paid homage to the elder monks, and sat down on his own seat.
Having recited the Vinaya, the Venerable Mahākassapa, desiring to recite the Dhamma, asked the bhikkhus:
"When reciting the Dhamma, with what person as the authority should the Dhamma be recited? The bhikkhus replied: "With the Elder Ānanda as the authority."
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa informed the Saṅgha:
"Let the venerable Saṅgha listen to me. If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, I would question Ānanda concerning the Dhamma."
Then the Venerable Ānanda informed the Saṅgha:
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, I shall answer the questions on the Dhamma posed by the Venerable Mahākassapa."

Then the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his robe over one shoulder, paid homage to the elder bhikkhus, and sat down at the Dhamma-seat, taking up an ivory-inlaid fan. Then the Venerable Mahākassapa asked the bhikkhus:
"Friends, which Piṭaka shall we recite first?"—"The Sutta Piṭaka, Bhante."—"In the Sutta Piṭaka..."
“There were four councils; among them, which was the first council? “The Dīgha Saṅgīti, venerable sir.
“In the Dīgha Saṅgīti there are thirty-four suttas in three sections;
among them, which was the first section? “The Sīlakkhandha Vagga, venerable sir. “In the Sīlakkhandha Vagga there are thirteen suttantas; among them, the first—”
“Which discourse? “Venerable sir, it is the discourse named the *Brahmajālasutta*, adorned with the threefold morality, which destroys various kinds of wrong livelihood, deceit, and flattery;
it unravels the net of the sixty-two views and causes the ten-thousandfold world system to tremble.
Let us recite that first.”
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa said this to the Venerable Ānanda: “Friend Ānanda, where was the *Brahmajāla* spoken?
“Between Rājagaha and Nāḷandā, at Ambalaṭṭhikā in the royal rest-house, venerable sir.
“With reference to whom? “With reference to the wanderer Suppiya and the young Brahmin Brahmadatta. “On what subject?”

“Regarding ‘Praise and Dispraise’”: Then the Venerable Mahākassapa asked the Venerable Ānanda about the introduction (*nidāna*) of the *Brahmajāla Sutta*, he asked about the persons (*puggala*), and he asked about the subject matter (*vatthu*). The Venerable Ānanda answered.
At the conclusion of the answer, five hundred arahants performed a communal recitation (*gaṇasajjhāya*). And in the manner already described, there was an earthquake.

Having thus chanted the *Brahmajāla*, they thereafter chanted all thirteen discourses together with the *Brahmajāla* according to the sequence of questions and answers beginning with, "But where, friend Ānanda, was the *Sāmaññaphala* spoken? and so forth;
and having designated it as "This is the section named the Sīlakkhandha-vagga," they established it.
Immediately after that, the Mahāvagga; and immediately after that, the Pāṭhakavagga.

Having thus recited this textual tradition—comprising three divisions, adorned with thirty-four suttas, and measuring sixty-four bhāṇavāras—they declared, “This is called the Dīghanikāya,” and entrusted it to the Venerable Ānanda, saying, “Friend, teach this to those who depend on you.”

Immediately after that, having recited the *Majjhima Nikāya*, which consists of eighty *bhāṇavāras*, they entrusted it to the disciples of the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, saying: "You must preserve this.

Immediately after that, having recited the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*, which consists of one hundred *bhāṇavāras*, they entrusted it to the Elder Mahākassapa, saying: "Venerable sir, you should teach this to your own disciples."

Immediately after that, having recited the Aṅguttara Nikāya, which consists of one hundred and twenty recitation sections (*bhāṇavāra*), they entrusted it to the Elder Anuruddha, saying: "Recite this to those who rely upon you.
Immediately after that, the Abhidhamma—consisting of the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, Vibhaṅga, Dhātukathā, Puggalapaññatti, Kathāvatthu, Yamaka, and Paṭṭhāna—is spoken of.
Having thus recited this scripture, the domain of subtle knowledge, which has been so elaborated, [they said]: "This..."
Having said, "This is called the Abhidhamma Piṭaka," the five hundred arahants recited it.
Just as previously described, an earthquake occurred.
Following that were the Jātaka, the Niddesa, the Paṭisambhidāmagga, the Apadāna, the Suttanipāta, and the Khuddakapāṭha.
The Dīgha-bhāṇakas say that after reciting this collection consisting of the *Dhammapada*, *Udāna*, *Itivuttaka*, *Vimānavatthu*,
*Petavatthu*, *Theragāthā*, and *Therīgāthā*, and declaring, "This is called the *Khuddakagantha*," they included it within the Abhidhamma Piṭaka itself.
The Majjhima-bhāṇakas, however, [include it] with the *Cariyāpiṭaka* and the *Buddhavaṃsa*.
Together with all of this, they say that it is called the *Khuddakagantha* (Minor Collection) and is included within the Sutta Piṭaka.

Thus, this entire word of the Buddha (*buddhavacana*) is of one kind by way of its flavor (*rasa*), of two kinds by way of the Dhamma and the Vinaya, and of three kinds by way of the first, middle, and last [teachings].
Likewise, it is of five kinds by way of the Piṭakas, and of five kinds by way of the Nikāyas.
It should be understood that [the Dhamma] is ninefold by way of its factors (*aṅga*) and eighty-four thousandfold by way of the aggregates of the Dhamma (*dhammakkhandha*).

How is it onefold by way of its flavor (*rasa*)? For, from the time the Blessed One fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment until he attained final nibbāna in the element of nibbāna without residue—in this interval of forty-five years—[it was onefold].

Whether spoken by one instructing gods, humans, nāgas, yakkhas, and so forth, or by one reflecting [upon it], all that has the single flavor of the flavor of liberation (vimuttirasa) alone. Thus, it is of one kind by way of flavor.
How is it of two kinds by way of Dhamma and Vinaya? All of this is reckoned as both Dhamma and Vinaya.
It proceeds. In this context, the Vinaya Piṭaka is the Vinaya, and the remainder of the Buddha’s word is the Dhamma. For this very reason it was said:
“What if we were to recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya together? and “I would ask Upāli about the Vinaya, and Ānanda about the Dhamma.
Thus, it is twofold by way of the Dhamma and the Vinaya.
How is it threefold by way of first, middle, and last? All of this indeed is divided into three types: the first Buddha-word, the middle Buddha-word, and the last Buddha-word. Among these:
“I have wandered through the saṃsāra of many births, Seeking, but not finding, the builder of the house; For birth again and again is suffering.”
"House-builder, you have been seen; you shall build no house again.
All your rafters are broken, the ridgepole is shattered.
The mind has reached the unconditioned; it has attained the destruction of craving."
This is the first word of the Buddha. Some say that the verse from the Khandhaka, “When indeed phenomena become manifest,” is this [first utterance].

However, it should be understood that this is the verse of exultation (*udāna*) that arose on the day of the full moon of Āsāḷha, when he had attained omniscience, as he was reflecting upon the mode of conditions with a mind filled with joy.
Furthermore, that which he spoke at the time of his final *parinibbāna*—“Come now, monks, I exhort you:
all conditioned phenomena are subject to decay; strive with diligence”—this is the final word of the Buddha.
That which was spoken between these two is called the intermediate word of the Buddha. Thus, it is threefold by way of the first, intermediate, and final words of the Buddha.
How is it threefold by way of the Piṭakas? All this consists of exactly three divisions: the Vinaya Piṭaka, the Sutta Piṭaka, and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka.

Therein, having combined everything—both that which was recited and that which was not recited at the First Council—the two Pātimokkhas, the two Vibhaṅgas, the twenty-two Khandhakas, and the sixteen Parivāras constitute this [Vinaya Piṭaka].

The Vinaya Piṭaka is [the basket of discipline]. The Dīghanikāya is the collection of thirty-three suttas beginning with the Brahmajāla; the Majjhimanikāya is the collection of one hundred and fifty-two suttas beginning with the Mūlapariyāya;
the Saṃyuttanikāya is the collection of seven thousand seven hundred and sixty-two suttas beginning with the Oghataraṇa;
and the Aṅguttaranikāya is the collection of nine thousand five hundred and fifty-seven suttas beginning with the Cittapariyādāna.

The Khuddakanikāya, which has fifteen divisions—namely, the Aṅguttaranikāya; and the Khuddakapāṭha, Dhammapada, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Suttanipāta, Vimānavatthu, Petavatthu, Theragāthā, Therīgāthā, Jātaka, Niddesa, Paṭisambhidāmagga, Apadāna, Buddhavaṃsa, and Cariyāpiṭaka—is called the Suttantapiṭaka.
The Dhammasaṅgaṇī, Vibhaṅga, Dhātukathā, Puggalapaññatti, Kathāvatthu, Yamaka, and Paṭṭhāna—this is called the Abhidhammapiṭaka. Therein—
“Because it possesses various specific characteristics, and because it disciplines both body and speech,
this is declared as ‘Vinaya’ by those who know the meaning of Vinaya.

For here, there are various [elements], including the fivefold recitation of the Pātimokkha, the seven classes of offenses beginning with the Pārājikas, and the divisions such as the Mātikā and the Vibhaṅga.
The methods of subsequent rules (*anupaññatti-naya*) serve the purpose of strengthening or relaxing what has already been established.

Because they restrain misconduct of body and speech, they discipline both body and speech; therefore, it is called *Vinaya* (Discipline) due to its manifold methods, its specific methods, and because it disciplines body and speech.
Thus, for the sake of proficiency regarding the meaning of this term, it was said: [...]* *Note: The ellipsis indicates the omitted portion of the original text.*
“Because it possesses various specific characteristics, and because it disciplines both body and speech,
this is declared as ‘the Discipline’ (vinaya) by those who know the meaning of discipline.
As for the other [definition]:

“It is called ‘Sutta’ because it indicates meaning, because it is well-spoken, because of its being heard, because of its leading forth, because of its stringing together, and because of its similarity to a thread.

For it indicates meanings divided into categories such as one’s own welfare and the welfare of others. And herein, the meanings are well-spoken, in accordance with the inclinations of those to be trained.”
Because it has been so stated. It "flows" (savati) toward its purpose like a crop toward its fruit;

what is meant is that it brings forth. It "exudes" (sūdati) like milk from a cow; what is meant is that it causes [the meaning] to flow out. And it "well protects" (suṭṭhu tāyati) them; what is meant is that it guards them.
Furthermore, this is similar to a measuring line: just as a carpenter’s line serves as a standard of measurement, so too does this for the wise.
And just as flowers gathered by a string are not scattered nor destroyed, even so are the meanings gathered by it.
Therefore, this was said for the sake of skill in the meaning of its words:
"Because of indicating meanings, because of being well-spoken, because of hearing, and because of leading forth;"
“Because it is similar to a thread (*sutta*) in its continuity, it is called a ‘discourse’ (*sutta*).
But the other [teacher] says: “That which herein possesses growth, has its own characteristic, is honored, and is well-defined;”
“And the teachings (dhammas) spoken in addition [to those already taught], by that [reason] it is called Abhidhamma.
For this prefix *abhi-* is seen in the senses of increase (*vuḍḍhi*), characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*), honored (*pūjita*), delimited (*paricchinna*), and additional (*adhika*).

Thus, in such passages as “My intense painful feelings are increasing (*abhikkamanti*), they do not subside,” it occurs in the sense of increase. Likewise, in the passage beginning “Those nights... [it occurs in the sense of characteristic].

In such passages as “well-known” (*abhiññāta*) and “distinguished” (*abhilakkhita*), it refers to a specific characteristic (*salakkhaṇa*). In “the king of kings, lord of men” (*rājābhirājā manujinda*), it refers to what is honored (*pūjita*).
In “capable of instructing in the Abhidhamma and the Abhivinaya,” it refers to what is delimited (*paricchinnā*);
that is to say, in the Dhamma and Vinaya which are free from mutual confusion. In “with surpassing beauty” (*abhikkantena vaṇṇena*), it refers to what is superior (*adhika*).

And herein, by way of such passages as “he develops the path for rebirth in the form realm” and “he dwells pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with loving-kindness,” there are states that possess growth.

By way of such passages as “having a visible form as its object, or a sound as its object,” they are also characterized because they are to be defined by their objects and so forth. “States of those in training, states of those beyond training... [and so on].
Although they are honored by way of such expressions as “dhammas, supramundane dhammas,” the intended meaning is that they are worthy of honor.

Although they are delimited because their individual natures are defined by way of such expressions as “there is contact, there is feeling,” dhammas are also spoken of as superior by way of such expressions as “lofty dhammas, immeasurable dhammas, unsurpassed dhammas. Therefore, this [is the case] for him.
It is said for the sake of skill in the meaning of words:
“Because the phenomena herein are grown, possess their own characteristics, are honored, are delimited,
and are stated in addition [to those in the Suttas], it is therefore called Abhidhamma.”
As for what is not specifically distinguished here, it is said:
"Those who know the meaning of the Piṭakas say that 'piṭaka' refers to the scriptures (pariyatti) and the container (abhājana);
having combined them accordingly, the three—Vinaya and the rest—are to be understood."
For the word *piṭaka* is used to denote "the teaching" (*pariyatti*) in such passages as, “Do not [rely] on the acquisition of the *piṭakas*,” and so forth;

and it is used to denote any kind of container in such passages as, “Then a man might come along carrying a hoe and a basket,” and so forth. Therefore, those who know the meaning of the word *piṭaka* have said that it signifies both the teaching and a container.
Now, regarding the statement, “By combining these, the three—the Vinaya and the rest—are to be known”: by means of this word *piṭaka*, which thus has two meanings, [the three are to be understood].

Having formed a compound, it is called the *Vinayapiṭaka* because it is both the discipline (*vinaya*) and a basket (*piṭaka*), since it is the "learning" (*pariyatti*) by nature and because it contains the various meanings [of the training].
In the same manner as previously stated, it is called the *Suttantapiṭaka* because it is both the discourses (*suttanta*) and that basket;
and it is called the *Abhidhammapiṭaka* because it is both the higher doctrine (*abhidhamma*) and that basket. Thus, these three—the Vinaya and the others—are to be known.
Having understood this, and furthermore, for the sake of proficiency in the various aspects of those very Piṭakas, one should elucidate:
"The distinctions between teaching, the dispensation, and the discourse therein as appropriate;
and the state of training, abandonment, and profundity."
"One should also analyze in detail how a bhikkhu attains, in each case, the various distinctions of the scriptures, as well as success and failure. Herein, this is the exposition and the analysis:
for these three Piṭakas are, respectively, teachings on the command, on conventional usage, and on the ultimate meaning.

They are called the teachings according to the offense, according to conformity, and according to the Dhamma; and they are also called the discourse on restraint and non-restraint, the unraveling of views, and the analysis of name-and-form.
For herein, the Vinaya Piṭaka is a teaching by way of command (*āṇādesanā*), because it was taught by the Blessed One, who possesses authority, out of an abundance of commands;

and the Sutta Piṭaka is a teaching by way of conventional expression (*vohāradesanā*), because it was taught by the Blessed One, who is skilled in conventional usage, out of an abundance of conventional expressions.
The Abhidhamma Piṭaka is called the "Teaching of Ultimate Meaning" because it was taught by the Blessed One, who is skilled in the ultimate meaning, due to its abundance of ultimate meaning.
Likewise, the first [Piṭaka] is the "Instruction according to Offense," because those beings who have committed many offenses are disciplined therein according to their respective offenses;

the second is the "Instruction according to Inclination," because beings with various underlying tendencies, latent dispositions, temperaments, and resolutions are disciplined therein in accordance with their respective inclinations.

Regarding the teaching in accordance with the natural order, the third is called the "Teaching in Accordance with Dhamma" because it is said: "Beings who perceive a mere heap of phenomena as 'I' and 'mine' are here taught according to the Dhamma.
Likewise, the first is called the "Discourse on Restraint and Non-restraint" because restraint and non-restraint, which are the opposites of misconduct, are explained therein.
"Restraint and non-restraint" refers to both minor and major restraint, like "action and non-action" or "fruit and non-fruit.
Second: "The unraveling of views, which serves as the antidote to the sixty-two views, is explained here"—this is the discourse on the unraveling of views.
Third: "The discernment of name-and-form, which serves as the antidote to lust and the other defilements, is explained here..."
The phrase "thus it has been told" refers to the discourse on the discernment of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Within these three [baskets], one should understand the three trainings (*sikkhā*), the three abandonments (*pahāna*), and the fourfold profundity.
For thus, in the Vinaya Piṭaka, the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*) is specifically taught; in the Sutta Piṭaka, the training in higher consciousness (*adhicitta-sikkhā*).
In the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, there is the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā).
In the Vinaya Piṭaka, there is the abandoning of transgression, because virtue is the antidote to the transgression of the defilements (kilesa).

In the Sutta Piṭaka, there is the abandoning of the obsessions (pariyuṭṭhāna), because concentration is the antidote to the obsessions. In the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, there is the abandoning of the underlying tendencies (anusaya).

This is because wisdom is the antidote to the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*). In the first [truth], there is abandonment by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgappahāna*); in the others, there is abandonment by suppression (*vikkhambhanappahāna*) and abandonment by eradication (*samucchedappahāna*).
In the first, there is the abandonment of the defilement of misconduct; in the others, there is the abandonment of the defilements of craving and views.
Furthermore, in each one of these, the fourfold profundity—of the phenomenon (*dhamma*), the meaning (*attha*), the teaching (*desanā*), and the penetration (*paṭivedha*)—is to be understood.

In this context, "dhamma" refers to the textual tradition (*tanti*). "Meaning" (*attha*) is the meaning of that very same tradition. "Teaching" (*desanā*) is the teaching of that textual tradition as it has been determined by the mind.

"Penetration" (*paṭivedha*) is the realization, in accordance with reality, of both the textual tradition and the meaning of the textual tradition. And these—dhamma, meaning, teaching, and penetration—are present in all three [collections].
Because they are difficult for those of dull intellect to fathom, like the great ocean for crocodiles and other such creatures.
And because it has no foothold that can be grasped, it is profound. Thus, in each individual case here, the fourfold profundity should be understood.
Another method: "Dhamma" means cause; for this has been said: "Knowledge regarding the cause is the analytical knowledge of Dhamma (dhamma-paṭisambhidā).
"Attha" means the fruit of the cause; for this has been said: "Knowledge regarding the fruit of the cause is the analytical knowledge of meaning (attha-paṭisambhidā). "Desanā" means designation.

The intended meaning is that the expression of the Dhamma is in accordance with the Dhamma. Alternatively, it is the act of explaining by way of direct order, reverse order, summary, detailed exposition, and so forth.
"Penetration" (paṭivedha) means clear realization (abhisamaya); and this is both mundane and supramundane, according to its object and its non-delusion.
It is the awakening to phenomena in accordance with their meaning, to meanings in accordance with the phenomena, and to designations in accordance with the paths of designation.
The unerring intrinsic nature, characterized by specific marks, is to be penetrated regarding those various phenomena taught here and there.
Now, since within these Piṭakas whatever category of Dhamma or category of meaning there may be,
and whatever meaning is to be made known becomes manifest to the knowledge of the listeners, there is accordingly a teaching that illuminates that meaning.

And herein, "penetration" (paṭivedha) refers either to the non-erroneous realization itself, or to the non-erroneous intrinsic nature (sabhāva) of those respective phenomena which is to be penetrated, characterized by their specific marks (salakkhaṇa).

All this is profound because it is difficult for those of poor wisdom who have not accumulated the requisites of merit to plunge into, and because it provides no foothold, just as the great ocean is to crocodiles. Therefore, it is profound.
In this way, the fourfold profundity should be understood here for each individual aspect.
And to this extent:
“The discourse on the teaching and the dispensation— Their distinction, as appropriate, [is as follows]…”
“And reveal the profundity of the abandonment of training, as well as its nature”—
this verse has already had its meaning explained.
“The distinctions of the scriptures, excellence, and likewise failure, wherever they may be found;”
“And whatever a bhikkhu attains, let him analyze all that as well.

In this context, one should see the threefold division of the scriptural tradition (*pariyatti*) within the Three Piṭakas. For there are three kinds of scriptural tradition: the tradition likened to a water-snake (*alagaddūpamā*), the tradition for the sake of deliverance (*nissaraṇatthā*), and the tradition of the storekeeper (*bhaṇḍāgārikapariyatti*).
Among these, that which is wrongly grasped and studied for the sake of criticism and so forth is the tradition likened to a water-snake. With reference to this, [the Blessed One said]:
It is said: “Bhikkhus, suppose a man needing a viper, seeking a viper, wandering in search of a viper, were to see a large viper and were to seize it by its coils or by its tail;
that viper would then turn back upon him and bite his hand or his arm or some other limb.”
If he were to seize it, he might on that account meet death or suffer pain amounting to death. Why is that?
Because, monks, the water-snake was wrongly grasped. Even so, monks, here some foolish men master the Dhamma—the discourses...
[and so on] ...the expositions; having mastered that Dhamma, they [misinterpret] those teachings.
They do not examine the meaning with wisdom; because they do not examine the meaning with wisdom, those teachings do not satisfy them through contemplation.
They master the Dhamma for the sake of finding fault and for the sake of escaping from debates;
yet they do not experience the purpose for which they master the Dhamma—those teachings [do not lead them to that goal].
“Misapprehended, they lead to harm and suffering for a long time. Why is that?
Because, monks, the teachings have been misapprehended.
But those which are well-apprehended—studied by one desiring only the fulfillment of the aggregate of virtue and so forth, and not for the sake of finding fault or the like—...
This is for the purpose of escape. With reference to this it was said:
"Those teachings, when well grasped by them, lead to their welfare and happiness for a long time. For what reason? Because the teachings have been well grasped, monks.
Furthermore, one who has fully understood the aggregates, abandoned the defilements, developed the path, penetrated the unshakable, and realized cessation—
One whose taints are exhausted studies solely for the purpose of maintaining the lineage and for the purpose of preserving the tradition; this is the "learning of the storekeeper.

Furthermore, a bhikkhu who is well-practiced in the Vinaya attains the three types of higher knowledge (tisso vijjā) by relying on the perfection of virtue (sīlasampadā), because it is therein that their detailed exposition is found.
One who is well-practiced in the Sutta attains the six direct knowledges (cha abhiññā) by relying on the perfection of concentration (samādhisampadā).

One attains them, because their specific classifications are explained therein. One who is well-practiced in the Abhidhamma, by relying on the perfection of wisdom, attains the four analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), because their specific classifications are also explained in that very work.

Thus, one who is well-practiced in these [teachings] attains, in due order, this excellence consisting of the threefold clear knowledge (*vijjāttaya*), the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*), and the four analytical knowledges.

In the Vinaya, however, one who has practiced wrongly perceives as blameless those contacts involving clinging—such as those of touch that are prohibited—even though they are similar in nature to the permitted pleasant contacts of rugs, coverings, and so forth. For it is said:
"Thus do I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One: those things which have been called obstructive by the Blessed One are indeed obstructive."
“By the Blessed One, for one who practices them, they are not sufficient to cause an obstacle. Thereby, he falls into a state of immorality.

One who has practiced wrongly regarding the Suttas—failing to understand the intended meaning (*adhippāya*) in passages such as, “Bhikkhus, there are four persons existing and found among you”—grasps the teaching incorrectly.
It was with reference to this that it was said: “Through our own incorrect grasp, both we and...”
“He misrepresents [the Dhamma], he wounds himself, and he produces much demerit. Thereby he falls into wrong view.
One who is ill-practiced in the Abhidhamma, rushing beyond the reflection on the Dhamma, reflects even upon things that should not be reflected upon.
Thereby he falls into mental derangement; for this has been said: “Bhikkhus, there are these four things that should not be reflected upon. Not…”
“Those things should not be thought about, for by thinking about them one would partake of madness and distress.
Thus, practicing wrongly with respect to these [five objects], one successively reaches this failure consisting of immorality, wrong view, and derangement of mind.
And at this point—
“Whatever distinction of mastery, and whatever failure, a bhikkhu may attain here or there—the Teacher has explained all that as well. This verse also has its meaning already stated.
Thus, having understood the Piṭakas in their various aspects, it should be known that this word of the Buddha is threefold according to them.
How is it fivefold by way of collection (*nikāya*)? All of this consists of five divisions:
the Dīghanikāya, the Majjhimanikāya, the Saṃyuttanikāya, the Aṅguttaranikāya, and the Khuddakanikāya. Among these, what is the Dīghanikāya?
It consists of thirty-four discourses (*sutta*), beginning with the Brahmajāla, which are comprised in three groups (*varga*).
“Thirty-four discourses, whose collection is in three sections—this is the Dīghanikāya, the first [nikāya] in the forward order.
But why is this called the Dīghanikāya? Because it is a collection of suttas of long extent, and because it is their dwelling place.

For a "group" (*nikāya*) is said to be a collection of dwellings. "Monks, I do not see even a single other group so mentally unified as this group of animals," and such statements from both the Teaching and common worldly usage—as in "the *poṇika* group" or "the *cikkhallika* group"—are the proofs here for their status as groups.
In this same way, the etymological meaning of the term *nikāya* should be understood for the remaining [groups] as well.
What is the Majjhima Nikāya? It consists of one hundred and fifty-two discourses, beginning with the Mūlapariyāya Sutta, which are of middle length and are comprised within fifteen sections.
As it is said: “That collection of discourses, where there are one hundred and fifty suttas and two additional suttas, is the Majjhima Nikāya, comprising five [vaggas] and ten sections.”
What is the Saṃyutta Nikāya? It consists of seven thousand, seven hundred and sixty-two discourses spoken by way of the *Devatāsaṃyutta* and others, beginning with the *Oghataraṇa*.
"Seven thousand discourses, And seven hundred discourses, And sixty-two discourses as well— This is the compendium of the Saṃyutta."

What is the Aṅguttara Nikāya? It consists of nine thousand, five hundred, and fifty-seven discourses (suttas) taught according to the progressive increase of single factors, beginning with the Cittapariyādāna and others.
“Nine thousand discourses, And five hundred discourses, And fifty-seven discourses— This is the number in the Aṅguttara.”

What is the Khuddakanikāya? It consists of the entire Vinaya Piṭaka, the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, and the fifteen divisions previously shown beginning with the Khuddakapāṭha—namely, the remainder of the Buddha’s word after setting aside the four Nikāyas.
“Setting aside these four Nikāyas, beginning with the Dīgha, whatever other word of the Buddha there is, that is considered the Khuddaka Nikāya.”
Thus, it is fivefold by way of collection (*nikāya*).
How is it ninefold by way of constituent parts (*aṅga*)? For all this [Dhamma] consists of nine divisions:
*sutta*, *geyya*, *veyyākaraṇa*, *gāthā*, *udāna*, *itivuttaka*, *jātaka*, *abbhutadhamma*, and *vedalla*. Therein:

The two Vibhaṅgas, the Niddesa, the Khandhaka, and the Parivāra; and in the Sutta Nipāta, the Maṅgala Sutta, the Ratana Sutta, the Nālaka Sutta, the Tuvaṭṭaka Sutta, and whatever other words of the Tathāgata are titled "Sutta"—all these should be understood as Sutta.
Furthermore, every discourse accompanied by verses should be understood as Geyya.
Specifically, in the Saṃyutta Nikāya, the entire Sagāthāvagga and likewise...
The Abhidhamma Piṭaka, the prose-less suttas (niggāthaka-sutta), and whatever other word of the Buddha is not included within the eight divisions (aṅga) should be understood as *veyyākaraṇa*.
The *Dhammapada*, the *Theragāthā*, the *Therīgāthā*, and the pure verses (*suddhikagāthā*) in the *Suttanipāta* that do not bear the title "sutta" should be understood as *gāthā*.
There are eighty-two verses associated with joy and knowledge.

The Suttantas should be understood as the Udānas. Those one hundred and ten Suttantas that proceed according to the method beginning with “This was said by the Blessed One” should be understood as the Itivuttakas.
The more than five hundred Jātakas, beginning with the Apaṇṇaka-jātaka, should be understood as the Jātakas.
[And those passages] that proceed according to the method beginning with “Monks, these four wonderful and marvelous qualities are in Ānanda”...
All discourses connected with wonderful and marvelous phenomena (*acchariya-abbhuta-dhamma*) should be understood as *abbhutadhamma*.

All discourses such as the *Cūḷavedalla*, *Mahāvedalla*, *Sammādiṭṭhi*, *Sakkapañha*, *Saṅkhārabhājaniya*, and *Mahāpuṇṇama Sutta*—those which were requested again and again until both knowledge (*veda*) and satisfaction (*tuṭṭhi*) were attained—should be understood as *vedalla*.
Thus, [the Dhamma] is ninefold by way of its divisions (*aṅga*).
How is it eighty-four thousandfold by way of the aggregates of the Dhamma? This entire word of the Buddha is as follows:
“I received eighty-two thousand [teachings] from the Buddha, two thousand from the bhikkhus;
eighty-four thousand are the teachings that have been transmitted to me.”
Thus, by way of the categories of Dhamma thus elucidated, there are eighty-four thousand divisions.

Among these, a single discourse (*sutta*) with a single thematic connection (*anusandhi*) constitutes one category of Dhamma. Where there are multiple thematic connections, the count of categories of Dhamma is according to those connections.
In the compositions in verse, the posing of a question is one category of Dhamma, and the answer is another. In the Abhidhamma, each individual [topic]...
The Triads and Duads constitute one vessel; each individual turn of thought constitutes another vessel; and each category of the Dhamma (dhammakkhandha) constitutes yet another.

In the Vinaya, there is the narrative background (vatthu), there is the matrix (mātikā), there is the word-by-word commentary (padabhājanīya), there is the intermediate offense (antarāpatti), there is the offense (āpatti), there is the non-offense (anāpatti), and there is the cutting off of the triad (tikaccheda).
In this context, it should be understood that each single division is one category of the Dhamma.
Thus, by way of the categories of Dhamma, it consists of eighty-four thousand divisions.

Thus, this word of the Buddha (buddhavacana) is of one kind when considered without distinction according to its flavor (rasa), but of two kinds and so forth when distinguished according to the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and so on.
By the assembly of masters headed by Mahākassapa, who were chanting [it], [it was established as]: "This is the Dhamma; this is the Vinaya..."
“This is the word of the Buddha spoken in the first period; this is the word of the Buddha spoken in the middle period;
this is the word of the Buddha spoken in the final period; this is the Vinaya Piṭaka; this is the Sutta Piṭaka; this is the Abhidhamma Piṭaka;
this is the Dīgha Nikāya… [and so on] …this is the Khuddaka Nikāya; these are the nine divisions beginning with the Suttas; these are the eighty-four thousand aggregates of the Dhamma.”

Having established this classification, the recitation was performed. Not only this one, but having also established many other varieties of classification found within the Three Piṭakas—such as the *Uddānasaṅgaha*, *Vaggasaṅgaha*, *Peyyālasaṅgaha*, the groupings of the *Ekakanipāta*, *Dukanipāta*, and so forth, as well as the *Saṃyuttasaṅgaha* and *Paṇṇāsasaṅgaha*—the recitation was completed in seven months.
At the conclusion of the recitation, it was said: "This teaching of the One Possessed of Ten Powers has been entrusted by the Elder Mahākassapa to last for a period of five thousand years."

Thinking, "It has been made capable of being recited," this great earth—bounded by the waters—trembled, shook, quaked, and vibrated in many ways as if giving a cry of "Sādhu! out of joy born from that realization;
and many wonders appeared. This is called the First Great Council (Paṭhama Mahāsaṅgīti). Regarding which it is said in the world:
“Because they were made by five hundred [people], she is called ‘The Five Hundred’;
and because she was made by elders, she is called ‘The Elder Nun.
1. Commentary on the Brahmajāla Sutta.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Wanderers:

While this First Great Council was being held, at the conclusion of the compilation of the Vinaya, the Venerable Mahākassapa asked for the first sutta of the first Nikāya within the Sutta Piṭaka—the *Brahmajāla*—saying: "Friend Ānanda, the *Brahmajāla*..."

At the conclusion of such statements as "Where was it spoken?", the Venerable Ānanda spoke the words beginning with "Thus have I heard," revealing everything—both where it was spoken and on account of what it was spoken. Therefore it is said:
"For the *Brahmajāla Sutta* as well, the introduction beginning with 'Thus have I heard' was spoken by the Venerable Ānanda at the time of the First Great Council."

1. In this context, *evaṃ* is a particle (*nipāta-pada*). *Me* and so forth are noun-terms (*nāma-pada*). In the phrase *paṭipanno hoti*, *paṭi* is a prefix (*upasagga-pada*), and *hoti* is a verb-phrase (*ākhyāta-pada*). By this method, first of all, the analysis of the words is to be understood. As for the meaning:
the word *evaṃ* has many distinct senses, such as comparison, instruction, praise, censure, acceptance, manner, indication, and restriction.
For instance, it occurs in the sense of comparison in such passages as: "By a mortal born in this way, much wholesome [deed] should be performed. And so forth.
In such cases as “Thus you should advance; thus you should retreat,” it is used in instruction (*upadesa*). In such cases as “So it is, Blessed One;
so it is, Sublime One,” it is used in encouragement (*sampahaṃsana*).
In such cases as “In this very way, this outcaste woman praises that shaveling ascetic here and there,” it is used in censure (*garahaṇa*). “‘Yes, venerable sir,’ he replied... [and so forth].
In such passages as "Those monks replied to the Blessed One," it refers to the acceptance of speech.

In such passages as "Thus indeed, venerable sir, do I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One," it refers to a manner of speaking. In such passages as "Come, young man, go to where the ascetic Ānanda is;
having approached him, in my name [inquire after] the ascetic Ānanda’s health... it refers to a command.

“Ask after his freedom from illness, his lightness of body, his strength, and his well-being: ‘The young brahmin Subha, son of Todeyya, asks whether the venerable Ānanda is free from affliction, free from illness, light in body, strong, and dwelling in comfort.
And say this as well: ‘It would be well indeed if the venerable Ānanda would go to the residence of the young brahmin Subha, son of Todeyya.’”
In such passages as "Let him approach out of compassion," it is used for illustration.
"What do you think, Kālāmas, are these states wholesome or unwholesome? "Unwholesome, venerable sir. "Blameworthy or blameless?
"Blameworthy, venerable sir. "Censured by the wise or praised by the wise? "Censured by the wise, venerable sir. "When fully undertaken and practiced..."
“Do they lead to harm and suffering or not? What is your view in this matter? “Venerable sir, when they are fully undertaken and observed, they lead to harm and suffering;
such is our view in this matter. In such passages, it is used in the sense of emphasis. Here, however, it should be understood in the senses of manner, indication, and emphasis.
Therein, by the word *evaṃ* in the sense of manner, he illustrates this meaning: [the teaching] which is skillful in various methods and originates from many underlying tendencies.

Who is capable of understanding in every way the word of that Blessed One— which is perfect in both meaning and phrasing, possesses manifold miracles, is profound in its penetration of the teaching on the Dhamma and its meaning, and reaches the range of hearing for all beings according to each one’s own language—
even by generating the desire to hear with all one's might, [one says] "Thus have I heard" (*evam me sutam*)? Even by me...
"In one sense it is 'heard' (suta)":

by way of indication, [the phrase] "Thus have I heard" indicates the entire discourse to be spoken hereafter, while liberating himself from the charge—“I am not self-become; this was not realized by me”—by saying, "It was heard by me thus," or "It was heard by me in this manner.
By way of restriction: "Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my disciples, the bhikkhus, who are learned..."
"That is to say, Ānanda, among those who possess wisdom, mindfulness, steadfastness, and who are attendants— namely, Ānanda. Thus,
because he had been praised by the Blessed One as "the Venerable Ānanda is skilled in the meaning, skilled in the Dhamma, skilled in the phrasing, skilled in etymological interpretation,
and skilled in what precedes and follows," and likewise by the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta), his own power of retention was commensurate with that state of praise.
By declaring this, he generates in beings a desire to hear: "Thus have I heard," and that indeed—whether in meaning or in phrasing—is neither deficient nor redundant;
it is to be seen exactly thus and not otherwise.
The word *me* (by me) is seen in three senses. For instance, in such passages as, "A song sung to me in verse is not fit to be eaten," and so forth.
The meaning is "by me. In such passages as, "It would be well, Bhante, if the Blessed One were to teach me the Dhamma in brief," the meaning is "to me.
In such passages as, "Be my heirs to the Dhamma, bhikkhus," the meaning is "my.
But here, both of the two possible meanings—“heard by me” and “my hearing”—are applicable.

The word *suta*—this term *suta*, both with and without prefixes—is divided into many meanings, such as going, renowned, soiled, accumulated, application, cognizable by the ear, following the door of the ear, and cognized.

For instance, in expressions such as "gone forth with the army" (*senāya pasuto*), the meaning is "going. In expressions such as "of one who sees the Dhamma heard" (*sutadhammassa passato*), the meaning is "of one whose Dhamma is renowned.
In expressions such as "the lustful toward the lustful" (*avassutā avassutassa*), the meaning is "the soiled toward the soiled."
In such passages as “You have accumulated no small merit,” the meaning is “accumulated. In such passages as “The wise who are intent on jhāna,” the meaning is “devoted to jhāna.

In such passages as “Seen, heard, and sensed,” the meaning is “cognizable by the ear. In such passages as “One who retains what is heard, one who stores what is heard,” the meaning is “one who retains what has been cognized by following the door of the ear. But here, it is by means of the door of the ear...
The meaning is either "retained" (*upadhārita*) or "the act of retaining" (*upadhāraṇa*).

For when the word *me* has the sense of "by me," it is appropriate to say, "Thus have I heard," meaning it was retained by means of the ear-door. When it has the sense of "mine," it is appropriate to say, "Thus have I heard," meaning it was the act of retention by me through the ear-door.

Thus, among these three terms: *evaṃ* (thus) is an indication of the function of consciousness, such as ear-consciousness and so forth; *me* (by me) is an indication of the person possessing the aforementioned consciousness;
*sutaṃ* (heard) is an indication of an apprehension that is neither deficient nor excessive and is non-perverted, by way of negating the state of not having heard.
Likewise, *evaṃ* (thus) is a manifestation of the mode of occurrence of that stream of consciousness proceeding through the ear-door upon a manifold variety of objects.
“Me” (by me) is a declaration of the person; “sutaṃ” (heard) is a declaration of the Dhamma. This is the summary here:
“Nothing else was done by me through the course of consciousness proceeding toward various kinds of objects; rather, this was done—this Dhamma was heard.

Likewise, “evaṃ” (thus) is a declaration of the Dhamma to be demonstrated; “me” is a declaration of the person; “sutaṃ” (heard) is a declaration of the person’s function. This is what is meant: “The discourse that I shall demonstrate, that was thus heard by me.”

"Thus" (*tathā*) means "in this way" (*evam*). For that continuum of consciousness (*cittasantāna*) which, through its occurrence in various modes, has the apprehension of various meanings and verbal expressions, there is the description of those various modes.

Indeed, "thus" (*evam*) is a designation for the mode (*ākāra-paññatti*). "Me" (*me*) is a designation for the agent (*kattuniddesa*). "Heard" (*suta*) is a designation for the object (*visayaniddesa*).
At this point, by means of the continuum of consciousness occurring in various modes, the conclusion regarding the apprehension of the object by the agent who possesses it is established.

Alternatively, *evaṃ* is a designation for the function of the person; *sutaṃ* is a designation for the function of consciousness; and *me* is a designation for the person endowed with both functions.

This, however, is the summary here: "It was heard by me—a person possessing the consciousness whose function is hearing—by way of that consciousness, using the conventional expression 'heard' which has acquired its function through hearing."
In this context, "thus" (*eva*) and "mine" (*me*) are designations of what does not exist according to the true and ultimate sense (*saccikaṭṭhaparamatthavasena*).
For what is there here that exists ultimately which could receive the designation "thus" or "mine"?
"Hearing" (*suta*), however, is a designation of what does exist. For that which is apprehended here by the ear exists ultimately. Likewise with "thus."

And "meti" (thus) is a designation by way of dependence (*upādāpaññatti*), because it is spoken in dependence upon this or that [object]. "Sutaṃ" (heard) is a designation by way of comparison (*upanidhāpaññatti*), because it is spoken in comparison with what is seen and so forth.
And here, by the word "evam" (thus), he illustrates non-delusion;
for one who is deluded is not capable of penetrating things in their various aspects. By the word "sutaṃ," he illustrates the non-forgetfulness of what has been heard. Of whom...
For what has been heard becomes forgotten; one does not claim, "I did not hear it," at a later time.

Thus, through non-delusion, wisdom (*paññā*) is accomplished, and through non-forgetfulness, mindfulness (*sati*) is accomplished. In this regard, there is the capacity to grasp the phrasing (*byañjana*) by means of mindfulness preceded by wisdom, and the capacity to penetrate the meaning (*attha*) by means of wisdom preceded by mindfulness. Through the conjunction of these two capacities, [one attains] that which is endowed with both meaning and phrasing.
Because he is capable of preserving the treasury of the Dhamma, his status as the Dhamma-treasurer is established.
According to another method: by the word "thus" (evam), he illustrates wise attention (*yoniso manasikāra*), for one who attends unwisely lacks various kinds of penetration.
By the word "heard" (*suta*), he illustrates non-distraction, because there is no hearing for one whose mind is distracted. For indeed, one whose mind is distracted...
Even when told of every possible attainment, a person says, "I have not heard this; say it again.
