Herein, through wise attention (*yoniso manasikāra*), one accomplishes right self-application and previous merit-making; for these are absent in one who is wrongly applied or who has not made merit in the past.
Through non-distraction, one accomplishes hearing the true Dhamma and reliance upon a superior person (*sappurisa*).
He accomplishes it. For one whose mind is distracted is unable to hear, and there is no hearing for one who does not attend upon a true person (sappurisa).

Another method: because of the phrase "thus" (*evaṃ*), for that continuum of consciousness in which there is the grasping of various meanings and phonemes due to the occurrence of various modes, there is the designation of various modes;
and that auspicious mode is not [present] in one whose self is not rightly directed.
"Or for one who has not previously performed merit"—therefore, by the phrase "thus," he demonstrates his own attainment of the latter two wheels in this auspicious manner.
"Hearing" (*suta*) refers to the attainment of the former two wheels through the application of listening;
for there is no hearing for one dwelling in an unsuitable place or one devoid of reliance upon virtuous persons (*sappurisa*). Thus, by means of the accomplishment of these latter two wheels...
The purification of intention (*āsaya*) is established through the accomplishment of the first two wheels;

through that purification of intention, the excellence of realization (*adhigama*) is accomplished, and through the purification of practice (*payoga*), the excellence of scripture (*āgama*) is accomplished.

Thus, the speech of one whose practice and intention are purified, and who is endowed with both scripture and realization, is like the dawn preceding the rising of the sun, and like wise attention (*yoniso manasikāra*) preceding wholesome action (*kusala-kamma*).
Thinking, "He ought to be the precursor to the Blessed One’s word," he spoke the words beginning with "Thus have I heard" while establishing the introductory setting (*nidāna*) for the occasion.

According to another method: by the word "thus" (*evaṃ*), which indicates penetration in its various modes, he demonstrates the presence of his own perfection in the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) of meaning (*attha*) and eloquence (*paṭibhāna*).

By the word "heard" (*suta*), which indicates penetration into the various categories of what is to be heard, he demonstrates the presence of his perfection in the analytical knowledges of phenomena (*dhamma*) and language (*nirutti*).
By speaking this word "thus" (*evaṃ*), which illustrates wise attention (*yoniso manasikāra*), he demonstrates: "These teachings have been examined by me with the mind and well-penetrated by view.
By speaking this word "heard" (*suta*), which illustrates application to hearing, he demonstrates:
"Many teachings have been heard by me, retained, and mastered by speech. By both of these, [he demonstrates] the perfection of both the meaning and the phrasing.
By illuminating this, he generates reverence for listening.

For one who does not listen with reverence to the Dhamma, which is perfect in both meaning and phrasing, is excluded from great benefit; therefore, having generated reverence, this Dhamma should be heard with careful attention.
Furthermore, by means of this entire statement, "Thus have I heard," the Venerable Ānanda [establishes] that which was proclaimed by the Tathāgata...
By not withholding the Dhamma from himself, he transcends the plane of the unworthy person; by professing discipleship, he enters the plane of the worthy person.
Likewise, he causes the mind to emerge from what is not the true Dhamma and establishes the mind in the true Dhamma.
By declaring, "This has been heard by me in its entirety; it is the word of that Blessed One himself," he liberates himself and [honors] the Teacher.
He refers back [to the source], applies the word of the Conqueror (jinavacana), and establishes the guide of the Dhamma.
Furthermore, without claiming for himself the state of having produced [the teaching] by his own effort, saying "Thus have I heard," he explains the previous statement:
"This was received by me directly from that Blessed One, who is confident in the four grounds of self-confidence and who possesses the ten powers."

“This is the word of the Perfectly Enlightened One— the one who stands in the place of the bull, the one who roars the lion’s roar, the supreme among all beings, the Lord of Dhamma, the King of Dhamma, the Sovereign of Dhamma, the Island of Dhamma, the Refuge of Dhamma, the Wheel-turning Monarch of the sublime Dhamma; herein,
no doubt or uncertainty should be entertained regarding the meaning, the doctrine, the phrasing, or the syllables.”
It destroys lack of faith in this Dhamma among all gods and humans, and it generates the perfection of faith. Therefore, this is said:
"It destroys lack of faith and increases faith in the Teaching;
Thus have I heard—so saying, the disciple of Gotama."
This is the exposition of the delimitation by number. "At one time" (*samaya*) is an exposition of the delimited. "At one time" (*ekaṃ samayaṃ*) is an indication of the unspecified.
In this context, the word *samaya* is seen to apply to: "conjunction, moment, time, collection, cause, view, acquisition, abandoning, and penetration."
For instance, in such passages as, “Perhaps tomorrow we might approach him, taking into account the time and the occasion,” the meaning is *samavāya* (conjunction).
In such passages as, “Monks, there is indeed only one moment and one occasion for living the holy life,” the meaning is *khaṇa* (moment).
In such passages as, “The time of heat, the time of fever,” the meaning is *kāla* (time). In such passages as, “A great assembly in the forest,” the meaning is *samūha* (multitude).
“Bhaddāli, you had not even realized this circumstance: ‘The Blessed One is staying at Sāvatthī;
the Blessed One will know me as the bhikkhu named Bhaddāli, who does not fulfill the training in the Teacher’s dispensation.
This too, Bhaddāli, was a circumstance that you had not realized. In such passages, it is the *hetu* (reason). “Now at that time... [and so forth].
In such passages as, “The wanderer Samaṇa Muṇḍikāputta, while learning [his doctrine], dwells in Mallikā’s Park, in the Tindukācīra grove of the Ekasālaka,
which is frequented by those who propound various doctrines,” it refers to *diṭṭhi* (view).
“Whatever benefit there is in this present life, and whatever benefit there is in the future life...”
In such passages as, “The steadfast one who has realized the goal is called wise,” it refers to acquisition (*paṭilābha*).
In such passages as, “Through the realization of conceit, he brought suffering to an end,” it refers to abandoning (*pahāna*).

In such passages as, “The meaning of suffering is oppression, the meaning of being conditioned, the meaning of burning, the meaning of changeability, and the meaning of realization (*abhisamaya*),” it refers to penetration (*paṭivedha*).

But here, "time" (kāla) is the meaning. By this, he indicates a single occasion (*samaya*) among the various divisions of time, such as the year, the season, the fortnight, the day and night, the morning, midday, evening, the first watch, the middle watch, the last watch, the hour, and so forth.
In that regard, although among these occasions—such as the year and the rest—whatever discourse [was spoken] in whichever year...
Whether it was spoken in a particular season, month, fortnight, during the night-time portion, or the day-time portion—all that is well-known and well-determined by the Elder’s wisdom.

For if one were to say, "Thus have I heard: in such-and-such a year, in such-and-such a season, in such-and-such a month, in such-and-such a fortnight, in such-and-such a part of the night, or in such-and-such a part of the day," it would not be possible to [easily]...
Whether for the purpose of memorizing, reciting, or causing others to recite it, there is much that would have to be said;
therefore, having condensed that entire meaning into a single phrase, he said, "At one time. Or else, [it refers to] these times:

the time of descent into the womb, the time of birth, the time of spiritual urgency, the time of the Great Renunciation, the time of practicing austerities, the time of conquering Māra, and the time of full enlightenment.
The "time" (samaya) refers to such occasions as the time for dwelling in happiness in this very life, the time for teaching, and the time for final Nibbāna;
these are the various types of times of the Blessed One, which were exceedingly renowned among gods and humans. Among those times, he indicates one specific time known as the "time for teaching.

Furthermore, regarding the times for the functions of wisdom and compassion, it is the time for the function of compassion; and regarding the times for practice for one's own welfare and for the welfare of others—
The time for practicing for the welfare of others; among the times for the two duties of those assembled, the time for a discourse on the Dhamma;
and among the times for the practice of teaching, the time for the teaching—it was with reference to one such occasion that he said, "at one time.

But why, in this instance, is it not expressed as "at whatever time" (*yasmiṃ samaye*) as in the Abhidhamma, "at whatever time [a state] belonging to the sense-sphere," and so forth in other Sutta passages?
—“Why, monks, when it is said, ‘At a time when a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures...

is an indication using the locative case (*bhummavacana*), and in the Vinaya it is expressed by the instrumental case (*karaṇavacana*) as ‘At that time the Buddha, the Blessed One,’ yet here, instead of doing so, an indication using the accusative case (*upayogavacana*) is made as ‘At one time’?
In this regard, it is because the meaning is possible both there [in the Vinaya] and here [in the Sutta], though in different ways. There...

For in the Abhidhamma and in other scriptural passages besides this, both the sense of locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and the sense of characterizing a state by means of another state (*bhāvena bhāvalakkhaṇa*) are possible.

For "occasion" (*samaya*) has the sense of time and the sense of a collection; thus, by means of the state of that "occasion"—which is reckoned as the momentary convergence of causes for the phenomena such as contact mentioned in various places—their own state is characterized.
Therefore, the locative case is employed there for the purpose of indicating that object.
Furthermore, both the sense of cause (*hetu*) and the sense of instrument (*karaṇa*) are possible in the Vinaya.

For, when that occasion for the promulgation of the training rules was difficult even for Sāriputta and others to discern, he was one who, by means of that occasion acting as both cause and instrument, promulgated the training rules.
Considering the reason for the promulgation of the training rules (*sikkhāpada*), the Blessed One dwelt here and there;
therefore, for the purpose of illustrating that meaning, the locative case was employed in those instances.
However, in this case and in other similar instances, the sense of absolute conjunction (*accantasaṃyoga*) is possible. For at whatever time the Blessed One—
He taught this or another sutta; at that very time, he dwelt exclusively in the abiding of compassion.
Therefore, for the purpose of illustrating that meaning, the dative case is employed here.
Thus it is said:

“Depending on the specific meaning intended, [the word *samaya*] is stated here as the locative, the instrumental, and—except for the case where it is called ‘an occasion’ (*samaya*)—as the accusative.
However, the ancient commentators explain it thus: “at that time,” “by that time,” or “on one occasion.”

Or rather, this is merely a distinction of expression; in all cases, the meaning is simply the locative case. Therefore, even when "at one time" (*ekaṃ samayaṃ*) is stated, the meaning should be understood as "at one time" (*ekasmiṃ samaye*).

"Bhagavā" means venerable. For in the world, they call what is venerable "Bhagavā. And he is venerable to all beings because he is distinguished by all supreme qualities; therefore, he is to be known as "Bhagavā. It has also been said by the Ancients:
“‘Bhagavā’ is the best word; ‘Bhagavā’ is the supreme word.
He is venerable and worthy of reverence; therefore he is called ‘Bhagavā.
Moreover—”
“Fortunate (bhāgyavā), one who has destroyed (bhaggavā), one who is endowed with (yutto), one who has analyzed the fortunes (bhagehi ca vibhattavā);
one who has enjoyed (bhattavā), one who has gone beyond (vantagamano) states of existence—therefore he is the Blessed One (bhagavā).

The detailed meaning of this term should be understood by means of this verse, which is indeed already stated in the *Visuddhimagga* in the exposition on the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati-niddesa*).
In this context, by stating "Thus have I heard," he demonstrates the Dhamma exactly as it was heard, thereby making the Dhamma-body of the Blessed One manifest.
By doing so, he consoles those people who are distressed by not seeing the Teacher, saying: "This teaching is not one whose Teacher has passed away; this is your Teacher."
By the words "At one time the Blessed One," he demonstrates that at that time the Blessed One was no longer present, thereby establishing the parinibbāna of the physical body (rūpakāya).

By this, [the meaning is]: "Even the Blessed One—the teacher of such noble Dhamma as this, the possessor of the ten powers, whose body was like a mass of thunderbolts—has attained parinibbāna; who else could possibly conceive hope for life?"
He arouses a sense of urgency in people intoxicated by the pride of life and inspires them toward the True Dhamma.

By saying "Thus," he indicates the excellence of the teaching (*desanā-sampatti*). By "heard by me" (*me sutaṃ*), he indicates the excellence of the disciple (*sāvaka-sampatti*). By "at one time" (*ekaṃ samayaṃ*), he indicates the excellence of the time (*kāla-sampatti*). By "the Blessed One" (*bhagavā*), he indicates the excellence of the teacher (*desaka-sampatti*).
Regarding the phrase "between Rājagaha and Nāḷanda," the word *antara* is used in the sense of a cause, a moment, the middle of the mind, an interval, and so forth.
It is seen [in such contexts]. For instance, in passages such as, “Who could know that interval other than the Tathāgata? and “People gather and deliberate;

what is the difference between me and them?”, the word *antara* refers to a cause. In passages such as, “Venerable sir, I saw a certain woman washing a vessel in the interval between lightning flashes,” it refers to a moment. And in passages such as, “In whom there are no angers from within,” it refers to the interior.
In the word *citte*, it means "in the middle," as in such passages as "one falls into despondency midway.
In such passages as "Moreover, monks, this Tapodā flows through the interval between two great hells," it means "in the gap. Here, however, it is used in the sense of a gap;
therefore, the meaning should be understood as "in the gap between Rājagaha and Nālandā. Furthermore, by the word *antarā*—
Because it is connected [to both], the accusative case has been employed.
In such instances, grammarians employ the word *antarā* only once—as in "he goes between the village and the river"—and that [single] word must be construed with the second member as well;
if it were not so construed, the accusative case would not apply. However, in this case, it is stated precisely after having been so construed.
“He has set out on a journey” means he has set out upon a path reckoned as a journey; the meaning is “a long road.

For according to the *Vibhaṅga* on the occasion of traveling a journey, it is stated that one may eat [before departing] with the thought, “I shall go half a *yojana*,” and thus even half a *yojana* constitutes a journey-path.
However, from Rājagaha to Nāḷandā is exactly one *yojana*.
"With a great community of bhikkhus": it is "great" both by greatness of virtue and by greatness of number.
For that community of bhikkhus was great in virtue because it was endowed with qualities such as fewness of desires;
it was also great in number because it consisted of five hundred. A "community of bhikkhus" (*bhikkhusaṅgha*) is a group of bhikkhus; [the phrase means] "with that community of bhikkhus."
The meaning is: "by a community of recluses (samaṇagaṇa) designated as a collection characterized by [right] view and virtue.
"Together" (saddhiṃ) means "in one place. Regarding "with about five hundred bhikkhus": those of whom there are about five are "about five" (pañcamattāni). "About" (matta) is said to mean a measure;
therefore, just as when it is said, "one who knows the measure in food," it means "he knows the measure in food, he knows the limit."
Just as there is such a meaning [in other contexts], so here too the meaning should be understood as: "approximately five hundred" (*pañcamatta*) means "measuring five" (*pañcapamāṇa*).
"Bhikkhusatāni" means "hundreds of bhikkhus"; [the phrase] "by those approximately five hundred bhikkhus" (*pañcamattehi bhikkhusatehi*).
"Suppiyo the wanderer" (*suppiyopi kho paribbājako*): "Suppiyo" is his name. The particle "pi" [is used] because of his similarity to one who has entered upon the path.
The purpose of the word *puggala* (person) is for the sake of grouping individuals. The particle *kho* serves to connect the words;
it is used here for the sake of the smoothness of the phonetic flow (*byañjana-siliṭṭhatā*). "Paribbājaka" refers to Channa the wanderer, a pupil of Sañjaya. This is what is meant:
"When the Blessed One had set out upon that journey, at that time the wanderer Suppiya also had set out. Here, the word *hi* has the sense of the past tense.
“Together with his pupil, the young brahmin Brahmadatta”—here, one who dwells near (*ante vasati*) is a *antevāsī*.
The meaning is: a student (*sissa*) who moves about in close proximity and remains in attendance. *Brahmadatta* is his name. *Māṇava* refers to a child, a thief, or a youth.
“Young men who, when exhorted by the messengers of the gods, remain heedless...”
In such passages as, “Those men who have entered a low state grieve for a long time,” the term *satto* (being) is used.
In such passages as, “They associate with young brahmins (*māṇava*), both those who have performed their duties and those who have not,” it refers to a thief.
In such passages as, “The young brahmin Ambaṭṭha, the young brahmin Aṅgaka,” it refers to a youth as a “young brahmin. Here, too, this is the very same meaning.
This is what is meant: "together with a young pupil named Brahmadatta.
Therein (*tatra*) means on that journey, or regarding those two persons. *Sudam* is merely a particle.
As for the word *pariyāya*, it applies to repetition, teaching, and cause. "Ānanda, whose turn is it today? [Thus it is said.]
In such passages as “to exhort the bhikkhunīs,” the word *pariyāya* refers to a turn or occasion.

In such passages as “remember this as the ‘Honey-Ball Discourse’ (*madhupiṇḍika-pariyāya*),” it refers to a teaching. In such passages as “by this method (*pariyāya*) also, O Prince, let it be so for you,” it refers to a reason.
Here, too, it is used in the sense of a reason; therefore, the meaning here is: “by way of many kinds of reasons.”
"By many reasons" is what is meant.
"He speaks dispraise of the Buddha": although the Blessed Buddha is free from dispraise and endowed with immeasurable praise, [he speaks of him] thus:
"That respectful service such as salutation which is to be performed toward those advanced in age in the world is called 'the essence of harmony'."

It is said that the ascetic Gotama does not possess this; therefore, the ascetic Gotama is one who lacks true flavor, one who is without enjoyment, a proponent of non-action, a proponent of annihilationism, one who is loathsome, a disciplinarian, an ascetic, and one who has passed beyond the womb.
The ascetic Gotama possesses no superhuman state, no distinction in noble knowledge and vision. The ascetic [speaks] what is struck down by mere reasoning...
“Gotama teaches the Dhamma through the pursuit of inquiry, according to his own inspired intuition.

The ascetic Gotama is not omniscient, nor a knower of the world, nor unsurpassed, nor the foremost person. Thus, having stated various reasons that are not reasons at all, he speaks in such a manner, uttering dispraise, faults, and censure.
And just as he did regarding the Buddha, so too regarding the Dhamma, having stated various things that are not reasons as if they were reasons,
he speaks dispraise in this way and that: "The Dhamma of the ascetic Gotama is ill-proclaimed, ill-penetrated, not leading out, and not conducive to peace."
And just as he did regarding the Dhamma, so too regarding the Saṅgha, he speaks dispraise in various ways by stating whatever is not a reason as a reason:
“The Saṅgha of the ascetic Gotama’s disciples has entered upon a wrong path;
it has entered upon a crooked path, a contrary path, a non-conforming path, a path that conforms to what is not the Dhamma.”
But his pupil thought: "Our teacher touches what should not be touched; he treads upon what should not be trodden upon.

He is like one swallowing fire, like one touching the edge of a sword with his hand, like one wishing to split Mount Sineru with his fist, like one playing with the rows of teeth of a saw, or like one approaching a fierce elephant in rut."
Like one grasping with his own hand, he who speaks ill of the Triple Gem—which is worthy of praise—will meet with ruin and disaster.
Furthermore, when a teacher steps upon excrement, fire, a thorn, or a black snake;
or climbs onto a stake; or eats the *halāhala* poison; or wades through alkaline water; or falls into the abyss of hell...
Or they fall away; yet it is not the case that everything must be followed by the pupil.
For beings are the owners of their own karma and go only according to their own karma. A father does not go by the karma of his son, nor a son by the karma of his father;
a mother does not go by the karma of her son, nor a son by the karma of his mother; a brother does not go by the karma of his sister, nor a sister by the karma of her brother.
"The teacher does not follow the pupil's business, nor does the pupil follow the teacher's business.
Yet my teacher speaks in dispraise of the Three Jewels; indeed, reviling the Noble Ones is a most blameworthy thing.
Having thus emerged with wise discernment, crushing the teacher's doctrine and citing the correct reason as the reason, he [spoke] in many ways regarding the Three...
He began to speak in praise of the Jewels, as is the way of a wise young man of good family. Thus it was said:
“The young Brahmin Brahmadatta, a pupil of the wanderer Suppiya, spoke in many ways in praise of the Buddha, in praise of the Dhamma, and in praise of the Saṅgha.”
In this context, as for the word *vaṇṇa*: the term *vaṇṇa* is seen to refer to shape, genus, the sense-sphere of visible form, cause, measure, quality, praise, and so forth.
Among these, in such passages as "having manifested the form of a great king of serpents," it refers to shape (*saṇṭhāna*).

In such passages as "The brahmin caste alone is the best caste; other castes are inferior," it refers to genus (*jāti*). In [the passage] "with supreme beauty of complexion... it refers to the sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*).
In such passages as "endowed with," it refers to the sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*).
[And as in the verse: "I do not take away, nor do I break; I simply smell the water-born flower from afar.
Now, by what quality is one called a 'thief of fragrance'?"—
In such cases as these, it means "cause. In such cases as "three qualities of the bowl," it means "measure.
In such cases as "But when, householder, were these qualities of the ascetic Gotama acquired? it means "virtue. In such cases as "He speaks praise of one worthy of praise," it means "praise.
Here, it means both virtue and praise. Indeed, by pointing to each respective actual cause, he [the Blessed One] has explained it in many ways.
He spoke praise associated with the qualities of the Triple Gem. Therein, by way of the formula beginning, "Thus indeed is that Blessed One:

worthy, perfectly enlightened," and by way of the formula beginning, "Bhikkhus, those who have confidence in the Buddha have confidence in the foremost," and also by way of the formula beginning, "Bhikkhus, one person, arising in the world, arises... [as he is] peerless, equal to the unequaled."
The praise of the Buddha should be understood by way of this method:

"The Dhamma has been well-expounded by the Blessed One," and "It is the uprooting of attachment and the cutting off of the round [of existence]," and "Those, monks, who have confidence in the Noble Eightfold Path have confidence in the foremost"—the praise of the Dhamma should be understood by such methods as these. "The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples has practiced well."
Furthermore, the praise of the Saṅgha should be understood through such methods as: “Bhikkhus, those who have faith in the Saṅgha have faith in the foremost,” and so forth.

Moreover, a capable Dhamma-preacher, having plunged into the five Nikāyas, the ninefold teaching of the Master, and the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dhamma, should proclaim the praise of the Buddha and the others. For in this regard:
In such instances, one who elucidates the virtues of the Buddha and others cannot be called a "Dhamma-preacher who has leaped across where there is no ford.

For in such cases, the true power of the Dhamma-preacher must be recognized. However, the young Brahmin Brahmadatta speaks in praise of the Triple Gem by relying merely on his own power derived from hearsay and the like.
"Thus both teacher and pupil"—in this way, those two, the teacher and the pupil. "Of one another" means one to the other.
"Speaking direct opposition" means speaking various forms of opposition directly without avoiding even the slightest [point];
the meaning is that they became speakers of contradiction on many occasions. For when the teacher spoke dispraise of the Triple Gem...

The pupil speaks praise, while the other speaks dispraise; then the other speaks praise again—in this way, like one striking a wedge into a solid wooden plank, the teacher repeatedly speaks dispraise of the Triple Gem.
But the pupil, like one driving back that wedge with a pin made of gold, silver, or gems, repeatedly [speaks praise] of the Triple Gem.
He speaks in praise. Therefore it is said: “They speak directly contrary [to the truth].
They follow closely behind the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus;
that is, they follow by maintaining their postures without ever losing sight of the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus from behind, keeping their heads turned toward them.
The meaning is that they followed after having offered [the sacrifice].
But why did the Blessed One set out on that journey? And why did Suppiya follow him?
And why did he speak dispraise of the Triple Gem? First, at that time, among those residing around Rājagaha, the Blessed One...
Having resided in one of the eighteen great monasteries, he would attend to his body at dawn and, at the time for alms-round, wander for alms in Rājagaha surrounded by the community of monks.

On that day, having made alms-food easily available to the community of monks, he returned from the alms-round after the meal; then, having had the community take up their bowls and robes, he said: "To Nāḷandā..."
“I shall go,” he thought, and having departed from Rājagaha, he set out on that journey.
At that time, Suppiya was staying in a certain wanderers’ park near Rājagaha, and surrounded by a retinue of wanderers, he was walking for alms in Rājagaha.
On that day, he had made it easy for the assembly of wanderers to obtain alms.

Having finished his morning meal and having had the wandering ascetics take up their requisites, he followed after the Blessed One, thinking, "I shall go to Nāḷandā," without even knowing that the Blessed One had set out on that path. Had he known, he would not have followed.
As he went along without knowing, he raised his neck and looked about, and there he saw the Blessed One with the splendor of a Buddha.
He was resplendent like the moving peak of a mountain of gold encircled by a crimson woolen cloth.
At that time, it is said, six-colored rays issued forth from the body of the One Possessing Ten Powers and streamed and radiated all around for a distance of eighty cubits,
appearing as if strewn with jeweled garlands, jeweled necklaces, and scattered jeweled powders, or like a spread-out golden cloth variegated with jewels.
That forest interior became as if sprinkled with the liquid of red gold, as if crowded by the falling of hundreds of meteors,

like kaṇikāra flowers scattered without interval, like powdered Chinese lac thrown about by the force of the wind, and as if radiantly spread and dispersed by the outpouring of the splendor of Indra’s bow, lightning, and the host of stars.
Furthermore, the Blessed One’s body, adorned with the eighty minor marks, was like a blooming lotus or water-lily, like a *pāricchattaka* tree in full flower,
or like the vault of heaven radiant with the shimmering rays of stars; it seemed to mock that very sky with its splendor, while the garland of his thirty-two excellent major marks,
beautified by the encircling halo of fathom-wide radiance, appeared like a garland of thirty-two moons strung together and set in place.

It was as if it were overwhelming with its splendor the glory of the thirty-two suns, the thirty-two wheel-turning monarchs, the thirty-two divine kings of the gods, and the thirty-two great Brahmās, all arranged in successive rows.
And surrounding the Blessed One stood all the monks—
few in desire, contented, secluded, unattached, reprovers of evil, censurers of sin, exhorters, and patient with admonition.
They were perfected in virtue, and perfected in concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
In their midst stood the Blessed One, like a golden pillar surrounded by a rampart of red woolen cloth; like a golden ship situated in the middle of a cluster of red lotuses;
like a mass of fire encircled by a coral railing; like the full moon surrounded by a host of stars.
It gladdened the eyes of even the birds, let alone those of gods and humans. On that day, for the most part, eighty great elders—

like fragrant elephants clad in well-fashioned armor, free from faults, having cast out faults, with defilements shattered, their matted locks untangled and their bonds severed— placed their rag-robes, the color of clouds, over one shoulder and took up their walking staffs.
They surrounded the Blessed One. He himself, free from passion, was surrounded by those free from passion; he himself, free from hatred, by those free from hatred;
he himself, free from delusion, by those free from delusion; he himself, free from craving, by those free from craving; he himself, free from defilement, by those free from defilement;
he himself, a Buddha, was surrounded by those who had awakened after him—like the filaments surrounded by petals, and the petals surrounded by the filaments.
Like the pericarp of a lotus; like the six-tusked king of elephants surrounded by eight thousand other elephants;
like Dhatarattha, the king of swans, surrounded by ninety thousand swans; like a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) surrounded by his military divisions;

like Sakka, the king of the gods, surrounded by hosts of deities; like Hārita the Great Brahmā, surrounded by hosts of Brahmas—[he appeared] through the power of merit accumulated over immeasurable time.
With the inconceivable and incomparable play of a Buddha, he proceeded along that path like the moon across the vault of the sky. Then,
seeing the Blessed One proceeding in such an incomparable manner with the play of a Buddha, and seeing the monks with downcast eyes, their faculties stilled and their minds at peace,
paying homage only to the Blessed One as if to the full moon stationed in the upper sky, [the people were struck with wonder].

The wanderer looked at his own assembly. It was burdened with many requisites: carrying staffs with leather thongs hanging from them, broken and shattered wooden walking sticks, peacock-feather fans, clay bowls, bags, water-pots, and so forth.
They were talkative and loose-tongued, uttering such useless words as, "Such-and-such a person has beautiful hands," or "Such-and-such a person has beautiful feet.
They were unsightly and unpleasing to behold. Upon seeing this, remorse arose within him.
Now, he ought to have spoken in praise of the Blessed One. However, because he constantly envies the Blessed One both for the loss of his own gain and honor,
and for the decline of his following— since it was only as long as the Buddha had not yet appeared in the world that the gain and honor of the other sectarians flourished,
but from the time of the Buddha’s appearance onwards, their gain and honor have diminished— [he speaks thus].
Like glow-worms at the rising of the sun, they fall into a state of utter lack of splendor.
Furthermore, as soon as Upatissa and Kolita had gone forth under Sañjaya, the wandering ascetics became a great assembly;
however, when they departed, that assembly of theirs was also broken. Thus, for these two reasons, this wandering ascetic [became] constantly...
He envies the Blessed One; therefore, it should be understood that while vomiting forth this vomit of envy, he speaks only dispraise of the Triple Gem. 2.
Then the Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, took up residence for one night at the Royal Lodge in Ambalaṭṭhikā.
As the Blessed One proceeded with that grace of a Buddha, he eventually reached the Ambalaṭṭhikā gate; looking at the sun,
he thought, "It is no longer time to go, for the sun has drawn near to its setting," and so he took up residence for one night at the royal rest-house in Ambalaṭṭhikā.
In that context, *Ambalaṭṭhikā* is the king’s pleasure grove.

It is said that near its gate there was a young mango tree (*amba-rukkha*), which they called *Ambalaṭṭhikā*. Because it was situated not far from that [tree], the grove itself came to be designated as *Ambalaṭṭhikā*.
It was endowed with shade and water, surrounded by a wall, with well-constructed gates, and was beautiful.
...as if well-guarded. There, they built a house for the king’s amusement, variegated with painted designs;
it is called the "King’s House.
And Suppiya too—having looked at the sun in that place—[thought]: "It is now the wrong time to go; there are many..."
"There are many small and large wanderers, and this road is full of dangers from thieves, fierce yakṣas, and wild beasts.

But this ascetic Gotama has entered the park, and deities take up their protective guard over the dwelling place of the ascetic Gotama; well then, let me also stay here for one night and depart tomorrow."
“I shall go,” he said, and entered that very garden. Then the community of monks, having performed their duties toward the Blessed One, each took note of his own dwelling place.

The wanderer also, having set down his wanderer’s requisites on one side of the garden, took up residence there together with his own retinue. However, according to what is recorded in the canonical text (Pāḷi): “Together with...”
"by his own pupil, the young Brahmin Brahmadatta," it was said.
Having thus taken up residence, that wanderer gazed upon the One of Ten Powers during the night.
At that time, lamps were burning all around like scattered stars; in their midst sat the Blessed One, together with the community of monks.
And they surrounded the Blessed One. There, not even a single monk had any fidgeting with his hands or feet, nor was there the sound of coughing or sneezing.
Indeed, that assembly sat perfectly still, like the flame of a lamp in a windless place, due to two reasons: their own mastery of the training and their reverence for the Teacher.
It came to pass. When the wanderer saw that splendor, he looked at his own assembly. There, some were throwing up their hands, some their feet;
some were babbling, while others lay with their tongues lolling out, saliva trickling from their mouths, gnashing their teeth, whimpering like crows, and gasping with rattling breaths.
Even though it was the time to speak in praise of the virtues of the Triple Gem, he—
Out of envy, Suppiya again began to speak in dispraise, while Brahmadatta spoke in praise in the same manner as previously described. Therefore it was said:
“There too, indeed, the wanderer Suppiya... and so on; all should be recited. In that context, “there too” (*tatrāpi*) means “in that very place, in the Ambalaṭṭhikā garden.”
3. *Sambahulānaṃ* means "of many. In this context, according to the method of the Vinaya, three persons are called "a number" (*sambahulā*);
beyond that, it is the Saṅgha. However, according to the method of the Suttanta, three and even more than that are "a number.
Here, they should be understood as "a number" according to the method of the Suttanta. Regarding *maṇḍalamāḷe*, in some places two central pillars (*kaṇṇikā*) are taken [as the defining feature].
Even a gabled hall (*kūṭāgāra-sālā*) constructed with a roof covered by *haṃsavaṭṭaka* tiles is called a "round pavilion" (*maṇḍalamāḷa*).
In some cases, even an assembly hall (*upaṭṭhāna-sālā*) constructed by taking a single central pillar and surrounding it with a row of pillars is called a "round pavilion.
However, in this context, the sitting hall (*nisīdana-sālā*) should be understood as the "round pavilion. "Of those who have sat down" means by way of their sitting.
“Of those assembled” means by way of their coming together. “This is a discourse on the wonderful” (*saṅkhiyadhammo*): *saṅkhiyā* is called a discourse; the meaning is “a discourse on the wonderful.
“Arose” (*udapādi*) means it appeared. But what is it? “It is wonderful, friends,” and so forth.

In that context, it is “wonderful” because it does not happen constantly, like a blind man’s climbing of a mountain. This, first of all, is the method according to the word (*saddanayo*). This, however, is the method according to the commentary (*aṭṭhakathānayo*).
“*Accharāyoggaṃ*”: it is wonderful (*acchariya*). The meaning is that it is worthy of clapping one’s hands.

“*Abbhūtaṃ*”: what has never been before has come to be. Both of these are synonyms for amazement. “*Yāvañcidaṃ*”: by this, he shows the immeasurability [of the Buddha] due to the fact that this has been so well-penetrated.
"By that Blessed One who knows... well-penetrated"—this is the summary of the meaning here.
That Blessed One, having fulfilled the thirty perfections and shattered all defilements, has awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment;
by that Blessed One, who knows the underlying tendencies and latent dispositions of various beings as clearly as an *āmalaka* fruit placed in the palm of the hand.
...by one who sees all knowable phenomena as if they were before his eyes;
moreover, by one who knows through the recollection of past lives and so forth, and sees with the divine eye;

or by one who knows through the three clear knowledges (*tisso vijjā*) or the six direct knowledges (*cha abhiññā*), and sees with the unimpeded universal eye (*samantacakkhu*). [This is] for the sake of the capacity to know all phenomena.
Or, by one who knows with wisdom, seeing with the extremely purified flesh-eye forms that are beyond the range of the eyes of all beings,
even those situated behind walls and so forth; or by one who knows with the wisdom of penetration, which has concentration as its proximate cause and accomplishes one’s own welfare,
and sees with the wisdom of teaching, which has compassion as its proximate cause and accomplishes the welfare of others.

He is an *arahant* because he has slain (*hatatta*) his enemies and because he is worthy (*araha*) of such requisites as robes and alms. He is a *sammāsambuddha* because he has perfectly and individually awakened (*buddhattā*) to all phenomena.
Alternatively, he is an *arahant* because he knows the obstructive phenomena, sees the phenomena leading to liberation, and has slain the enemies that are the defilements.
He is a *sammāsambuddha* because he has perfectly and individually awakened to all phenomena. Thus...
By means of the four kinds of intrepidity, praised in four ways, the diversity of inclinations and the diversity of dispositions of beings have been well-penetrated, even thoroughly penetrated.
Now, in order to show the state of their being well-penetrated, he said, "For this," and so forth. This is what is meant: and this...
The Blessed One said: "Monks, beings come together and unite by way of their elements (*dhātu*);
those of inferior inclinations come together and unite with those of inferior inclinations; those of noble inclinations come together and unite with those of noble inclinations.
Monks, even in the past, beings came together and united by way of their elements; those of inferior inclinations..."
Those of inferior disposition... [as before] ...those of noble disposition harmonized and united with those of noble disposition.
In the future too, monks, ... [as before] ...they will harmonize and unite;
and even now, monks, in the present time, beings harmonize and unite according to their own elements: those of inferior disposition [with those of inferior disposition].

“Those of inferior inclinations... [and so on]... those of noble inclinations associate and harmonize with those of noble inclinations”—thus, by means of the knowledge of omniscience, which knows the diversity of beings’ inclinations, dispositions, views, acceptances, and tastes, just as one measuring with a tube or weighing with a balance, there is the knowledge of the diversity of inclinations.
It was known, even well-penetrated. Indeed, two beings with the same inclination are rare in the world:
when one wishes to go, the other wishes to stay; when one wishes to drink, the other wishes to eat.
And of these two—the teacher and the pupil—this wanderer Suppiya followed closely behind the Blessed One... [as before]... following right after him.
“And they belong to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. In this context, *itihamete* means “thus these,” which is to say, “in this way these. The rest is exactly as previously stated. 4.
Then the Blessed One, having understood this summarized teaching for those bhikkhus—here, “having understood” (*viditvā*) means having known by means of omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
For the Blessed One knows by seeing with the fleshly eye in some instances—as [the text continues]: “He saw...”
It is as in such passages as: "The Blessed One [saw] a great log being carried away by the current of the river Ganges," and so forth.

In some instances, he knows after seeing with the divine eye—as in: "With the purified divine eye, which surpasses that of humans, the Blessed One saw those deities surveying the sites for the village of Pāṭaligāma, even as many as a thousand."
In some cases, he knows by hearing with his natural ear—as in such passages as: “The Blessed One heard this conversation between the Venerable Ānanda and the wanderer Subhadda.
In other cases, he knows by hearing with the divine ear—“The Blessed One heard with the purified divine ear-element, which surpasses that of humans... and so forth.
...as in the case of the conversation and dialogue between the householder Sandhāna and the wanderer Nigrodha, and so forth.
But here, having heard it with the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), he knew it. Doing what did he know it? He performed the duty of the last watch;
and this duty is of two kinds: purposeful and purposeless. Of these, the purposeless duty—
The Blessed One eradicated [the defilements] by means of the path of Arahantship while still on the seat of enlightenment itself.

However, the Blessed One’s duty remains purposeful; that is fivefold: the duty before the meal, the duty after the meal, the duty during the first watch of the night, the duty during the middle watch of the night, and the duty during the last watch of the night.
In this regard, the duties before the meal are as follows:
Having risen early in the morning, the Blessed One—both for the sake of favoring his attendants and for the sake of bodily comfort—performs his personal grooming such as washing his face.
Then, until the time for the alms-round, he passes the time in a secluded seat. At the time for the alms-round, he puts on his lower robe.

Having fastened his waist-band, put on his robe, and taken up his bowl, he would enter a village or town for alms—sometimes alone, sometimes surrounded by the community of monks; sometimes in his ordinary manner, and sometimes while performing many miracles.
For instance, as the Lord of the World entered for alms, gentle winds would blow ahead of him.
The clouds clear the earth, releasing droplets of water to settle the dust on the road and remaining above as a canopy;
other winds gather flowers and scatter them upon the path;
elevated ground-sites sink down, while depressed ones rise up; at the moment of setting foot down, the ground becomes level and pleasant to the touch.
Or lotus flowers receive his feet. As soon as his right foot is placed within the threshold (indakhīla), six-colored rays of light issue forth from his body;

adorning the palaces, gabled chambers, and other structures—which appear as if stained with molten gold or draped in variegated cloths—they stream hither and thither, [reaching] elephants, horses, birds, and so forth.
Standing in their respective places, they made sounds in a sweet manner; likewise did the musical instruments, such as drums and lutes, and the body-ornaments of the people.
By that sign, the people knew: "Today the Blessed One has entered here for alms.
Dressed well and properly robed, they took perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and went out from their houses.
Having entered the street and respectfully honored the Blessed One with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, they paid homage and requested:
"Venerable sir, give to us ten bhikkhus, twenty, fifty... [and so on]... a hundred.
Then, taking the Blessed One’s bowl and preparing a seat, they served him the almsfood with great care. The Blessed One—

Having finished his meal, he observed the mental continuums of those beings and taught the Dhamma in such a way that some were established in the taking of the refuges, some in the five precepts, and some in one of the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, or non-returning;
while others, having gone forth, attained the supreme fruit of Arahatship. Having thus assisted the great multitude, he rose from his seat.
He goes to the monastery. Having gone there, he sits upon the excellent Buddha-seat prepared in the pavilion, awaiting the conclusion of the monks' meal.
Then, at the conclusion of the monks' meal, the attendant informs the Blessed One. Thereupon, the Blessed One enters the fragrant chamber. This, first of all, is the duty before the meal.

Then the Blessed One, having thus finished his meal and sat down in the attendance hall of the Gandhakūṭī, washed his feet, stood upon the footstool, and exhorted the Saṅgha of bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, strive with diligence!
Rare is the arising of a Buddha in the world; rare is the attainment of human birth; rare is prosperity; rare is the going forth.”
“Rare is the hearing of the True Dhamma. Therein, some ask the Blessed One for a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
The Blessed One also gives them a meditation subject according to their respective temperaments (*carita*).
Then, all of them pay homage to the Blessed One and go each to his own night-quarters or day-quarters—some to the forest, some to the foot of a tree, and some to the mountains and so forth.
Some [say it was] the abode of one of the Four Great Kings... some say the abode of Vasavatti.
Then the Blessed One, having entered the fragrant chamber, if he so desires, lies down for a while in the lion’s posture on his right side, mindful and clearly comprehending.
Then, having arisen with a tranquil body, during the second watch of the night, he surveys the world.
During the third watch, in whatever village or town he dwells depending upon, the great multitude there, having given alms before the meal,
assembles at the monastery after the meal, well-robed and well-clad, bringing perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. Then the Blessed One,
having approached with a miracle suited to the assembled company, proceeds to the Dhamma Hall and ascends the excellent Buddha-seat prepared there.

Seated, he teaches the Dhamma appropriate to the time and appropriate to the occasion; then, having discerned the right moment, he dismisses the assembly, and the people, having paid homage to the Blessed One, depart. This is the duty after the meal.
Having thus completed his post-meal duties, if he wishes to bathe his limbs, he rises from the Buddha’s seat.
Having entered the bathhouse, he allows his limbs to be warmed by the water prepared by his attendant.
The attendant, having brought the Buddha’s seat, arranges it in the courtyard surrounding the Fragrant Chamber.
The Blessed One, having put on his well-dyed inner robe, fastened his waistband, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and gone there, sits down all alone.
Having secluded himself for a short while, the bhikkhus then come from here and there to attend upon the Blessed One.
There, some ask questions, some seek a meditation subject, and some request a teaching on the Dhamma.
The Blessed One spends the first watch of the night fulfilling their intentions. This is the duty of the first watch.
But at the conclusion of the duties of the first watch, when the bhikkhus had paid homage to the Blessed One and departed, the deities of the entire ten-thousandfold world system,
seeking an opportunity, approached the Blessed One and asked questions— even those as brief as four syllables— just as they had prepared them.
The Blessed One spent the middle watch answering the questions of those deities.
This is the duty of the middle watch.

As for the last watch, however, having divided it into three parts, he spends one part in walking meditation in order to relieve the body’s weariness caused by sitting from the time of the morning meal onwards. In the second part...
Having entered the fragrant chamber, he lies down on his right side in the lion’s posture, mindful and clearly comprehending.

Rising in the third watch, he sits up and surveys the world with his Buddha-eye for the purpose of seeing those individuals who have performed meritorious deeds—such as through generosity and virtue—in the presence of previous Buddhas. This is the duty of the final watch.
On that day, however, the Blessed One, having completed his morning duties in Rājagaha, set out on the road after his meal;
having taught the meditation subject to the bhikkhus during the first watch of the night, and answered the questions of the deities during the middle watch,
he ascended the walking path in the last watch and, while walking back and forth, [spoke] this to the five hundred bhikkhus.
Having heard with his own omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa) the discourse that had arisen concerning that very omniscient knowledge, he understood it.
Therefore it was said: "While performing the duties of the last watch of the night, he understood.
And having understood this, it occurred to him: "These bhikkhus are speaking of my qualities concerning my omniscient knowledge."
Furthermore, the function of omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) was not manifest to them, but it was manifest to me alone.
When I had gone there, they would have related their own discourse to me without interruption;

then, making that the occasion (*aṭṭhuppatti*), I would have analyzed the threefold morality (*sīla*), uttered the lion’s roar (*sīhanāda*) which is unassailable in sixty-two points, and [explained] the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*).
Having brought these together and made the qualities of the Buddha manifest, I shall teach the Brahmajāla Sutta—
shaking the ten-thousandfold world system as if lifting up Mount Sineru or striking the sky with a golden pinnacle— concluding it with the peak of Arahantship.
Even after I have attained Parinibbāna, that teaching of mine will [benefit] beings for five thousand years.
"it will lead to the attainment of the deathless, the great Nibbāna. Having thought thus, he approached the circular pavilion (*maṇḍalamāḷa*).
"Yena" means by which direction or region it is to be approached. Or, this instrumental case is used in the sense of the locative;
the meaning here is that he went to that place where the circular pavilion was located.
"He sat down on the prepared seat. It is said that during the Buddha's time, wherever even a single bhikkhu dwelt, a Buddha-seat was always prepared there.

Why? It is said that the Blessed One would keep in mind those who, having received a meditation subject from him, were dwelling in comfortable places, thinking: "Such-and-such a person, having received a meditation subject from me..."
“Has he gone? Will he be able to produce some distinction or not? Then, if he sees him having abandoned the meditation subject and engaging in unwholesome thoughts, he thinks:
“How is it that unwholesome thoughts have overcome this clansman, who dwells here having received a meditation subject from a Teacher such as I?”
“...will wander through the cycle of existence in the beginningless suffering of saṃsāra.
Out of compassion for him, [the Buddha] manifested himself right there, instructed that clansman, and having leapt into the air, returned once more to his own dwelling place.
Then, being thus instructed, those bhikkhus thought: “The Teacher, knowing our minds, has come to us...”
He shows himself standing right nearby. At that moment, seeking out a seat by saying, "Venerable sir, sit here;
sit here," is indeed a burden. Therefore, they dwell having already prepared a seat.
Whoever has a bench prepares it; whoever does not have one prepares a bed, a plank, or a wooden log.

[They] prepared a stone or a heap of sand. Not finding those, they even gathered old leaves and spread out their rag-robes (*paṃsukūla*) there to set them down. But here, there was already a seat for the king;
having dusted it off and prepared it, they sat around it, and those bhikkhus, beginning with the Blessed One’s knowledge of inclinations (*adhimuttika-ñāṇa*), [praised] his virtue.
They sat down while being honored. With reference to this, it is said: "He sat down on the prepared seat.
Once seated, however, knowing [the situation] already, he questioned the bhikkhus for the purpose of initiating the discourse.
They told him everything. Therefore, it is said: "Then the Blessed One, having sat down," and so forth. In that context, "by what" (*kāya nu*) means "by which" (*katamāya*).
The meaning is: "Why are you sitting here in conversation? There is also a textual reading *kāya netthā*, which means "by what [conversation] are you here?
There is also a textual reading *kāya notthā*, which has the same meaning as the former. Regarding the term *antarākathā*:
it is another kind of talk occurring in the interval between such things as the attention to meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*), recitations, and inquiries.
"Unfinished" means that because of my arrival, it remains incomplete and has not reached its conclusion. What does this show?

"I have not come to interrupt your discourse; rather, I have come with the intention that, by means of my omniscience, I shall bring your discussion to its conclusion and demonstrate its ultimate point.
Having said this, he invited [the Buddha] to exercise his omniscience while remaining seated. This...
"Venerable sir, our conversation was interrupted when the Blessed One arrived; this is the intended meaning here as well.

Venerable sir, this conversation of ours concerning the qualities of the Blessed One’s omniscient knowledge was interrupted—it was not frivolous talk such as talk about kings and so forth—and now that the Blessed One has arrived, please complete it for us and teach it."
And at this point, by the Venerable Ānanda, for the sake of easy descent into the lotus and water-lily pond whose waters were bright,

stainless, and sweet in taste, a jeweled staircase was fashioned, its beauty enhanced by the arrangement of pure stone slabs; and the area of the ground was strewn with white sand resembling a bed of scattered pearls—
[a place] surrounded by well-proportioned walls and variegated railings, as if desiring to touch the path of the stars.
Like a staircase for the easy ascent of a magnificent palace with a towering structure, radiant with the massed splendor of the light from clusters of gems set in gold vines and bound to smooth,
soft ivory slabs; like a wide, well-set doorframe, illuminated by the radiance of gold, silver, gems, pearls, coral, and other jewels,

for the easy entrance into a great mansion adorned with noble sounds and wealth, where the household folk move about with sweet voices of speech and laughter mingled with the clinking of golden bracelets and anklets.
And just as a great gateway, so too has this Nidāna— adorned with the factors of time, place, teacher, subject matter, assembly, and location—

been spoken for the sake of easy comprehension of this Sutta, which is endowed with both meaning and phrasing and reveals the majesty of the Buddha’s qualities; thus ends the commentary on its meaning.
5. Now, the opportunity has arrived for the commentary on the discourse (sutta) set forth by the Blessed One in the manner beginning with: “Monks, others might speak dispraise of me,” and so forth.
This commentary on the discourse, however, becomes clear when it is spoken after investigating the setting-forth of the discourse;
therefore, we shall first investigate the setting-forth of the discourse. There are four...

For there are these four ways in which the discourses are set forth: those arising from one's own inclination, those arising from the inclination of others, those occasioned by a question, and those arising from a particular circumstance.

Among these, those discourses that the Blessed One spoke solely out of his own inclination without being requested by others—namely, the *Ākaṅkheyya-sutta*, the *Vattha-sutta*, the *Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna*, and the *Mahāsaḷāyatanavibhaṅga-sutta*—are those arising from his own inclination.

The *Ariyavaṃsa-sutta*, the carrier of the discourses on the right efforts (*sammappadhāna*), the carrier of the discourses on the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*), the faculties (*indriya*), the powers (*bala*), the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*), and the path-factors (*maggaṅga*)—these and others like them are examples of the "deposition according to one's own inclination" (*attajjhāsaya-nikkhepa*).

However, those such as: "Rāhula’s qualities conducive to the ripening of liberation have indeed matured; what if I were now to [instruct] Rāhula... are examples of the "deposition according to another's inclination" (*aññajjhāsaya-nikkhepa*).

"Having overcome [them], one should further bring about the destruction of the taints (*āsavā*). Thus, having considered the inclinations, patience, intentions, aspirations, and capacity for awakening of others, these were spoken according to the inclinations of others;
namely, the *Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta*, the *Mahārāhulovāda Sutta*, the *Dhammacakkappavattana*, the *Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta*, and so forth. Of these:
The relinquishing [of the teaching] is according to another’s inclination.

However, having approached the Blessed One, the four assemblies, the four castes, the nāgas, the supaṇṇas, the gandhabbas, the asuras, the yakkhas, the Great Kings, the Tāvatiṃsa and other gods, Mahābrahmā, and so forth, [requested]: “The factors of enlightenment...”
"…are called 'factors of enlightenment' (bojjhaṅga)," it is said, Bhante. "The hindrances (nīvaraṇa), the hindrances," it is said, Bhante;
"are these, Bhante, the five aggregates of clinging (pañcupādānakkhandhā)? They ask questions in such a manner as, "What indeed is the best wealth for a person?

When thus questioned, whatever [teachings] were spoken by the Blessed One—such as those in the Saṃyutta Nikāya on the Factors of Enlightenment (Bojjhaṅgasaṃyutta) and so forth—[those are the ones referred to].
Or else there are others such as the Devatā-saṃyutta, Māra-saṃyutta, Brahmā-saṃyutta, Sakkapañha, Cūḷavedalla, Mahāvedalla, Sāmaññaphala, Āḷavaka, Sūciloma, Kharaloma Suttas, and so forth;
their presentation is dependent upon a question.
But those which were spoken in dependence on a specific occasion that had arisen—such as the Dhammadāyāda and the Cūḷasīhanāda—[their presentation is dependent on a cause].

The simile of the moon, the simile of one’s own son’s flesh, the simile of a block of wood, the simile of a mass of fire, the simile of a lump of foam, and the simile of the Pāricchattaka tree—these and others like them are instances of contextual introduction (*aṭṭhuppatti*).
Among these four types of introduction, this sutta belongs to the contextual introduction. By way of contextual introduction...

For this was laid down by the Blessed One. On what occasion (aṭṭhuppatti) did it arise? On the occasion of praise and dispraise. A teacher spoke dispraise of the Triple Gem, while his pupil spoke praise.

Having made this occasion of praise and dispraise the starting point, the Blessed One, who is skilled in teaching, began the instruction: "Bhikkhus, others may speak dispraise of me... and so forth. In that regard:
*Mamaṃ* is a term of possession (*sāmivacana*), meaning "mine. The word *vā* has the sense of an alternative. *Pare* refers to beings who are hostile.
*Tatra* means "among those" who speak ill [of them].
Although by the words "no resentment" (*na āghāto*) and so forth it is shown that those monks have no resentment at all, nevertheless, for the sake of future sons of good family...
In such instances as these, he establishes the guide to the Dhamma by preventing the arising of unwholesome states. Therein, "āhanati cittaṃ" means "it strikes the mind";
this is a designation for anger (kopa). "Appatītā honti tena atuṭṭhā asomanassikā" means "they are not pleased, dissatisfied, and unhappy because of it";
this is a designation for dejection (domanassa). "It does not accomplish the welfare of oneself nor of others" means...
*Anabhiraddhi* is a designation for anger. Thus, here by two terms the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*) is stated, and by one term the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*);
in this way, two aggregates have been mentioned. By means of these, the cause for the remaining associated phenomena is also effectively excluded.
Having thus prevented mental corruption through the first method, he shows the danger therein through the second method:
He said: “If you were to be angry or displeased in that regard, the obstacle would belong to you alone.
Therein, “if you were to be [thus]” means: if you were to be toward those who speak dispraise, or if you were to be toward that dispraise;
the sense is: if you should be so. “Angry” means through anger; “displeased” means through mental distress. “The obstacle would belong to you alone...”
"By that, there would be an obstacle for you"—that is, by that anger and that dissatisfaction, there would be an obstacle to the first jhāna and the others.
Having thus shown the disadvantage by way of the second method, he spoke the passage beginning with "Would you [be able] to others...
by way of the third method, showing their incapacity even for the mere discernment of the meaning of words. In that context, "of others" refers to whomever...

For one who is angry does not understand the meaning of what is well-spoken or ill-spoken, whether it concerns the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, or Noble Disciples, nor even his own parents or enemies. As it is said:
"An angry person does not know the meaning; an angry person does not see the Dhamma."
"Blinding darkness then arises for the man whom anger overcomes.
Anger produces harm; anger agitates the mind.
People do not realize that this fear has arisen from within themselves."

Having thus in every way restrained the mental corruption of ill-will regarding dispraise, he now speaks the words beginning with “In that regard, you should disentangle what is untrue as untrue,” in order to show the manner in which one should proceed.
Therein, “in that regard, by you” means: in that matter of dispraise, by you. “What is untrue should be disentangled as untrue” means:
whatever is untrue, that should be removed precisely by its state of being untrue. How? By the method beginning with, “Thus this is untrue.”
In this regard, the application is as follows: having heard such things as, "Your teacher is not omniscient; the Dhamma is ill-proclaimed;
the Saṅgha has entered upon a wrong path," one must not remain silent. Rather, one should speak thus: "This which you have said is indeed false;
for this reason also it is false, for this reason also it is untrue; 'this does not exist among us.'"
“Moreover, this is not found among us; our Teacher alone is omniscient, the Dhamma is well-expounded, and the Saṅgha is practicing rightly;
herein lies such-and-such a reason. And here it should be understood that the second phrase is a synonym for the first, and the fourth for the third.
Furthermore, this withdrawal [of blame] should be made only regarding what has been criticized.
Not in all cases. For if, when it is said, "You are immoral; your teacher is immoral; this and that was done by you;
this and that was done by your teacher," one remains silent and accepts it, he becomes suspicious. Therefore, without harboring mental malice, the censure should be withdrawn.
However, by means of the ten grounds for abuse, according to the method beginning with "You are a camel" or "You are an ox," [one may continue].
Having looked with equanimity upon a person who reviles one, one should simply exercise patience through endurance.

6. Having thus shown the characteristic of being a "Tādi" (one who is such) regarding the ground of dispraise, he now spoke the passage beginning with, “Or, monks, others might speak praise of me,” in order to show it regarding the ground of praise. In this context, “others” refers to any gods or humans who are full of faith.
It is called *ānanda* because they rejoice by means of it; this is a designation for *pīti* (rapture). The state of being well-minded is *somanassa*;

this is a designation for mental pleasure (*cetasika-sukha*). The state of one who is elated is *uppilāvitatta*. Of what is there the state of being elated? It is of the mind (*cetaso*). This is a designation for the rapture that causes elation and brings about agitation (*uddhacca*).
Here too, the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*) is expressed by two terms, and the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) by one.
Having thus prevented elation by means of the first method, he says, “If you were to be there,” etc., showing the danger therein by means of the second.

Here too, the meaning should be understood as follows: “That would be an obstacle for you alone” means that through that elation, there would be an obstacle for you alone regarding the first jhāna and so forth. But why is this?
Is it not said by the Blessed One:
"The rapture that arises in the body for one who praises 'the Buddha'—
that rapture alone is better than even the whole of Jambudīpa"?
The rapture that arises in the body for one who praises the Dhamma is indeed superior even to the entire Jambudīpa filled with wealth.
The rapture that arises in the body for one who praises the Saṅgha...
For it has been said: "That joy alone would indeed be better than even the whole of Jambudīpa," and "Those who, monks, have faith in the Buddha, have faith in the Supreme One.
By such hundreds of suttas as these, joy and gladness alone toward the Triple Gem are praised. It is true that they are praised, but that [joy] is based on renunciation (*nekkhamma*).
Here, what is intended is that worldly joy and gladness similar to what arose in the Venerable Channa in the manner of saying, "The Buddha is ours, the Dhamma is ours," and so forth.
For this acts as an obstacle to the attainment of jhāna and the like.
It was for this very reason that even the Venerable Channa was unable to produce any distinction until the Buddha had passed away into final Nibbāna.
But at the time of his final Nibbāna, being urged by the "Brahma-punishment" (brahmadaṇḍa) thus prescribed, he abandoned that joy and gladness and produced a distinction [of attainment].
Therefore, it should be understood that this was said with reference specifically to what constitutes an obstacle.
For this joy is accompanied by greed, and greed is indeed like anger. As it has been said:
“The greedy one does not know the goal; the greedy one does not see the Dhamma.
Blind darkness then arises when greed overcomes a man.
Greed is the producer of misfortune; greed is the agitator of the mind.”
“Fear born from within, that people do not perceive.

Furthermore, it should be understood that although the third section has not been included here [in the text], it is indeed included by implication. For just as one who is angry does not understand the matter, so too one who is greedy does not understand the matter.
As for the section showing the manner in which one should practice, this is the application: “Your Teacher is omniscient, an arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha.”
Having heard such things as, "The Dhamma is well-expounded; the Saṅgha has practiced rightly," one should not remain silent.
Rather, one should acknowledge it thus: "This which you have said is indeed real; for this reason also it is real, and for this reason also it is true.
For that Blessed One is indeed an Arahant, and indeed a Perfectly Enlightened One; the Dhamma..."
“Thus well-expounded,” “thus visible here and now”; “the Saṅgha is thus practicing rightly,” “thus practicing straightly.
When asked, “Are you virtuous? if one is indeed virtuous, one must certainly acknowledge, “I am virtuous.
When asked, “Have you attained the first jhāna… [and so on] …are you an arahant? one should acknowledge this only among fellow bhikkhus who are of like status.
For in this way, both evil desire is avoided and the fruitfulness of the Dispensation is demonstrated.
The remainder should be understood according to the method already stated. This concludes the Short Exposition on Virtue.
7. But as for this phrase, “Bhikkhus, this is a trifle,” what is the connection? This sutta is bound by two terms: praise and blame.
Therein, blame is expressed thus: “This is unreal, this is untrue”;
having reached the limit of the water, one turns back like a fire. Praise, however, is that which should be acknowledged as real, exactly as it is.
— "Thus it is a departed being (peta)," thinking this, he simply followed along. That [praise] was twofold:

the praise spoken by Brahmadatta, and the praise initiated by the Saṅgha of monks in the manner beginning with, "It is wonderful, friends! Among these, he will show the connection for the exposition of emptiness following the praise uttered by the Saṅgha of monks;
but here, [the connection follows] that which was spoken by Brahmadatta.
In order to show the connection to what was previously stated, the teaching begins with the words, "But this, bhikkhus, is a trifle.
In this context, *appamattakaṃ* is a name for that which is limited (*paritta*). *Oramattakaṃ* is a synonym for the same.
*Mattā* means measure (*pamāṇa*). That of which the measure is small is *appamattakaṃ*. That of which the measure is low is *oramattakaṃ*.

“Virtue alone, a mere trifle of virtue. This is what is meant: “But this, monks, is indeed a mere trifle, a small thing, a mere trifle of virtue,” such that even an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), making an effort by saying, “I shall speak in praise of the Tathāgata,” might speak in praise [of it].
Herein, one might ask: Is this so-called virtue not the supreme ornament of the yogi? As the ancients have said:
“Virtue is the adornment of the practitioner; virtue is the embellishment of the practitioner.
Adorned with virtue, the practitioner has reached the pinnacle of all embellishments.
And by the Blessed One, in many hundreds of discourses, virtue has been spoken of as being of great importance. As it was said: “If one should desire…”
“Monks, when a monk thinks, ‘May I be dear to my fellow celibates, agreeable, respected, and esteemed,’ he should be one who fulfills the precepts themselves. And:
“As a hen guards her eggs, as a yak guards its tail;”
"Just as one protects a beloved son or one's only eye,
even so, while guarding your virtue,
may you be well-behaved and always full of reverence."
“The fragrance of flowers does not go against the wind,
nor that of sandalwood, tagara, or jasmine.
But the fragrance of the virtuous goes even against the wind.”
The person of noble character wafts his fragrance in every direction.
Whether it be sandalwood, tagara, blue lotus, or jasmine—
of all these varieties of scents, the fragrance of virtue is unsurpassed.
Faint is this fragrance of tagara and sandalwood;
but the supreme fragrance of those possessed of virtue wafts even among the gods.
Of those who are perfected in virtue and dwell in heedfulness—
“Māra finds no path for those who are liberated through right knowledge.
And: “A wise man, established in virtue, developing the mind and wisdom—a bhikkhu ardent and discerning—he shall unravel this tangle.”
“Just as, monks, whatever plants and seeds attain growth, increase, and abundance, they all do so by depending on the earth and being established upon the earth;
it is thus that these plants and seeds attain growth, increase, and abundance. Even so, monks, a monk, depending on virtue and being established in virtue...”
“Developing the seven factors of enlightenment and cultivating the seven factors of enlightenment, one attains growth, increase, and abundance in the qualities.
Thus, many other suttas should also be seen. In this way, in hundreds of suttas, virtue has been described as being truly great. Why, then, does he say here that it is “insignificant”?
"By comparison with what is higher. For virtue does not reach the level of concentration, nor does concentration reach the level of wisdom;
therefore, by comparison with what is above, what is below is called "inferior. How is it that virtue does not reach the level of concentration?
At the seventh year after his full enlightenment, the Blessed One, at the gate of the city of Sāvatthī—
Seated upon a jeweled throne one *yojana* in measure, within a jewel-pavilion twelve *yojanas* wide at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree,
while a divine white parasol three *yojanas* in height was being held over him, he— amidst an assembly extending twelve *yojanas*—
demonstrated his own majesty and crushed the heretics by manifesting a mass of fire from the upper part of his body and a stream of water from the lower part of his body.
He displays the Twin Miracle proceeding in such a manner as this: "A mass of fire issues from each single pore, a stream of water issues from each single pore," and so forth regarding the six colors.

From his body, which is golden-hued, rays of golden light shoot forth and reach as far as the peak of existence (*bhavagga*), pervading the entire ten-thousandfold world system (*dasasahassacakkavāḷa*).
It is like the time for adorning oneself; each successive ray proceeds as if in tandem with the preceding one, as if they were yoked together and occurring at the same moment.
Yet, there is no such thing as the simultaneous occurrence of two consciousnesses. However, for the Blessed Buddhas, regarding the duration of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga)...
Due to their lightness and because he has mastered them through five modes of practice, they proceed as if simultaneously.
However, for each individual ray, the acts of adverting, preparatory work, and resolution are distinct and separate.
For the Blessed One enters the blue kasiṇa attainment for the sake of the blue ray, and the yellow kasiṇa for the sake of the yellow ray.
One enters the red and white *kasiṇa* for the sake of red and white rays; one enters the fire *kasiṇa* for the sake of a mass of fire;
one enters the water *kasiṇa* for the sake of a stream of water. When the Teacher walks in meditation, the emanation stands, sits, or lies down—all this should be detailed in full.
Herein, there is not even a single function of virtue (*sīla*); everything is solely the function of concentration (*samādhi*).
In this way, one does not attain concentration through mere virtue.

However, the Blessed One, having fulfilled the perfections for four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons, departed from his palace—which had been the dwelling place of the glory of a universal monarch—at the age of twenty-nine;
he went forth on the bank of the Anomā River and, having renounced the world, [attained it].
Having practiced the yoga of striving for six years, on the full moon day of Visākha, after partaking of the honey-milk-rice mixed with divine essence offered by Sujātā in the village of Uruvelā,
he entered the seat of enlightenment from the south-east at the time of evening. Having circumambulated the king of trees,
the Assattha, three times, he stood on the north-eastern side, spread out a layer of grass, and assumed the cross-legged posture with its three joints.
Having sat down cross-legged, making the meditation subject of loving-kindness endowed with its four factors his precursor,
and having resolved upon the foundation of energy, he placed the fifty-cubit trunk of the Bodhi tree— resembling a mass of silver set upon a golden seat—
behind him as he sat upon his excellent fourteen-cubit couch, just as one might place a jeweled parasol above the branch of a Bodhi tree.
While being supported by robes the color of gold, as the sprouts of enlightenment—resembling coral—fell away and the sun was setting, he shattered the army of Māra;
in the first watch of the night, he recollected his former births;
in the middle watch, he purified his divine eye; and at the time of dawn, he applied his knowledge to the principle of dependent origination, which is the customary practice of all Buddhas.
Having produced the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing, taking that very state as a basis, he developed insight;
then, having exhausted all defilements by means of the fourth path attained through the sequence of the paths, he realized all the qualities of a Buddha—this was his function of wisdom.
Thus, concentration does not reach the level of wisdom.
In this regard, just as water in the hand does not reach the bowl, water in the bowl does not reach the jar,
water in the jar does not reach the water-pot, water in the water-pot does not reach the large cauldron, and water in the large cauldron [does not reach...]
The water in a small pool does not reach the water in a ravine; the water in a ravine does not reach the water in a mountain stream;
the water in a mountain stream does not reach the water in the five great rivers;
the water in the five great rivers does not reach the water in the great ocean of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa-mahāsamudda*); [the water] in the great ocean of the world-system...
