The water in a bowl does not equal the water in the great ocean at the base of Sineru. Compared to the water in a bowl, the water in the hand is small...
[and so on] ...compared to the water in the great ocean at the base of Sineru, the water in the world-ocean is small.
Thus, taking the water as it becomes greater and greater above, the water below each level is small.

In the same way, by taking each successive higher quality into account, the virtue of each preceding stage should be understood as trifling and limited. Therefore it was said: “But this, bhikkhus, is a trifling matter, a limited matter, merely a matter of virtue. Regarding the phrase “by which one is a worldling,” it is said here:
“Two kinds of worldlings were spoken of by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun:”
“The blind worldling is one, the noble worldling is another.

In this context, he who lacks study, inquiry, hearing, retention, and reflection regarding the aggregates, elements, bases, and so forth, is the blind worldling. He who possesses these is the noble worldling. Furthermore, both of these types are called “worldlings” (puthujjana) for various reasons, such as being born among the many (puthu):
“Because of being born among the many, and other such causes, one is a worldling;”
“Because he is included among ordinary people, or because this person is ‘many’ (puthu), he is thus called an *puthujjana*.
For he is an *puthujjana* because of such reasons as generating (*janana*) various kinds of defilements (*kilesa*), and so forth. As it has been said:
“They generate various defilements, thus they are *puthujjanas*; they possess various, unshattered views of individuality (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), thus they are *puthujjanas*; various...”
Ordinary persons (*puthujjana*) are those who look to the faces of teachers; ordinary persons are those who have not emerged from the various states of existence;
ordinary persons are those who perform various volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*);

they are carried away by various floods (*ogha*), tormented by various fevers (*santāpa*), consumed by various burning pains (*pariḷāha*), and are attached to the five strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*).
“Worldlings (puthujjana) are greedy, clinging, infatuated, obsessed, attached, fastened, and entangled;
worldlings are individually shut in, covered, enveloped, blocked, concealed, and enclosed by the five hindrances.

They are so called because they are included among the multitude of people who have passed beyond the path of counting, who are turned away from the noble Dhamma, and whose conduct consists of lowly things.

A *puthujjana* is so called because he is an individual (*puthu*) who has gone his own way, reckoned separately, and is dissociated from the noble ones (*ariya*) who are endowed with virtues such as morality and learning; thus he is a *puthujjana*. Regarding the phrase "of the Tathāgata":
the Blessed One is a *tathāgata* for eight reasons. He is a *tathāgata* because he has come (*āgata*) in such a way (*tathā*). Thus...

He is a Tathāgata because he has gone thus; he is a Tathāgata because he has come to the characteristic of suchness; he is a Tathāgata because he has perfectly awakened to the true nature of phenomena as they really are;

he is a Tathāgata by virtue of seeing things as they truly are; he is a Tathāgata by virtue of speaking things as they truly are; he is a Tathāgata by virtue of acting as he speaks; and he is a Tathāgata in the sense of overcoming.
In what sense is the Blessed One a Tathāgata because he has come thus? Just as the previous Perfectly Enlightened Ones came having exerted themselves for the welfare of the entire world;

just as the Blessed Vipassī came, just as the Blessed Sikhī, just as the Blessed Vessabhū, just as the Blessed Kakusandha, just as the Blessed Koṇāgamana, and just as the Blessed Kassapa came—so has he come. Thus is he a Tathāgata.
"He has come. What is meant by this? By the same resolve through which these Blessed Ones came, our Blessed One has also come.

Or else, just as the Blessed Vipassī... [and so on] ...just as the Blessed Kassapa, having fulfilled the perfection of generosity, and having fulfilled the perfections of virtue, renunciation, wisdom, energy, patience, truthfulness, determination, loving-kindness, and equanimity, [has come].
Having fulfilled these thirty perfections— namely, the ten pāramīs, the ten upapāramīs, and the ten paramattha-pāramīs—
and having made the five great renunciations, namely the relinquishing of limbs, eyes, wealth, kingdom, children, and wife;
and having fulfilled the preliminary efforts, the former conduct, the teaching of the Dhamma, the conduct for the benefit of others, and so forth, through the practice of wisdom...
Having reached the limit [of his goal], he has come; likewise, our Blessed One has also come. Or else, just as the Blessed Vipassī...

[and so on] ...the Blessed Kassapa, having developed and cultivated the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path, has come.
In the same way, our Blessed One has also come. Because he has come in that manner, he is called the Tathāgata.
"Just as the sages such as Vipassī and the others have attained omniscience here in this world," so too has he.
"Likewise, this Sage of the Śākyas has also come;
therefore, he who possesses the eye is called the Tathāgata.
Thus, he is a Tathāgata because he has come in such a way.
In what sense is he a Tathāgata? He is a Tathāgata because just as the Blessed One Vipassī went [at birth], and... the Blessed One Kassapa went, so too did he go.
And how did that Blessed One go? For immediately upon being born, having stood with level feet upon the earth, he went seven steps facing north.
As it is said: "Immediately upon being born, Ānanda, the Bodhisatta..."
Standing with even feet, he proceeds seven steps facing north;
while a white parasol is held over him, he surveys all directions and utters this lion’s roar:
“I am the foremost in the world, I am the eldest in the world, I am the best in the world. This is the final birth; now there is no further becoming.”
And was that movement of his true? It was indeed not false, because it served as a precursor to many distinguished attainments.
For the fact that he stood with level feet immediately upon birth was a precursor to his acquisition of the four bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*).
Furthermore, his facing toward the north was a precursor to his state of transcendence over the entire world.
The taking of seven steps signifies the attainment of the seven jewels of the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*).
As for the waving of the yak-tail fans mentioned in the phrase "Yak-tail fans with golden handles are waved," it signifies the crushing of all rival teachers.
The holding of the white parasol signifies the attainment of the supreme, stainless white parasol of the liberation of *arahantship*.
Standing upon the seventh step, he surveyed all directions; this was the omen for the attainment of the unobstructed knowledge of omniscience.
His uttering of the "Bull's Voice" was the precursor to the irreversible turning of the supreme Wheel of Dhamma.
Likewise, the Blessed One has gone there, and that journey of his was true and not false, by virtue of being the omen for those very same specific attainments.
Therefore the ancients said:
“Just as a newborn calf,
with even feet, touches the earth.”
Thus Gotama strode seven steps,
while the Maruts held up a white parasol for him.
Having gone those seven steps, Gotama—
He surveyed the directions all around with equanimity;
he uttered speech endowed with the eight factors,
like a lion standing upon a mountain peak.
Thus he has gone to suchness, therefore he is the Tathāgata.
Or alternatively, just as the Blessed One Vipassī … [and so on] … just as the Blessed One Kassapa [attained], this Blessed One likewise has gone by means of renunciation, abandoning sensual desire;
by means of non-ill will, abandoning ill will; by means of the perception of light, abandoning sloth and torpor; by means of non-distraction … [and so on].
Having abandoned restlessness and remorse through the discernment of phenomena,
having shattered ignorance with knowledge, having dispelled discontent with gladness, having thrown open the door-panel of the hindrances with the first jhāna,
having stilled applied and sustained thought with the second jhāna, having faded away from rapture with the third jhāna, and [having abandoned] pleasure and pain with the fourth jhāna...
Having abandoned [them], and having transcended the perception of form, the perception of sensory resistance, and the perception of diversity through the attainment of the base of infinite space;

having transcended the perception of the base of infinite space through the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness; having transcended the perception of the base of infinite consciousness through the attainment of the base of nothingness;
and having transcended the perception of the base of nothingness through the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—he has gone.
By contemplating impermanence, one abandons the perception of permanence; by contemplating suffering, the perception of pleasure;
by contemplating non-self, the perception of self; by contemplating disenchantment, delight; by contemplating dispassion, lust; by contemplating cessation, arising;
by contemplating relinquishment, grasping; and by contemplating destruction, the perception of compactness; and by contemplating vanishing...
Accumulation [is abandoned] by the contemplation of change; the perception of permanence by the contemplation of the signless;

the wish for gratification by the contemplation of the desireless; misapprehension of individuality by the contemplation of emptiness; misapprehension of grasping at a core by the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena;

misapprehension of delusion by the knowledge and vision of things as they truly are; misapprehension of attachment by the contemplation of danger; and misapprehension of non-reflection by the contemplation of reflection.
He has gone by way of non-reflective attachment to fetters through the contemplation of turning away;

having broken the defilements associated with views by means of the stream-entry path, having abandoned gross defilements by means of the once-return path, having eradicated subtle defilements by means of the non-return path, and having completely severed all defilements by means of the arahant path—he has thus gone. In this sense also, he is the Tathāgata.
How is he a Tathāgata because he has come to the characteristic of suchness (*tathalakkhaṇa*)?
The characteristic of hardness in the earth element is such, it is not otherwise. The characteristic of flowing in the water element; the characteristic of heat in the fire element;

the characteristic of distension in the air element; the characteristic of non-obstruction in the space element; the characteristic of cognizing in the consciousness element. It is because he has come to these characteristics that he is a Tathāgata.
The characteristic of form is deformation. The characteristic of feeling is experiencing. The characteristic of perception is perceiving. The characteristic of volitional formations is forming.

The characteristic of consciousness is cognizing. The characteristic of applied thought is directing onto. The characteristic of sustained thought is examining. The characteristic of rapture is pervading. The characteristic of pleasure is gratification. The characteristic of one-pointedness of mind is non-distraction. The characteristic of contact is touching.

The characteristic of the faculty of faith is resolution; the characteristic of the faculty of energy is exertion; the characteristic of the faculty of mindfulness is establishment; the characteristic of the faculty of concentration is non-distraction; the characteristic of the faculty of wisdom is understanding.

The characteristic of the power of faith is unshakability by lack of faith; the characteristic of the power of energy is unshakability by indolence; the characteristic of the power of mindfulness is unshakability by forgetfulness; the characteristic of the power of concentration is unshakability by agitation; the characteristic of the power of wisdom is unshakability by ignorance.
The characteristic of the mindfulness enlightenment factor is establishment. The characteristic of the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor is discrimination.

The characteristic of the energy enlightenment factor is exertion. The characteristic of the rapture enlightenment factor is pervasion. The characteristic of the tranquility enlightenment factor is peace.
The characteristic of the concentration enlightenment factor is non-distraction. The [characteristic] of the equanimity enlightenment factor...
The characteristic of right view is reflective discernment; the characteristic of right intention is directing toward; the characteristic of right speech is encompassing;
the characteristic of right action is originating; the characteristic of right livelihood is purification.
Right effort has the characteristic of exertion. Right mindfulness has the characteristic of establishing. Right concentration has the characteristic of non-distraction.
Ignorance has the characteristic of unknowing. Formations have the characteristic of volition. Consciousness has the characteristic of cognizing.
Name has the characteristic of bending toward an object. Form has the characteristic of being afflicted. The six sense bases have the characteristic of being a base.
Contact has the characteristic of touching. Feeling has the characteristic of being felt. Craving has the characteristic of being a cause. Clinging has the characteristic of grasping.
Becoming has the characteristic of accumulation. Birth has the characteristic of arising. Aging has the characteristic of decaying.
Death has the characteristic of passing away.
The characteristic of the elements is emptiness. The characteristic of the sense bases is being a base. The characteristic of the foundations of mindfulness is establishing.

The characteristic of the right efforts is striving. The characteristic of the bases of psychic power is succeeding. The characteristic of the faculties is predominance. The characteristic of the powers is unshakability.
The characteristic of the factors of enlightenment is leading out. The characteristic of the path is causality.

The characteristic of the truths is suchness. The characteristic of serenity is non-distraction. The characteristic of insight is contemplation. The characteristic of serenity and insight is their single function (taste). The characteristic of the yoke-pair is their non-transgression [of each other].
The characteristic of purification of virtue is restraint. The characteristic of purification of mind is non-distraction. The characteristic of purification of view is seeing.
The characteristic of the knowledge of destruction is cutting off. The characteristic of the knowledge of non-arising is tranquility.
The characteristic of zeal is its root; the characteristic of attention is its origination; the characteristic of contact is its convergence; the characteristic of feeling is its meeting place;
the characteristic of concentration is its predominance; the characteristic of mindfulness is its sovereignty;
the characteristic of wisdom is its transcendence; the characteristic of liberation is its core; and the characteristic of Nibbāna, which plunges into the Deathless, is its culmination.

It is thus, it is not otherwise. Thus, because he has arrived at the characteristic of suchness (*tathalakkhaṇa*) by way of the path of knowledge, having reached it without missing it, he is the *Tathāgata*.
Because he has arrived at the characteristic of suchness in this way, he is the *Tathāgata*.
How is he the *Tathāgata* because he has perfectly awakened to the phenomena of suchness as they truly are? The "phenomena of suchness" are the four [noble truths].
The Noble Truths. As it is said: “Bhikkhus, these four are such, not otherwise, not different.
Which four? ‘This is suffering,’ bhikkhus—this is such, this is not otherwise, this is not different,” and so on in detail.
And the Blessed One has fully awakened to them; therefore, because he has fully awakened to those such (tatha) phenomena, [he is called the Tathāgata].
He is called the Tathāgata. Here, the word *gata* has the sense of "fully awakened.
Furthermore, the fact that aging-and-death has arisen and come about with birth as its condition is *tatha* (such), not otherwise, not different...
[and so on] ...the fact that volitional formations have arisen and come about with ignorance as their condition is *tatha*, not otherwise, not different... [and so on] ...thus.
The meaning of conditionality for volitional formations in relation to ignorance, the meaning of conditionality for consciousness in relation to volitional formations...
[and so on] ...the meaning of conditionality for aging and death in relation to birth is such, not otherwise, and not different. The Blessed One has fully awakened to all that;
therefore, because he has fully awakened to those such (tatha) phenomena, he is called the Tathāgata. Thus, regarding such phenomena...

He is the Tathāgata because he has awakened to things as they truly are (*yāthāvato*). How is he the Tathāgata by virtue of seeing things as they are? The Blessed One, regarding the objective base of visible form that comes within the range of the eye-door of immeasurable beings in immeasurable world-systems throughout the world with its devas... [and so on] ...among the generation including devas and humans: *The Tathāgata knows that visible form as it really is.* *The Tathāgata sees that visible form as it really is.* *The Tathāgata understands that visible form as it really is.* *The Tathāgata penetrates that visible form as it really is.* *The Tathāgata breaks through that visible form as it really is.* *The Tathāgata pierces that visible form as it really is.* *The Tathāgata fathoms that visible form as it really is.* *The Tathāgata surveys that visible form as it really is.* *The Tathāgata encompasses that visible form as it really is.* *The Tathāgata masters that visible form as it really is.* In this way, the Blessed One is the Tathāgata by virtue of seeing things as they are. He is the Tathāgata by virtue of seeing things as they are. He is

There is a name; he knows and sees it in all its aspects. For one who thus knows and sees—whether by way of the desirable and undesirable, or by way of the terms applicable to what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized—it is as follows: "What is that form which is the form-base (*rūpāyatana*)?
That form which, derived from the four great elements, is a manifestation of color, visible and impinging, blue..."
When analyzed by way of many names—such as "yellow" and so forth—through thirteen sections and fifty-two methods, it remains exactly as it is;
there is nothing false. This same method applies to sounds and other objects that come into the range of the ear-door and the other sense-doors.
And this was said by the Blessed One: "Monks, whatever in the world with its devas... [and so on] ...among the generation including devas and humans..."
"Whatever has been seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, or pondered by the mind—that I know.

That I have directly known; that is understood by the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata does not stand [clinging] to that. Thus, he is the Tathāgata because of his seeing of things as they truly are (*tathadassitāya*).
In this context, the etymological derivation of "Tathāgata" should be understood as "one who sees things as they truly are" (*tathadassī atthe tathāgato*).
In what sense is the Tathāgata one who speaks truthfully? From the night the Blessed One sat upon the invincible throne at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa),
crushed the heads of the three Māras, and fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (anuttara-sammāsambodhi),

until the night he attained final nibbāna in the element of nibbāna without residue (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu) between the twin sāla trees— within this interval of forty-five years— [he spoke only that which is so].

Whatever was spoken by the Blessed One during the first, middle, or final enlightenment—whether it be a discourse (*sutta*), mixed prose and verse (*geyya*), or even the analytical treatises (*vedalla*)—all of that is irreproachable in both meaning and phrasing;
it is neither deficient nor redundant, complete in every aspect, and it crushes the intoxication of lust, hatred, and delusion. Not even so much as a hair’s tip of fault exists therein.

Whatever has been omitted, all that is exactly as it was—neither false nor otherwise—just as if marked with a single seal, measured with a single reed-measure, or weighed on a single scale. Therefore he said:
"Cunda, between the night when the Tathāgata awakens to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment and the night when [he passes away] into the Nibbāna-element without residue..."
“He attains final Nibbāna; whatever he speaks, utters, or explains in the interval between [his birth and that moment], all that is exactly so and not otherwise.

Therefore, he is called the ‘Tathāgata. Here, the word *gata* has the sense of “spoken. Thus, he is a Tathāgata because of his speaking truthfully (*tathavāditā*). Furthermore, *āgada* means “speaking”; the meaning is “speech.
Since he possesses unerring speech (*aviparīta-āgada*), by changing the letter *da* to *ta*, the term *tathāgata* is formed. In this sense, the derivation of the word should be understood.
In what sense is the Tathāgata so called because of acting accordingly? For the body of the Blessed One conforms to his speech, and his speech conforms to his body;
therefore, he is one who acts as he speaks and speaks as he acts. And for one such as this, the body has gone (gata) and proceeded (pavatta) in accordance with his speech—this is the meaning.
Furthermore, just as the body has gone, so too has his speech gone and proceeded; thus he is the Tathāgata.
For this very reason it was said: “Bhikkhus, as the Tathāgata speaks, so he acts; as he acts, so he speaks.
Thus, as he speaks, so he acts, and as he acts, so he speaks. Therefore he is called the ‘Tathāgata. In this way, he is a Tathāgata by virtue of acting accordingly.
How is he a Tathāgata in the sense of overcoming? Having made the peak of existence above and the Avīci hell below his limits—
Horizontally, throughout immeasurable world-systems, he surpasses all beings in virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation;

there is no equal or measure for him. He is incomparable, immeasurable, unsurpassed—the king of kings, god of gods, the Sakka beyond Sakkas, the Brahmā beyond Brahmās. Therefore it was said: "In the world with its devas..."
“Monks, in the world... among the generation with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, the Tathāgata is the conqueror, unconquered, the all-seeing, who wields mastery;
therefore he is called ‘Tathāgata.
In this regard, the derivation of the word should be understood as follows: it is like a medicine (*agada*); and what is this? It consists of the splendor of his teaching.

And there is the medicinal elixir of merit (*puññussaya*). For by means of this, this physician of great power overcomes all proponents of other doctrines and the world with its devas, just as one overcomes snakes with a divine antidote.
Thus, in the overcoming of the entire world, his medicine consists of the splendor of his teaching and the elixir of merit; it is true and unerring.
By changing the letter *da* to the letter *ta*, he should be understood as the "Tathāgata."
Thus, the Tathāgata is so called in the sense of overcoming.

Furthermore, he is the Tathāgata because he has gone to suchness (*tathāya gato*), and he is the Tathāgata because he has gone to reality (*tathaṃ gato*). "Gone" (*gato*) means understood, transcended, reached, or entered; this is the meaning.

In that regard, he is the Tathāgata because he has gone to, or understood, the entire world through the full understanding of its delimitation (*tīraṇapariññā*). [He has likewise understood] the origin of the world...

He is a *tathāgata* because he has gone (*gato*) and passed beyond (*atīto*) to suchness (*tathāya*) by means of the full understanding of abandoning (*pahānapariññā*). He is a *tathāgata* because he has gone to and attained suchness by means of the realization (*sacchikiriyā*) of the cessation of the world (*lokanirodha*).
He is a *tathāgata* because he has gone to and entered upon the true path leading to the cessation of the world (*lokanirodhagāminī paṭipadā*).
Therefore it was said by the Blessed One:
“Bhikkhus, the world has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata is detached from the world.
The origin of the world, bhikkhus, has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; the origin of the world has been abandoned by the Tathāgata.
The cessation of the world, bhikkhus, has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; the cessation of the world has been realized by the Tathāgata. The way leading to the cessation of the world...”
“Bhikkhus, the path to the cessation of the world has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; the path leading to the cessation of the world has been developed by the Tathāgata.
Whatever, bhikkhus, in this world with its devas… all that has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata.
Therefore, he is called the ‘Tathāgata.’”

The meaning of this should also be understood in this way. And this is merely a brief introduction for illustrating the state of a Tathāgata. However, only a Tathāgata himself could describe the state of a Tathāgata in its entirety.

"And what is that, monks?"—by asking "What is that?", he asks: "What is it by which a worldling, through something trifling, something insignificant, mere virtue alone, might speak in praise of the Tathāgata? In this context, "question" (pucchā) means...

There are five kinds of questions: the question for the illumination of what has not been seen, the question for the correlation of what has been seen, the question for the cutting off of doubt, the question for assent, and the question out of a desire to speak.
Among these, what is the question for the illumination of what has not been seen? It is when the characteristic of a thing is naturally unknown, unseen, and unmeasured.
That which has not been crossed over, not manifested, and not fully clarified—one asks a question for the sake of its knowledge, seeing, weighing, scrutinizing, and full clarification;
this is a question for the purpose of illuminating what has not been seen.
What is a question for the purpose of correlating what has been seen? It is when the characteristic is already known by nature, having been seen, weighed, and scrutinized.
It has been abandoned and thoroughly cultivated; he asks a question for the purpose of cross-examining it with other wise men—this is a question for the purpose of cross-examining what has been seen.
What is a question for the purpose of cutting off doubt? He is by nature prone to uncertainty, prone to perplexity, and possessed of indecision.
“Is it thus? Is it not thus? What indeed is it? How indeed is it? He asks this question for the purpose of cutting through doubt.
This is the question for cutting through doubt.
What is the question for seeking consent? The Blessed One asks a question with the consent of the bhikkhus: “What do you think of this?”
“Bhikkhus, is form permanent or impermanent? “Impermanent, Bhante. “And that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?
“Suffering, Bhante. All this should be stated; this is a question for assent (*anumatipucchā*).
What is a question from a desire to speak (*kathetukamyatāpucchā*)? The Blessed One asks a question because of his desire for the bhikkhus to speak.
“Bhikkhus, there are these four foundations of mindfulness. Which four? … [as above] … Bhikkhus, there are these eight factors of the path.
Which eight?”—this is a question asked out of a desire to speak.
Thus, since among these five types of questions there is no phenomenon whatsoever that has not been seen by the Tathāgata, [he knows them all].

There is no question for the purpose of clarifying what has not yet been seen. Nor is there a question for the purpose of correlating with what has been seen, because even the mental application [thinking], "I shall teach this after comparing it with other wise recluses and brahmins," does not arise.
This is because for the Buddhas, there is no approaching toward or circling around even a single dhamma; [this was already accomplished] at the very seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).

All doubts have been severed; therefore, there is no longer even a question regarding the cutting off of uncertainty. However, two remaining types of questions do exist for Buddhas, among which this is called a "question out of a desire to speak.
8. Now, in order to explain the matter asked about by that question of desire to speak, he said: "Having abandoned the taking of life," and so forth.
In this context, “pāṇātipāta” means the taking away of life (pāṇassa atipāto), the killing of a living being (pāṇavadho), the destruction of a living being (pāṇaghāto).
Here, “living being” (pāṇo) refers conventionally to a sentient being, but in the ultimate sense to the life-faculty (jīvitindriya).

Regarding that living being, “killing of a living being” is the volition of a killer—arising through either the door of body or the door of speech—which, while perceiving that living being as a living being, initiates the effort that cuts off the life-faculty. This [volition] occurs toward those devoid of virtues...
Among animals and other such beings, the offense is slight when the creature is small and grave when the body is large; why is this?

Because of the greatness of the effort (*payoga*). Even when the effort is equal, it is because of the greatness of the object (*vatthu*). Among humans and others who possess virtues, the offense is slight when the being has few virtues and grave when they have great virtues.
However, when there is equality in both physical size and virtue, [the gravity depends on] the defilements (*kilesa*).
It should be understood that [the offense] is of slight censure when the effort is mild, and of great censure when it is intense.
It has five constituent factors: a living being, the perception of it as a living being, the intention to kill, the effort, and death by means of that.

There are six modes of application: by one's own hand, by command, by relinquishing [an object], by remaining stationary, by means of knowledge (*vijjā*), and by means of psychic power (*iddhi*). In this regard...
If this were explained in detail, it would become excessively prolix; therefore, we do not elaborate upon it, nor on other matters of a similar kind.
Those who desire to know the full meaning should consult the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya.
"Having abandoned" means having relinquished this immorality, which consists of the volition of taking life. "Abstaining" refers to the period from the moment it has been abandoned...
From that point on, he is indeed one who abstains from immorality.

By this very method—that there are no phenomena cognizable by the eye or ear which he would transgress, let alone those cognizable by the body—the meaning should be understood in other such passages as well.
"Ascetic" (samaṇa) is a designation given to the Blessed One because his evil has been stilled (samita-pāpa). "Gotama" is by way of his clan. And not only...
The Blessed One himself abstains from taking life, and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus also abstains;
however, the teaching has come down from the beginning in this way. But when explaining the meaning, it is appropriate to explain it by way of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus as well.
"One who has laid aside the rod, one who has laid aside the weapon" means that he does not take up a rod or a weapon for the purpose of harming others.
The meaning is: one who has laid aside the stick and laid aside the weapon.
In this context, with the exception of the staff, all remaining implements should be understood as "weapons" because they have the nature of harming living beings.
However, when monks go about carrying a walking-stick, a tooth-stick, a small adze, or a gimlet, that is not for the purpose of injuring others.
Therefore, he is reckoned as one who has laid aside the rod and laid aside the weapon.
"Conscientious" means endowed with a sense of shame characterized by a loathing for evil. "Compassionate" means having attained a state of loving-kindness (*mettā*).
"Sympathizing with the welfare of all living beings" means being compassionate toward all living beings through their welfare. By virtue of that state of compassion...
The meaning is: one whose mind is intent on the welfare of all living beings. "Dwells" (*viharatīti*) means he moves about, carries on, maintains himself, and protects.

"Thus indeed, monks" (*iti vā hi, bhikkhave*) means "in this way, monks. The word *vā* (or) is stated here in the sense of an alternative (*vikappa*), having regard for what follows later, such as "having abandoned taking what is not given," and so forth;
thus, in every instance, the nature of being an alternative should be understood by regarding either what precedes or what follows.
This, however, is the summary here: Monks, an ordinary person, speaking in praise of the Tathāgata, might say:
"The ascetic Gotama does not kill living beings, nor does he cause them to be killed, nor does he approve of such acts;
he is abstinent from this immorality; oh, how great indeed are the qualities of a Buddha! Having thus made a great effort, he speaks in praise.
"Even though he wishes to speak, he will speak only of what is trifling, insignificant, and merely a matter of conduct and virtue.

He will not be able to speak of the praise based on the state of being uncommon [to others] hereafter. Not only ordinary worldlings, but even stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arahants, and even paccekabuddhas are likewise unable to do so;
only a Tathāgata is able to do it, and I shall explain that to you further."
This concludes the commentary on the meaning with its underlying intention (*sādhippāya*). Hereafter, however, we shall explain only the previously unexplained words.

Regarding the phrase "having abandoned taking what is not given" (*adinnādānaṃ pahāya*): here, "taking what is not given" means the taking of that which has not been given, the seizing of another's property, theft, or robbery.
In this context, "what is not given" refers to that which is possessed by another, over whom another exercises control according to their own will.

One who commits [the act] is not subject to punishment and is blameless. When there is what is possessed by another and one perceives it as such, the volition of theft—which originates from the effort of taking that object—is *adinnādāna* (taking what is not given). This is less blameworthy when the property of another is inferior, and more blameworthy when it is superior; why?
Because of the superiority of the object (*vatthu*). When the object is equal, [the degree of blameworthiness depends on] the property of those possessing greater virtues.

In regard to the object, it is a grave offense. Depending on the specific person who possesses superior qualities, it is a minor offense in regard to an object belonging to one who possesses inferior qualities.
It has five constituent factors: the object being possessed by another, the perception that it is possessed by another, the intention to steal, [the act of taking, and the removal of the object].
"Exertion" means taking [the object] by that means. There are six modes of application—namely, those beginning with "by one's own hand.

These, moreover, proceed according to the following types of misappropriation: misappropriation by theft, misappropriation by force, misappropriation by concealment, misappropriation by scheming, and misappropriation by trickery.
This is the summary here; the detailed exposition, however, is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*.

"One who takes only what is given" (*dinnādāyī*) means one who takes only what has been offered. "One who expects only what is given" (*dinnapāṭikaṅkhī*) means one who even with the mind desires only what has been given.

"Stealth" (*thena*) means taking by stealth; "not by stealth" (*athena*) means not by stealth. "By means of the pure self" (*athenattāya*) means precisely because of being free from stealth, it is pure. "By the self" (*attanā*) means by the personal existence (*attabhāva*).
What is meant is: "Having made his own self pure and free from stealth, he dwells. The remainder is as in the first training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
It should be applied in the same manner as previously stated. And just as it is here, so it is everywhere.
"Unholy life" (*abrahmacariya*) means a non-noble way of life. One who practices the holy (*brahma*), that is, the noble conduct, is a "practitioner of the holy life" (*brahmacārī*).
An "ārācārī" is one who lives far removed from unholiness. Because they are similar by virtue of being overwhelmed by lust, they are called "those engaged in sexual intercourse" (*methunaka*).

Unwholesome practices (*asaddhamma*) are so designated because they are to be indulged in by those who have acquired the conventional designation "sexual intercourse. "Village-dharma" (*gāmadhamma*) refers to the practices of village-dwellers.
9. "Having abandoned false speech": here, "false" (*musa*) refers to either a verbal or bodily exertion that destroys one's purpose when preceded by the intent to deceive;
or, it is the volition (*cetanā*) that, with the intention to deceive, originates a bodily or verbal exertion intended to mislead another. This is false speech (*musāvāda*).
Another method: “False” (*musā*) refers to a matter that is unreal and untrue. “Speech” (*vāda*) refers to the communication of that [matter] as real and true.

By way of its characteristic, however, false speech is the volition that originates the act of communicating a matter that is not so as being so, by one who desires to make another understand it as such.
Regarding the object [of the speech], it is less blameworthy when that object is small, and more blameworthy when it is great.
Moreover, for householders, a statement such as "I have nothing," uttered out of a lack of desire to give away what belongs to them, is slightly blameworthy;
whereas one uttered by acting as a witness for the purpose of destroying another's case is greatly blameworthy.

For those who have gone forth, even having obtained a small amount of oil or ghee, to speak with a sense of humor in the manner of an exaggeration—saying, "Today in the village the oil flows like a river"—is [greatly blameworthy].
For those who speak according to the method of saying "what was not seen was indeed seen" and so forth, it is a grave offense (*mahāsāvajja*).
It has four constituent factors (*sambhāra*): an untrue basis, the intention to deceive, the corresponding effort, and another’s understanding of that meaning.
There is a single mode of application (*payoga*), which is exclusively by means of one's own hand; [this is done] either by body, by what is connected to the body, or by speech.
Or it should be understood as the act of deceiving another.
If the other person understands that matter through that act, this volition that originates the act is bound by the kamma of false speech at that very moment.
For just as one deceives another by means of body or speech connected to the body, so too [one deceives] by saying, "Speak this to him."

This includes one who has something sent by means of a letter, one who places it before [the recipient] after writing a note, or one who writes "this matter should be understood in this way" on a wall or similar surface and leaves it there.
Therefore, in this case, the modes of action involving commissioning another (*āṇattika*), relinquishing (*nissaggiya*), and fixed objects (*thāvara*) are applicable;
however, since they have not been mentioned in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), they should be accepted only after careful investigation.
One who speaks the truth is a "truth-speaker" (*saccavādī*). One who joins truth with truth, unites it with truth, is a "truth-uniter" (*saccasaṃdho*);

the meaning is that he does not speak falsehood from time to time. For a person who sometimes speaks falsehood and sometimes the truth, his truth is not joined with truth because it is interrupted by false speech;
therefore, such a person is not a truth-uniter. But this one is not like that.
"Truth-firm" (*saccasaṃdha*) means that even for the sake of life one does not speak falsely, but rather adheres to truth with truth.
"Firm" (*theta*) means stable; the meaning is one whose speech is stable.

For one person is not of stable speech—like turmeric dye, like a wooden stake driven into a heap of chaff, or like a gourd placed on the back of a horse—whereas another is like a line carved in stone.
He is firm in speech like a city gatepost; even when his head is being cut off with a sword, he does not utter two different words. This is called "steadfast" (*theto*).
"Trustworthy" (*paccayiko*) means one who is to be trusted, whose word is to be believed.
For some individuals are not trustworthy; when it is said, "Who said this? It was so-and-so," they are subject to being told, "Do not believe his word."
He becomes one who relies on others. When it is said, "By whom was this spoken?
By so-and-so," he falls into the state of saying, "If it was spoken by him, then that alone is the authority; there is nothing further to be examined; it is exactly thus.
This is called being one who relies on others. "One who does not deceive the world" means that by virtue of his truthfulness, he does not deceive the world.

Regarding the phrases "having abandoned malicious speech" (*pisuṇaṃ vācaṃ pahāya*) and so forth: that speech by which, when one speaks it to someone, it creates a sense of intimacy in one's own heart while making the other person feel empty—that is malicious speech.
That speech by which one makes both oneself and another harsh, or which is itself harsh, neither pleasant to the ear nor reaching the heart—that is harsh speech.
That by which one prattles nonsense, which is meaningless, is idle chatter (*samphappalāpa*).
The volition that is their root also receives the name "slanderous speech" (*pisuṇavācā*) and so forth; and it is precisely this [volition] that is intended here.
In this context, slanderous speech is the volition that, arising from a defiled mind, instigates bodily or verbal effort for the purpose of dividing others or out of a desire for one's own favor.
That [volition] is less blameworthy when the person whom it divides has few virtues, and more blameworthy when that person has great virtues.
Its four constituent factors are: another person who is to be divided;

either the intention to cause division, thinking, "In this way they will become separate, they will be parted," or the desire for affection, thinking, "In this way I will become beloved and trustworthy";
the corresponding effort; and the recognition of that purpose. "For the sake of dividing these" means: in the presence of those who were referred to by the word "these."
He hears [words] for the purpose of dividing them;

or he reconciles those who are divided—meaning that having approached each one individually of two friends, or of those who share the same preceptor and so forth, who have become estranged for some reason, he says: "For you, born into such families and so learned..."

Having said such things as "it is not fitting," one who performs reconciliation (*sandhāna*) and subsequent repair (*anukatta*). "From the granting of gifts" (*anuppadātā*) means one who grants gifts for the sake of reconciliation (*sandhānānuppadātā*). The meaning is:
seeing two people in harmony, one who performs strengthening by saying, "For those born in such a family and endowed with such virtues, this is appropriate," and so forth.
One whose pleasure grove (*ārāma*) is harmonious is "one whose pleasure grove is harmonious" (*samaggārāmo*).
The meaning is that he does not even wish to dwell where there is no harmony. There is also a textual reading *samaggarāmo*, which has this very same meaning.
*Samaggarato* means "delighting in harmony"; the meaning is that he does not wish to go elsewhere, having abandoned them.
He rejoices upon seeing or hearing of harmony, thus he is "one who delights in harmony" (*samagganandī*). Or, he is one who speaks words that create harmony (*samaggakaraṇiṃ vācaṃ bhāsati*).
Whatever speech brings beings into harmony, that speech he utters which illuminates the quality of concord, and not the other kind.
Harsh speech is an exclusively cruel volition that gives rise to bodily and verbal applications which cut into the vital parts of another.
To illustrate this, there is the following account: it is said that a certain boy, disregarding his mother’s words, went into the forest.
His mother, unable to turn him back, cursed him, saying, "May that fierce female buffalo pursue you!
Then, right there in the forest, a female buffalo rose up before him. The boy made a declaration of truth: "May that which my mother spoke with her mouth not come to pass;
may that which she thought in her heart come to pass. At that very spot, the buffalo stood as if bound fast.
He stood there. Thus, even an action that cuts the vitals does not become harsh speech because of the gentleness of the mind.

For parents sometimes say to their children, "May robbers cut you into pieces," yet they do not wish for even a single lotus leaf to fall upon them. And teachers and preceptors sometimes say to their dependents:
—“Why do these shameless and fearless ones wander? Expel them! And yet they desire their success in learning and realization.
Just as harsh speech does not occur because of gentleness of mind, so too non-harsh speech does not occur because of gentleness of speech.
For one who wishes to have someone killed, the words “Let this person sleep comfortably” are certainly not non-harsh speech.
It exists as speech; however, because of its harshness of mind, it is indeed harsh speech.
It is less blameworthy when directed toward one of little virtue, and more blameworthy when directed toward one of great virtue. Its three constituent factors are:
another person who may be reviled, a mind of anger, and the act of reviling itself.
*Neḷā*: *Ela* is said to mean fault (*dosa*); that which has no *ela* is *neḷa*, meaning "faultless.

It is like the word *neḷa* used in the phrase, "The white-canopied chariot with faultless wheels" (*nelaṅgo setapacchādo*). *Ear-pleasing* (*kaṇṇasukhā*): Because of the sweetness of its phrasing (*byañjana*), it is pleasant to the ears;
it does not produce earache, as if pierced by a needle. Because of the sweetness of its meaning (*attha*), it generates affection rather than irritation throughout the entire body.
It is "pleasing" (*pemanīyā*). It is "heart-reaching" (*hadayaṅgamā*) because it reaches the heart, entering the mind with ease without being obstructed.
It is "urbane" (*porī*) because it exists in the city due to its perfection of qualities; it is also called "urbane" because it is as refined as a woman raised in the city.

Alternatively, it is "urbane" because it belongs to the city (*purassa esā*). The meaning is "the speech of city-dwellers," for city-dwellers indeed possess appropriate speech. This much is the measure.
They call one who is a father "father," they call one who is merely a brother "brother," and they call one who is merely a maternal uncle "maternal uncle.
Such talk is "dear to many people" (*bahujanakantā*). Because it is dear, it is "pleasing to many people" (*bahujanamanāpā*), meaning it is agreeable to many and increases their mental well-being.
Idle chatter (*samphappalāpa*) is unwholesome volition that manifests as useless talk and gives rise to bodily and verbal exertion. Due to its weakness in repetition (*āsevanamandatāya*), it...

It is slightly blameworthy, yet becomes greatly blameworthy due to the magnitude of its habitual practice. It has two constituent factors: a preoccupation with useless talk such as the Mahābhārata war or the abduction of Sītā, and the actual telling of such stories.

One who speaks at the proper time is called a "speaker at the right time" (kālavādī); the meaning is that he speaks after having observed the appropriate occasion for what ought to be said. That which is real is "suchness" (tathaṃ).
He speaks only that which is true to its own nature; thus, he is a speaker of truth (*bhūtavādī*). He speaks only by relying on what is beneficial for both the present life and the future life;
thus, he is a speaker of the good (*atthavādī*). He speaks by relying on the nine supramundane states (*dhamma*); thus, he is a speaker of the Dhamma (*dhammavādī*).
He speaks by relying on the discipline of restraint and the discipline of abandoning; thus, he is a speaker of the Vinaya (*vinayavādī*).
“Nidhāna” means a place for depositing; thus, “nidhānavatī” means one who possesses such a place. The meaning is: she speaks words that are worthy of being deposited in the heart.
“At the proper time” means that even while speaking such words, she does not speak at an improper time with the thought, “I shall speak words worthy of being deposited”;
rather, the meaning is that she speaks only after considering the appropriate occasion. “With a reason” (sāpadesaṃ).
"With a simile" means with a reason. "With a limit" means he speaks in such a way that its limit is made known by showing its boundary.
"Connected with the goal" means he speaks in a manner endowed with meaning because it cannot be exhausted even when analyzed through many methods;
or rather, by that very meaning which he, as a speaker of the goal, expresses.
Because he is composed, he speaks speech that is meaningful; it is said that he does not set aside one thing and speak another.

10. "The destruction of seed-life and plant-life" refers to the fivefold class of seed-life—namely, root-seeds, stem-seeds, joint-seeds, crown-seeds, and seeds from seeds—as well as any class of plant-life such as green grass, trees, and so forth.
The meaning is: one who abstains from the disturbance [of living beings] by means of undertaking activities such as cutting, splitting, and cooking.
"One who eats but one meal" refers to two meals: the morning meal (*pātarāsa-bhatta*) and the evening meal (*sāyamāsa-bhatta*).
Of these, the morning meal is delimited by the middle of the day; the other is from after midday until before dawn. Therefore, within the middle of the day...
Even if he eats eight times a day, he remains a "one-meal-eater" (*ekabhattika*). It is with reference to this that it is said, "a one-meal-eater. Eating at night is "night";
one who abstains from that is "abstaining from night" (*rattūparata*). Eating after midday until the setting of the sun is called "untimely eating" (*vikālabhojana*).
Because of his abstinence from that, he is "abstaining from untimely eating. When did he abstain? On the bank of the river Anomā.
From the day of one’s going forth [into homelessness].
Because it is not in conformity with the Teaching (*sāsana*), "visūkadassana" means a sight that is a spectacle and an obstacle.

It refers to dances, songs, and instrumental music—whether performed by oneself through dancing or causing others to dance, and so on, or even those occurring as the dancing of peacocks and the like—which have become mere spectacles.
"And spectacles" refers to watching dancing, singing, instrumental music, and performances.
Indeed, for neither monks nor nuns is it permissible to perform dances and so forth themselves, to have others perform them, or even to watch them when performed by others.
Regarding "garlands" and so on: "garland" means any kind of flower; "scent" means any kind of fragrant substance; "unguent" means that which colors the skin.
In this context, "wearing" means to put on; "adorned" means to fill out deficiencies;
and "decorated" means to take pleasure in them by way of fragrance and the coloring of the skin. "Place" (ṭhāna) refers to the cause. Therefore, the meaning is:
one who abstains from that unvirtuous volition (*dussīlya-cetanā*) by which the great multitude performs those acts such as wearing garlands and so forth.
"High bed" refers to one that exceeds the prescribed measure. "Large bed" refers to an unworthy covering. "Abstaining from these" is the meaning. "Jātarūpa" means gold.
"Rajata" refers to those things that enter into commerce, such as the kahāpaṇa coin, the copper māsaka, the lac māsaka, and the wooden māsaka.
He abstains from the acceptance of both of these; he neither acquires them nor accepts them.
The meaning is: he does not cause [them] to be acquired, nor does he consent to what has been set aside.
Regarding "the acceptance of raw grain": this refers to the acceptance of all seven kinds of raw grain, namely, rice, paddy, barley, wheat, millet, panicled millet, and kudrūsa grass.
And it is not only the acceptance of these that is forbidden for monks; even the touching of them is prohibited.

It is indeed not permissible. Regarding "accepting raw meat": here, for monks, the acceptance of raw meat and fish—except when specifically permitted—is not allowed; however, the mere touching of them is not forbidden.

Regarding "accepting women or girls": here, a "woman" refers to one who has entered into marriage with a man, while the other is called a "girl"; the acceptance of either, as well as the touching of them, is likewise unallowable.

Regarding "accepting female and male slaves": here, their acceptance specifically as female and male slaves is not permitted. However, it is permitted if one says, "I give [this] as a kitchen worker," or "I give [this] as a monastery attendant.
As for the items beginning with goats and sheep and ending with fields and land, the method for determining what is allowable and what is unallowable should be examined according to the Vinaya.
In that context, a "field" (khetta) is that in which grain crops grow; a "site" (vatthu) is that in which other crops grow.
Alternatively, that wherein both [seed and soil] flourish is a field (*khetta*). A plot of ground prepared for that purpose is a site (*vatthu*).
Here, by way of the terms "field" and "site," planted ponds and the like are also included.
"Messengership" (*dūteyya*) refers to the work of a messenger; it means taking a letter or a message sent by householders and [delivering it] there.
In this context, "going" refers to the minor journey of one sent from house to house; "errand" (pahiṇagamana) is said to be that same minor journey.
"Service" (anuyoga) means performing both of those tasks. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as "service consisting of errands and journeys.
"Buying and selling" means both buying and selling. Regarding "fraudulent scales" and so forth, "fraud" (kūṭa) means deception. Among these, "fraudulent scales" is...
There are four kinds of cheating: cheating by name, cheating by form, cheating by the measure, and cheating by concealment.
Among these, "cheating by form" means making two scales equal in appearance, taking with the larger one when receiving, and giving with the smaller one when giving.
"Cheating by the measure" means that when receiving, one presses down on the scale with the hand at the rear part, and when giving, one does so at the front part.
Regarding "the deception of taking" (*gahaṇakūṭa*): when taking, one takes the rope at the base; when giving, one holds it at the tip.
Regarding "the deception of concealment" (*paṭicchannakūṭa*): having made a scale hollow and filled it inside with iron filings, when taking, one places it at the rear;
when giving, one places it at the front. "Kaṃsa" refers to a golden bowl; deception by means of that is "the deception of the golden bowl" (*kaṃsakūṭa*). How so? Having made one golden bowl...
He made two or three other iron bowls appear as if they were made of gold;
then, having gone to the countryside and entered some wealthy household, he said, “Buy these golden vessels. When asked their price, they wished to give a higher price.
Then, when they asked, “How can it be known that these are gold? he replied, “After testing them...”
"Take it! Having thus struck the golden bowl against the stone and given away all the bowls, he departs.

There are three kinds of cheating with measures (*mānakūṭa*): by breaking the heart, by breaking the crest, and by breaking the cord. Among these, "breaking the heart" occurs at the time of measuring ghee, oil, and so forth.
For one who takes those [liquids] using a measure with a hole at the bottom—[saying], "Slowly..."
Having said, “Pour it out,” he takes it after causing much [liquid] to flow into the inner vessel; the giver, having closed the opening, gives it quickly, filling it completely.

The "breaking of the crest" occurs at the time of measuring sesame, rice, and so forth. For when taking those, one takes them by slowly raising a crest; when giving, one gives by filling it swiftly while cutting off the crest.
The "breaking of the measuring line" occurs at the time of measuring fields and land. For those who do not receive a bribe measure even a small field as large;

those who do receive a bribe, however, measure it as larger than it actually is. Regarding "opening up again" (*ukkoṭana*) and so forth: "opening up again" means taking a bribe in order to make one who is not the owner the owner.
"Deception" (*vañcana*) means deceiving others by various means. In this regard, there is this story: it is said that a certain hunter [caught] both a deer and a fawn...
Having taken it, he was returning when a certain rogue said to him: "Sir, what is the deer worth? What is the fawn worth?

When he replied, "The deer is worth two kahāpaṇas; the fawn is worth one," the rogue gave him one kahāpaṇa, took the fawn, and after going a short distance, turned back and said: "Sir, I have no need for the fawn; give me the deer."
He said, "In that case, give me two kahāpaṇas. He replied, "But, sir, did you not already give me one kahāpaṇa?
"Yes, it was given. "Take this young fawn; thus there will be two kahāpaṇas—one kahāpaṇa and this young fawn, which is worth a kahāpaṇa.
Perceiving that he was speaking with reason, [he took] the young fawn.

"Having taken [it], he gave it to the deer. "Deceit" (*nikati*) means deception by means of a trick (*yoga*) or by means of illusion (*māyā*), such as making a garland-ornament appear as a garland-ornament, a non-jewel appear as a jewel, or non-gold appear as gold;
it is deception by means of a counterfeit. "Crooked application" (*sāciyoga*) means crooked practice;
this is a name for those very things, such as extortion and so forth. Therefore: "extortion and crooked application," "deception and crooked application," and "deceit and crooked application."
The meaning here should be understood in this way. Some say that "crooked practice" (*sāciyoga*) refers to the substitution of one thing for another after showing something else;
however, that is already included under "deception.
Regarding "cutting" and so forth: "cutting" refers to the cutting off of hands and the like; "killing" refers to slaughter; "binding" refers to binding with ropes and the like.
Bondage. "Robbery" (*viparāmosa*) is of two kinds: snow-robbery (*himaviparāmosa*) and thicket-robbery (*gumbaviparāmosa*).
That which consists in plundering people traveling on a road who have been concealed by snow at the time of a snowfall is snow-robbery.
That which consists in plundering those who have been concealed by thickets and the like is thicket-robbery. "Plunder" (*ālopa*) refers to [the seizure of] villages, market towns, and so forth.
“An instrument of plunder. “Violence” means a rash act. It is the seizing of desired goods after entering a house and placing a weapon upon people’s chests.
Thus, monks, an ordinary person, when speaking in praise of the Tathāgata, might say: “The ascetic Gotama abstains from this kind of cutting...
[and so on] ...from violence. It is in this way, monks, that an ordinary person might speak in praise of the Tathāgata.
To this extent, the *Cūḷasīla* (Shorter Section on Virtue) is completed.
Now, in expanding upon the *Majjhimasīla* (Intermediate Section on Virtue), he says: "Or, as some venerable sirs... and so forth. Herein, this is the commentary on the words not previously explained.
“Gifts given out of faith” means those given having placed one’s trust in karma, its fruit, this world, and the world beyond.
The meaning is that they are not given with the thought, “This person is my relative,” or “He is my friend,” or “He will repay me for this,” or “He has done this for me before.
For gifts given in such a manner are not called “gifts given out of faith. “Meals” is merely a heading for the teaching.
In terms of meaning, however, all this has already been stated: having eaten meals given out of faith, having put on robes, having used lodgings, and having consumed medicines for the sick.
*Seyyathidaṃ* is a particle; its meaning is: "What is that seed-life and vegetation-life, the destruction of which they are devoted to?"
"They dwell" means: showing that, he said "root-seed," and so forth.
Therein, "root-seed" refers to turmeric, ginger, *vacā*, *vacatta*, *ativisa*, *kaṭukarohiṇī*, *usīra*, *bhaddamuttaka*, and so on.
"Stem-seed" refers to the *assattha*, the *nigrodha*, the *pilakkha*, the *udumbara*, the *kacchaka*, and the *kapittha*.
And so forth. "Fruit-seed" (*phalabīja*) refers to sugarcane, *naḷa* reeds, bamboo, and so on.
"Apex-seed" (*aggabīja*) refers to *ajjaka*, *phaṇijjaka*, *hirivera*, and so on. "Seed-of-seeds" (*bījabīja*) refers to paddy, legumes, and so on.
All of these, when separated from the tree and capable of growing, are called "the class of seeds" (*bījagāma*). However, that which is not separated from the tree and is not withered—

“Bhūtagāma” (a collection of living beings) is what is said. In this context, it should be understood that the destruction of a collection of living beings is an offense entailing expiation (*pācittiya*), whereas the destruction of a collection of seeds is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). 12.
Regarding “use of what has been stored”: this refers to the use of something that has been kept in storage. In this regard, there are two types of explanations, according to the Vinaya.

[This applies] both by way of the rule of discipline (*vinaya*) and by way of austerity (*sallekha*). First, by way of the rule of discipline: whatever food has been received today becomes "stored" (*sannidhikāraka*) by the following day;
if one consumes it, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
However, having given what one has received oneself to novices (*sāmaṇera*), it is permissible to eat on the second day after they have set it aside; yet, in this case, there is no austerity.

The same principle applies to the storage of drinks (*pāna-sannidhi*). In this context, "drink" refers to the eight kinds of drinks, beginning with mango juice, as well as those that are compatible with them; their detailed classification is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*.

Regarding the storage of robes (*vattha-sannidhi*), when a robe is neither formally resolved upon (*an-adhiṭṭhita*) nor assigned for use (*a-vikappita*), it constitutes storage and brings about a loss of austerity (*sallekha*);
this is the figurative explanation. However, in the literal sense, one should be content with the three robes (*ticīvara*); a fourth...

Having received it, one must give it to another. If one is unable to give it to anyone at all, but wishes to give it to someone who has gone for the purpose of receiving a recitation or for the purpose of inquiry, it must be given as soon as that person returns; it is not permitted not to give it.

However, if robes are insufficient, it is permitted to set aside a period of time authorized by the expectation of further acquisitions. [This applies] to those who work with needles, thread, and robes.
If it cannot be obtained, it is permissible to set it aside after performing a formal act of the Vinaya (vinayakamma).

However, it is not permissible to set it aside thinking, "Now that this one is worn out, where else shall I find such another? For in doing so, there is accumulation (sannidhi), and it violates the austerity of spiritual refinement (sallekha).
Regarding the accumulation of vehicles: a vehicle is defined as a draft-ox cart, a chariot, a wagon, a carriage, a palanquin, or a litter.
This is not a vehicle for one who has gone forth. However, sandals are indeed a vehicle for one who has gone forth.
For a single bhikkhu, one pair is permitted for traveling in the forest and one for washing the feet; at the most, two sets of sandals are allowed.
If a third is obtained, it must be given to another. One should not keep them [thinking], "When this one is worn out, where will I get another?"
It is permissible, provided there is storage and it does not cause the destruction of austerity.
Regarding "bedding" in the context of "storage of bedding": a bed is a couch. For a single bhikkhu, up to two couches are permitted—one in a private room and one in the daytime quarters.
If more than that is obtained, it must be given to another bhikkhu or to a group.
It is not permissible to keep [medicines] for oneself. Furthermore, this constitutes storing them up and violates the practice of effacement (*sallekha*).
Regarding the storage of medicinal scents: when a monk suffers from ailments such as skin eruptions, itch, or skin diseases, the use of scents is permitted.
Having had those scents brought in, once that illness has subsided, they should be given to others who are ill, or used for purposes such as fumigating the five-finger marks at the gate.

Or they should be brought [to him]. However, it is not permissible to set them aside thinking, "They will be useful when there is illness again," for that constitutes hoarding and violates the practice of effacement (*sallekha*).
By "worldly goods" (*āmisa*), one should understand what remains after what has been mentioned. For example, here a certain bhikkhu, at such a time—
Thinking, "This will be of benefit," he had sesame, rice, mung beans, peas, salt, fish, meat, dried meat, ghee, oil, sugar, vessels, and other such items brought and set aside.

During the rainy season, having had rice-gruel prepared by the novices early in the morning and having eaten it himself, he said, "Novice, it is difficult to enter the village because of the water and mud; go to such-and-such a family and [inform] me..."
He sent word, saying: "Inform him that he is seated in the monastery; fetch curds and other provisions from such-and-such a family.
Even when the monks asked, "Venerable sir, will you enter the village?", he replied, "Friends, it is difficult to enter the village now.
They said, "Very well, venerable sir; you stay here, and we shall go and seek almsfood," and so they departed.
Then the novice, having brought curds and other items and prepared the meal and its condiments, brings them forward;
even as he is eating that, his attendants send more food, and from that too he eats what is most agreeable.
Then the monks arrive bringing almsfood, and from that too he eats only what is most agreeable and neck-deep.
In this way, he passes even four months [in such accumulation]. This is called: "The bhikkhu lives the life of a shaven householder, not the life of a recluse.
Such is what is known as the storage of material goods (āmisasannidhi).
Furthermore, in the dwelling place of a bhikkhu, there might be a single measure of rice, a single lump of sugar, and a quarter-measure of ghee.
It is permissible to store this much for the sake of thieves who might arrive unexpectedly;
for if they did not receive even this much hospitality of food, they might deprive one of life. Therefore, if this much is not available, it is permissible to have it brought and stored.
And during times of discomfort, whatever here is allowable (*kappiya*) may be used by oneself as well. [In the] *kappiya-kuti*...
However, even for one who sets aside much, there is no such thing as "storing up" (sannidhi). For the Tathāgata, however, there is nothing whatsoever—
whether a handful of rice or a mere four-finger-breadth of cloth— that has been set aside with the thought, "This shall be mine today or tomorrow."
13. Regarding "spectacles": as for "dancing," whatever kind of dancing it may be, it is not permitted to watch it even while walking along the road by craning one's neck.
Furthermore, the detailed analysis here should be understood according to the method stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*.
And just as it is here, so it is with all the passages in the Suttas connected with the training rules (*sikkhāpada*). Hereafter—
Without saying even this much, we shall describe only the purpose [of each] here and there.
They watch a theatrical performance (*naṭasamajja*). A recitation (*akkhāna*) refers to the *Bhārata* war and so forth;
it is not even permissible to go to the place where such a thing is being told. A *pāṇissara* is a gong (*kaṃsatāḷa*); some also call it a hand-clapper (*pāṇitāḷa*). A *vetāḷa*...
Some say that *ghanatāḷaṃ* refers to the raising of a dead body by means of a spell (*manta*). *Kumbhathūṇaṃ* is a square drum made of leather;
some also say it is the sound of a water-jar (*kumbha-sadda*). *Sobhanakaṃ* is the scattering [of flowers] by actors, or that which makes beautiful;
what is meant is a "splendid display. *Caṇḍālaṃ* is the game of iron balls; they also say it is the game of winnowing baskets played by *caṇḍālas*. *Vaṃsaṃ*...
“Playing after raising up a bamboo pole.
Regarding “washing”: it is the washing of bones. It is said that in certain regions, when a relative has died, they do not cremate them but bury them.
Then, having recognized that their bodies have become putrid, they exhume them, wash the bones, and [dispose of them].

They smear [the bones] with perfumes and set them out. At the time of a festival, having placed the bones in one spot and liquor and such in another, they drink the liquor while weeping and lamenting. And this has been said:
"Monks, there is among the people of the Southern Countries what is called the 'washing of the bones'; there, there is both food and drink."
“Whether it be food to be chewed, food to be swallowed, food to be tasted, or food to be drunk; whether it be dancing, singing, or instrumental music—this, monks, exists;
I say this is not non-existent. However, some say that the washing of bones with a net of illusions is also a form of washing.
In elephant battles and the like, a monk must neither fight with elephants and such creatures himself, nor cause them to fight.
It is not proper to watch them fighting. *Nibbuddha* means wrestling (*mallayuddha*). *Uyyodhika* refers to where a clash is seen.
*Balagga* is the place for counting the troops. *Senābyūha* is the array of the army; it is the deployment of the army by way of the wagon-array (*sakaṭabyūha*) and so forth.
*Anīkadassana* is according to the method beginning with: "Three elephants constitute the rear elephant division," and so on.
The viewing of the arrayed troops. 14.

That wherein negligence stands is a ground for negligence (*pamādaṭṭhāna*). It is both gambling and a ground for negligence, thus it is a "ground for negligence consisting of gambling" (*jūtappamādaṭṭhāna*).
Since there are eight squares in each row, it is called "eight-squares" (*aṭṭhapada*); the same method applies to the "ten-squares" (*dasapada*) as well. "Space" (*ākāsa*)...
It is a game played in the air itself, like the games of *aṭṭhapada* and *dasapada*. *Parihārapatha*:
having made various circular paths on the ground, one must move about therein; it is a game for those moving along the paths. *Santikā*: the game of *santikā*.
Pieces of wood or pebbles placed together are moved away and brought back by the fingernail alone, without shaking them.
And if anything moves there, it is a defeat; this is a designation for such a game.
*Khalika* refers to playing with dice on a gaming board. *Ghaṭikā* is said to be a game played by striking a short stick with a long stick.
*Salākahattha* refers to moistening the hand with lac, madder, or flour-water, and then...
"Kiṃ hotu" refers to the game of striking the ground or a wall to produce the appearance of elephants, horses, and so forth.
"Akkhā" refers to the game of marbles. "Paṅgacīraṃ" means a leaf-blade; they play by blowing through it.
"Vaṅkakaṃ" refers to a small plough used as a toy by village children. "Mokkhacikā" refers to the game of tumbling over.
It means playing by turning [objects] upside down, either by taking a stick in the air or by placing one’s head on the ground.
A *ciṅgulika* is called a spinning wheel made of palm leaves and the like that revolves through the force of the wind.
A *pattāḷhaka* is called a leaf-tube; people play by measuring sand and such things with it. A *rathaka* is a small chariot.
*Dhanukanti* refers simply to a small bow. *Akkharikā* is said to be a game for guessing letters either in the air or on the back [of one's hand].
*Manesikā* is a game for knowing what has been thought by means of the mind.
*Yathāvajjaṃ* is a game of showing [something] by employing whatever defect there may be—such as being one-eyed, having a withered arm, or being hunchbacked.

15. *Āsandi* refers to a high seat that exceeds the prescribed measure. The word is put in the accusative case in all instances because it is dependent on the phrase *anuyuttā viharanti* (they dwell devotedly).
A *pallaṅka* is one made by placing animal figures on the legs. A *gonaka* is a large woolen rug with long hair;
it is said that its wool is more than four finger-breadths in length. A *cittaka* is a woolen covering decorated with various woven patterns.
*Paṭika* is a white woolen covering. *Paṭalika* is a thick, flowered woolen covering;
it is also called an "āmalaka-leaf" [cover]. *Tūlika* is a stuffed cover filled with one of three types of cotton-down.
*Vikatika* is a woolen covering variegated with the forms of lions, tigers, and so forth. *Uddalomi* is a woolen covering with fringes on both sides; some call it "single-sided upraised-flower."
They say: "Ekantalomi" refers to a woolen rug with hair on one side only.
Some say it is "ubhatouggatapuppha. "Kaṭṭissa" is a silk rug inlaid with jewels.
"Koseyya" is likewise a silk rug inlaid with jewels; however, a plain silk rug is also permitted.

This is stated in the Vinaya. However, in the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*, it is said: "With the exception of the *tūlikā* (down mattress), all [other types] such as the *gonaka* (wool blanket) and so forth, even if sewn with jewels, are not permitted.
*Kuttaka* refers to a woolen spread suitable for sixteen dancing girls to stand upon and perform a dance. *Hatthattharaṃ* (elephant-spread).
"Spreadings for horses" refers specifically to the rugs used as coverings on the backs of elephants and horses. The same principle applies to "chariot-spreadings.
"Antelope-skin mats" refers to mats made by sewing together antelope skins to the size of a bed. "Exquisite spreadings of kadali-deer skin":
there is indeed such a thing as a kadali-deer skin, and an exquisite spreading made from it means a superior, high-quality spread.
The meaning is this: it is said that they make it by spreading out a panther skin over a white cloth, sewing it together.
"With a canopy above" (*sauttaracchadaṃ*) means together with a red canopy (*vitāna*) tied above;
even a white canopy is not permitted if there is an improper rug beneath it, but it is permitted if there is none. "With red pillow-cases on both sides" (*ubhatolohitakūpadhānaṃ*).
A pillow for the head and a pillow for the feet—meaning a pair of red pillows at both ends of a bed—is not allowable.
However, if there is only one pillow that is red on both sides, or has the color of a lotus, or is variegated, it is permissible provided it is of the proper measure.
But a large pillow is prohibited. Two pillows that are not red are also permitted.
These are indeed permissible. Having obtained more than that, they should be given to others.

If one is unable to give them away, one may even lie down after spreading them crosswise on a bed and placing a coverlet over them. However, regarding high chairs (*āsandi*) and the like, one should proceed according to the method already stated.
For it has been said: "Monks, I allow you to cut off the legs of a high chair and then use it."
“Having torn apart the hair-ornaments of the couch, one may use them; having unraveled the cotton stuffing, one may make a bolster;
and the remainder may be made into a floor-covering. 16.
Regarding the anointing and so forth: the body odor of children who have emerged from their mother’s womb [is such that] at the time they reach twelve years of age—
When [the child] has passed away, they rub the body with scented powders and the like in order to remove the foul odor from the corpse;

such rubbing is not permitted. However, when they place virtuous children on their laps, anoint them with oil, and massage them for the purpose of developing the symmetry of the hands, feet, thighs, navel, and so forth—such massaging is not permitted.
"Bathing" means bathing those very children with perfumes and other such substances.

"Massaging" means increasing the bulk of the arms by striking the hands and feet with clubs and similar implements, as is done by great wrestlers. "A mirror" means that it is not permitted to carry any kind of mirror.
"Collyrium" refers specifically to decorative collyrium. "Garland" means either a woven garland or one that is unwoven. "Ointment" means...
Whatever makes for the coloring of the skin: facial powder and facial ointment. They give clay-based paste for the purpose of removing black spots and the like on the face;
when the blood has been stirred up by that, they give mustard-seed paste; when the affliction has been consumed by that, they give sesame paste;
when the blood has settled by that, they give turmeric paste; and when the complexion of the skin has been restored by that, [they apply] facial powder.
They powder their faces; all of that is not permitted.
Regarding hand-bands and the like: they wander about having bound various conch shells, skull-cups, and so forth to their hands; whether those or any other hand-ornaments, none are permitted.
Others wander about with their hair tied in topknots, [adorned] with golden leaf-patterns, pearl necklaces, and the like.
And they surround him; all of that is improper. Others wander about carrying a four-cubit staff or some other decorated staff.
Likewise, others have a medicine tube adorned with various figures of women, men, and so forth, well-surrounded and slung over their left side.
Others carry a sheath encrusted with gems and gold, which is not sharp.
A sword; a parasol adorned with five-colored threads and variegated with makara-teeth and other motifs;
sandals variegated with gold, silver, and the like, and fringed with peacock feathers;
