some, showing a hairline four finger-breadths wide and a span in length, bind a turban-band upon the forehead like a flash of lightning from a cloud's mouth, and they wear a crest-jewel.
Holding yak-tail fans (*cāmara-vāla-bījanī*)—all of that is not permitted.
17. Because it does not lead to the paths of heaven or liberation, it is called "animal talk" (*tiracchānakathā*).
Regarding that, [talk] concerning kings occurs in such a manner as: "Mahāsammata, Mandhātā, Dhammāsoka—such was their great majesty," and so forth.

"Talk" refers to talk about kings. This same principle applies to talk about thieves and so forth. Among these, talk such as "that king is handsome and beautiful to behold" is merely worldly talk and constitutes "animal talk" (*tiracchānakathā*).

However, talk that proceeds in the manner of "even he, who possessed such great power, has come to destruction," remains within the state of being a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). Regarding thieves, [talk such as] "Mūladeva was so powerful, or Meghamāla... [is likewise].
"Such great power he has"—speaking thus of their deeds with the thought, "Oh, what heroes!"—is merely talk about houses; it is frivolous talk (*tiracchānakathā*).

Even regarding battles such as the *Bhārata* war, to speak of how one was killed by another or how one was pierced, motivated solely by a craving for sensual pleasure (*kāmasādavasena*), is frivolous talk.
But when such talk proceeds with the thought, "Even they have indeed reached destruction," it is in every case simply a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).

...it exists. Furthermore, it is not proper to speak of food and so forth with a sense of sensual gratification (*kāmasāda*), saying, "We ate and consumed such food as was thus endowed with color, fragrance, flavor, and texture.
However, having performed it for a purposeful end, one may say:
"In the past, we gave to those possessed of virtue—and at the *cetiya*—food, drink, clothing, bedding, garlands, and perfumes that were thus endowed with color and the rest."

It is permissible to say, "We shall perform an offering. However, in conversations regarding relatives and the like, it is not permissible to speak out of a sense of attachment, such as saying, "Our relatives are brave and capable," or "In the past, we used to travel about in such various vehicles.
But if one speaks for a purposeful reason, it is permissible to say, "Those relatives of ours have also passed away," or "In the past, we wore such sandals..."

It is permissible to say, "We have given it to the Saṅgha. However, talk about villages—whether concerning their being well-situated or poorly situated, having plenty of food or a scarcity of food, and so forth—or saying, "The inhabitants of such-and-such a village are brave and capable," is not permissible when done out of a sense of gratification (*assāda*).

But if it is spoken for a beneficial purpose (*sātthaka*), it is permissible to say, "They are faithful and confident," or "They have reached destruction and decline. The same principle applies to talk concerning towns, cities, districts, and so on.

Talk about women is not appropriate when based on their complexion, shape, and so forth, in the sense of relishing them; it is only appropriate in the sense that "she was faithful, confident, and has passed away.
Talk about heroes is not appropriate when based on the thought, "The warrior named Nandamitta was a hero," in the sense of relishing him;
it is only appropriate in the sense that "he was faithful and has passed away. Talk about streets is also [not appropriate] regarding "such-and-such a street..."

"To say, 'Well-placed, ill-placed, brave, capable,' by way of gratification (assāda) is not permissible. To say, 'Faithful, confident, they have reached destruction and passing away'—this alone is permissible.

"The discourse on the water-pot stand" (kumbhaṭṭhānakathā) means a discourse on a place for water; it is also called a discourse on a bathing ford (udakatittha), or a discourse on a water-carrier woman (kumbhadāsī).
Or, even if she is "charming and skilled in dancing and singing," it is not permitted by way of enjoyment; it is only permitted in the manner of "having faith, being confident," and so forth.
"Talk about the departed" refers to talk concerning those who have passed away. The determination regarding that is similar to the determination regarding talk about living relatives.
"Diverse talk" refers to all other useless talk of various kinds that is distinct from the aforementioned preceding and succeeding types of talk.
"Speculations about the world" (*lokakkhāyikā*) refers to such Lokāyata sophistry and contentious talk as: "By whom was this world created? It was created by a certain [being named] so-and-so";
"The crow is white because its bones are white; the crane is red because its blood is red," and so forth.
"Speculations about the ocean" (*samuddakkhāyikā*) refers to: "Why is the ocean called 'Sāgara'? It was dug by the god Sāgara; therefore it is 'Sāgara. It was dug..."
Because it was personally announced by the hand gesture "meti," talk such as "the ocean" and so forth is meaningless talk about proclaiming the ocean.

"Bhava" means growth; "abhava" means decline. Thus, talk that proceeds after stating some cause or other—whether meaningful or meaningless—regarding "this is existence" and "this is non-existence" is talk about existence and non-existence (itibhavābhavakathā).

18. *Viggāhikakathā* (contentious talk) means talk involving dispute, talk involving provocation. In this context, "what is relevant to me" (*sahitaṃ me*) means my statement is relevant, coherent, connected with the meaning, and connected with the reason. "What is irrelevant to you" (*asahitaṃ te*) means your statement is irrelevant and incoherent.
"What has long been practiced by you is overturned" (*adhiciṇṇaṃ te viparāvattaṃ*) refers to that which has been practiced by you for a long time.
"Suppaguṇaṃ": that which was well-strung has been turned back and twisted by me with a single word; the meaning is, "you know nothing. "Āropito te vādo":
the fault has been leveled against you by me. "Cara vādappamokkhāya": go forth for the sake of releasing yourself from the censure;
wander about; the meaning is, go and train yourself here and there. "Nibbeṭhehi vā sace pahosi": or untie it, if you are able. Thus, if you are capable... [the rest of the sentence follows].
"You were capable [of this] yourself; now, release [yourself] right now.
Regarding the discourse on errand-running: "Go here" means go from here to such-and-such a place. "Come there" means come from that place to such-and-such a place.
"Take this" means take this from here. "Bring this from there" means [bring it] from such-and-such a place.

"Bring this name here. In brief, however, with the exception of these five types of fellow practitioners of the Dhamma and messages concerning assistance to the Triple Gem, it is not permissible for laypeople to act as messengers for others.
20. Regarding the term "deceivers" (kuhakā) and so forth: they are called deceivers because they deceive the world and cause it to be bewildered by means of the threefold basis of deception.
They are "flatterers" (*lapaka*) because they speak while desiring gain and honor. They are "hinters" (*nemittika*) because hinting is their habit.
They are "schemers" (*nippesika*) because scheming is their habit. They are "those who seek gain through gain" because they strive for, pursue, and seek out gain by means of gain.
These are: hypocrisy (*kuhanā*), flattery (*lapanā*), hinting (*nemittikatā*), scheming (*nippesikatā*), and seeking gain through gain (*lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanatā*).
This is a designation for persons endowed with these [faults]. This is the summary here.

However, in detail, these [faults] beginning with hypocrisy (*kuhana*) have been explained by citing both the canonical texts (*pāḷi*) and the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) in the "Description of Virtue" (*Sīlaniddesa*) in the *Visuddhimagga*.
At this point, the middle virtue is completed.
The Explanation of the Great Virtue (Mahāsīlavannanā). 21.
Following this is the Great Virtue. "Aṅga" refers to the science of bodily marks (*aṅgasattha*), which proceeds in such a manner as:
"One endowed with any such limb among the hands, feet, and so forth, becomes long-lived, famous," and so on. "Nimitta" refers to the science of omens (*nimittasattha*).
It is said that King Paṇḍu, having placed three pearls in his fist, asked a fortune-teller, "What is in my hand?
The man looked here and there; at that moment, a pearl was being carried off by a fly that had seized it from a house-lizard, so he replied, "Pearls.
When asked again, "How many?", he heard the sound of a cock crowing three times.
He said, “Three. Thus, having pointed out this and that, they dwell devoted to signs (*nimitta*). Regarding “portents” (*uppāta*):
it refers to the occurrence of great portents such as the falling of lightning; for upon seeing these, they predict, “This will happen,” or “It will happen thus.
Regarding “dreams” (*supina*): if one sees a dream at the time of forenoon, such is its ripening (*vipāka*).
They dwell devoted to dream-interpretation (*supinaka*) according to such methods as: "Whoever sees this particular thing in a dream, for him this particular thing will happen," and so forth.
"Characteristics" (*lakkhaṇa*) refers to such things as: "One endowed with this characteristic becomes a king; one with this, a viceroy," and so on.
"Torn by mice" (*mūsikacchinna*) means gnawed by rats. For even by that [mark], whether on a new cloth or an old cloth, from this...

From the very beginning, they declare: "When this has been cut, it becomes such-and-such. *Agnihoma* refers to the offering into the fire, meaning that when an oblation is sacrificed with such wood in this manner, it becomes such-and-such. *Dabbihoma* and the others are also indeed *agnihoma*s;

however, they are mentioned separately according to their specific modality, such as: "When an oblation is sacrificed with such a ladle (*dabbi*) using such grains (*kaṇa*) and so forth, it becomes such-and-such."
In this context, *kaṇa* refers to chaff. *Taṇḍula* refers to the grains of rice and other types of grasses. *Sappi* refers to cow’s ghee and so forth. *Tela* refers to sesame oil and so forth.
Furthermore, taking mustard seeds and other substances with the mouth and casting them into fire, or offering them after reciting a spell (*vijjā*), is called *mukhahoma*.
Offering oblations with blood from the right knee, the thigh, and so forth, is called *lohitahoma*.
*Aṅgavijjā* (the science of limbs) was previously described as a science based on making predictions after merely seeing a limb;

here, however, *aṅgavijjā* is described as making predictions such as whether this noble son is of high birth or not, or whether he is endowed with fortune or not, after examining a finger-bone and reciting a spell (*parijappita*).
*Vatthuvijjā* (the science of sites) is the science for discerning the merits and defects of house-sites, monastery-sites, and so forth.

For even by seeing a particular kind of clay or similar object, and having recited a spell (*vijjā*), they perceive virtues and defects in a space measuring thirty *ratana*s beneath the earth and eighty *ratana*s in the sky. "The science of the marks" (*khattavijjā*) refers to treatises such as the *Abbhayamāsurakkha-rāja-sattha*.

"The science of peace" (*sivavijjā*) refers to spells for bringing about tranquility upon entering a cemetery; some also call it the "science of jackal cries. "The science of spirits" (*bhūtavijjā*)...
*Bhūtavejjamanto*: spells for treating spirits. *Bhūrivijjā*: spells to be learned by one living in a great house. *Ahivijjā*:
both the spell for curing those bitten by snakes and the spell for summoning snakes. *Visavijjā*:

that by which they protect against old poison, produce new poison, or make even poison itself [neutral]. *Vicchikavijjā*: the spell for curing those stung by scorpions. Regarding *mūsikavijjā* as well...
The same method applies here. *Sakuṇavijjā* (the science of birds) is the knowledge of birds regarding their cries and so forth, pertaining to bipeds and quadrupeds that have wings or lack them.
*Vāyasavijjā* (the science of crows) is the knowledge of the cries of crows; this is a distinct treatise, which is why it is mentioned separately.
*Pakkajjhāna* is reflection that has reached maturity. Now, [it involves knowing]: "This one will live for this much; this one for that much."

The meaning is: "thus occurring" is the knowledge of signs (*ādiṭṭhañāṇa*). "Protection from arrows" (*saraparittāṇa*) is the science of charms for guarding against arrows, by which one acts so that they do not fall upon oneself.
"The deer-circle" (*migacakkam*): this is stated as a comprehensive term for the knowledge of the cries of all birds and quadrupeds.
22. Regarding the characteristics of gems and so forth: "Such a gem is praised; such a gem is not praised;
it is or is not a cause for the master’s health, prosperity, and so on"—thus they dwell devoted to the characteristics of gems and the like by way of their color, shape, and other qualities.
This is the meaning. In that context, "weapons" refers to all weapons with the exception of swords and the like. As for the characteristics of women and so forth, in whomsoever...
The men, women, and others residing in that family are to be understood solely by way of their increase or decline.
Furthermore, regarding the characteristics of goats and so forth, this distinction should be understood: "The meat of such goats and others may be eaten; the meat of such [others] must not be eaten.
Moreover, in this context, even with respect to the characteristics of a monitor lizard (*godhā*)—such as in paintings, jewelry, and the like—if such a monitor lizard is present, then this...
This distinction should be understood: "it is called [so-and-so]. Here is the background story:
it is said that in a certain monastery, they had a lizard blowing fire depicted in a mural. From that time on, a great dispute arose among the bhikkhus.
When a visiting bhikkhu saw this, he mocked it. From then on, the dispute subsided. This is also the characteristic of an earring: even with an earring used as an ornament...
It should also be understood by way of the house-eaves. The characteristics of the tortoise are exactly like those of the monitor lizard.
The characteristics of wild animals are stated as a comprehensive summary of the characteristics of all four-footed creatures. 23.
"The departure of kings will take place": on such-and-such a day, under such-and-such a lunar mansion, for a king named so-and-so...
"The conclusion will come"—thus he explains the departure of kings on foreign expeditions. This same method applies everywhere.
However, "non-departure" here refers to the return of those who have been away.
"There will be an approach of internal kings" means that our king within the city has become hostile toward external kings; "there will be a withdrawal of external kings" [means the same].
"He will approach; from that, there will be his departure"—thus he explains the arrival and departure of kings.
The same method applies to the second phrase as well. Victory and defeat are already evident.
Regarding lunar eclipses and so forth, they are to be understood through the very manner of prediction, such as: "On such-and-such a day, Rāhu will seize the moon."
Moreover, even the conjunction of a constellation with Mars and other planets is simply a "planetary conjunction.
A "falling meteor" is the descent of meteors from the sky. A "blazing of the quarters" is like the state of the directions being turbid and agitated by crests of fire and crests of smoke.
A "thundering of the gods" is the roaring of dry clouds. "Rising" means appearing; "setting" means disappearing.

"Defilement" (*saṃkilesa*) means impurity. "Purification" (*vodāna*) means purity. "Thus is its result" (*evaṃ vipāko*) means that it brings about such various kinds of pleasure and pain for the world.

25. "Good rain" (*suvuṭṭhi*) refers to the god's bestowing of a proper downpour. "Bad rain" (*dubbuṭṭhi*) refers to drought; what is meant is the obstruction of the rains. "Hand-sign" (*muddā*) refers to hand gestures.
"Calculation" (*gaṇanā*) is said to be counting by means of the *acchiddaka* (unbroken) method. "Arithmetic" (*saṅkhāna*) refers to the methods of addition, subtraction, and so forth.
Counting by clusters (*piṇḍagaṇanā*). One for whom this is well-mastered knows, upon seeing even a tree, "there are this many leaves here. Regarding poetry (*kāveyya*):
"Bhikkhus, there are these four poets. Which four? The poet of thought, the poet of what is heard, the poet of meaning, and the poet of inspired wit.
Of these four poets, [one composes] either by means of one's own thought, or—as in the case of the one named Vessantara—...

The composition of poetry for the sake of a livelihood occurs either by hearing such things as “He was a king,” and so forth, according to what has been heard; or by way of meaning, thinking, “This is its meaning;
I shall construe it thus”; or by way of spontaneous wit, thinking upon seeing something, “I shall compose something that corresponds to it.
The Lokāyata has already been described.
26. *Āvāhana* (Bringing Home): This refers to the act of bringing home a girl from such-and-such a family under such-and-such a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) for this boy.
*Vivāha* (Marriage): This refers to the act of giving this girl to a boy named so-and-so under such-and-such a lunar mansion, thinking, "In this way, her prosperity will come about.
*Saṃvaraṇa* (Engagement): Engagement means... "Today is the lunar mansion... [text continues]
"Beautiful! Be united this very day; thus there shall be no separation for you"—this is the means of creating union.
"Opening" (*vivaraṇa*) means: "If you wish to separate, separate this very day; thus there shall be no further reunion for you"—this is the means of creating disunion.
"Mixing" (*saṅkiraṇa*) refers to [the mixing of] "earnings, debt, or wealth given..."
"Today, gather it up; for what has been gathered today becomes stable"—this is the accumulation of wealth. "Scattering" means the employment of wealth, such as saying:
"If you wish to employ wealth through investment, loans, and so forth, what is employed today will become double or fourfold.
"Making fortunate" means making beloved and pleasing, or making beautiful.
Or, "making unfortunate" (*dubbhagakaraṇa*) is the opposite of that.

"Causing a hostile conception" (*viruddhagabbhakaraṇa*) means causing a conception that is hostile, dissolved, unstable, or dead. The meaning is the giving of medicine so that it does not perish again.
For a conception perishes due to three causes: wind, microbes, and karma. Among these, regarding that which perishes due to wind:
He gives cooling medicine that brings about quenching; he provides a remedy for living beings when they are being destroyed by parasites;
yet when one is being destroyed by *kamma*, even the Buddhas are unable to prevent it.
"Binding the tongue" means binding the tongue with a mantra. "Locking the jaw" refers to the mantra for binding the mouth.
Binding is that by which they are unable to move their jaws. "Chanting over the hands" (*hatthābhijappana*) is the recitation of a mantra for the purpose of turning back the hands.
It is said that when the mantra is recited while standing within seven paces of him, the other person turns his hands back and hurls them away.
"Chanting over the ears" (*kaṇṇajappana*) is [the use] of a spell (*vijjā*) for the purpose of not hearing sounds with the ears.
*Jappanaṃ*: Having muttered that [incantation], it is said, one says whatever one desires at the place of legal decision;
the opponent does not hear it, and thus cannot provide a reply. *Ādāsapañhaṃ*: asking a question after causing a deity to descend into a mirror.
*Kumārikapañhaṃ*: asking a question after causing a deity to descend into the body of a young girl.
“Devapañha” (The Questions of the Deity) refers to the posing of questions after a deity has been made to descend into the body of a female slave.
“Ādiccupaṭṭhāna” (Sun-worship) is the service rendered to the sun for the sake of a livelihood. “Mahatupaṭṭhāna” (Great Worship) is likewise the service rendered to the Great Brahmā.

“Abbhujjalana” (Fire-spitting) is the issuing of flames from the mouth by means of a mantra. “Sirivhāyana” (Invocation of Fortune) is [the practice of saying]: “Come, O Fortune, establish yourself upon my head.”
Thus is the invocation by means of the head and glory. 27.
*Santikamma* (the rite of propitiation) is the act of making a promise to the deities (*santipaṭissavakamma*) after going to a shrine for the gods, saying:
"If this or that of mine succeeds, I shall offer you such and such an oblation. This is to be performed at the time of success. In that regard...

But when [the means] are fully prepared, the performance of that is called *paṇidhikamma*. *Bhūrikamma* is the performance of the ritual application by one who has resided in a *bhūrighara* and mastered the spells.
Regarding *vassakamma* and *vossakamma*: here, *vassa* means a man, and *vossa* means a eunuch.
Thus, making a man out of a eunuch is *vassakamma*, and making a eunuch out of a man is *vossakamma*.
But while performing that [act], one merely brings about a state of lack of desire; one is not able to make the gender-sign disappear.

*Vatthukamma* is the establishing of a house site on ground where none has been established. *Vatthuparikamma* is the performance of the ritual offering for the site after saying, "Bring this and that.
*Ācamana* is the cleansing of the mouth with water. *Nhāpana* is [the bathing] of others...
Bathing (*nhāpanaṃ*). Offering oblations (*juhanan ti*): making fire-offerings for their sake. Emetics (*vamananti*): administering a medicinal agent (*yoga*) to induce vomiting.
The same principle applies to purgatives (*virecana*). Upper purgation (*uddhaṃvirecanan ti*): the removal of humors (*dosa*) from above. Lower purgation (*adhovirecanan ti*):
the removal of humors from below. Head-purgation (*sīsavirecanan ti*): a head-purification treatment (*sirovirecana*). Ear-oil (*kaṇṇatailan ti*): [oil] for the purpose of lubricating the ears.

Or the cooking of medicinal oils for the purpose of removing wounds. "Eye-drops" refers to oil for anointing the eyes. "Nasal therapy" (natthukamma) is the administration of medicine through the nose after mixing it with oil.
"Collyrium" (añjana) is an alkaline ointment capable of removing two or three layers of film from the eye.
"Counter-collyrium" (paccañjana) is a cooling medicinal ointment used to soothe inflammation. "Surgery" (sālākiya) is the medical work performed with a probe or surgical instrument.
"Surgery" (sallakattiya) refers to the medical work of a surgeon. "Treatment of children" (dārakatikicchā) is said to be the medical work of a pediatrician (komārabhacca).
By the phrase "the non-provision of medicinal roots," he indicates the treatment of the body.
"The removal of medicinal herbs" (osadhīnaṃ paṭimokkho) refers to the extraction of caustic substances and the like once the wound has healed accordingly.
To this extent, the Great Precept (*mahāsīla*) is concluded.

Having thus explained the threefold morality by way of the connection to the praise spoken by Brahmadatta, [the commentary] now— [...proceeds with the Exposition of the Eternalist Theory of the Speculators on the Past (*pubbantakappikasassatavāda*): 28. Thus, having explained the threefold morality by way of the connection to the praise spoken by Brahmadatta, now—

Following the sequence of the praise spoken by the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus, he began the exposition of emptiness (*suññatā*) in the manner beginning with: “There are, bhikkhus, other phenomena (*dhammā*) that are deep and hard to see.
In this context, the word *dhamma* is used in such senses as quality, teaching, scripture, and insubstantiality.
“For indeed, neither Dhamma nor non-Dhamma have equal results;
non-Dhamma leads to hell, while Dhamma brings about a happy rebirth.
In such passages as these, the word *dhamma* refers to a quality (*guṇa*). In such passages as “I shall teach you, O bhikkhus, the Dhamma that is good in the beginning,” it refers to the teaching.

In the phrase "in the teaching" (*desanāyaṃ*), it refers to the teaching itself, as in "Here, a bhikkhu masters the Dhamma: the discourses (*sutta*), the mixed prose and verse (*geyya*)," and so forth.
In the phrase "At that time, indeed, there are mental phenomena (*dhammā*), there are aggregates (*khandhā*)," and so forth, it refers to non-sentient things.
But here it applies to a quality (*guṇa*). Therefore, the meaning here should be understood thus: "There are, bhikkhus, other qualities of the Tathāgata."
"Profound" means that, like the great ocean, it cannot find a footing for the knowledge of others—except for that of a Tathāgata—even with the needle-point of a gnat's snout;
because of its profundity, it is difficult to see. Because it is difficult to see, it is difficult to realize.

It is peaceful because all fevers have been extinguished, and it is peaceful also because it proceeds toward peaceful objects. It is sublime in the sense of providing no satiety, like a meal of exquisite flavor.

Because they are the domain of supreme knowledge, they are not to be traversed by reasoning; thus, they are "beyond the sphere of reasoning" (*atakkāvacara*). Because their intrinsic nature is subtle and delicate, they are "subtle" (*nipuṇa*).
Because they are not the domain of fools, they are to be known only by the wise; thus, they are "to be experienced by the wise" (*paṇḍitavedanīya*).
"Those things which the Tathāgata, having realized them for himself through direct higher knowledge, has proclaimed" refers to those phenomena which the Tathāgata knows without depending on others.
The meaning is: having sacrificed [his own views] and having made it manifest for himself through his own preeminent knowledge, he proclaims, illuminates, explains, and reveals it.
"By which" means by which qualities and dharmas. "According to reality" means as it truly is (*yathābhūtam*).
"Those who would speak rightly of his praise" means that those desiring to speak the praise of the Tathāgata should speak rightly—that is, they should speak without omission.
The meaning is "they would be able. And what are those qualities praised by the Blessed One in this way? They are the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
If that is so, why is there an expression in the plural? It is because of its association with various types of consciousness and because it has various objects.
For that [knowledge] is found in the four great functional consciousnesses associated with knowledge, and no single phenomenon is its exclusive object.
There is no such thing [as a single consciousness that knows all]. As it has been said: "The knowledge that knows everything past is 'omniscience' (sabbaññutaññāṇa);

because there is no obstruction therein, it is 'unobstructed knowledge' (anāvaraṇañāṇa)," and so forth. Thus, the use of the plural number is made because of the association with various states of mind arising again and again, and because of the various objects [of those minds].

The phrase “But it is another” (*aññeva*) here is a term for differentiation; it should be construed with all the following terms as follows: “It is another, not the abstention from taking life and so forth;

it is profound, not superficial. For while the knowledge of the disciple’s perfections (*sāvakapāramīñāṇa*) is profound, the knowledge of private enlightenment (*paccekabodhiñāṇa*) is even more profound than that—thus there is no such differentiation there—and as for the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), [it is likewise distinguished].
"Even deeper than that"—therein, too, there is no further determination; yet there is nothing else deeper than this.
Therefore, the determination "they are deep" is obtained. Likewise, everything should be understood as "hard to see" or "hard to penetrate.
"And which are they, monks?"—this, however, is a question expressing the desire to speak about those phenomena. "They exist..."
"Monks, some recluses and brahmins... and so forth is the response to the question. But why was this begun in such a manner?
For when the Buddhas reach four specific occasions, their thundering becomes great;
wisdom enters [them]; the greatness of the Buddha-wisdom becomes manifest; and the teaching becomes profound, struck by the three characteristics, and connected with emptiness.
Which four? The formulation of the Vinaya, the difference in grounds, the mode of conditions, and the difference in occasions.

Therefore: “This is light; this is heavy; this is curable; this is incurable; this is an offense; this is no offense; this leads to cutting off; this leads to rehabilitation; this leads to confession; this is a worldly transgression.”
"This is a transgression of the formal rule; regarding this matter, this should be prescribed"—this is what is called the promulgation of a training rule when a case has thus arisen.
In this regard, others have neither the capacity nor the power; this is not within the domain of others, but is the domain of the Tathāgata alone.
Thus, once the promulgation of the Vinaya has been reached, the thundering of the Buddhas becomes great.
Knowledge enters into it... [and so on] ...connected with emptiness.
Likewise, these are called the four foundations of mindfulness... [and so on] ...the noble eightfold path, the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, and the four noble truths.
There are twenty-two faculties, nine roots, four nutriments, seven contacts, seven feelings, seven perceptions, seven volitions, and seven consciousnesses.

Among these, so many are called phenomena belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), and so many are phenomena included within the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) and the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*). So many...

There is no power or strength in others to analyze and expound the Abhidhamma Piṭaka with its twenty-fourfold system of relations and infinite methods, declaring, "These are mundane phenomena; so many are supramundane phenomena. This is beyond the scope of others;
it is the domain of the Tathāgata alone. Thus, when the range of the Buddhas' roar reaches the delimitation of the various planes of existence (bhūmantara), it is truly a thundering roar.
It becomes great; it enters into knowledge... [and so on]... associated with emptiness.
Likewise, this ignorance is a condition for volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) in nine ways:
by being a condition as arising, as occurrence, as a sign, as accumulation, as conjunction, as an impediment, as origin, as cause, and as condition.
In the same way, formations and the other factors are conditions for consciousness and the rest. As it is said:
"How is wisdom in the discernment of conditions knowledge of the stability of phenomena? Ignorance is the arising-stability and the occurrence-stability of formations;
it is their sign-stability, accumulation-stability, bondage-stability, impediment-stability, origination-stability, and cause-stability."
Ignorance is a condition in nine ways: as arising, presence, non-disappearance, support, foundation, cause, origin, nutriment, and condition; and formations are arisen through conditions.
The wisdom that, in this way, grasps the conditions—that both these phenomena are arisen through conditions—is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*).
In the past time and in the future time, ignorance is the arising and presence of formations... [and so on] ...birth is the condition for aging-and-death.
“Arising and presence … [and so on] … and the presence of conditions: by these nine aspects, birth is the condition and aging-and-death is what has arisen through conditions;
both these states have arisen through conditions. Wisdom in the discernment of conditions is ‘knowledge of the stability of phenomena.
Thus, this threefold cycle and threefold time, which occurs as the state of condition for each respective phenomenon in such and such a way—
No one else possesses the power or strength to analyze and explain dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) with its three connections, four groups, and twenty modes;
this is not the domain of others, but the domain of the Tathāgata alone.
Thus, when reaching the aspect of conditions (paccayākāra), the thundering of the Buddhas becomes great, and their knowledge penetrates it... [and so on] ...connected with emptiness (suññatā).
Likewise, there are four who are eternalists; four who are partial-eternalists; four who hold to the finite and infinite views;
four who are eel-wrigglers; two who are fortuitous-originationists; sixteen who are proponents of perception; eight who are proponents of non-perception;
eight who are proponents of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; seven who are annihilationists; and five who are proponents of Nibbāna in this very life.

"There is no power or strength in others to explain these sixty-two views by breaking them down, stripping away their roots and their thickets; this is not within the scope of others, but is the domain of the Tathāgata alone.
Thus, having reached another occasion, the thundering of the Buddhas becomes great, and wisdom enters [the world].
The greatness of the Buddha’s knowledge is made manifest; the teaching is profound, struck by the three characteristics, and connected with emptiness.

At this point, however, a change of context occurs; therefore, in order to demonstrate the greatness of omniscient knowledge and to reveal and clarify the teaching on emptiness, the King of Dhamma enters into another context:
“There are, bhikkhus, some recluses and brahmins”—thus he began the response to the question.
29. Therein, *santi* means there are, they exist, they are found. *Bhikkhave* is a form of address. *Eke* means some. *Samaṇabrāhmaṇā* means:
they are recluses (*samaṇā*) by virtue of having gone forth, and brahmins (*brāhmaṇā*) by birth; or [they are so called] by the world...

They are thus recognized as "ascetics" (*samaṇa*) and "brahmins" (*brāhmaṇa*). They are called "speculators about the past" (*pubbantakappika*) because they grasp [theories] after having speculated about and deliberated upon the past (*pubbanta*).
Alternatively, they are called "speculators about the past" because the speculation concerning the past belongs to them.

In this context, the word *anta* is seen to signify "end," "interior," "boundary," "inferiority," "further part," and "portion. For example, in such expressions as "full to the end" (*antapūra*) or "full to the belly" (*udarapūra*).

Indeed, the word *anta* has various meanings. In such passages as, “They wander in the world, concealed by their retinues, impure within yet appearing beautiful without,” it means *abbhantara* (the interior).

In such passages as, “It wears out at the end of the waist-band (*kāyabandhana*)” or “She [reaches] the edge of the greenery, or the edge of the path, or the edge of the rock, or the edge of the water,” it means *mariyādā* (a boundary).
In such passages as, “This, monks, is the lowest of livelihoods, namely, mendicancy (*piṇḍolya*),” it means... [the lowest].
In such passages as “This, indeed, is the end of suffering,” it refers to the subsequent state; for the destruction of all conditions is called the subsequent state or the limit of suffering.
In such passages as “Personal existence, friend, is one extreme,” it refers to a portion;
and this term is used here also in the sense of a portion.

The word *kappa* also occurs in many senses, such as in the phrases: “May the Blessed One remain, venerable sir, for an *kappa*,” “there is time (*kappa*) to lie down,” and “what is made allowable (*kappakata*) by one is joined with what is not made allowable.
Thus it applies to various meanings such as a lifespan, a portion of time, a rule of discipline, and so forth.
Here, however, it should be understood to apply to craving and views. And this has been said: “*Kappa*s...”

“There are two kinds of *kappa*: the *kappa* of craving and the *kappa* of views. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as follows: they are “speculators about the past” (*pubbantakappika*) because they exist having imagined (*kappetvā*) and fabricated (*pakappetvā*) a portion of the past aggregates by way of craving and views.
Since their views follow after the past itself, arising again and again for those who thus exist having imagined the past, they are called [views] that follow the past.
Those who hold views regarding the past, having such views, and depending upon and relying on that past, cause other people as well to fall into speculative views;
they assert various kinds of propositions based on eighteen grounds.
In this context, "various kinds" means of many sorts. "Propositions" (*adhimuttipadāni*) means terms of designation (*adhivacanapadāni*). Alternatively:
Because they proceed by overriding actual reality and by not grasping things according to their true nature, these are called "resolutions" (*adhimutti*), which is to say, "views" (*diṭṭhi*).
"Resolution-terms" (*adhimuttipada*) means terms that indicate resolutions; the meaning is: words that point out views.
"By eighteen bases" (*aṭṭhārasahi vatthūhi*) means by eighteen reasons.

30. Now, in order to explain those eighteen grounds by which they assert [their views], he asks them with the intention of making them speak, using the method beginning with "But those venerable ones," and so forth; having asked thus, he says "There are, monks," and so on, in order to analyze and demonstrate those grounds.
In this context, "doctrine" (*vāda*) means that by means of it they speak; this is a designation for a speculative view (*diṭṭhigata*). [The term] *sassata*...
"Those who hold a doctrine" are the eternalists (*sassatavāda*); the meaning is "those with the view of eternalism.
In this same manner, the meaning of subsequent similar terms should be understood. Regarding the phrase "the self and the world are eternal":
having apprehended one among the aggregates such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth as both "self" and "world," they proclaim that it is eternal, deathless, permanent, and stable. As it has been said:
—“They proclaim both self and world as ‘form is self and the world, and it is eternal’;
likewise they proclaim feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as ‘feeling... consciousness is self and the world, and it is eternal. 31.

Regarding the phrase “exerting ardor” (*ātappa-manvāya*) and so forth: energy (*vīriya*) is called “ardor” (*ātappa*) because of its nature of burning away (*ātāpana*) the defilements (*kilesa*). That very same [energy]...
"Exertion" (*padhāna*) is so called by way of striving. "Application" (*anuyoga*) is so called by way of repeated engagement. Thus, the meaning is:
having followed, approached, and depended upon energy that is threefold in its classification. "Heedfulness" (*appamāda*) is said to be non-separation from mindfulness.
"Right attention" (*sammā-manasikāra*) is attention as a means, attention as a path; in terms of its actual meaning, it is said to be knowledge. For in whatever attention...
For one who is established [in concentration], the knowledge of recollecting past lives succeeds; this refers to the attention directed toward this state.
Therefore, the summary meaning here is: "having relied upon energy, mindfulness, and wisdom. "Of such a kind" means of such a nature.
"Mental concentration" (*cetosamādhi*) means concentration of the mind. "Touches" means experiences or attains. "As the mind is concentrated" means...
The meaning of "the manifold former existences" and so forth, when the mind is rightly placed and well-established by means of that concentration, has been explained in the *Visuddhimagga*.
"He spoke thus": having become endowed with such power of meditation, the one holding to wrong views (diṭṭhigatika) speaks as follows. "Vaṃjhā" means...
Like a barren cow, a barren palm tree, and so forth, it is fruitless and does not produce anything for anyone.
By this, he rejects the idea that those things grasped as "self" and "world"—namely, the meditative absorptions (jhānas) and so on—possess the quality of producing form and other phenomena.
It is "immovable" (kūṭaṭṭha) because it stands like a mountain peak. It is "standing like a pillar" (esikaṭṭhāyiṭṭhita) because it stands having become like a pillar; just as...
"A pillar of reeds firmly planted stands immovable"—this means it stands thus. By both [phrases], he illustrates the impossibility of the world's destruction.
However, some, citing the reading *īsikaṭṭhāyiṭṭhito*, say it stands like a reed in a clump of muñja grass.
In that case, the intended meaning is this: that which is called "born" exists already, just as the reed exists within the muñja grass.
It emerges. And because it stands like a reed-stalk, the meaning is that those very beings run about, going from here to elsewhere.
"Transmigrating" means they move from one state to another. "Passing away" means they undergo such a reckoning. Likewise, "re-arising.
In the Commentary, however, after previously stating, "The self and the world are eternal," it now says, "And those beings run about," and so forth.
By this statement, this proponent of a speculative view (diṭṭhigatika) undermines his own position;
for the view of a speculative proponent is not fixed, but is as unstable as a stake driven into a heap of chaff.

It is said that here, just as in a madman’s basket there may be pieces of cake, excrement, cow dung, and so forth, what is beautiful becomes indeed ugly. "It exists eternally" (atthitveva sassatisamam).

In this context, "eternal" (sassata) means that one conceives of the self as being permanent and existing, like the great earth; likewise, one conceives it to be like Mount Sineru, the moon, and the sun.
Thus, conceiving the self to be equal to those things, they say, "It exists eternally.
Now, in order to provide the reason for proving the proposition beginning with "the self and the world are eternal," he shows the cause: "That..."
"And for what reason? Because I have applied myself with ardor," he said, beginning thus. Therein, "By this I know this" means:
"By this specific attainment, I know this through direct personal experience; I do not speak merely on the basis of faith alone.
The letter *m* here is used for the purpose of euphonic junction (*sandhi*). "This, monks, is the first ground... [he said].
"By four grounds": regarding the four locations expressed by the word *vatthu*, this is the first location;
the meaning is that this recollection of approximately one hundred thousand births is the first cause. 32–33.
The same method applies to the two subsequent occasions as well. For this particular occasion [differs] only insofar as it concerns the recollection of many hundreds of thousands of births.
It was said [in reference to the first]. The others [were said] by way of recollecting forty-one aeons of world-dissolution and evolution.
For a heretic of dull wisdom recollects only as much as several hundreds of thousands of births; one of medium wisdom, ten aeons of dissolution and evolution;
and one of sharp wisdom, forty, but not beyond that.
34. In the fourth section: one who reasons is a *takkī*; or, one who possesses reasoning is a *takkī*.
This is a designation for those who grasp at views after having reasoned and deliberated. One who is endowed with investigation (*vīmaṃsā*) is an *vīmaṃsī*.
Investigation means weighing, approving, and tolerating. Just as a man, having investigated the water with a staff, enters it, even so, one who [enters] after having weighed...
Having found it pleasing and having asked for forgiveness, he adopts that view; he is to be understood as "one who investigates" (*vīmaṃsī*).
"Struck by reasoning" (*takkapariyāhataṃ*) means struck by reasoning; the sense is: having reasoned in various ways.
"Followed by investigation" (*vīmaṃsānucaritaṃ*) means followed by that aforementioned kind of investigation. "Self-evident" (*sayaṃpaṭibhānaṃ*) means produced merely from one's own intuition.
"He speaks thus" means he says this having grasped the view of eternalism (*sassatadiṭṭhi*).

In that regard, there are four types of reasoners (*takkī*): the one who relies on hearsay (*anussutika*), the one who knows by birth (*jātissara*), the one who gains through profit (*lābhī*), and the pure reasoner (*suddhatakkikā*).
Among these, the one who has heard such things as "there was a king named Vessantara" and [thinks], "In that case, if the Blessed One is indeed Vessantara, then he is eternal... [continues].

One who, while reasoning, grasps the view that "the self [exists]," is called one who reasons based on what has not been heard (anussutika-takkiko). One who, having remembered two or three births, reasons—thinking, "In the past I was such-and-such a person;
therefore, the self is eternal"—is called one who reasons based on recollection of past births (jātissara-takkiko).
Furthermore, one who, because of his own attainment, reasons—"Just as my self is happy now, so it was in the past and will be in the future... [is called one who reasons based on present experience].
Having reasoned, "It will be so," one adopts a view; this is called a "speculator based on gain" (*lābhītakkiko*).
On the other hand, one who adopts [a view] by mere reasoning alone, thinking, "When this exists, that comes to be," is called a "pure speculator" (*suddhatakkiko*).
35. "By one or another of these" means by one or another of these very four grounds, whether by one or by two.
Or with three [reasons]. With these grounds—that there is no other single reason outside of these for the proclamation of eternalism—he utters an irreversible lion’s roar.
"36. This, monks, the Tathāgata understands": monks, this refers to those fourfold types of speculative views.
The Tathāgata knows in various ways. Demonstrating that mode of understanding, he said: "These are the bases of views," and so forth.
In this context, the views themselves are called "bases of views. Furthermore, the cause of views is also a "basis of views.
As it is said: "What are the eight bases of views? The aggregates are a basis of views; ignorance is a basis of views; contact is also [a basis of views]."
“Perception, applied thought, improper attention, evil friends, and the voice of another are bases for views.
“The aggregates are the cause, the aggregates are the condition, in the sense of being the source from which [views] arise; thus the aggregates are also bases for views.
Ignorance is the cause... [and so on] ...evil friends are the cause. The voice of another is the cause, the voice of another is the condition.”
"By way of being a basis for views in the sense of their origination, even the voice of another is a basis for views. Thus they are "taken up":
first, those bases for views known as views—such as "the self and the world are eternal"—are taken up, that is, grasped;
the meaning is that they have been set in motion. Thus they are "clung to": because of a mind free from doubt, they are repeatedly touched and clung to.
"This alone is the truth, all else is vain"—thus they have reached a final conclusion. However, as for the grounds for views (*diṭṭhiṭṭhāna*), which are reckoned as causes:
when they are grasped in such a way, they give rise to views. They are grasped by way of their object (*ārammaṇa*), by way of their occurrence (*pavatta*), and by way of their repetition (*āsevana*).
Because of not seeing the danger (*ādīnava*) in them, they are adhered to (*parāmaṭṭha*) through repeated grasping. Thus they have such a destination (*evaṃgatika*).
Thus [there are those] belonging to any one of the destinies of hell, the animal realm, or the sphere of hungry ghosts.
"Thus in the future life" (*abhisamparāya*) is a synonym for the preceding term; it means "such a world beyond.
And the Tathāgata understands that: not only does the Tathāgata understand the destination of views (*diṭṭhigata*) together with its cause and its destiny, but...
He understands; moreover, he understands all that, and beyond that, he understands both virtue and concentration as well as the knowledge of omniscience.

"He does not misapprehend that understanding" means that even while understanding such an unsurpassed distinction, he does not misapprehend it by way of craving, views, pride, or misapprehension, thinking, "I understand."

"And for one who does not cling, Nibbāna is personally realized"—thus, for one who does not cling, by reason of that non-clinging, the extinction of those defilements of clinging is realized by oneself, through one's own self. This shows, O monks, that Nibbāna is manifest to the Tathāgata.
Now, in order to show the practice by which that Nibbāna was attained by the Tathāgata as he practiced accordingly, [he says] "in which..."
“Attached to feelings, the followers of other sects enter the thicket of views, thinking, ‘We shall be happy here; we shall be happy there.
Teaching the meditation subject by means of those very feelings, he said, “The origin of feelings,” and so forth.
Therein, “having known it as it really is” means: “The origin of feelings is from the origin of ignorance,” in the sense of the origin of conditions.

He sees the arising of the aggregate of feeling; he sees the arising of the aggregate of feeling in the sense of the arising of conditions, thinking, "With the arising of craving, there is the arising of feeling";
he sees the arising of the aggregate of feeling in the sense of the arising of conditions, thinking, "With the arising of kamma, there is the arising of feeling";
[he sees the arising of the aggregate of feeling] in the sense of the arising of conditions, thinking, "With the arising of contact, there is the arising of feeling."
“He sees the arising of the aggregate of feeling. Even while seeing the characteristic of production, he sees the arising of the aggregate of feeling.
Having thus understood the origin of feelings as they really are by way of these five characteristics, [he understands]:
“With the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of feeling”—this is the passing away of the aggregate of feeling in the sense of the cessation of conditions.
He sees: "With the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of feeling"—he sees the passing away of the aggregate of feeling in the sense of the cessation of conditions.
He sees: "With the cessation of karma, there is the cessation of feeling"—he sees the passing away of the aggregate of feeling in the sense of the cessation of conditions.
He sees: "With the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of feeling"—he sees the passing away of the aggregate of feeling in the sense of the cessation of conditions.
He sees it. Even while seeing the characteristic of change, he sees the passing away of the aggregate of feeling.
Having thus understood, as they truly are, the subsiding of feelings by way of these five characteristics, he understands the gratification as it truly is:
"The pleasure and joy that arise dependent upon feeling—this is the gratification of feeling."
Having understood this, and having understood the danger as it really is— namely, that "feeling is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, and this is the danger in feeling"—
and having understood the escape as it really is— namely, that "the removal of desire and lust for feeling, the abandoning of desire and lust for feeling,
is the escape from feeling"— one becomes free from desire and lust.
"Monks, the Tathāgata is without clinging and liberated through non-clinging. Whatever clinging might exist, he would cling to something;
and because of that clinging, there would be a constituent aggregate (khandha). Since that does not exist, the Tathāgata, monks, is liberated precisely by not clinging to any phenomenon whatsoever."
37. "These, monks, are those very things regarding which I asked: 'And what, monks, are those teachings that are profound?

It should be understood that these teachings of omniscient knowledge—which I have thus pointed out as 'these, monks, are those things that the Tathāgata understands, and he understands even more than that'—are profound, difficult to see... [and so on] ...to be realized by the wise."
Since neither an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) nor anyone among those such as stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*) is able to speak of the Tathāgata’s praise as it truly is,
but rather the Tathāgata alone could speak of his praise correctly as it truly is— even by one who asks in this way,
only omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) has been asked about, and by one who provides the answer, only that has been explained; however, in the interim, various views (*diṭṭhi*) have been analyzed.
The commentary on the first recitation section is finished.
Commentary on the Theory of Partial Eternity (Ekaccasassatavāda): 38.

"Partial-eternalists" (ekaccasassatikā) refers to those who maintain the theory of partial eternity. They are of two kinds: those who hold that some sentient beings (satta) are eternal, and those who hold that some conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) are eternal. Both of these types are included here.
39. *Yanti* is merely a particle. *Kadāci* means "at some time. *Karahaci* is a synonym for the same.
*Dīghassa addhuno* means "of a long duration. *Accayena* means "by the passing. *Saṃvaṭṭati* means "it perishes.
*Yebhuyyena* is said with reference to those remaining after those who are reborn in the higher Brahma-worlds or in the formless realms [have departed]. By means of jhāna.
They are "mind-made" (manomaya) because they are produced by mind. They are "joy-fed" (pītibhakka) because joy is their food and sustenance.
They are "self-luminous" (sayampabha) because their own radiance is their light. They are "sky-walkers" (antalikkhacara) because they move through the atmosphere.

They are "dwellers in beauty" (subhaṭṭhāyino) because they abide in beautiful places such as gardens, celestial palaces, and wish-fulfilling trees; or alternatively, they are called "dwellers in beauty" because they abide having become beautiful with delightful garments and ornaments.
"For a long, extended period" means, at the maximum, eight eons.
"It evolves" (vivaṭṭati) means it forms [the world]. "Empty of the Brahma-palace" means empty due to the absence of beings who have naturally arisen there;
the meaning is that the plane of the Brahmakāyika deities comes into being. There is no creator or instigator of it, as stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.
However, according to the method already described, a jeweled ground arises through kamma-condition and temperature-originated production.

And it is precisely in these natural places of production that pleasure groves, wish-fulfilling trees, and so forth, come into being. Then, an attachment arises for beings toward their habitual dwelling places;
they develop the first jhāna and subsequently descend from it. Therefore, he said: "Then a certain being," and so on.
"Either through the exhaustion of the life-span or through the exhaustion of merit":
those who, having performed sublime meritorious deeds, are reborn in some short-lived divine world, are unable to remain by the power of their own merit;

they pass away simply according to the measure of that divine world's life-span, and thus they are said to "pass away through the exhaustion of the life-span. However, those who have performed limited meritorious deeds...
Having performed [meritorious deeds], they are reborn in the world of long-lived devas; yet, they are unable to remain for the full duration of their lifespan and pass away prematurely.
Thus, it is said that they "pass away through the exhaustion of merit. "For a long period" means for a *kappa* or half a *kappa*. 41.
"Discontent" (*anabhirati*) is the longing for another being to come. However, that dissatisfaction which is associated with aversion (*paṭigha-sampayutta*)—
That does not exist in the Brahma-world. "Agitation" (*paritassanā*) means fear and trembling; furthermore, this agitation is fourfold:
agitation due to fear, agitation due to craving, agitation due to views, and agitation due to knowledge. In this regard:
"In dependence on birth there is fear, terror, trepidation, horripilation, and mental dread. In dependence on aging... sickness... death... [and so on]... there is dread."
This is called trembling out of fear (*tāsatassaṇā*). “Oh, may other beings too come to this state!”—this is called trembling out of craving (*taṇhātassaṇā*).
“It is merely the agitation and vacillation [of the mind]”—this is called trembling out of views (*diṭṭhitassaṇā*).
“Having heard the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma, they for the most part fall into fear, agitation, and terror”—this is trembling out of knowledge (*ñāṇatassaṇā*).
[This is] the name. Here, however, both the search for craving (*taṇhātassanā*) and the search for views (*diṭṭhitassanā*) are applicable.
As for "the Brahma-palace" (*brahmavimāna*), it is not said here to be empty because of the existence of those who have first been reborn there.
"They are reborn" (*upapajjanti*) means they approach by way of rebirth. "Companionship" (*sahabyata*) means co-existence.
42. "Abhibhū" means standing having overcome [others], thinking, "I am the eldest. "Anabhibhūto" means not overcome by others. "Aññadatthu" is a particle used for emphasis.
"Daso" refers to seeing; the meaning is, "I see everything. "Vasavattī" means I bring all people under my control. "Issaro, kattā, nimmātā" means:
"In this world, I am the lord, I am the maker, I am the creator. I am the lord of the world.
"I am the maker and the creator; the earth, the Himavat, Sineru, the world-systems, the great oceans, the moon, and the sun were created by me.
"I am the best and the ordainer of the world," he said;
"you shall be called a khattiya, you a brahmin, a vessa, a sudra, a householder, or a renunciant—even down to an outcaste."
"Be! Become a bull!"—thus he conceives: "I am the one who directs beings in this way. "A master, a father of what has been and what is to be"—through his mastery over the practice, he conceives:

"I am the master; I am the father of both what has come to be and what is yet to be. In that regard, beings born from eggs and from a womb are called "what is to be" while still within the eggshell and within the womb; from the moment they have emerged outside, [they are no longer so].
"Beings" (bhūta) means: those born from moisture are "candidates" (bhavya) at the first moment of consciousness, and from the second moment onward they are "beings" (bhūta).
Those of spontaneous birth (opapātika) are to be understood as "candidates" during the first posture (iriyāpatha), and from the second posture onward they are "beings.
Thinking "all of them are my sons," he conceives: "I am the father of beings and candidates."
Now, desiring to establish this through reasoning, he made the declaration, "These beings were created by me," and then said, "For what reason?
and so forth. "Itthattaṃ" means "this state of being," that is to say, the state of Brahmā.
By this [phrase], even though they have passed away and been reborn according to their own karma, they merely imagine out of conceit, "We were created by him."
"Thinking thus, she bends down like a crooked beam entering a crooked hole and goes to his very feet.

(43) "More beautiful" (*vaṇṇavantataro*) means more beautiful; the meaning is that he is handsome and pleasing. "Of greater power" (*mahesakkhataro*) means of greater renown by virtue of his sovereignty and retinue.
(44) "But it is possible" (*ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ*) means this is indeed the reason: having passed away from there, he does not go elsewhere.
"He comes right here"—this was said with reference to that. "From the home" means from the house. "The homeless life" means the going forth (*pabbajjā*).
For it is called the "homeless life" because, in that state, there is no such work as farming or cattle-tending belonging to a household;
therefore, it is called the homeless life. "He goes forth" means he approaches it. "Beyond that he does not recollect" means beyond his previous births (*pubbenivāsa*).
He does not remember; being unable to remember, he stands there and adopts a view.
Regarding [the self] as "eternal" and so forth, seeing no rebirth for it, he says it is "eternal" (*nicca*); seeing no death, he says it is "permanent" (*dhruva*);

because of its constant existence, he says it is "everlasting" (*sassata*); and because there is no change even by way of aging, he says it is "of an unchanging nature" (*avipariṇāmadhamma*). The rest here is...
In the first instance, it is self-evident. 45–46.
In the second instance, they are corrupted and ruined by play; thus they are "corrupted by play" (*khiḍḍāpadosika*).

Some also write the Pāḷi as *padūsika*, but that is not found in the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*). "Excessively" (*ativela*) means "at the wrong time" (*atikāla*), the sense being "for too long. "Engaged in the nature of laughing, playing, and delighting" (*hassakhiḍḍāratidhammasamāpanna*).
"Addicted to the nature of laughter and the nature of play" means they have attained and are devoted to the nature of laughter and the nature of play;
the meaning is that they dwell possessing the aforementioned natures of delight, being devoted to the pleasure of merriment and laughter as well as the pleasure of physical and verbal play.
"Mindfulness fails" means mindfulness regarding edible and consumable foods fails. It is said that by means of what was obtained through a particular excellence of merit...

While sporting in the festival with their own great majesty and splendor, they were so overwhelmed by the magnitude of that attainment that they did not even know whether they were consuming food or not.
Then, from the moment one meal had passed, though they continued to eat and drink incessantly, they still fell away and did not remain. Why? Because of the heat born of karma (*kammaja-tejo*).

Because of the strength [of the divine heat] and the weakness of the physical body—since for human beings the kamma-born heat is weak and the physical body is strong—it is possible, even after seven days have passed, to support the physical basis with warm water, thin gruel, and so forth, due to the weakness of their heat and the strength of their physical bodies.
However, for devas, the heat is strong and the physical body is weak. They [can remain] for one...

They are unable to remain once the time for food has passed. Just as, for example, a lotus or a water lily placed upon a heated stone at midday during the summer heat does not return to its natural state even if it is sprinkled with a hundred jars of water in the evening, but rather perishes;
even so, those who eat and drink continuously thereafter still pass away.
They do not remain. Therefore he said: "Through the loss of mindfulness, those devas fall away from that body.
But who are those devas? There is no specific investigation in the *Aṭṭhakathā* as to which devas these are;

however, because it is stated without distinction that "the kamma-born fire of devas is powerful, while the physical [fire] is weak," it refers to whichever devas subsist on solid food (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*). Thus...
It should be understood that those very beings who perform [such acts] are the ones who pass away. However, some say: "Those gods are the Nimmānarati and Paranimmitavasavatti [gods].
They are called *khiḍḍāpadosika* (corrupted by play) merely because they are corrupted by play. The rest here should be understood in the same manner as previously explained.
47–48. In the third instance, they are corrupted and destroyed by mind; thus they are *manopadosika*. These are the Cātumahārājika [gods].
It is said that among them, one son of the gods, thinking, "I shall play at the festival," set out upon the street in his chariot with his retinue;
then another, coming out and seeing him going ahead, thought, "O, this wretch!"— seeing him as if he had never seen him before—
and became angry, thinking, "He goes along bloated with joy and as if he were bursting."
Even while walking ahead, if he sees that the other has turned back and is angry—realizing the state of his anger because "those who are angry are easily recognized"—he counters with anger, thinking:

"You are angry; what can you do to me? This prosperity was obtained by me through the power of generosity, virtue, and so forth, not by your power. For when one person is angry, the other who is not angry protects himself.
But when both are angry, the anger of one becomes a condition for the other’s, and the anger of that one also becomes a condition for the other’s;
thus they both pass away while their retinues are still weeping. This is the natural law (*dhammatā*) here. The rest should be understood according to the method already stated.
49–52. In the doctrine of Takki, he perceives the dissolution of the eye and so forth, but as for consciousness, because each preceding [moment]...
Having given a condition for each subsequent [moment], it ceases; therefore, one does not perceive the dissolution of the mind as being more powerful than the dissolution of the eye and so forth.
Not seeing this, he assumes that when this personal existence is broken up, the mind goes elsewhere—just as, for example, a bird leaves one tree and alights on another.
Thus he spoke. The rest here should be understood according to the method already stated.
53. Regarding the "Eternalists" (Antānantikā):

this means those who hold views concerning the finite, the infinite, both the finite and the infinite, or neither the finite nor the infinite; that is, doctrines that proceed by taking as their object that which is finite, or infinite, or both finite and infinite, or neither finite nor infinite.

54–60. "He dwells perceiving a limit in the world": having taken the counterpart sign—which has not been expanded as far as the limits of the world-system—and apprehending it as "the world," he dwells perceiving a limit in the world.
However, one who has expanded the kasiṇa up to the limits of the world-system is one who perceives the infinite.
Furthermore, one who does not expand upwards or downwards but expands only across, and thus perceives a limit above and below, is one who perceives a limit [in the world].
[One] perceives [beings] as infinite horizontally. The doctrine of the skeptic (takkīvāda) is to be understood in the same manner already described.
These four [views] are included among those who speculate about the past (pubbantakappika), because they are grasped as views based solely on what has been previously seen by oneself.
Commentary on the Eel-Wriggling Doctrine (amarāvikkhepavāda): [To be continued].

61. "Does not die" (*na marati*) means "immortal" (*amarā*). What is that? It is both the view and the speech of one who holds a speculative position, which—according to the method beginning with "Is it thus for me? (*evam-pi me no*)—is without limit. "Diverse shaking" (*vividho khepo*) means "perplexity" (*vikkhepa*);
the perplexity caused by such immortal views and speech is "the perplexity of the immortals" (*amarāvikkhepa*).
Those who possess this are the "Eel-Wrigglers" (*amarāvikkhepikā*). According to another method: "Amara" is the name of a certain species of fish.
Just as she, darting about in the water by means of surfacing and submerging, cannot be caught, so too this doctrine darts hither and thither and does not admit of being grasped;
thus it is called "the Eel-Wriggler" (*amarāvikkhepa*). Those who possess this are called "Eel-Wrigglers" (*amarāvikkhepika*).
62. “He does not understand ‘this is wholesome’ as it really is”: the meaning is that he does not understand the ten courses of wholesome action as they really are.
Regarding the unwholesome as well, the ten courses of unwholesome action are intended. “It would be a vexation for me”:
through the arising of remorse, thinking “I have spoken falsely,” there would be vexation for me; it would become suffering.
“Meaning”: “That would be an obstacle for me” means that it would be an obstacle for both my heavenly rebirth and the path [to liberation].
“Out of fear of false speech and out of loathing for false speech” means through moral dread (*ottappa*) and shame (*hiri*) regarding false speech.
“He falls into verbal evasion” means he falls into a verbal diversion. Of what kind? Into “endless equivocation” (*amarāvikkhepa*); the meaning is, into a limitless diversion.
In such passages as "Thus, too, it is not for me," "thus, too, it is not for me" refers to undetermined wavering.
"Likewise, too, it is not for me" rejects the eternalist view stated as "the self and the world are eternal.
"Otherwise, too, it is not for me" rejects partial eternalism stated as being otherwise than eternal. "Not, too, it is not for me" [refers to] "a Tathāgata does not exist after death..."
By saying "not after death," he rejects the doctrine of annihilationism. By saying "not even 'it is not,' nor 'it both is and is not,'" he rejects the speculative view of the logicians (*takkīvāda*).
Furthermore, when asked whether "this is wholesome" or "this is unwholesome," he does not give any answer at all. When asked, "Is this wholesome? he says, "Not even so for me. Then, "What...?"
When it was said, "Is it unwholesome? he replied, "It is not even so for me. When it was asked, "Is it otherwise than both? he replied, "It is not otherwise either for me.
Then, when it was asked, "If it is not in any of these three ways, what is your position? he replied, "It is neither 'it is' nor 'it is not' for me.
Then, when it was asked, "Is your position that it is 'not'? he replied, "It is neither 'not' nor 'not-not' for me. In this way, he merely displayed confusion.
He falls into error and does not stand firm even on one side.
63. Whether out of desire or passion, even if he does not know, he might hastily say of what is wholesome, "It is wholesome," and of what is unwholesome, "It is unwholesome.
Then, [when questioned], "I have explained it thus for such-and-such a person; was that well-explained? he [does not answer] other wise men...

When they had questioned him and it was said by them, “Well explained, good sir! You have indeed explained the wholesome as wholesome and the unwholesome as unwholesome,” [if one thinks], “There is no one as wise as I,” such would be my desire (*chanda*) or passion (*rāga*) therein;
this is the meaning. And here, *chanda* is weak passion, while *rāga* is strong passion. “Hatred (*dosa*) or aversion (*paṭigha*)” refers to the wholesome.
However, having said that what is unwholesome is wholesome, or that what is wholesome is unwholesome, and then having asked other wise people and been told by them,
"You have misstated it," [to think] "I do not even know this much"— this is the meaning of "there would be in me either hatred (dosa) or resentment (paṭigha).
Here too, *dosa* is weak anger, while *paṭigha* is strong anger.

"May that be my clinging; may that be my vexation": thus, that pair consisting of desire and lust would be my clinging (*upādāna*), while the pair consisting of hatred and aversion would be my vexation (*vighāta*).
Alternatively, both together constitute clinging by way of firm grasping, and vexation by way of striking down.
For lust grasps the object through a lack of desire to let go, like a leech; hatred [grasps it] through a desire to destroy.
Like a venomous snake. Both of these are called "clinging" (*upādāna*) and "affliction" (*vighāta*) because they both strike with the quality of causing torment.
The rest is exactly the same as in the first section.
64. "Wise" (*paṇḍita*) means endowed with wisdom. "Skillful" (*nipuṇa*) means possessing subtle and refined intelligence regarding subtle distinctions of meaning.
"Capable of penetration. "Having mastered the doctrines of others" means both having understood the doctrines of others and having gained proficiency in debate with them.
"Like a hair-splitter" means like an archer who splits a single hair.
"They move about as if piercing," meaning they conduct themselves as if piercing even the subtle views of others with their own wisdom, just as a hair-splitter pierces a hair.
The meaning is as follows: "They would question me there" means those ascetics and brahmins would question me regarding those wholesome and unwholesome states.
"They would cross-examine" means they would ask about my doctrine, saying, "State your own view: what is wholesome? What is unwholesome?
"They would press for reasons" means when I have stated, "It is this," they would ask for the reason, saying, "For what cause do you establish this point? "They would rebuke" means...
When it is said, “For this reason indeed,” they would point out a fault in the reason given and thus cross-examine him, saying, “You do not know this;
take this instead, discard that. “They would not succeed” (*na sampāyeyyuṃ*) means they would not achieve [their purpose];
the meaning is that they would not be able to speak after having achieved it. “That would be a distress for me” (*so mamassa vighāto*) refers to that which [happens] again and again.
"Even having spoken, not fulfilling [the promise]" means: "That would be a frustration for me; it would result only in the suffering of drying up my lips, palate, tongue, and throat.
The rest here is exactly the same as in the first section. 65–66.

"Dull-witted" (*mando*) is a name for one of weak wisdom, that is, one who lacks wisdom. "Deluded" (*momūho*) means excessively bewildered. Regarding the phrases "There is a Tathāgata," and so forth...

The term "being" (*satta*) is intended here as the "Tathāgata. The rest of this is self-evident. These four [theories] also fall among those who speculate about the past (*pubbantakappika*), because they are apprehended through views based solely on following phenomena that occurred in the past.
Commentary on the Theory of Fortuitous Origination (*Adhiccasamuppannavāda*):

67. “The self and the world have arisen by chance (adhiccasamuppanna)” — this view is that of chance-arising. Because they possess this [view], they are called “chance-arisers” (*adhiccasamuppannikā*).

“Chance-arisen” means arisen without a cause. 68–73. “Non-percipient beings” (*asaññasatta*) is merely a conventional designation for teaching; the meaning is that their individual existence (*attabhāva*) consists of mere matter (*rūpa*) due to the absence of mental states.
Their arising should be understood as follows: someone, having gone forth in a sectarian order, performs preparatory work on the wind-kasiṇa...
Having attained the fourth jhāna and emerged from that jhāna, he sees the fault in consciousness, thinking:
"In consciousness there is the suffering of having one's hands cut off and so forth, as well as all fears; enough with this consciousness; the state of being without consciousness alone is peaceful.
Having thus seen the fault in consciousness, and without falling away from his jhāna, he passes away and is reborn among the non-percipient beings.
With the cessation of his death-consciousness, his mind turns back right here; only the aggregate of form appears there.

Just as an arrow shot by the force of a bowstring travels through the air for as long as the force of that string lasts, even so, those who have been reborn, impelled by the force of jhāna, remain for as long as the force of that jhāna persists.
But when the momentum of the jhāna has been exhausted, the aggregate of form disappears there, and here the perception of rebirth-linking arises.
Since their passing away from that state is discerned by means of that perception which has arisen here, it is said:
"And with the arising of that perception, those devas pass away from that body. "Santatāya" means for the sake of peacefulness.
The rest here is self-evident. The doctrine of the rationalists (takkīvāda) should also be understood according to the same method already stated.
Thus ends the commentary on the eighteen theorists concerning the past; now, the forty-four theorists concerning the future (aparantakappika).

To show this, he said, "There are, bhikkhus," and so forth. In that context, they are called *aparantakappikā* because they speculate upon and grasp the future limit (*aparanta*), which is designated as a section of time;
or, they are called *aparantakappikā* because such speculation regarding the future limit exists for them.
The remaining [terms] should likewise be understood according to the method already explained above.

**Commentary on the Proponents of Consciousness (Saññīvāda)** 75. *Uddhamāghātanikā*: "Execution ground" (*āghātana*) is said to mean death; those who assert that the self exists after the execution ground are called *uddhamāghātanikā*. A doctrine that proceeds by way of "possessing consciousness" is the "doctrine of consciousness" (*saññīvāda*); those who hold this [view] are the *saññīvādā*. 76–77.
In the phrases "the self possesses form" (*rūpī attā*), etc., the kasiṇa-form is taken as "the self," and the perception occurring therein is taken as "consciousness."
Having grasped [this], like the Ājīvakas and others, or by mere reasoning alone, they describe him thus: "The self is material (rūpī), healthy after death, and percipient (saññī).

In that context, "healthy" means permanent. Or, having taken the sign of the formless attainment as "self" and the perception of that attainment as "perception," like the Nigaṇṭhas and others, or by mere reasoning alone, [they describe him as] "immaterial (arūpī)..."
They describe him thus: "The self exists, is healthy, and possesses perception after death. The third [view], however, proceeds by way of a mixed assumption.

The fourth proceeds solely by way of speculative reasoning. The second tetrad is to be understood in the same manner as that stated for the views concerning finitude and infinitude (*antānantika-vāda*).

In the third tetrad, one possesses a perception of unity by way of one who has attained meditative absorption (*samāpannaka*), and one possesses a perception of diversity by way of one who has not attained it.
It should be understood that one perceives the limited by way of the limited kasiṇa, and one perceives the immeasurable by way of the vast kasiṇa.
Furthermore, in the fourth tetrad, having seen a being being reborn in the plane of the three or four jhānas with the divine eye, one apprehends them as "exclusively happy.
Having seen one being reborn in hell, one apprehends them as "exclusively miserable. Having seen one being reborn among humans...
“Experiencing pleasure and pain”: seeing one being reborn among the Vehapphala devas, he apprehends them as “neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
For those who possess the knowledge of recollecting past lives are specifically speculators about the past, while those with the divine eye are speculators about the future.
Commentary on the Doctrine of Non-percipient Beings.
78–83. The doctrine of non-perception (*asaññīvāda*) is to be understood by way of the two tetrads stated at the beginning regarding the doctrine of perception (*saññīvāda*).

Likewise for the doctrine of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññīnāsaññīvāda*). For while those views were held there by those who grasp "the self is percipient," here they are held by those who grasp "the self is non-percipient" and "the self is neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient.
