In this regard, one need not seek a definitive reason.
For it has been said that the grasp of one who holds wrong views is like the back of a madman.
84. Commentary on Annihilationism:
"When annihilationism exists" means when it is present. "Annihilation" (uccheda) means cutting off. "Destruction" (vināsa) means non-appearance.

They "dissolve" (*vibhavanti*) means the disappearance of existence (*bhāva-vigama*). All these terms are merely synonyms for one another. In this regard, two types of people adopt the annihilationist view (*uccheda-diṭṭhi*):

the one who possesses [the divine eye] and the one who does not. The possessor, having seen with the divine eye the passing away (*cuti*) of an Arahant but not seeing their rebirth (*upapatti*), or whoever is able to see only the passing away and not the rebirth, adopts the annihilationist view.

And one who has not attained [the path] might grasp at annihilationism either out of greed for sensual pleasure, thinking, "Who does not know the next world?", or through reasoning such as, "Just as leaves fallen from a tree do not grow again,
so too are sentient beings. However, it should be understood that these seven views arise here precisely by way of craving and views, having been conceptualized both in that manner and otherwise.
85. Therein, "possessing form" (*rūpī*) means having form. "Consisting of the four great elements" (*cātumahābhūtika*) means made of the four great elements.

"Belonging to mother and father" (*mātāpettika*) refers to what belongs to the mother and father; what is that? It is semen and blood. "Born and produced from what belongs to mother and father" (*mātāpettikasambhava*) means born and arisen from the maternal and paternal [elements].
Thus, by way of the term "form-body," he calls the human existence "self. "In this way, some" (*ittheketi*) means "thus, some"; such is the meaning.

86. The second [type of being], having rejected that [state], speaks of a divine existence (*dibbattabhāva*). "Divine" (*dibba*) means born in the world of the gods (*devaloka*). "Belonging to the sense-sphere" (*kāmāvacara*) means included among the six classes of sense-sphere gods. "One who eats edible food" (*kabaḷīkārāhārabhakkha*) means one who consumes material food consisting of morsels.

87. "Mind-made" (*manomaya*) means produced by means of meditative absorption (*jhāna*). "Possessing all limbs and parts" (*sabbaṅgapaccaṅgī*) means endowed with every limb and member. "With unimpaired faculties" (*ahīnindriya*) means possessing complete faculties.
This is stated both with reference to those [faculties] that exist in the Brahma-world and by way of the configuration of others.
88–92. The meaning of "by completely surmounting perceptions of form" and so forth has been explained in the *Visuddhimagga*.

Regarding the phrases "one who has reached the base of infinite space" and so on, however, the meaning should be understood as "one who has attained existence in the base of infinite space. The rest here is self-evident.
Commentary on the Doctrine of Nibbāna in the Present Life.
93. Regarding the doctrine of Nibbāna in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammanibbānavāda*): "the present life" (*diṭṭhadhamma*) refers to the directly perceived phenomenon;
it is a designation for the individual existence obtained here and there. "Nibbāna in the present life" means Nibbāna within this very individual existence;
the meaning is the pacification of suffering in this very selfhood. Those who propound that [Nibbāna] are called "proponents of Nibbāna in the present life."
"Supreme Nibbāna in this very life" (*parama-diṭṭhadhamma-nibbāna*) means the supreme, highest Nibbāna in the present life; this is the meaning.
(94) "With the five strands of sensual pleasure" (*pañcahi kāmaguṇehi*) means with the five divisions of sensual desire, such as agreeable forms and so forth, or with the fetters thereof.

"Endowed" (*samappita*) means being thoroughly endowed or closely attached. "Possessed" (*samaṅgībhūta*) means being fully equipped. "He enjoys" (*paricāreti*) means [he indulges] in those strands of sensual pleasure.
He moves and shifts his faculties as he pleases, leading them here and there. Or else, he frolics, delights, and plays.
And herein, sensual pleasures are of two kinds: human and divine. Human sensual pleasures should be regarded as similar to those of King Mandhātu;
divine sensual pleasures are like those of the divine king Paranimmitavasavatti. For those who have approached such sensual pleasures...
They proclaim the attainment of Nibbāna in this very life.

In the second section, they should be understood as impermanent in the sense of non-existence, suffering in the sense of oppression, and subject to change in the sense of abandoning their natural state.
Their "change and alteration" refers to the change of those sensual pleasures known as...
Through change, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise according to the method already stated:
"What was mine no longer is mine. In this context, sorrow has the characteristic of inward brooding; lamentation has the characteristic of outward wailing based upon that [sorrow];

pain has the characteristic of bodily oppression; grief has the characteristic of mental affliction; and despair has the characteristic of despondency. The meaning of the passage beginning with "quite secluded from sensual pleasures" is as follows:
This is stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.
96. "Thought" (*vitakkita*) refers to the initial application of mind (*vitakka*) that functions by way of directing the mind toward the object.

"Discursive thought" (*vicārita*) refers to the sustained application of mind (*vicāra*) that functions by way of continued examination. "By this" (*etena*) means by this initial application and by this sustained examination; "this" refers to the first jhāna.
It appears coarse, as if it were covered with thorns.
97–98. *Pītigataṃ* means rapture itself. *Cetaso uppilāvitattaṃ* means that which causes the mind to become elated.
*Cetaso ābhogo* means the repeated application of the mind and attention toward that bliss after emerging from the jhāna.
"Application" (*samannāhāra*)—the rest here is self-evident in the doctrine of Nibbāna in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammanibbānavāda*).
Up to this point, all sixty-two views have been explained. Of these, seven are annihilationist views (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*), while the remainder are eternalist views (*sassatadiṭṭhi*). 100–104.
Now, by means of this section beginning with "These, monks," all those speculators regarding the future limit (*aparantakappika*) are addressed.
Having brought them all together at once, he expounds that very knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
Again, with the section beginning "These, monks," he likewise brings together all those speculators on the past and future and expounds that same knowledge.
Thus, even when asking "And what, monks, are those phenomena? and so forth, he is asking precisely about the knowledge of omniscience.

Even when answering, as if weighing the inclinations of beings with a balance or drawing up sand from the foot of Mount Sineru, he sets aside the sixty-two types of views and answers only with the knowledge of omniscience. Thus this teaching has come down according to its sequence.
For there are three sequences of a sutta: the sequence of questioning, the sequence of intention, and the sequence of natural progression.
In that context, according to the suttas answered by the Blessed One for those who asked thus: "When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
'Venerable sir, what is the near shore? What is the far shore? What is the sinking in midstream? What is the high ground on dry land? What is the seizure by humans?
What is the seizure by non-humans? What is the whirlpool? What is the state of internal putrefaction?'"—it is by means of these [answers].
The connection of the question is to be understood.
Then, a reflection arose in the mind of a certain bhikkhu: "Thus, indeed, form is non-self...
feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness is non-self; surely actions performed by what is non-self..."
“...will touch their own self? Then the Blessed One, having known with his own mind the reflection in the mind of that bhikkhu, addressed the bhikkhus:
“It is possible, bhikkhus, that some foolish man here, being ignorant and immersed in ignorance, might—his mind dominated by craving—think that the Teacher’s instruction should be overstepped.”
—“Thus, indeed, friends, form is not-self... [and so on] ...will they experience it? “What do you think, monks, is form permanent or impermanent?
Having thus understood the inclination of others, the sequence of the underlying intention should be understood according to the suttas spoken by the Blessed One.

However, regarding the sequence of the discourse (*anusandhi*), it should be understood according to those suttas in which the subsequent teaching occurs either by way of a corresponding state (*anurūpadhamma*) or by way of an opposite state (*paṭipakkha*) to that teaching with which the instruction began.
For example, in the *Ākaṅkheyya-sutta*, the teaching begins below with virtue (*sīla*), while above it follows with the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*).
It has arrived. In the *Vattha-sutta*, the teaching arose from defilement below, while the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) appear above.
In the *Kosambaka-sutta*, it arose from quarreling below, while the qualities of conciliation (*sāraṇīya-dhamma*) appear above.
In the *Kakacūpama-sutta*, it arose from impatience below, while the simile of the saw appears above. In this *Brahmajāla-sutta* as well, the teaching [arose] from views below.
Having arisen, the subsequent exposition on emptiness (*suññatā*) follows. Therefore it was said: "Thus this teaching has come down by way of its internal connection.
This concludes the commentary on the section concerning agitation and vacillation ( §§ 105–117).
Now, for the purpose of showing the delimitation of the boundaries, the teaching beginning with "In this regard, monks" (*tatra bhikkhave*) is commenced.
Even that which is experienced by those venerable recluses and brahmins— who do not know and do not see, who are immersed in craving—

is merely the agitation and vacillation of one who is distressed. And that through which they, having become joyful by means of the gratification of views, the pleasure of views, and the feeling of views,
proclaim on four grounds an eternal self and world— that too belongs to them.
For you recluses and brahmins, who do not know and do not see the true nature of phenomena as it really is,
that feeling belongs solely to those possessed by craving; indeed, that feeling is merely a state of agitation and vacillation,
caused by the agitation known as views and the agitation known as craving.
It shows that [the view] is merely quivering, merely moving, merely shaking—like a post driven into a heap of chaff—and not unshakable like the vision of a stream-enterer.
This same method applies to the various eternalist views and so forth.
Commentary on the Section on Contact as Condition.
118–130. Furthermore, the passage beginning with, “In this regard, monks, those recluses and brahmins who are eternalists,” etc., is undertaken for the purpose of showing the chain of conditions.

Therein, the phrase “that too has contact as its condition” means that by whatever gratification in views, pleasure in views, and feeling born of views they experience joy, they proclaim the self and the world to be eternal on four grounds; and that [joy] is also a vibration of craving and views.
This shows that feeling has contact as its condition. This same method applies everywhere.
Now, in order to demonstrate the powerful nature of that condition within the feeling of views, he further says:
"In this regard, bhikkhus, those recluses and brahmins who are eternalists," and so forth. Therein, "those indeed [who hold such views] apart from contact..."
That those ascetics and brahmins will experience that feeling without contact—
there is no such possibility. For just as a pillar is a powerful support for propping up a falling house,
and that house cannot remain standing without being supported by the pillar, even so, contact is a powerful condition for feeling.
He shows that without that [consciousness], this "seen-experience" does not exist. This same method applies everywhere.
144. Commentary on the Cyclic Discussion Based on the Adherence to Views:
Now, monks, as for those recluses and brahmins who are eternalists, [claiming] the self and the world are eternal...

They propound [their views] on four grounds; by the method beginning with "those recluses and brahmins who are partial-eternalists," etc., he groups together all the feelings associated with all views.
Why? For the purpose of including them within contact (*phassa*) above. How?
Because "all those experience [feelings] by repeatedly contacting through the six bases of contact. In that context, the six bases of contact are: [The list of the six bases of contact follows.]
As for the name: there are these six—eye-contact-sphere, ear-contact-sphere, nose-contact-sphere, tongue-contact-sphere, body-contact-sphere, and mind-contact-sphere.
For this term *āyatana* (sphere) occurs in the senses of birth, meeting together, cause, and mere designation.
In that regard: "Kamboja is the sphere (*āyatana*) of horses; the Southern Road is the sphere of cattle."
It occurs in the sense of birth; the meaning is "in the place of birth. In the phrase "Birds frequent that delightful abode," it refers to a meeting place.
In the phrase "Whenever there is a suitable occasion (*āyatana*)," it refers to a cause. In the phrase "They dwell in leaf-huts in forest regions (*araññāyatane*)," it refers to a mere designation.
Now, this term is applicable here in all three senses, beginning with birth. For, in the case of the eye and so forth, the phenomena—of which contact is the fifth—arise (*sañjāyanti*).
They converge, and these are their causes; thus they are called *āyatanas*. However, here, by following the method of the teaching, "Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises;

the meeting of the three is contact," and having introduced the instruction with contact as its head, the sense-bases of contact and so forth are mentioned in order to show the succession of conditions beginning with contact.
"Experiencing by touching again and again" means experiencing after having touched again and again.
And although here it is stated as if the bases (āyatana) have the function of touching, nevertheless their function of touching is not to be understood in that way.
For the bases do not touch; rather, contact (phassa) alone touches each respective object, while the bases [serve as the support] for the contact.

Having been set down, they were shown; therefore, the meaning here should be understood as follows: all those [beings], having touched the objects such as visible forms through contact arising from the six bases of contact (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), experience that feeling born of view (*diṭṭhi-vedanā*).

In the passage beginning "With feeling as condition, craving" (*vedanā-paccayā taṇhā*), "feeling" refers to the feeling arising from the six bases of contact. That [feeling] is divided into craving for visible forms (*rūpa-taṇhā*) and so forth.
Craving is a condition for [clinging] by way of the aspect of decisive support (*upanissaya*). Therefore it was said: "With feeling as condition, craving arises.
Furthermore, that craving is a condition for the fourfold clinging both by way of the aspect of decisive support and by way of the aspect of co-nascence (*sahajāta*).
Likewise, clinging is a condition for becoming. Becoming is a condition for birth by way of the aspect of decisive support.

In this context, "birth" (jāti) should be understood as the five aggregates together with their modifications. Birth is a condition for aging-and-death and for sorrow and the rest by way of decisive support (upanissaya).
This is the summary here; however, the detailed exposition on dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) has been set forth in the *Visuddhimagga*.
Here, only its purpose should be understood. For the Blessed One [taught] the discourse on the round of existence (vaṭṭakathā).
Speaking thus: "Bhikkhus, no prior limit of ignorance is discerned such that one could say, 'Before this, ignorance did not exist;
then afterwards it came into being. Even though this is said, bhikkhus, ignorance is nevertheless discerned as having this specific condition (*idappaccaya*).
Thus, under the heading of ignorance... Bhikkhus, no prior limit of craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*) is discerned... [and so on].
“‘With this as condition, there is craving for existence’—thus, monks, he spoke from the perspective of craving; or ‘the prior limit of the view of existence is not discerned’...
‘With this as condition, there is the view of existence’—thus he spoke from the perspective of views.
But here, speaking from the perspective of views, having explained the views that arise through attachment to feeling, [he speaks] regarding that which is rooted in feeling.
He taught dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*). By this he shows:

"In this way, these proponents of views, having grasped this perspective, run and wander from here to there and from there to here—among the three realms of existence, the four modes of birth, the five destinations, the seven stations of consciousness, and the nine abodes of beings—like oxen yoked to a machine, [tethered] to a post."
"Like a dog tied by a leash, or like a ship driven off course by the wind, they revolve only within the suffering of saṃsāra;
they are unable to lift their heads out from the suffering of saṃsāra. This concludes the commentary on the discourse concerning the turning away from saṃsāra (*vivaṭṭakathā*).
145. Having thus explained the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) based on those who hold to views, the Blessed One now spoke the passage beginning with, "But when, monks, for a monk...
in order to demonstrate the turning away from the cycle (*vivaṭṭa*), taking as his basis a monk who is devoted to the practice of yoga. In this context, "when" (*yataḥ*) means at which time.
"Of the six bases of contact" (*channaṃ phassāyatanānaṃ*) refers to those six bases of contact by means of which, having touched [objects], they experience [feelings].
The cycle of existence turns for those who hold to views; it turns for those very same six bases of contact (*phassāyatana*).

Regarding "origination" and so forth, the origination and other aspects of the bases of contact should be understood according to the method explained in the meditation subject on feeling (*vedanā-kammaṭṭhāna*) by way of such statements as "with the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of the eye," and so on.
However, just as it was stated there: "With the arising of contact, with the cessation of contact..."
In this way, here in regard to the eye and so forth, it should be understood as: "from the arising of nutriment, from the cessation of nutriment. In the sense-base of mind, it is:
"from the arising of name-and-form, from the cessation of name-and-form.
"He understands more excellently" means that one who holds to a speculative view knows only the view; but this [wise person] knows both the view and the view-possessor.
And he knows the higher degrees of virtue, concentration, wisdom, and liberation, up to the stage of Arahantship. Who knows this?

One whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) knows it; an Anāgāmī, a Sakadāgāmī, a Sotāpanna, a learned bhikkhu who has mastered the scriptures, and one who has initiated insight (āraddhavipassaka) know it.
However, the teaching is brought to its conclusion by means of the pinnacle of Arahantship alone.

146. Having thus explained the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭa*), he now began with the words, “Bhikkhus, whoever they may be,” in order to demonstrate that there is no one who holds a speculative view (*diṭṭhigatika*) that is not liberated by this net of teaching.
In this context, “caught within the net” means they have been placed right inside this net of my teaching. “Attached to this” means attached to this net of my teaching.
"Dependent" means "stuck. What is meant by "emerging while emerging"? Even as they sink down and even as they rise up, they remain caught within the net of my teaching; thus they sink and they rise.
"Included herein" means included within this net of my teaching; being bound by it and enclosed within the net, they emerge.
They dive in; there is no one here who is not included among those holding views.
"With a fine-meshed net" means with a soft-meshed net, that is, one with fine openings.

For the Blessed One is like a fisherman, the teaching is like a net, the ten-thousandfold world system is like the small amount of water, and the sixty-two types of theorists are like the coarse creatures.

Just as one standing on its bank and looking out sees that large creatures have been caught within the net, so too does the Blessed One see that all speculative views have been caught within the net of his teaching; in this way, the application of the simile should be understood here.
(147) Thus, because all views are subsumed under these sixty-two views, [the Blessed One knows] all those who hold to speculative views.

Having shown that [the Tathāgata] is included within this web of teachings, he now says, "Bhikkhus, the body of the Tathāgata has cut off the cord of existence," and so forth, in order to show that he himself is not included anywhere therein.
In this context, it is called *netti* because by means of it they lead (*nayanti*). They lead means they drag along, binding them by the neck; this is a term for a rope.
In this context, however, craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*) is intended by the term "rope" (*nettī*) because of its similarity to a rope.

For it leads and draws the great multitude of people toward various states of existence by binding them around the neck; thus, it is called the "rope of existence" (*bhavanetti*). One who has had the rope of existence cut by the sword of the path of Arhatship is "one whose rope of existence is severed" (*ucchinnabhavanettiko*).
"With the breakup of the body" means after the breakup of the body. "With the exhaustion of life" means because of the total exhaustion and complete wasting away of life;
the meaning is that there will be no further rebirth-linking.
"They shall not see him" means they shall not see that Tathāgata—neither gods nor humans shall see him; the meaning is that he will have entered the state of non-designation (*apaṇṇattika*).
"Monks, it is just as if," this is the application of the simile. For the body of the Tathāgata is like the mango tree;
the great stalk that grew on the tree is like the craving that previously existed dependent upon it.
The cluster of mangoes—measuring five hundred, twelve hundred, or eighteen hundred fruits—attached to that stalk is like the things bound by craving when craving exists.
Having sacrificed [the cause], there arise in the future the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements.

Just as when that stalk is cut, all those mangoes follow along with it, having followed that very stalk, and by the cutting of the stalk they are indeed cut—this is the meaning; even so, because the stalk of the "net of existence" has not been severed...

The five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements that might arise in the future—all those phenomena follow in its wake and are governed by the conduit to existence (*bhavanetti*); when that conduit is cut, they are indeed cut—this is the meaning.
Just as, moreover, in that same tree, through contact with the poison of the *maṇḍūka* thorn, [the tree] gradually withers away.
In common parlance, one might say, "In this place there was such-and-such a tree," yet no one actually sees that tree;
likewise, when this body has been broken— having gradually withered away due to the exhaustion of the moisture of craving through contact with the Noble Path—
then after the breaking up of the body and the termination of life, they will not see it.
"Even gods and humans shall no longer behold the Tathāgata; indeed, there will remain nothing more than the mere conventional expression, 'This is the teaching of such a Teacher as this.
Having thus brought [the Buddha] to the element of Nirvana without remainder (*anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu*), he concluded the discourse. 148.
When this had been said, the Venerable Ānanda—thus, when the Blessed One had spoken this Sutta, the Elder [Ānanda] from the beginning...
Having considered the entire discourse and thus illuminated the power of the Buddha, he thought, "The Blessed One has not mentioned the name of the discourse that was spoken;
let me cause its name to be taken. Having reflected thus, he said this to the Blessed One.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Therefore, Ānanda," the construction of the meaning is as follows: Ānanda, because in this Dhamma exposition there is both the benefit here [in this world]...
It is also analyzed according to its benefit for others; therefore, you should remember this discourse on the Dhamma as the "Net of Meaning" (*Atthajāla*).
Furthermore, because many threads of the Dhamma are spoken of herein, you should remember it as the "Net of the Dhamma" (*Dhammajāla*).
And because the supreme knowledge of omniscience is analyzed here in the sense of being sublime (*brahma*), you should remember it as the "Supreme Net" (*Brahmajāla*).
Remember it as "The Net of Views," because sixty-two views are analyzed herein.
Furthermore, remember it as "The Unsurpassed Victory in Battle," because having heard this Dharma discourse,
one is able to crush even the Māra of the Son of a Deva, the Māra of the Aggregates, the Māra of Death, and the Māra of Defilements.

"Thus spoke the Blessed One": from this point, beginning with the conclusion of the introduction up until the words "You may also remember him as 'the unsurpassed victor in battle,'" the Blessed One spoke this entire sutta while revealing his omniscient knowledge— which is supremely profound and finds no footing in the wisdom of others—
just as the sun dispels darkness, he dispersing the great darkness of the various speculative views.
149. "Those bhikkhus were delighted" means those bhikkhus were glad and content; it is said that they became uplifted in mind through the joy directed toward the Buddha.

"The discourse spoken by the Blessed One" refers to this Sutta, which is endowed with the elegance of teaching through various methods, possessing a voice as sweet as the song of the *karavīka* bird, pleasing to the ear, and like a consecration of the Deathless for the hearts of wise people.
The words of the Blessed One, speaking with the Brahma-voice, they rejoiced in, approved of, and accepted.
For this word *abhinandati* occurs in the sense of craving in such passages as "he rejoices in and speaks of";
it also occurs in the sense of approaching in such passages as "both gods and humans rejoice in food."
“In relatives, friends, and dear ones, they rejoice at the arrival of a man who has lived abroad for long and has returned safely from afar. In such passages as these, it refers to welcoming.

In such passages as “having rejoiced and having expressed appreciation,” it refers to expressing appreciation. Here, however, it is appropriate in the sense of both expressing appreciation and welcoming. Therefore it was said: “They rejoiced means they both expressed appreciation and welcomed.”
“The well-spoken, the well-uttered—‘Excellent, excellent!’—thus did the bhikkhus, rejoicing with their heads bowed, receive [the words] of the Tathāgata.
And as for the phrase “in this exposition,” it refers to this sutta devoid of verses (*niggāthaka-sutta*); for it is called an exposition because it is devoid of verses.
"A ten-thousandfold world-system" means a world-system measuring ten thousand world-spheres (*cakkavāḷa*).
Regarding "it shook," it should not be understood that it shook only at the conclusion of the discourse; for it is said, "while it was being recited.
Therefore, as each of the sixty-two views was being dispelled and taught, at the conclusion of each respective view—that is, at each of the sixty-two points—it shook.
It should be understood that [the earth] shook.

In this regard, the earthquake should be understood through eight causes: by the disturbance of the elements, by the power of one possessing psychic potency (iddhimā), by the descent of a Bodhisatta into the womb, by his emergence from his mother’s womb, by his attainment of full enlightenment, and by the setting in motion of the Wheel of Dhamma.
[The Buddha spoke of] the relinquishing of the life-formations and the final Nibbāna.

We shall explain the analysis of these [earthquakes] at the time of commenting on the passage found in the *Mahāparinibbāna Sutta*: "Ānanda, there are these eight causes, eight conditions for the manifestation of a great earthquake. However, this great earth shook on eight other occasions as well.

—In the Great Renunciation, in the approach to the seat of enlightenment, in the taking up of refuse-rags, in the washing of refuse-rags, in the Kāḷaka-ārāma Sutta, in the Gotamaka Sutta, in the Vessantara Jātaka, and in this Brahmajāla [Sutta].
Therein, during the Great Renunciation and the approach to the seat of enlightenment, he was unshaken by the power of energy.
During the taking up of refuse-rags, [he was unshaken] regarding the four great continents surrounded by two thousand islands.

Overcome by the force of wonder, she trembled, thinking: "It was difficult for the Blessed One to do what he has done—renouncing his home, going forth, and going to the charnel ground to take up a rag-robe.
She trembled because of the trembling at the improper time during the *Paṃsukūladhovana* and *Vessantara Jātaka*.
In the *Kāḷakārāma* and *Gotamaka Suttas*, she trembled because of his being a witness, as he said, "I am a witness, Blessed One."

However, it should be understood that when these sixty-two positions of views (*diṭṭhigata*) were being taught by the Elder Mahinda after he had disentangled and cleared them away within this *Brahmajāla Sutta*, the earth shook as a sign of approval.
Moreover, it was not only at these specific points that the earth shook; rather, it also shook during the three communal assemblies (*saṅgaha*) of the Elder Mahinda.
On the day he arrived at this island, sat in Jotivana, and taught the Dhamma, it shook.
Furthermore, when he had swept the courtyard of the Piṇḍapātiya Thera’s cetiya in the Kalyāṇiya Monastery, sat right there, and attained rapture with the Buddha as its object, he began this sutta;
at the conclusion of the sutta, it shook as far as the ocean's edge.
The place to the east of the Lohapāsāda was known as Ambaḷaṭṭhika.
There, while seated, the Dīghabhāṇaka Theras began reciting the Brahmajāla Sutta; even at the conclusion of their rehearsal, the earth shook with its very waters as its boundary.
Thus, by whose power it shook on many occasions—
Having carefully mastered both the Dhamma and the meaning of that *Brahmajāla*, the supreme sutta taught here by the Self-Existent One,
let the wise practice it with systematic attention.
Thus ends the commentary on the Brahmajāla Sutta in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya. 2.
Commentary on the Sāmaññaphala Sutta.

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Ministers of the King (Rājāmaccakathāvaṇṇanā) 150. “Thus have I heard... at Rājagaha” refers to the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta*. Herein is the commentary on the previously unexplained words:
“At Rājagaha” means in the city of that name. For it is called Rājagaha because it was occupied by Mandhātu, Mahāgovinda, and others.
It is so called. Others also describe various other modes here, but what is the use of them? This is merely the name of that city.

Furthermore, this city exists during the time of a Buddha and during the time of a Wheel-turning Monarch (cakkavatti); at other times it is empty, being possessed by *yakkhas*, and remains as a forest inhabited by them.

"Dwells" (*viharatī*) refers, without distinction, to the postures (*iriyāpatha*), the divine dwellings (*dibba-vihāra*), the brahma-dwellings (*brahma-vihāra*), and the noble dwellings (*ariya-vihāra*).

This is an indication of one who possesses a particular abode. Here, however, it is an indication of association with one of the postures—among the divisions of standing, walking, sitting, and lying down.

By this, it should be understood that the Blessed One both dwells and is perceived as dwelling whether standing, walking, sitting, or lying down. For he [relieves] the discomfort of one posture by means of another posture.
Having severed [the continuity], he carries on and maintains his personal existence (attabhāva) without it falling away; therefore, he is said to "dwell" (viharati).
"In Jīvaka Komārabhacca’s mango grove" indicates the location near which he dwells, being dependent upon that village as his resort.
Therefore: "He dwells at Rājagaha in Jīvaka Komārabhacca’s [mango grove]."
"In the mango grove" means that he was dwelling in the mango grove of Jīvaka Komārabhacca near Rājagaha;
this is how the meaning here should be understood. This locative case is used in the sense of proximity. In that regard, he "lives" (jīvati), thus he is Jīvaka;
he is "nourished by a prince" (kumāreṇa bhato), thus he is Komārabhacca. As it is said: "What is this, my man, surrounded by crows? "It is a child, Your Majesty."
“‘Does he live, sir? ‘He lives, Your Majesty. ‘In that case, sir, take that boy to our inner palace and give him to the nurses to raise.
Because they said, ‘He lives (jīvati),’ they gave him the name Jīvaka. Because he was raised by the prince, they gave him the name Komārabhacca.
This, then, is the summary here; for the detailed account, however, it is in the *Jīvakavatthu-khandhaka*.
It has indeed been explained. His account of the legal decision (*vinicchayakathā*) is also stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya.

On one occasion, however, after Jīvaka had purged the Blessed One’s body which was saturated with bile and presented him with a pair of Siveyyaka cloths, he established himself in the fruit of stream-entry at the conclusion of the recitation of the thanksgiving for the robes and thought: "By me..."

"One should go to attend upon the Buddha two or three times a day; however, this Veḷuvana is too far away, whereas my mango grove park is closer. What if I were to have a monastery built for the Blessed One here?
Having thus arranged for night-quarters, day-quarters, caves, huts, pavilions, and so forth in that mango grove, he prepared what was suitable for the Blessed One.

Having had a fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭi) constructed and having had the mango grove enclosed by a wall eighteen cubits high and the color of copper-plate, he gratified the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha with a meal provided with robes, offered the water of dedication, and presented it as a monastery.
It was with reference to this that it was said: "in Jīvaka Komārabhacca’s mango grove."
"With twelve hundred and fifty bhikkhus" means with thirteen hundred bhikkhus less one hundred. Regarding the words "king" and so forth:
he is a *rājā* because by means of his own perfection of sovereignty and the four bases of sympathy (*saṅgahavatthu*), he pleases (*rañjeti*) and increases the great multitude.
He is a *Māgadha* because he is the lord of the Magadhas. By the fortune-tellers it was said: "Even while still unborn, he will become the king's enemy."
"Niddiṭṭho" refers to Ajātasattu.
It is said that when he was conceived in the womb, such a craving arose in the queen: "O, would that I might drink the blood from the king’s right arm!
Thinking, "A craving has arisen for a grave matter; it is not possible to tell anyone," she did not speak of it.
Unable [to fulfill her desire], she became emaciated and disfigured. The king asked her, “My lady, your physical form is not its natural color;
what is the reason? “Do not ask me, Great King,” she replied. “My lady, if you do not tell me your own intention, to whom will you tell it?
Thus, by pressing her in various ways, he made her speak. Having heard it, he said, “Foolish woman, what is there here—”

"Did you perceive it as heavy? Having summoned a physician, she had him cut her arm with a golden knife, took blood in a golden bowl, mixed it with water, and made her drink it. When the fortune-tellers heard of this, they prophesied:
"This fetus will become the king's enemy; by him the king will be slain. When the queen heard this...
Thinking, "It is said that one born from my womb will kill the king," she, desiring to cause an abortion, went to the pleasure grove and had her womb massaged;
yet the fetus did not fall away. She went there again and again and acted in the same manner.
The king, investigating why she was going to the pleasure grove so frequently, heard the reason for it.
“Lady, it is not yet known whether there is a son or a daughter in your womb;
if you act thus toward the child born of yourself, a great heap of demerit will manifest upon the surface of Jambudīpa. Do not do this!
Having thus restrained her, he provided a guard. At the time of her delivery, she thought, “I shall kill him. Even then, the men on guard—
They removed the boy. Then, at a later time, they presented the prince, who had reached maturity, to the queen.
As soon as she saw him, she conceived a motherly affection for him; because of that, she was unable to have him killed. In due course, the king also gave the vice-regency to his son.
Then, on one occasion, Devadatta, having gone into seclusion, thought: "Sāriputta’s retinue belongs to Mahāmoggallāna..."
“The assembly of Mahākassapa is his assembly; thus these are separate responsibilities, and I too shall bring forth my own responsibility.
Thinking, “It is not possible to produce an assembly without material gain;
well then, let me procure some gain,” he reflected, and according to the method set forth in the *Khandhaka*, he won over Prince Ajātasattu with a miracle of psychic power, morning and evening.
Knowing that he was coming for an audience with five hundred chariots and perceiving him to be utterly confident, [the brahmin] approached him one day and said this:
"In the past, young man, humans were long-lived; nowadays they are short-lived.
Therefore, young man, kill your father and become king; I shall kill the Blessed One and become a Buddha. Thus he incited the prince to the murder of his father.
Thus, thinking, "The noble Devadatta is of great power;

there is nothing unknown to him," he bound a pillow to his thigh and, throughout the day, filled with fear, agitation, suspicion, and terror, entered the inner palace and caused the aforementioned disturbance.
Then the ministers seized him and, having interrogated him—[saying], "The prince must be killed, as must Devadatta..."
Having resolved, "And all the bhikkhus must be slain," they informed the king, saying, "We shall act according to the king's command.

The king stripped of their offices those ministers who desired to kill him, and having appointed those who did not desire to kill him to high positions, he asked the prince: "But why, prince, do you wish to kill me?"
“I desire the kingdom, O King,” he said. The king gave him the kingdom.
He informed Devadatta, saying, “My heart’s desire has been fulfilled. Then Devadatta said to him:
“You think you have done well, like a man who has covered a jackal inside a drum; in just a few days, you will—”
“Having considered the insult done to him by her, his father himself will become king. Then [the son asked], “Venerable sir, what shall I do?
“Have him executed by the root. “But, venerable sir, is my father not exempt from the sword?
“Kill him by cutting off his food. He had his father cast into a house of torment; for a “house of torment” is a place for inflicting punishment.
He said, "Build a smoke-house. He then said, "Do not let anyone else see me except my mother.
The queen would place food in a golden bowl, carry it in her lap, and enter. The king, having eaten that, sustained himself.
When the prince asked, "How does my father sustain himself? and heard of this occurrence, he said, "Having made my mother’s lap [his vessel]..."
"Do not allow her to enter," he said. From then on, the queen would enter after placing food inside her hair-tuft.

Hearing of that as well, [the king] said, "Do not allow her to enter with her hair-tuft tied up. Then, having placed food in her golden sandals, she would close them and enter while wearing the sandals.
The king sustained himself by means of that. Again, having asked, "How does she sustain herself?"...
Having heard this matter, he said, "Do not even allow her to enter while wearing sandals.
From that time on, the queen would bathe with scented water, anoint her body with the four sweets, put on her robes, and then enter. The king sustained himself by licking her body.
When he questioned again and heard of this occurrence, he said, "From now on, prevent my mother from entering."
She said: "Lord Bimbisāra, standing at the threshold, she wept and cried out, 'You did not allow them to kill him when he was a youth;
you yourself nourished your own enemy! But this is now your last sight of him;
from now on, I shall no longer be permitted to see you. If I have done you wrong, forgive me, O King! Having spoken thus, she turned back."
From that time on, the king had no food. He sustained himself by walking meditation (*caṅkama*) through the bliss of the path and its fruition.
His physical form shone with extraordinary splendor. Having asked, "My man, how does my father sustain himself?

and hearing the reply, "Your Majesty, he sustains himself by walking meditation; his physical form shines with extraordinary splendor," [the prince thought], "I shall deprive him of his walking meditation."
Having thought, "Cut my father's feet with a razor, smear them with salt and oil, and roast them over glowing acacia coals," he sent for the barbers.
When the king saw them, he thought, "Surely my son must have been instigated by someone;
these men have come to shave my beard. They went and paid their respects.
They stood there. When asked, "Why have you come?", they reported that message.
When told, "Do as your king wishes," they said, "Be seated, Your Majesty," and having paid homage to the king, they said:
"Your Majesty, we are carrying out the king's command; do not be angry with us, for this is not worthy of righteous kings such as yourself."
Having said this, he seized the man’s ankle with his left hand, took a razor in his right hand, slit the soles of his feet,
smeared them with salt and oil, and roasted them over glowing acacia embers. It is said that in the past,
the king had gone onto the courtyard of the cetiya wearing sandals, and had stepped upon a wooden plank prepared for him to sit on with his unwashed feet.
They say that this was the result of that [act]. A powerful pain arose in the king. As he was recollecting, "O Buddha! O Dhamma!
O Saṅgha!", he withered away like a garland of flowers cast upon a shrine courtyard and was reborn in the world of the Four Great Kings as a yakkha named Janavasabha, an attendant of Vessavaṇa.
On that very day, a son was born to Ajātasattu. Two letters arrived simultaneously to announce both the birth of the son and the death of the father.
The ministers, thinking, "We shall report the birth of the son first," placed that letter in the king's hand.
At that very moment, paternal affection for his son arose within the king and pervaded his entire body.
Having shattered [the bone] down to the marrow, he stood there pressing against it. At that moment, he recognized his father’s virtue, thinking:
"Even though I was born, such affection as this arose in my father. He said, "Go, men, and release my father!
They asked, "Why should we release him, Your Majesty? and placed another letter in his hand.
Having heard of that event, he went weeping to his mother and asked, "Mother, did my father have any affection for me when I was born?
She replied, "Foolish son, what are you saying? When you were a small child, a boil broke out on your finger.
Then, unable to console you while you were crying, they took you to the court of justice."
They went into the presence of your father as he was sitting there. Your father placed his finger in his mouth; the abscess burst right in the mouth.
Then, out of affection for you, your father swallowed that pus mixed with blood without even spitting it out.
Such was your father’s affection for you. Having wept and lamented, he performed the funeral rites for his father’s body.
Devadatta also approached Ajātasattu and said, "Great King, command men who will deprive the ascetic Gotama of his life.
Having sent the men provided by the king, he himself climbed Vulture Peak, hurled down a boulder with a machine,
and even released the elephant Nālāgiri, yet he was unable to kill the Blessed One by any means whatsoever.

Unable to recover his lost gains and honor, he requested five specific points; failing to obtain them, he thought, "I shall win over the people by means of these," and thus created a schism in the Saṅgha.

When Sāriputta and Moggallāna departed, taking their following with them, Devadatta vomited warm blood from his mouth and lay upon his sickbed for nine months. Then, overcome with remorse, he asked: "Where..."
Having asked, "Does the Teacher reside here now? and being told, "In the Jeta Grove," he said, "Bring me on a litter and show me the Teacher.

But as he was being brought there, because he had not performed the deed worthy of seeing the Blessed One, he split the earth right there near the lotus pond in the Jeta Grove and fell into the Great Hell. This is the account in this matter.
This is the summary. The method of the detailed exposition is found in the Khandhaka; however, because it has already been included there, it is not stated in its entirety here.
Thus, he was designated by the fortune-tellers as "Ajātasattu" (Unborn Enemy) because he would become the king's enemy even while still unborn.
As for the name "Vedehiputta," he is the son of the daughter of the King of Kosala, not of the King of Videha. Furthermore, "Vedehī" is a synonym for "wise woman."
As it is said: “The housewife Vedehikā; the noble Ānanda is a sage of Vedeḥ. Herein, this is the etymological analysis:
by means of this one knows, thus it is *veda*; this is a designation for knowledge. One who strives, exerts himself, or endeavors by means of *veda* is a *vedehī*.
The son of a *vedehī* is a *vedehiputta*.
*Tadahūti* means "on that day. *Uposatho* (fast-day) is so called because they dwell (*upavasanti*) there;
"they dwell" means they live having become endowed with virtue or fasting. Herein, this is the extraction of the meaning:
in such passages as "Come, friend Kappina, let us go to the Uposatha," the Uposatha is the recitation of the Pātimokkha. [In the passage] "Thus, endowed with the eight factors..."

In such passages as, “The Uposatha has been observed by you, Visākhā,” it refers to virtue (*sīla*). In such passages as, “For the pure one, there is always the month of Phagguna; for the pure one, there is always the Uposatha,” it refers to the observance (*upavāsa*).

In such passages as, “The Uposatha is the name of a king of nāgas,” it refers to a designation (*paññatti*). In such passages as, “Monks, on that very day of the Uposatha, [one should not depart] from a residence where monks are present,” it refers to the day on which one should observe the fast. Here too, that very same meaning is intended. Furthermore, this...

It is threefold, according to the division into the eighth, the fourteenth, and the fifteenth [of the lunar fortnight]. Therefore, in order to exclude the remaining two, it is stated as "the fifteenth.
For this very reason it was said: "It is called *uposatha* because they observe the fast (*upavasanti*) therein.
"On the *Komudī*" means on the night of the full moon when water-lilies (*kumuda*) abound; for at that time, it is said, the water-lilies are in full bloom, and they are present there.
*Komudī*. Regarding *cātumāsiniyā*: it is *cātumāsiyā*, for that is the conclusion of four months;
thus it is called *cātumāsī*. Here, however, it is called *cātumāsinī*. It is "full" (*puṇṇā*) because it is full of months, full of seasons, and full of years;
thus it is "complete" (*sampuṇṇā*). "Mā" refers to the moon; when that is full, it is "the full moon" (*puṇṇamā*). Thus, [it means] "on the full moon" (*puṇṇāya puṇṇamāyā*).
And the meaning should be understood from these two phrases:
"surrounded by royal ministers" [refers to her] being as if the quarters of space were being washed by streams of milk issuing from silver jars, and being completely encircled by strings of pearls,
garlands of *sumana* flowers, white silk garments, and clusters of white lotuses falling from a silver palace.
And the meaning is that he was surrounded by royal ministers on a night illuminated by the rising radiance of the full moon, which is free from the four types of defilements.
"Having gone to the excellent upper palace" means having gone to the top of the excellent palace. He was seated upon a golden throne beneath a costly, raised white parasol.
Why was he seated there? For the purpose of dispelling sleep. For this king, from the day his father passed away...
Having set out with the thought, "I shall go to sleep," as soon as his eyes were closed, he woke up crying out as if struck by seven hundred spears.
When asked, "What is this?", he replied, "Nothing. Thus, sleep was unpleasant to him;
therefore, he sat down for the purpose of dispelling that sleep. Moreover, on that day, the festival had been proclaimed.
It was so. The entire city was sprinkled and swept, strewn with sand, its doorways adorned with jars filled with five-colored flowers and parched grain;
all quarters were decorated with raised banners and flags and illuminated by rows of brilliant lamps.
It was crowded with great crowds of people enjoying the festival of the constellations along the lanes, the squares, and the streets. Thus, it was also because it was a day of the constellations.
“They say he is sitting,” they said. Yet, even after saying this, they reached the conclusion: “For a royal family, there is always a festival;
he is merely sitting here for the sake of dispelling sleep.
He uttered an *udāna*—that is, he uttered an exclamation—just as oil that cannot be contained in a measure overflows.
That which flows [into a pond] is called an *avaseka*. And that water which is unable to enter a pond, but passes over it, is called a *ogha* (flood).
In the same way, that joyful speech which is unable to enter the heart, but being excessive, does not settle within and exits outward, is called an *udāna*. Such is this joy-filled [utterance].
The meaning is that he uttered these words.
"Dosiṇā" means free from fault; it is said to be devoid of these five secondary defilements: clouds, mist, smoke, dust, and Rāhu.
Therefore, "ramanīyā" and so forth are the five words of praise. For she [is] to the great multitude...

It is "delightful" (ramaṇīyā) because it delights the mind. It is "beautiful" (abhirūpā) because it is exceedingly well-formed due to being illuminated by moonlight free from the aforementioned defects.
It is "worth seeing" (dassanīyā) because it is fit to be seen. It is "gracious" (pāsādikā) because it gladdens the heart.
It is "characteristic" (lakkhaññā) because it is fit to serve as a sign for days, months, and so forth.
"Who indeed today, who indeed today—whether a *śramaṇa* or a *brāhmaṇa*? One is a *śramaṇa* by virtue of having stilled evil;
one is a *brāhmaṇa* by virtue of having banished evil. The grammatical construction here is "whom we might attend upon"; the meaning is:
"Whom, while attending upon him by way of asking questions, our minds might become serene upon hearing the sweet Dhamma. Thus, with this [the King spoke].
With every word he uttered, he performed the preliminary rite for the appearance of a vision. For whom did he perform it? For Jīvaka. For what purpose?
For the sake of seeing the Blessed One. Was he unable to approach the Blessed One himself to see him?
Yes, he was unable. Why? Because of his great transgression.
"In that case, the noble disciple who was the Blessed One’s attendant had his own father killed, and Devadatta, relying on him, caused much harm to the Blessed One;
thus he is one of great offense. Because of that great offense, he is unable to go himself.
But Jīvaka is the Blessed One’s attendant; thinking, 'I shall see the Blessed One in the shadow of his back,' [he goes]."
He performed the act of producing a sign of light. But did Jīvaka know, "This is my act of producing a sign of light"?
Yes, he knew it. Then why was he silent? For the purpose of cutting off distraction.
For in that assembly many attendants of the six teachers had gathered; they were untrained...

Because they had not themselves trained through such attendance, when I began to speak of the Blessed One’s virtues, they would repeatedly rise from their seats to speak of the virtues of their own teachers;
thus, my discourse on the Teacher’s virtues would not reach its conclusion.
However, the King, having approached these family attendants, was captivated by their lack of essence and was won over by their talk of their own virtues.

“Thinking, ‘If he remains displeased, he will question me; then, having recounted the Teacher’s virtues without hesitation, I shall take the king to the Teacher’s presence,’ I remained silent for the purpose of cutting off his distraction, even though I knew this.
Those ministers also thought thus: “Today the king has praised [the Buddha] with five verses throughout the night; surely there must be something...”
“Having approached either a recluse or a brahmin and asked him a question, he desires to hear the Dhamma;
and having heard the Dhamma from whomsoever he gains confidence, he will pay great honor to that person.
But as for the recluse who frequents his family, if he frequents the royal court, it is well for him.”
151–152. Having thought thus—“I will go, taking the king with me, after speaking in praise of my own personal attendant ascetic;
I will go”—they began to speak in praise of their respective personal attendants. Therefore he said:
“When this was said, a certain royal minister,” and so forth. In that context, *Pūraṇa* is the name of that one who claimed to be a teacher.
“Kassapa” is his clan name. It is said that he was born as the one who completed a family’s ninety-nine servants;
therefore, they gave him the name Pūraṇa (The Completer). Because he was a lucky servant, there was no one to tell him, “This is ill-done,” or “This has not been done.
He thought, “Why do I live here? and fled. Then robbers stripped him of his clothes.
Not even knowing how to cover himself with leaves or grass, he entered a village with nothing but his gold.
Seeing him, people thought, "This ascetic is an arahant of few desires; there is no one like him," and they approached him bringing cakes, rice, and other offerings.
He thought: "It is because I am without a garment to wear that this has arisen for me. Then—
From that time on, even after receiving a garment, he did not wear it; instead, he took up the going-forth (pabbajjā).

In his presence, others and yet others—five hundred people in all—went forth. With reference to him, it says: "Pūraṇa Kassapa. He is called *saṅghī* because he possesses a *saṅgha*, which is a collection of those who have gone forth.
He is called *gaṇī* because he possesses a *gaṇa*, which is that very same group.
A teacher of a group (*gaṇācariyo*) is one who is the teacher of that group by way of training them in conduct (*ācāra*). "Renowned" (*ñāto*) means well-known or famous.
"Famous" (*yasassī*) means he possesses a reputation that has arisen in this way: "He is of few desires and content; out of fewness of desires, he does not even wear a robe.
A "founder of a sect" (*titthakaro*) is one who establishes a doctrine (*laddhi*). "Esteemed as good" (*sādhusammato*) means: "This one is good, beautiful, a true person (*sappuriso*)."
Thus he is esteemed. "Of many people" means of the unlearned, blind, foolish worldling.
He is called *rattaññū* because he knows that many nights have passed since his going forth. He is one who has gone forth for a long time (*cirapabbajita*);
for the talk of one who has recently gone forth is not easily accepted as authoritative, hence he says "one who has gone forth for a long time. He is one who has reached a great age (*addhagata*).
"Who has gone on a journey" means one who has passed through two or three royal successions; this is the intended meaning.
"One who has reached old age" means one who has arrived at the final stage of life. Both of these [terms] were spoken with reference to the statement: "A story told to a youth is not to be trusted.
"He remained silent" refers to a man who, desiring to eat a golden-colored, sweet-tasting mango fruit, had it brought and placed in his hand.

Seeing that [the Buddha] was like a dish of *kājarapaka* (a sweetmeat) set before him, he desired to hear the sweet discourse on the Dhamma—endowed with the qualities of the jhānas and higher knowledges (*abhiññā*), and struck by the three characteristics (*tilakkhaṇa*). Previously, even at the sight of Pūraṇa, he had been displeased;
now, becoming even more displeased by this talk of virtues, he remained silent. Although he was displeased, he thought: "If I were to rebuke him and seize him by the neck..."

Thinking, "Having seized him, I will have him led away; then, fearing that 'the king does this to whoever speaks,' no one else will say anything," he consented even to that unpleasant speech and remained silent.
Then another, thinking, "I shall speak in praise of my own family priest," began to speak. Thus it was said:
"—Another one too," and so forth. All of that is to be understood according to the method already stated.
Herein, "Makkhali" was his name; because he was born in Gosālā, "Gosāla" was his second name.
It is said that as he was walking on muddy ground carrying an oil jar, his master said to him, "Dear boy, do not stumble (mā khalī)."
Thus, having stumbled and fallen through negligence, he began to flee out of fear of his master.
His master ran after him and seized him by the hem of his garment. He cast off his cloth and fled naked.

The rest is exactly like the account of Pūraṇa. "Ajita" is his name. Because he wears a blanket of hair, he is called "Kesakambala. Thus, by combining these two names, [he is known as Ajita-kesakambala].
He is called Ajita Kesakambala. In this context, "hair-cloth" (kesakambala) refers to a blanket made from human hair;
there is no garment more wretched than that. As it has been said:
"Bhikkhus, just as among all garments woven from threads, the hair-cloth is declared to be the most wretched. The hair-cloth, bhikkhus..."
"In cold weather he is cold; in hot weather he is hot; he is ill-favored, foul-smelling, and unpleasant to the touch.
"Pakudha" is his name, and "Kaccāyana" is his clan. Thus, combining both name and clan, he is called Pakudha Kaccāyana.
He is one who rejects cold water; even after defecating, he does not perform the act of washing with water.
Having obtained hot water or sour gruel, he prepares it;
or, having crossed a river or a puddle on the road, thinking "my virtue is broken," he builds a mound of sand, resolves upon his virtue, and goes on his way.
Such a person is one who has acquired a lack of dignity. "Sañcaya" is his name. "Belaṭṭha’s son" means the son of Belaṭṭha.

156. Because he was given the name "Nigaṇṭha" (Fetterless) due to his claim, "We have no fetters of grasping, no fetters of attachment; we are free from the fetters of the defilements," he is called Nigaṇṭha.
He is the son of Nāṭa, thus "Nāṭaputta. 157. Then the king...
[The king, it is said, having heard their words, thought: "I shall [investigate] the statement of whomever..."

He did not wish to hear it, so he spoke for himself alone. But as for the one who wished to hear my words, he remained silent like a garuḍa that has drunk the elixir of the nāgas; alas, this is a loss for me! Then it occurred to him:
“Jīvaka is an attendant of the peaceful Buddha, the Blessed One; he too is peaceful, and therefore, like a bhikkhu perfected in his duties...”
"He sits there as if silent; he will not speak unless I speak first. When an elephant is trampling, one must seize the elephant's very foot.
Thinking thus, he began to deliberate with him himself. Therefore it is said: "Then the king... In this context, "why silent?
means for what reason was he silent? [He thought: "Of these ministers, each for himself..."
When they speak in praise of his personal attendant monk, his face does not brighten.
He asks: "Is it because your personal attendant monk is not like theirs? Are you poor? Was authority not granted to you by my father? Or is it that you lack faith?"
Then it occurred to Jīvaka: "This king is having the virtues of the ascetic who attends upon my family recounted. It is no longer time for me to remain silent;

however, just as these [other] ascetics who attend upon his family have remained seated after bowing to the king and recounted the virtues of their own teachers, it is not fitting for me to recount the virtues of the Teacher in such a manner. Having risen from his seat, he approached the Blessed One.
Facing the monastery, he prostrated with the fivefold contact and, raising his hands in a brilliant añjali with the ten nails joined together to his head, said:
"Great King, do not think of me thus: 'This man approaches some ascetic or other.
For when my Teacher descended into his mother’s womb, when he emerged from his mother’s womb, and at his Great Renunciation—"

“At the time of his full enlightenment and at the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, the ten-thousandfold world system trembled; likewise he performed the Twin Miracle, and likewise the Descent from the Heavens.
I shall speak of the Teacher’s virtues; listen with a one-pointed mind, O Great King. Having said this, he spoke:
“This, O King, is the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One,” and so forth. Therein, that indeed...
"Bhagavantam" is the accusative case used in the sense of describing one who has become such [an exalted being];
its meaning is "to that Blessed One. "Kalyāṇa" means endowed with excellent qualities; what is meant is that he is supreme. "Kittisaddo" is simply fame, or the sound of praise.
"Abbhuggato" means risen up, having spread over the world including the devas. How so? "Thus indeed is the Blessed One..."
“The Blessed One is an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One...
[etc. ...the Blessed One. Herein, this is the connection of the words: “That Blessed One is indeed an Arahant, indeed a Perfectly Enlightened One... [etc. ...indeed the Blessed One.

This means: “for these and those reasons. In that context: because he is far from (ārakatta) defilements, and because he has slain (hata) his enemies (arīnaṃ) and the spokes (arānaṃ) of the wheel of existence.

Because he is worthy (arahant) of requisites and so forth, and because he is devoid of worthiness (rahābhāva) for the performance of evil—it is by such reasons as these that the Blessed One should be understood as "Worthy" (Arahan).
Having thus set forth the outline (mātikā), all these terms have been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga* in the section on the Recollection of the Buddha;
therefore, their detailed exposition should be taken from there.

But Jīvaka, having explained the meaning of each word, said: "In this way, Great King, the Blessed One is my Teacher; in this way he is the Perfectly Enlightened One... [and so on] ...in this way he is the Blessed One.
Then he added: "May Your Majesty attend upon that Blessed One; perhaps as Your Majesty attends upon him, your heart will find confidence. And here—
Saying, "Let the King attend upon him," he said, "Great King, even if you were to question my Teacher— a hundred times, a thousand times, or a hundred thousand times like yourself—
I have both the power and the strength to capture the minds of them all and explain it;
therefore, Great King, approach him with confidence and ask."
As the king listened to the discourse on the virtues of the Blessed One, his entire body was suffused without interruption by five-colored rapture (*pīti*).
Desiring to depart at that very moment, he thought: "At this hour, no one other than Jīvaka will be able to yoke the vehicles quickly for me as I go into the presence of the One of Ten Powers."
Having reflected, he said: "In that case, my dear Jīvaka, have the elephant-vehicles prepared.
In this context, "tena hi" is a particle used for the purpose of exhortation; it means, "Go then, my dear Jīvaka. Regarding "elephant-vehicles":
although many vehicles such as horse-drawn chariots and others were available, the elephant-vehicle is the most excellent; [he sent him] to the presence of the Most Excellent One.
Thinking, "One must proceed by means of the supreme vehicle," and considering that while the sounds of horse-drawn carriages and chariots are heard from afar,
one does not even hear the sound of an elephant-vehicle when walking step for step behind it—
and that near the Blessed One, who has attained *nibbāna*, one must proceed by vehicles that have themselves attained *nibbāna*— he said, "elephant-vehicles."
"Five hundred female elephants" means five hundred she-elephants (*kareṇu*). "Having had them prepared" means having had them made ready for mounting.
"Fit for mounting" means suitable for riding; the sense is that they were covered with trappings. But what did he do—did he do what was commanded by the king, or what was not commanded?
He did what was not commanded. Why? Because of his wisdom. For it occurred to him thus: "The king says, 'I am going at this time.'"

Kings, indeed, have many enemies. If some obstacle should arise on the way, they will reproach me, saying, "Jīvaka is taking the king away even at an improper time, thinking, 'How shall I seize the king for myself?
They will also reproach the Blessed One, saying, "The ascetic Gotama, thinking 'my talk is proceeding,' has preached the Dhamma without even observing the proper time."
“...so he speaks. Therefore, thinking, “I shall act in such a way that neither blame arises for me nor for the Blessed One, and the King’s protection is well-arranged,” [he reflected]:
“There is no fear for men when they rely on women; thus, surrounded by women, I shall go in comfort.”
Having prepared five hundred female elephants and had five hundred women take on the appearance of men, he said, "Surround the king with swords and spears in hand," and then he thought:
"In this present existence, this king lacks the necessary support (upanissaya) for the paths and fruits;
and Buddhas, indeed, preach the Dhamma only when they perceive such support. Well then, I—"
“I shall assemble the great multitude; for if this happens, the Teacher will teach the Dhamma out of compassion for someone, and that will be of benefit to the great multitude.
Thus he sent messengers here and there and caused a drum to be beaten, proclaiming:
“Today the King goes into the presence of the Blessed One; let everyone provide protection for the King according to their own means.”
Then the great multitude thought: “It is said that the king is going for the purpose of seeing the Teacher; what kind of Dhamma teaching will there surely be?
What is the use of our festival games? We shall go right there.
Taking perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, they all stood on the road, longing for the king’s arrival. Jīvaka also informed the king: “The preparations have been made...”
“Your elephant-vehicles are ready, Your Majesty; now do as you deem it the right time.
In this context, the phrase “now do as you deem it the right time” is a formal expression of courtesy. This is what is meant:
“That which was commanded by you has been done by me; now, whether it be the time for going or not going, do exactly as you yourself desire.”
159. “Paccekā itthiyo” means separate women; it is said that for each female elephant there was one woman.
“Ukkāsu dhāriyamānāsu” means while torches—namely, staff-lamps—were being carried. “Mahacca rājānubhāvena” means with great royal majesty. The reading “mahaccā” also exists;
its meaning is “mahatiyā” (with a great [majesty]), this being a change of gender. Royal majesty...
This is called royal supernormal power (*rājiddhi*). What, then, is his royal supernormal power? It is the sovereign glory over two great kingdoms extending three hundred *yojanas*.

For on a certain day, even though there had been no prior arrangement that the king would approach the Tathāgata, at that very moment five hundred women took male attire, fastened turbans upon their shoulders, and—
Taking swords with blades drawn and lances with jeweled handles, they went forth. It was with reference to this that it was said:
"having mounted separate women.
Furthermore, sixteen thousand khattiya dancing-women surrounded the king; at their outer edge were the hunchbacks, dwarfs, Kirātas, and others.
At their edge were the palace guards, trusted men. At their edge were about sixty thousand high ministers, dressed in various colorful garments and ornaments.

At their edge were about ninety thousand sons of the nobility, adorned with diverse decorations and holding various kinds of weapons in their hands, like young masters of the *vidyādhara* arts. At their edge were [those worth] a hundred coins...

Having dressed themselves in robes worth five hundred pieces of gold, having arranged one shoulder bare, well-bathed, well-anointed, and adorned with various ornaments such as golden garlands, about ten thousand brahmins went along raising their right hands and shouting cries of victory.
Surrounding them were musical instruments of the fivefold type. Surrounding those was a perimeter of rows of bows. Of that—
At the edge were herds of elephants. At the edge of the elephants, they neighed as they struck neck against neck.
At the edge of the horses were chariots clashing with one another. At the edge of the chariots were warriors striking arm against arm.
At their edge stood the eighteen divisions of the army, resplendent with their respective wealth of ornaments.
Thus, just as an arrow shot while standing at the edge does not reach the king, so Jīvaka Komārabhacca, having made arrangements for the king’s retinue, went himself very close to the king, thinking:
"If any danger should arise, I shall first give the gift of life to the king. As for the torches, there were several hundreds or thousands of them.
It is said, “There was no distinction [in the scent],” with reference to such royal supernormal power (iddhi):
“By means of his great royal majesty, he went to where Jīvaka Komārabhacca’s mango grove was.
Regarding the phrase “fear indeed arose,” there is here fear as mental trepidation, fear as knowledge, fear as the object, and fear as moral dread (ottappa).

There are four kinds of fear. Among them, that which is described by way of the formula beginning, "In dependence on birth, there is fear, there is terror," is called the fear of mental trepidation (*cittutrāsabhaya*).

That which comes in such passages as, "Having heard the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma, they for the most part fall into fear, agitation, and terror," is called the fear of knowledge (*ñāṇabhaya*). [And as in: "Surely this fear and dread is coming."
Herein, what is called the fear of the object has been stated:
"They praise the timid one, for there is no hero therein;
for out of fear, the virtuous do not commit evil."
This is what is called the fear of moral dread (*ottappabhaya*). Among these, here it refers to the fear that is a trembling of the mind;
the meaning is "it has been," or "it occurred. *Chambhitatta* is the state of being tremulous; the meaning is the shaking of the entire body. *Lomahaṃsa* is the bristling of the hair;
the meaning is the standing up of the hairs on the body. Furthermore, this bristling of the hair may also occur through rapture (*pīti*) at times such as when hearing the Dhamma.
It occurs. It may also occur through fear in those of a timid nature when seeing battles, demons, and the like; here it should be understood as "fear and horripilation.
But why was he afraid? Some say it was because of the darkness. It is said that in Rājagaha there were thirty-two great gates and sixty-four small gates.
[The place] was between Jīvaka’s mango grove and the wall and Vulture Peak.
He went out by the eastern gate and entered the shadow of the mountain;
there, the moon was obscured by the mountain peak, and because of the mountain’s shadow and the shadows of the trees, it became dark—yet even this is not the cause.
For at that time, there would have been no distinguishing even a hundred thousand torches.
But this [king] was afraid because he suspected Jīvaka, owing to the quietness [of the place]. It is said that Jīvaka informed him from the upper palace itself:
"Great King, the Blessed One loves quiet; he should be approached only in silence.
Therefore, the king silenced the musical instruments. The instruments were merely held, and even speech was not raised loudly.
Moving about without making a sound by means of the perception of a celestial nymph, they proceeded; not even the sound of a fruit falling from anyone’s tree in the mango grove could be heard.
Kings, it is said, are fond of noise. On account of that silence, the king became dissatisfied and conceived suspicion toward Jīvaka, saying:
"This Jīvaka has brought twelve hundred and fifty bhikkhus into my mango grove."
"And here not even the sound of a thrown object is heard; I think it is a fabrication.
This man, having deceived me and led me out of the city, has stationed a military force in front and intends to seize me for himself so that he may raise the royal parasol.
For he possesses the strength of five elephants, and he is walking close behind me, right near me."
"I do not have even a single man with a weapon in his hand. Alas, what a calamity for me! Having thus become afraid, he was unable to maintain an appearance of fearlessness;
he revealed his state of terror to him. Therefore it is said: "Then the king... [there was] no sound.
In that context, *samma* is a term of address for a friend, meaning "Friend, how is it with me?"
It was said: "Do you not deceive me? means: having said that what does not exist exists, do you not mislead me?
"The sound" refers to the sound of conversation and discourse.
"Do not fear, Great King," Jīvaka [said], thinking: "This king does not know me, thinking, 'This man does not deprive another of life.'"

Thinking, "If I do not reassure him, he will perish," and having resolved to reassure him firmly, he said, "Do not fear, Great King," and spoke the words beginning with, "It is not you, O Deva. "Abhikkama" means "come forward," that is, go toward [me];
the sense is "enter. Since saying it only once would not be firm enough, he spoke it twice while hurrying. These...
"Great King, lamps are burning in the assembly hall. A band of thieves does not remain having lit a lamp;
yet these lamps are burning in the assembly hall. 'Go, Great King,' he says, by means of this perception of a lamp.
*Commentary on the Question on the Fruits of the Ascetic Life* (Sāmaññaphala-pucchā-vaṇṇanā)
160. "The ground for an elephant" (*nāgassa bhūmi*) refers to that place where one who has mounted an elephant is able to go;
this is what is called the ground for an elephant. "Having dismounted from the elephant" means having descended from the elephant at the outer gatehouse of the monastery.
At the very moment he set foot upon the ground, the majesty (*tejo*) of the Blessed One pervaded the King’s body. Then, at that very instant—
Sweat poured from his entire body; his robes seemed as if they had to be wrung out and removed.

Remembering his own transgression, a great fear arose within him. Unable to go straight into the presence of the Blessed One, he took Jīvaka by the hand and, as if walking through the monastery grounds, said: "This, my dear Jīvaka, has been well done by you; this..."
Praising the monastery by saying, "It has been well constructed," he gradually approached the door of the assembly hall;
the meaning is that he arrived there.
But why did he ask, "Where is the Master? Some say it was because he did not know. It is said that during his youth...
[The opponent argues: "The Blessed One had previously been seen coming together with his father;

however, later, through association with evil friends, having committed patricide, dispatched assassins, and caused Dhanapāla to be released, he became a great offender and had never before approached the presence of the Blessed One.
[The author replies: He asks this because he does not recognize [the truth]. That is not the reason, for the Blessed One is endowed with the most excellent marks (*ākīrṇavaralakṣaṇa*).

Adorned with the secondary marks and illuminating the entire monastery with six-colored rays of light, he sat in the center of the circular pavilion surrounded by a host of monks like the full moon surrounded by a multitude of stars—who would not know him?
Yet, he asks this out of the playful exercise of his sovereignty; for it is the nature of royal families that even when they know [the answer], they inquire.
They ask as if they were ignorant. But Jīvaka, having heard that, thought: "This king stands before the One of Ten Powers and asks, 'Where is the Blessed One?

like one who, while standing on the earth, asks 'Where is the earth?', or looking up at the sky, asks 'Where are the moon and sun?', or standing at the foot of Sineru, asks 'Where is Sineru? He thought, "I shall show him the Blessed One."
Thinking, "I shall point him out," he extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One and said, "This one, O Great King," and so forth.
"Purakkhato" means sitting in front of one who is seated surrounded by a retinue.
"Yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami" means he went to where the Blessed One was; that is, he approached the presence of the Blessed One.

The meaning is "having approached. "He stood to one side" means that, without obstructing either the Blessed One or the community of monks, he paid homage to the Blessed One and stood alone in a place suitable for himself to remain.
"Silent, silent" means that wherever he looked, he saw only those who were likewise silent. For in that place—
Not even a single bhikkhu displayed fidgeting with his hands or feet, nor was there the sound of sneezing;
not even a single bhikkhu looked toward the king or the royal assembly standing before the Blessed One, though they were adorned with every ornament and surrounded by dancers.
All sat gazing only at the Blessed One.

The king, having gained confidence in their tranquility and repeatedly gazing upon the Saṅgha of bhikkhus whose faculties were calmed—like a lake that is clear and free from mud—uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*).

In this context, "by this" means by that tranquility of virtue (*sīla-upasama*) consisting of bodily, verbal, and mental conduct, by which the Saṅgha of bhikkhus is peaceful; [it is] "by this tranquility."
