He illuminates this point. In that context, he did not say this with the thought, "Oh, may my son, having gone forth, become as peaceful as these bhikkhus.
Rather, having seen the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and being inspired with confidence, he recollected his son.
For it is a common occurrence in the world that when one has obtained what is difficult to find, or upon seeing something wonderful, one recollects those dear to one, such as kinsmen and friends.
It was his natural disposition. Thus, seeing the community of monks and recollecting his son, he spoke these words.
Moreover, out of concern for his son and desiring his welfare, he spoke thus.
For it occurred to him: "My son will ask, 'My father was young; where is my grandfather? To which I shall reply, 'He was killed by your father.'"
Having heard this, he will think, "I too shall have my father killed and rule the kingdom.
Thus, desiring his pacification out of apprehension regarding his son, he spoke in this way. For even though he spoke thus, his son would surely have him killed;
for in that lineage, the killing of a father had occurred five times in succession. Ajātasattu [killed] Bimbisāra.
Udaya killed Ajātasattu. His son was named Mahāmuṇḍika; he killed Udaya. His son was named Anuruddha; he killed Mahāmuṇḍika.

His son was named Nāgadāsa; he killed Anuruddha. But as for Nāgadāsa, the inhabitants of the kingdom, being incensed, had him executed, saying, "These are kings who have cut off our lineage; what is the use of these?"
Why did he say, "You have indeed come"? It is said that even before the King had uttered a word, the Blessed One thought:
"This king has arrived and stands silent and speechless; what is he thinking? Then, knowing his mind, [the Blessed One realized]:
"Being unable to converse with me, he has looked upon the Saṅgha of monks and remembered his son."
"However, he will not be able to say anything while I remain silent; therefore, I shall engage him in conversation.
Thus, immediately after the king spoke, he said, "You have come, Great King, according to your affection. The meaning of this is:
Great King, just as water that has fallen upon a high ground flows toward the lowlands, even so you—
"Having surveyed the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he went toward where his affection lay.
Then it occurred to the king: "Oh, how wonderful are the qualities of the Buddha! There is no one like me who has committed an offense against the Blessed One;
for I had my chief supporter killed, and having accepted the words of Devadatta, I plotted his murder."

“He was sent away, Nāḷāgiri was released, and because of me Devadatta hurled the rock—yet the face of the One Possessed of Ten Powers does not turn away even as he addresses me with such great offense!
Oh, how well-established the Blessed One is in the characteristics of an ‘Arahant’ (tādi) through these five ways!
Having abandoned such a Teacher, we shall not seek one elsewhere. Thus he was filled with joy.
Addressing the Blessed One, he said, "Venerable sir, you are dear to me," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "having extended his joined palms toward the community of bhikkhus": it is said that this thought occurred to him:

"If, after paying homage to the Blessed One, I were to go here and there and pay homage to the community of bhikkhus, the Blessed One would be left behind; yet [the community] must also be shown respect."
This was not the case. For even by one who, after bowing to the king, bows to the viceroy, disrespect is shown toward the king.
Therefore, having bowed to the Blessed One, he paid homage with joined palms to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus at the very spot where he stood and sat down to one side.
"A certain region" means a certain place.
Then the Blessed One, inspiring him to ask his question, said: "Ask, Great King, whatever you desire. The meaning of this is: "Ask if you so wish;

there is no burden for me in answering your questions. Or alternatively, he extended an invitation of omniscience, saying: "Ask whatever you desire; I shall answer it all," thus making an offering that is not shared by others.
[This is] by means of the Paccekabuddhas, the Chief Disciples, and the Great Disciples. For they do not say, "Ask whenever you wish," but rather, "Having heard [the question], we shall know.
The Buddhas, however, say: "Ask, friend, whenever you wish," or "Ask, Great King, whenever you wish," or:
"Ask me a question, Vāsava, whatever you desire in your mind."
“I shall bring you to the end of each and every question,” or:
“In that case, bhikkhu, sit down on your own seat and ask whatever you desire,” or:
“The doubts of all, both Bāvari’s and yours.”
“Permission has been granted; ask whatever you desire.
Or: “Ask me, Sabhiya, a question—whatever you desire—and for each and every question, I shall bring you to its conclusion.”
They invited the various yakkhas, lords of men, devas, recluses, brahmins, and wanderers to declare their omniscience.

And it is not surprising that the Blessed One, having reached the stage of a Buddha, should offer this invitation. But he who, while still on the stage of a Bodhisatta, stood in partial knowledge, said:
"Koṇḍañña, answer the questions!"
The seers of virtuous form entreat him:
"Koṇḍañña, this is the way among men:
that when one has grown old, this burden comes upon him."
Thus, when requested by the seers for the sake of Sakka and the others:
"May your honors ask whatever question you desire in your minds, having been granted leave."
"For I shall answer each of your questions, having known for myself this world and the next.
Thus it was during the time of Sarabhaṅga. And in the Sambhava Jātaka, after wandering throughout the whole of Jambudīpa three times, [he answered] the questions...

When the Brahmin Sucirata, having failed to see the one who brings an end [to suffering], had been granted the opportunity to ask a question, the seven-year-old boy—while playing in the dust on the street, sitting cross-legged right there in the middle of the road—said:
"Truly, I shall explain it to you, just as one who is skilled; even so."
"And the king indeed knows whether he will do it or not.
Thus did he offer the invitation of omniscience (*sabbaññu-pavāraṇā*).
When the Blessed One had thus offered the invitation of omniscience, the king, being satisfied, asked a question.
He said, beginning with, “Just as these, venerable sir,” and so forth. In that context, *sippa* (craft) itself is *sippāyatana* (the sphere of craft).

*Puthusippāyatanāni* means many crafts. *Seyyathidaṃ* means “which then?”—he shows who those are by means of the terms “elephant-riders,” and so on, namely those who live depending on this or that craft. For this is the intended meaning: “Just as for these who live by their crafts...”
“By means of that craft, the visible fruit of the craft is made known. Is it possible, in this way, to make known a visible fruit of recluseship?
Thus, having brought forward the various fields of craft, he shows those who live by crafts.
Therein, “elephant-riders” refers to all elephant trainers, elephant physicians, elephant tamers, and so forth. “Horse-riders” [refers to...].
All horse-trainers, horse-riders, and horse-grooms, and so forth. Charioteers: all chariot-trainers, chariot-warriors, chariot-guards, and so forth.
Archers: bow-experts and marksmen. Banner-bearers (*celaka*): those who go at the front carrying the victory banner in battle. Standard-bearers (*calaka*):
those who arrange the military formations, thinking, "Let this be the King’s position here; let that be the position of such-and-such a high official. Food-distributors (*piṇḍadāyaka*):...
"Bold great warriors. It is said that they enter the enemy's army and, having cut off the heads of their foes like lumps of meat, they distribute them;
the meaning is that they emerge after leaping up again and again. Or, it is the name for those who, in the midst of battle, take the food-bowls of the warriors and serve them.
"Ugga rājaputtā" means high-born sons of kings who have risen to the highest ranks as combatants.
“Princes. “Volunteers”: those who, having said, “Whose head or weapon shall we bring?
and being told, “Of so-and-so,” enter the battle and bring back exactly that; these are called “volunteers” because they volunteer.
“Great elephants”: like great elephants, they are great elephants; this refers to their fighting without turning back even when elephants and other such creatures are charging toward them.
This is a designation. "Brave men" refers to those who are exclusively brave, capable of crossing the ocean even while wearing their nets and skins.
"Shield-bearers" refers to those who fight having entered into leather armor or having taken up shields for protection against arrows.
"Sons of slave-girls" refers to household slaves who fight out of strong affection. "Cooks" refers to bakers. "Barbers" refers to bath-attendants. "Bathers" refers to...

"Those who wash" refers to bath-attendants. "Cookers" are those who prepare food. "Garland-makers" and the like are well known. "Accountants" are those who recite the *Acchiddaka* (the *Suttanipāta*).
"Finger-calculators" are those who live by means of counting with hand-gestures (*mudrā*). "Or whatever others" refers to iron-workers, ivory-workers, painters, and so forth.
"Thus engaged" means thus occupied. "In this very life" refers to those elephant-riders and others, and to those various fields of craft (*sippāyatana*).
Having demonstrated this, they receive great prosperity from the royal court and subsist upon the visible fruit of their craft itself.
"They gladden" means they make one happy. "They satisfy" means they make one full of joy, endowed with vigor and strength. Regarding the terms *uddhaggikā* and so forth:
because it produces fruit above, it has its summit directed upward (*uddhaṃ aggam assā atthīti uddhaggikā*). Because it is worthy of heaven, it is *sovaggikā*.
"Having a pleasant ripening" means having a pleasant result (*sukhavipāka*). "Leading to heaven" means it brings about or produces ten things that are preeminent:
visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, longevity, beauty, happiness, glory, and sovereignty. The meaning is that she establishes such a sacrificial gift (*dakkhiṇā*).
Regarding the term "fruit of recluseship" (*sāmaññaphala*): here, in the ultimate sense, the Path is "recluseship," while the Noble Fruit is the fruit.
The fruit of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*). As it is said: "And what, monks, is recluseship? It is this very Noble Eightfold Path.
That is to say: right view... [and so on] ...right concentration. This, monks, is called recluseship. And what, monks, are the fruits of recluseship?
The fruit of stream-entry... [and so on] ...the fruit of arahantship. That.
This king does not know [the answer]. However, he asks with reference to the simile of the slave and the farmer that appeared above.
Then the Blessed One, without yet answering the question, reflected: "Many disciples of other sects and royal ministers have come here;
if we were to explain by illustrating both the dark side and the bright side, our king [would be overwhelmed] by a great..."

"He has come here with great effort; from the moment of his arrival, people will complain, saying, 'The ascetic Gotama speaks only of the clamor and the wrangling of ascetics,' and they will not listen to the Dhamma with respect.
But when it is spoken by the king, they will not be able to complain; they will simply follow the king, for the world follows its lord. Come now, let me [speak] to the king himself."
Thinking, "I shall take up the burden," while taking up the burden for the king, he said, "Do you recollect...?
and so forth. 164. Therein, "abhijānāsi no tvam" means "do you indeed recollect.

And this word *no* should be construed with the word *pucchitā* that follows later. For this is what is meant: "Great King, do you recollect this question [having asked it] to other recluses and brahmins..."
"Have you been questioned, and do you remember having been questioned; has it not been forgotten by you?

"If it is not a burden for you"—that is, if it is not burdensome for you to speak here in the same manner as they have explained to you, provided there is no discomfort on your part, then please speak—this is the meaning.
"Indeed, venerable sir, [I cannot]," with reference to what did he say this? For those who merely resemble wise men...
It is difficult to speak in the presence [of others], for they point out faults at every step and at every syllable.
But those who are exclusively wise, upon hearing a discourse, praise what is well-spoken;
regarding poorly-spoken passages, they rectify whatever is inconsistent with the scripture, the words, the meaning, or the phrasing. Indeed, there is no one exclusively wise equal to the Blessed One.
There is none. Therefore he said: "Venerable sir, it is not that I feel any weightiness [of status] toward one where the Blessed One is seated, or one who is like the Blessed One.
Commentary on the Teaching of Pūraṇa Kassapa (165):

"Once upon a time, here" means: once, at this place, I was. "Having exchanged greetings and pleasantries" means: having brought to a conclusion the conversation that produces mutual joy and is worthy of being remembered.

166. Regarding the phrases “one who does, O Great King, or one who causes to be done,” and so forth: “does” refers to one who acts with his own hand; “causes to be done” refers to one who causes it to be done by command;
“cuts” refers to one who cuts off the hands and other limbs of others; “cooks” refers to one who oppresses others with punishment;
“grieves” refers to one who causes grief to another by stealing their goods and the like; “causes to grieve” refers to [causing] grief oneself...
"Whether doing it oneself or having others do it": "becoming weary" means becoming weary oneself through the deprivation of food, imprisonment, and so forth, or causing others to become weary;
"trembling or causing another to tremble" means trembling oneself at the time when another is trembling, or causing another to tremble;
"causing the destruction of life" means even while killing a living being oneself.
Even when causing to kill. Thus, in all instances, the meaning should be understood by way of both the action and its cause.
*Sandhi* means a house-break-in. *Nillopa* means a great plundering. *Ekāgārika* means plundering after surrounding a single house.
*Paripantha* refers to one standing on the road for the purpose of seizing those who come along. For one who acts, it is not as if he does not act.
Even if one acts with the perception, "I am committing some evil," no evil is committed; there is no evil.
However, this demonstrates that beings possess the perception, "We are committing evil. "With a razor-edge" means with a razor-rim, or with an edge like the blade of a razor.
"A single piece of flesh" means a single mass of flesh. "A heap" refers to that very same thing.
This is a synonym. "On that account" means on account of the making of a single meat-bowl.
Regarding the people on the southern bank who were harsh and cruel, he said, "Slaying," and so forth.
On the northern bank, beings are faithful, confident, devoted to the Buddha, devoted to the Dhamma, and devoted to the Saṅgha; they...
He spoke the words beginning with “giving with intention,” and so forth. In that context, “sacrificing” means performing a great sacrifice.
“By self-restraint” means by the restraint of the sense faculties or by the observance of the Uposatha. “By control” means by the control of moral discipline (*sīla*).
“By the utterance of truth” means by truthful speech. “Coming” (*āgama*) means arrival; the meaning is “occurrence. In every respect, he rejects the very performance of both evil and merit.

One who "answers a mango when asked about a breadfruit" is one who, when it is asked what a mango is like or what its trunk, leaves, flowers, and fruits are like, answers that the breadfruit is like this or that its trunk, leaves, flowers, and fruits are like this.

"In the conquered territory" means in the region where his command prevails. "Should be disparaged" means should be harassed. "Without rejoicing" means not saying, "Excellent, excellent! and so forth.
"Without praising" means without commending. "Without reviling" means without refuting by saying, "What you have spoken is the foolish speech of a fool.
"Not grasping" means not grasping it as being essential. "Not setting upright" means not fixing it in the heart with the thought, "This is the escape," or "This is the ultimate meaning.
However, the phrasing (*byañjana*) that he has mastered is both [grasped] and set upright.
Commentary on the Teaching of Makkhali Gosāla (167–169).
In the doctrine of Makkhali, the term "condition" (*paccaya*) is merely a synonym for "cause" (*hetu*).

By both terms, he rejects the very existence of a condition for defilement, such as bodily misconduct, and a condition for purification, such as bodily good conduct. [The phrase] "by one's own effort" (*attakāra*)...

"Self-action. By means of the karma performed by oneself, these beings attain even the state of a deva, a Māra, or a Brahmā, as well as the enlightenment of a disciple, the enlightenment of a paccekabuddha, or omniscience;

yet he rejects that as well. By the second phrase, [he rejects] that which depends on the action of another—the exhortation and instruction of another—by which all people, with the exception of the Great Being, attain human excellence.
Starting from the beginning up until the attainment of Arhatship, he rejects that which is produced by another. Thus, this fool is said to strike at the wheel of the Conqueror.
"There is no human effort" (natthi purisakāro): he rejects even that human effort by which beings attain the aforementioned forms of prosperity.
"There is no power" (natthi balaṃ): [he rejects] that power upon which beings are established.
Having exerted energy (*vīriya*), people attain those successes; [the view] rejects that power.
Phrases such as "there is no energy" and so forth are all merely synonyms for human effort (*purisakāra*).

However, these are taken separately by way of rejecting statements such as, "This has proceeded through our energy, this through human strength (*purisathāma*), and this through human prowess (*purisaparākrama*)."
"‘All beings’ (sabbe sattā)”: he includes without exception those such as camels, oxen, and donkeys. "‘All living things’ (sabbe pāṇā)”:

he speaks by way of the one-facultied living thing, the two-facultied living thing, and so forth. "‘All creatures’ (sabbe bhūtā)”: he speaks with reference to beings within egg-shells and womb-sheaths.
"‘All souls’ (sabbe jīvā)”: he speaks with reference to rice, barley, wheat, and so forth; for in them, there is the state of growing.
"Perceiving a living soul. "Powerless, weak, and lacking energy": they possess neither their own power, nor strength, nor energy.

Regarding the phrase "transformed by destiny, conjunction, and inherent nature": here, *niyati* means fixed or determined. *Saṅgati* means the movement from one place to another among the six classes of birth (*abhijāti*).
*Bhāva* means simply the inherent nature (*sabhāva*). Thus, by way of destiny, conjunction, and inherent nature...
And they have matured, having reached various states. This shows that whatever is destined to become as it should, that indeed becomes so;
and whatever is not destined to become, that does not become. "Only in the six classes of birth" means that standing only within these six classes of birth, they experience pleasure and pain.
This shows that there is no other ground for pleasure and pain.
"Hundreds of thousands of wombs" means one hundred and fourteen thousand of the primary wombs—the highest wombs—and another six hundred and sixty.

"And five hundred actions" means five hundred actions. [The author] merely demonstrates a useless view by means of mere reasoning. This applies to such passages as "five actions and three actions," and so forth.
The same method applies here. However, some say: "He speaks of 'five actions' by way of the five faculties (*indriya*), and 'three' by way of bodily action and so forth.
Regarding the terms "action" (*kamma*) and "half-action" (*upaḍḍhakamma*), his view is that bodily action and verbal action are "action," while mental action is "half-action.
He says that "the sixty-two ways of practice" (*dvaṭṭhipaṭipadā*) means sixty-two ways of practice. [He also says] "the sixty-two intermediate eons" (*dvaṭṭhantarakappa*).
In one eon (*kappa*), there are sixty-four intermediate eons (*antarakappa*). However, not knowing the other two [types of eons], he spoke thus.

Regarding the "six classes of birth" (*chaḷābhijāti*): he speaks of these six classes of birth, namely, the black class of birth, the blue class of birth, the red class of birth, the yellow class of birth, the white class of birth, and the supreme white class of birth.
Among those, [there are] the sheep-slaughterers, the bird-catchers, the hunters, and so forth.
He says that pig-butchers, hunters, fishermen, thieves, executioners, prison wardens, and whoever else performs cruel deeds belong to the dark class (*kaṇhābhijāti*).
He says that monks belong to the blue class (*nīlābhijāti*);
for it is said that they consume the four requisites after having placed thorns within them. Thus he says, "Monks live by means of thorns. This is his [view].
It is in the Pāli itself. Alternatively, he says that some who have gone forth live like thorns.
He says that the Nigaṇṭhas, who belong to the blood-red caste, are those clad in a single garment. It is said that these are indeed whiter than the previous two.
He says that the lay followers of the Acelakas, who wear white garments, belong to the turmeric-yellow caste. Thus, even compared to the Nigaṇṭhas, he considers his own supporters to be superior.
He says: "The Ājīvakas and Ājīvakinīs are of the 'white' high birth (sukkābhijāti). He says that they, it is said, are whiter than the previous four.
He says: "Nanda, Vaccha, Kisa, Saṅkicca, and Makkhali Gosāla are of the 'supremely white' high birth (paramasukkābhijāti). He says that they, it is said, are all whiter than everyone else.

"The eight stages of man" refers to these eight stages of man: the stage of dullness, the stage of play, the stage of testing one's way, the stage of straightforwardness, the stage of training, the stage of the recluse, the stage of the Victor, and the stage of wisdom.
Regarding this, from the day of birth for seven days, beings are dull and bewildered because they have just emerged from the cramped place [the womb]; this—
He says, "The stage of dullness. However, those who have come from an unhappy destination weep and wail frequently;
those who have come from a happy destination smile, recollecting that [former state]. This is called the "stage of play.
Taking hold of one's mother’s or father’s hand, foot, bed, or chair, and then placing one's own foot on the ground is the "stage of testing steps."

[This is] the name. When one is capable of walking on foot, it is called the level of the upright (ujugatabhūmi). When one is training in the crafts, it is called the level of the trainee (sekkhabhūmi).

When one has gone forth from the household life and become a renunciant, it is called the level of the ascetic (samaṇabhūmi). When one has served a teacher and attained knowledge, it is called the level of the Victor (jinabhūmi).

As it is said: "The bhikkhu is a victor who has reached the level of the wise; he does not crave for anything"—thus one calls such a non-gainer an ascetic who has reached the level of the wise (pannabhūmi).
"Ninety-nine hundred Ājīvaka sects" means ninety-nine hundred modes of livelihood for Ājīvakas. "A hundred wanderers' sects" means a hundred forms of renunciation for wanderers.
"A hundred Nāga abodes" means a hundred Nāga circles. "Twenty hundred faculties" means twenty hundred faculties.
"Thirty hundred hells" means thirty hundred hells. "Dust-places" refers to places where dust is scattered, such as the backs of hands, the backs of feet, and so forth.
He speaks with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). "Seven wombs of the percipient" (*saññīgabbha*)—he speaks with reference to camels, oxen, mules, goats, sheep, deer, and wild buffalo.
"Seven wombs of the non-percipient" (*asaññīgabbha*)—he speaks with reference to rice, paddy, barley, wheat, millet, panic seed, and kudrūsa grass.
"Wombs of the entwined" (*nigaṇṭhigabbha*)—wombs produced from knots; he speaks with reference to sugarcane, bamboo, reeds, and so forth. "Seven gods" (*deva*)...
There are many gods, yet he says they are "seven. Humans are infinite, yet he says they are "seven.

There are seven types of *pisāca* spirits; he says these very large *pisācas* are "seven. Regarding "lakes," he refers to the great lakes—namely, Kaṇṇamuṇḍa, Rathakāra, Anotatta, Sīhapapāta, Chaddanta, Mandākinī, and Kuṇāla—and speaks of them thus.
"Knots" (*pavuṭā*) means knots or joints. "Precipices" (*papātā*) means great precipices. "Hundreds of precipices" means hundreds of small precipices. "Dreams" (*supinā*)...
"Great dreams. "Hundreds of dreams" means hundreds of minor dreams. "Great aeons" (*mahākappā*) refers to great aeons.

Regarding this, it is said that when one removes a single drop of water from a great lake with the tip of a blade of *kusa* grass every hundred years, and after doing so seven times the lake becomes devoid of water, that constitutes one great aeon. There are eight million four hundred thousand such great aeons.
"Having exhausted both fools and the wise, they bring about the end of suffering"—this is his tenet.
For it is said that even the wise cannot attain purification in the interval, and the fool does not go beyond that [point].
"By virtue" means by the practice of nakedness (*acelaka*) or by whatever other practice; "by conduct" means by such conduct as that; "by austerity" means...
By means of ascetic practice (*tapokamma*): one who thinks "I am wise" and purifies himself prematurely is said to bring what is unripened to ripeness.
One who thinks "I am a fool" and proceeds only after the passage of the time specified for him is said to make what is ripened utterly clear (*byanti*) by repeatedly touching it.
"It is not thus" means it is not so; he demonstrates that neither of those two things can be accomplished.
"Measured by a *doṇa*" means as if measured by a *doṇa* (a measure of capacity). "Pleasure and pain" (*sukhadukkha*) is a compound of pleasure and pain.
"With its limit fixed" means having its limit established by the time already mentioned.

"There is no decrease or increase" means there are no decreases or increases. The meaning is: "The cycle of existence does not decrease for the wise, nor does it increase for the fool. "In its height and depth" (*ukkaṃsāvakaṃse*) refers to its maximum and minimum extents.
This is a designation for those who increase their years.
Now, establishing that meaning by means of a simile, he said, "Just as if," and so forth. Therein, "a ball of thread" refers to a ball of thread made by winding it together.
"It runs away even as it is being unwound" refers to [the ball] thrown while standing on a mountain or at the top of a tree.
Just as [a ball] moves only while being propelled by the force of the string, and when the string is exhausted it stops right there and does not go further—
so too, he shows that it does not proceed beyond the time stated.
(Commentary on the Doctrine of Ajita Kesakambalin)
170–172. In the doctrine of Ajita, the statement "there is no gift" is said with reference to the non-existence of the fruit of giving.

"Sacrifice" (yiṭṭha) refers to a great offering; "oblation" (huta) is intended to mean hospitality consisting of food offerings. He rejects both of these as well, with reference precisely to the non-existence of their fruit.
"Of good and evil deeds" (sukatadukkaṭānaṃ) means of good and evil deeds; the sense is "of wholesome and unwholesome [actions]. "Fruit" (phalaṃ)...
"Kamma-result" (*vipāka*): he says that there is no such thing as what is called "result" or "kamma-result.
"There is no this world": for one standing in the next world, this world does not exist; "there is no next world": for one standing in this world, the next world does not exist.
He shows that all things are annihilated right where they are. "There is no mother, there is no father": [he denies their existence].
Among these, he speaks by way of the absence of fruit for right practice and wrong practice.
"There are no beings who undergo spontaneous birth" means he says there are no such beings as those who, having passed away, are reborn.
"Consisting of the four great elements" means composed of the four great elements. "Earth, the body of earth" refers to the internal earth element.
The external earth element. "Anupeti" means it follows along (*anuyāyati*). "Anupagacchati" is a synonym for that same word; it also has the meaning of "it goes after.
By both terms, he shows that it approaches (*upeti*) and approaches closely (*upagacchati*). This same method applies to water and the other elements as well.
"The faculties" refers to the six faculties, with the mind as the sixth, which leap into space. "With the couch as the fifth" means with the bed upon which one lies as the fifth.
The meaning is: the bed itself and the four men standing holding the legs of the bed.

"As far as the cremation ground" means up to the cemetery. "Footprints" refers to the words concerning virtues and faults—such as "this person was thus virtuous" or "thus immoral"—that arise in such a manner;
or rather, in this context, "footprints" is intended to mean the physical body itself. "Dove-colored" means having the color of a dove.
The meaning is "having the color of a pigeon's wing. *Bhassantā* means "ending in ashes," or this is simply the original reading (*pāḷi*).
Regarding "oblations" (*āhutiyo*): whatever gift has been given, such as the various kinds of food parcels and honors, all that ends in ashes;
the meaning is that it does not proceed beyond that to yield fruit. *Dattupaññattaṃ* means "established by fools" (*dattu*), that is, by foolish people.
It is so designated. This is what is meant: "This gift was designated by fools, not by the wise;
it is the fools who give, while the wise receive"—thus he shows.
In that regard, Pūraṇa, by saying "evil is not done by one who acts," rejects the efficacy of kamma. Ajita [says] "of the body..."
By saying, "Differences are cut off," he rejects fruition (*vipāka*). Makkhali, by saying, "There are no causes," rejects both.
In this regard, by rejecting karma, one also rejects fruition;
and by rejecting fruition, one also rejects karma. Thus, all of these, in meaning, are rejectors of both.
They are proponents of causelessness, proponents of non-action, and proponents of nihilism.
Or else, those who adopt their doctrine and, sitting in their night-quarters or day-quarters, recite and investigate it, [hold that]:
"For one who acts, no evil is done; there is no cause, there is no condition; the dead are annihilated."
Wrong mindfulness settles upon that object; the mind becomes one-pointed, and impulsions (javana) surge forth.
In the first impulsion, they are curable; likewise in the second and so on. But in the seventh, even for Buddhas, they are incurable and irreversible, like the thorn of Ariṭṭha.
In this regard, someone enters one [of these wrong views], someone two, and someone even three; and once one has entered, even if it is among two...
Even when the three [refuges] have been entered, he remains one of fixed wrong view;

having become an obstacle to both the path to heaven and the path to liberation, he is incapable of going to heaven in the very next existence, let alone to liberation. This being is called a "stump in the cycle of existence" (*vaṭṭakhāṇu*), a guardian of the earth;
for such a person, there is generally no emergence from such a state of existence.
“Therefore, one who desires prosperity and possesses discernment should avoid an unwholesome person from afar, just as one would avoid a venomous serpent. —
Commentary on the Doctrine of Pakudha Kaccāyana.
173–175. In the doctrine of Pakudha, *akatā* means "unmade. *Akatavidhā* means "of unmade arrangement"; the sense is that they have not even been caused to be made by anyone saying, "Do it thus.
*Animmitā* means not even fashioned by supernormal power (*iddhi*). *Animmātā* means not caused to be fashioned;

some read the word as *animmāpetabbā* ("not to be caused to be fashioned"), but that is seen neither in the Canon (*pāḷi*) nor in the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*). The triad of terms beginning with "barren" (*vañjha*) [is to be understood].
The meaning is exactly as stated. "They do not stir" means they do not move because they stand firm like a pillar that has been fixed.
"They do not change" means they do not abandon their natural state. "They do not obstruct one another" means they do not harm one another. "Unable" means not capable.
In the phrases "the earth-body" and so forth, "earth-body" (pathavikāyo) refers either to the earth itself or to a collection of earth. "Therein" (tattha):

Regarding those seven bodies containing living beings: as to the phrase "among the seven bodies," just as a weapon struck against a heap of mung beans and so forth enters through the gaps between the mung beans, even so the weapon enters through a hole or opening among the seven bodies.
In that case, the thought "I am depriving this being of life" is merely a matter of perception; this is what he shows.
Commentary on the Doctrine of Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta (176–178).
Regarding the doctrine of Nāṭaputta: "Restrained by the fourfold restraint" (*cātuyāmasaṃvarasaṃvuta*) means restrained by a restraint consisting of four parts.
"Prevented from all water" (*sabbavārivārita*) means one who has prevented all water; the meaning is that he has rejected all cold water. It is said that regarding cold water...
He perceives a being; therefore, he does not utilize it. "Engaged in the warding off of all" means joined with the complete prevention of evil.

"Shaken off by the warding off of all" means one whose evil has been shaken off by the complete prevention of evil. "Pervaded by the warding off of all" means permeated by the complete prevention of evil.
"One who has gone beyond" means one whose mind has reached the ultimate limit. "Self-controlled" means one whose mind is restrained. "Stable" means one whose mind is well-established.
In this doctrine, there is something that accords with the Teaching; however, because it is based on an impure assumption, all of it has become mere speculative view.
179–181. Explanation of the Doctrine of Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta:
The doctrine of Sañjaya follows the same method as that stated under the "Eel-Wriggler" (Amarāvikkhepa).
**Commentary on the First Fruit of the Ascetic Life (Paṭhamasandiṭṭhikasāmaññaphalavaṇṇanā)** 182.

“I, venerable sir,” means: “I, venerable sir, not finding any essence in the doctrines of the other sectarians—just as one who, having crushed sand, finds no oil—ask the Blessed One. 183. “As it may seem good to you” means:

“In whatever way it pleases you. Regarding the term *dāsa* (slave): there are those born in the house, those purchased with wealth, those captured in war, those brought by force, and those who have entered into slavery of their own accord.

"A certain person. "A worker" (*kammakāra*) means one who is not lazy and whose very nature is to perform work. "One who rises early" (*pubbuṭṭhāyī*) means that having seen [the master] from afar, he rises first of all.
Having risen in this way, he prepares a seat for the master and performs the duties such as washing his feet;
then, he lies down or sits down later—thus he is "one who lies down or sits down later" (*pacchānipātī*). Or, even before the master has risen from his bed...
"He rises first" means he is one who rises before [others]. Having performed all duties from the time of dawn until the master goes to sleep at night, he lies down afterwards;
thus he is "one who lies down afterwards. He moves about responding to whatever needs to be done, saying, "What shall I do?
What shall I do?"—thus he is "one who responds to what is to be done. Only that which is pleasing...
One who performs service is "one who acts agreeably. One who speaks only what is pleasant is "one who speaks kindly.
One who moves about looking up at the master’s face, which is bright with joy, is "one who looks to the face.
"Like a god" means like a deity. "May I indeed do meritorious deeds" means "may I indeed become such as this."
"If he were to perform meritorious deeds"—this is the meaning. There is also a reading, "So vatassa'ssa" (it would indeed be for him), which has the same meaning.

"What if I were to give?"—this shows the state of his reflection after making an effort toward the going-forth, thinking: "If I were to give alms, even for the duration of my life, I would not be able to give even a hundredth part of what the king gives in a single day."
"Restrained in body" means having closed off the body, having shut the door through which unwholesomeness enters.
The same method applies to the other two phrases as well. "With food and clothing as the highest aim" means with food and clothing as the supreme or ultimate;
the meaning is that even for this purpose, having abandoned improper search, one is content with the foremost austerity. "Delighting in..."

Regarding "seclusion" (*paviveka*): he delights in the three kinds of seclusion thus described—namely, "bodily seclusion for those whose bodies are secluded from society; mental seclusion for those who delight in renunciation;
and the seclusion from acquisitions (*upadhiviveka*) for persons free from acquisitions who have reached the ultimate purification and entered the state beyond conditioned formations.
Having abandoned the company of crowds, he dwells alone in body, and [abandons] the company of mental defilements.

"Having abandoned [them], he dwells alone by means of the eight attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*); the meaning is that he dwells having reached Nibbāna after entering either the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) or the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). *Yaggha* is a particle used for the purpose of exhortation.
'We would also invite him with a seat' means we would clear away the seat where he is sitting and say, 'Please sit here.'"
"Even if we were to invite him" means that even after bringing [the requisites] to him, we would invite him. In this context, there are two kinds of "bringing":

by speech and by body. One who says, "At whatever moment you desire, tell us what you need from our robes and so forth," is said to invite by bringing through speech. Having observed a deficiency in robes and other necessities, [one brings them by body].
When giving those things while saying, "Take this," one invites by approaching with the body; referring to both of these, he said, "one might even invite.

And here, "requisites for medicinal support for the sick" refers to any medicine suitable for a sick person. The etymological explanation, however, is stated in the *Visuddhimagga*. "Protection, defense, and guardianship":
It is a protection consisting of both guarding and warding off. Furthermore, this righteous arrangement is not established merely by stationing men with weapons in hand;

rather, it is established by arranging things such that wood-gatherers, leaf-gatherers, and others do not enter the monastery at improper times, and that deer-hunters and others do not catch deer or fish within the monastery boundary. By arranging it in this way—
A "righteous" protection has been established; it is with reference to this that he says, "righteous.
(185) "If this being so": if your slave were to receive salutations and so forth from you, then "this being so.
"Addhā" is an expression of certainty. By saying "the first," he indicates that there is also something else.
And for that very reason, the King said, "But it is possible, venerable sir, that there might be another [fruit]," and so forth.
Commentary on the Second Fruit of the Homeless Life (Sāmaññaphala): 186–188. One who plows is a *kassaka* (farmer).

One who is the master of a house, a headman over even a single house, is a *gahapatika* (householder). One who performs labor consisting of a tax is a *karakāraka* (tax-payer). One who increases a heap of grain and a heap of wealth is a *rāsivaḍḍhaka* (one who increases the heap).
"Little" means small, even as little as a single stalk of rice. "Mass of wealth" means a heap of wealth.
He mentions both "great" and "vast" in order to show that just as it is difficult to renounce what is great, so too is it difficult to renounce what is small.
In the case of the slave, however, since the slave has no mastery over himself, much less over his wealth.
For whatever wealth he may have belongs only to his owners; therefore, the term "possessions" was not used. "Relatives" (*ñāti*) is the same as "the circle of relatives" (*ñātiparivaṭṭo*).
189. Regarding the commentary on the more excellent fruit of recluseship:
"But, venerable sir, is it possible [to see] another [fruit] even in this very life?"—here, it was not stated "in exactly this way. That...
And why? Because if it were said simply "in this very way," the Blessed One would be able to illuminate the fruit of recluseship with such similes for an entire day and night, or even more than that.

In this regard, although there is indeed no limit to hearing these words of the Blessed One, nevertheless, thinking that the meaning will remain exactly as it is, [he considers] the further distinction.

When he asked, instead of saying "just so," he said, "even more excellent and even more sublime. In this context, "more excellent" (*abhikkantatara*) means more agreeable to the mind or more pre-eminent;
"more sublime" (*paṇītatarā*) means superior. "Therefore then" (*tena hi*) is a particle used for the purpose of exhortation;
for he spoke thus to urge him toward listening: "Listen to that which is more excellent and more sublime."
“He hears of the fruit of recluseship.
‘Pay close attention,’ [it is said]; here, however, ‘pay close attention’ (*sādhukaṃ*) and ‘well’ (*sādhu*) have the same meaning.
For this word *sādhu* is seen used in such senses as entreaty, acceptance, encouragement, beauty, and strengthening. ‘It would be well for me, venerable sir...’”
In such passages as “May the Blessed One teach the Dhamma in brief,” it is seen in the sense of *āyācana* (requesting).

In such passages as “‘Very well, venerable sir,’ that bhikkhu, having rejoiced and expressed his appreciation for the Blessed One’s words,” it is seen in the sense of *sampatiggahaṇa* (acceptance/approval).
In such passages as “Excellent, excellent, Sāriputta,” it is seen in the sense of *sampahaṃsana* (encouragement/consolation).
“Excellent is the king who delights in the Dhamma; excellent is the person possessed of wisdom;
excellent is one who does not deceive friends; happiness lies in not committing evil.
In such instances, it means "beautiful. In such phrases as “Therefore, brahmin, listen and pay close attention,” it is the word *sādhuka* itself [that is used].
"Daḷhīkamme" is also called "āṇattiyaṃ. Here too, it should be understood in both the sense of strengthening (daḷhīkamme) and in the sense of an instruction (āṇattiyaṃ).
It is also appropriate in the sense of "sundaraṃ" (beautiful/excellent). For, in the sense of strengthening: "Listen to this Dhamma firmly, grasping it well-grasped.
In the sense of an instruction: "Listen according to my instruction. And in the sense of "sundaraṃ": "This is beautiful, auspicious."
"Listen to the Dhamma"—thus it is illuminated.
"Pay attention" means: reflect upon it; the sense is, "be attentive," meaning "having become undistracted in mind, observe"; the intention is, "make it an object of the mind.
Furthermore, here the phrase "listen" is intended to ward off distraction of the ear-faculty. "Thoroughly..."
"Pay attention" (*manasikarohi*) means the warding off of distraction of the mind-faculty (*manindriya*) through the application of firm mental engagement (*daḷhīkammaniyojana*).

Herein, the former [phrase] is for warding off the grasping of a distortion regarding the phrasing (*byañjana*), while the latter is for warding off the grasping of a distortion regarding the meaning (*attha*).
By the former, one is enjoined to listen to the Dhamma; by the latter, to the retention, investigation, and so forth, of the teachings already heard. By the former...

And because this Dhamma is accompanied by its phonemes, it indicates that it is "to be heard. By the latter [phrase], it indicates that it is "to be attended to thoroughly. Alternatively, connecting the word "thoroughly" with both preceding phrases:
because this Dhamma is profound in its nature and profound in its teaching, therefore listen thoroughly; because it is profound in its meaning and profound in its penetration...
And therefore, "you should attend carefully"—thus the construction is to be understood.

"I shall speak, O Great King"—this refers to the detailed exposition of the teaching on the fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*) which was promised. For "I shall teach" (*desessāmi*) is a concise indication, whereas "I shall speak" (*bhāsissāmi*) is a detailed indication. Thus said the Elder Vaṅgīsa:
“He teaches in brief and speaks in detail;
like the song of the maina bird, he utters inspired eloquence.
When this was said, King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha, filled with enthusiasm, replied to the Blessed One, saying, “So be it, Bhante,” thereby accepting and receiving the Blessed One’s words.
190. Then the Blessed One said this to him; that is to say, he spoke the entire sutta beginning with “Here, Great King,” which is the meaning.
In this context, *idha* is a particle used as a designation for a location (*desāpadese*).

This [term] is sometimes used in reference to the world, as it is said: “Here, the Tathāgata arises in the world. Sometimes it refers to the Dispensation (*sāsana*), as it is said: [“Here, a noble disciple hears the Dhamma”].
—“Right here, monks, is the first ascetic; right here is the second ascetic. [This refers to] some specific occasion. As it is said:
“While standing right here, having become a deity, I have regained my life-span once more; know this, O venerable ones.”
In some instances, it serves merely to complete the meter. As it is said: “Here, monks, I might have eaten and been invited.
But here, it should be understood as spoken with reference to the world. The address “Great King” is used again in order to deliver the teaching as previously promised.
This is what is meant: “Great King, in this world a Tathāgata arises...”
“An arahant... [and so on] ...the Buddha, the Blessed One. Herein, the term *tathāgata* is explained in the *Brahmajāla Sutta*. The terms beginning with *arahant* are detailed in the *Visuddhimagga*.
Regarding the phrase “he arises in the world,” here “world” (*loka*) is threefold: the world as space, the world of beings (*sattaloka*), and the world of formations (*saṅkhāraloka*).
However, in this context, the world of beings is intended. And although he arises in the world of beings, [the text continues:]
The Tathāgata does not arise in the world of the devas, nor in the world of Brahmā, but arises only in the world of humans.
Even within the human world, he does not appear in another world-system (*cakkavāḷa*), but only in this very world-system. Furthermore, he does not appear in all places;
rather, [he appears] to the east of the market town named Gajaṅgalā, beyond which is Mahāsāla, and further beyond that are the bordering provinces—within these limits.
In the center, in the southeastern direction, is the river named Salaḷavatī; beyond that are the bordering districts, and on this side is the center.
In the southern direction, there is the market town named Setakaṇṇika; beyond that are the bordering districts, and on this side is the center.
In the western direction, there is the brahmin village named Thūṇa; beyond that are the bordering districts.
"To the north, from the mountain named Usiraddhaja situated between the ocean and the middle region, the bordering districts lie beyond;
thus, within this delimited central region measuring three hundred yojanas in length, two hundred and fifty yojanas in width, and nine hundred yojanas in circumference, the Tathāgata arises.
And it is not only the Tathāgata, but also the Paccekabuddhas [who arise there]."
The chief disciples, the eighty great elders, the mother of the Buddha, the father of the Buddha, the wheel-turning monarch,
and other brahmins and householders who have attained the essence—
all these arise right here. Therein, the Tathāgata arises from the time he consumed the meal of honeyed milk-rice given by Sujātā until his attainment of the path of Arahatship.
It is called "arisen" when it has appeared in the fruit of arahantship. Or, from the Great Renunciation up to the path of arahantship; or from the Tuṣita heaven up to the path of arahantship;

or from the feet of Dīpaṅkara Buddha up to the path of arahantship—it is called "arising" during that interval, and it is called "arisen" upon reaching the fruit of arahantship. Here, the term "arises" refers to the state of having arisen for the very first time.
It has been said. "A Tathāgata has arisen in the world"—this is the meaning here.
"He, this world": that Blessed One [perceives] this world. He now points out what is to be said:
"together with devas" means *sadevaka*, together with devas. Likewise, "together with Māra" means *samāraka*; "together with Brahmā" means *sabrahmaka*; "together with recluses and brahmins."
"Together with recluses and brahmins": it is called "the people" (*pajā*) because of being born; that is "the people. "Together with gods and humans" means *sadevamanussam*.
Therein, by the term "together with gods," the inclusion of the five classes of sense-sphere gods (*kāmāvacara-deva*) should be understood.

By the term "together with Māra," the inclusion of the sixth class of sense-sphere gods is meant. By the term "together with Brahmā," the inclusion of the Brahmā-world deities, such as those of the Brahmakāyika realm, is meant. By the term "together with recluses and brahmins,"...

There is the inclusion of those ascetics and brahmins who are enemies and adversaries of the Dispensation, as well as the inclusion of those ascetics and brahmins who have stilled evil and cast out evil.
By the term "generation" (*pajā*), the world of beings (*sattaloka*) is included. By the term "together with devas and humans," conventional devas and the rest of humanity are included.

Thus, it should be understood that here, by means of three phrases, the world of beings is included along with the physical world (*okāsaloka*); whereas by means of two [phrases], only the world of beings is included.

There is another method: by the inclusion of "together with devas," the world of the formless-sphere devas is included; by the inclusion of "together with Māras," the six sense-sphere deva worlds are included;

by the inclusion of "together with Brahmās," the world of the form-sphere Brahmās is included; and by the inclusion of "together with recluses and brahmins," etc., either the human world together with the conventional devas according to the four assemblies is included, or else the entire world of all remaining sentient beings.
Moreover, by the expression "together with the devas" (sadevaka), he states that the entire world has been realized from the perspective of its highest limit.
Then, for those who might have thought, "Māra is of great power, the lord of the six sense-sphere realms, and possesses sovereign control;
has even he been realized by him?"—dispelling their doubt, he said "together with Māra" (samāraka). Furthermore, for those who thought, "Brahmā..."
"By means of a single finger, one of great power radiates light across a thousand world-systems; by two [fingers]... [and so on]...
by ten fingers, one radiates light across ten thousand world-systems. And one experiences the unsurpassed bliss of meditative attainment (*jhāna-samāpatti*);
has he too realized this?"—thus he spoke "together with Brahmā" (*sabrahmaka*) in order to dispel their doubt.
Then, in order to dispel the doubt of those who thought, "There are many ascetics and brahmins who are adversaries of the Teaching; have they too been realized?
he spoke the verse beginning with *sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiṃ pajam*.

Having thus declared that even the most eminent among the eminent had been realized, he then proceeded, taking as his upper limit the conventional deities (*sammutideva*) and the rest of humanity, to describe the extent of his realization.
He said "together with gods and humans" (sadevamanussa) in order to reveal that he has realized [this truth] for the rest of the world of beings.

This is the sequence of the meanings here. However, the Ancients have said: "Together with gods" (sadevaka) means the remainder of the world together with the gods; "together with Māra" (samāraka) means the remainder of the world together with Māra;
"together with Brahmā" (sabrahmaka) means the remainder of the world together with the Brahmās. Thus, all those who have entered the three realms of existence...
Having included sentient beings within three aspects in three locations, and then encompassing them again with two terms, he said:

"the generation including recluses and brahmins, together with devas and humans. Thus, by means of these five terms, in their respective ways, the entire threefold world-system (*tedhātuka*) alone is encompassed.

Regarding the phrase "having realized it for himself through direct knowledge and made it known": here, "for himself" (*sayaṃ*) means by oneself, having become independent of others. "Direct knowledge" (*abhiññā*)...

"Having directly known" (*abhiññāya*) means having known by means of superior knowledge (*adhika-ñāṇa*). "Having realized" (*sacchikatvā*) means having made it manifest to direct experience; by this, inference and other such means of cognition are excluded.
"He proclaims" (*pavedeti*) means he awakens, makes known, and reveals.
He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning... [as above] ...good in the end; that Blessed One, out of compassion for beings...

Even having abandoned the unsurpassed bliss of seclusion, he teaches the Dhamma. And whether teaching little or much, he teaches it as being good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end.
He teaches it having made it good, auspicious, and blameless in the beginning;
he teaches it having made it good, auspicious, and blameless in the middle; and he teaches it having made it good, auspicious, and blameless in the end.

This has been stated. In this context, there is the beginning, middle, and end of a teaching, and there is the beginning, middle, and end of the Dispensation (*sāsana*). First, regarding the teaching:
even in a four-line verse, the first line is called the beginning; the next two are called the middle; and the final one is called the end.
In a sutta consisting of a single sequence of meaning, the introduction (*nidāna*) is the beginning, and "Thus he spoke" (*idam avoca*) is the end.

The middle is between the two. For a sutta with many sections, the first section is the beginning, the final section is the conclusion, and one, two, or many sections in the middle are simply the middle.
Furthermore, for the Teaching (Sāsana), virtue, concentration, and insight are called the beginning. And this has been said: "And what is the beginning of wholesome states?"
Of phenomena? "Virtue that is perfectly pure and a view that is straight.
But when it is said, "Bhikkhus, there is a middle way realized by the Tathāgata," the Noble Path is what is called the "middle.
Both the fruit and Nibbāna are called the "end. "It is for this purpose, Brahmin, that this holy life is lived; this is its essence."
For in the passage, "This is the conclusion," it is the fruit that is called the conclusion.
In the passage, "Friend Visākha, the holy life is lived with Nibbāna as its abyss, Nibbāna as its final goal, and Nibbāna as its conclusion," it is Nibbāna that is called the conclusion.
Here, however, what is intended is the beginning, middle, and conclusion of the teaching. For the Blessed One, regarding the Dhamma—
Having shown virtue at the beginning, he shows the path in the middle and Nibbāna at the end. Therefore it is said:
"He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end.
Consequently, when another preacher of the Dhamma speaks the Dhamma—
“At the beginning one should show virtue; in the middle, one should clarify the path;
at the conclusion, Nibbāna—this is the established method for a speaker.

Regarding the phrase “with meaning and with phrasing”: for one whose teaching is based on descriptions such as rice porridge, meals, women, men, and so forth, [the discourse is considered to possess both meaning and phrasing].
He does not teach what is well-phrased (*sāttha*). The Blessed One, however, having abandoned such [unhelpful] teaching, teaches a discourse based on the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth;
therefore, it is said that he "teaches what is well-phrased.

But for one whose teaching consists of words joined with only a single consonant, or where all the consonants are retroflex (*niroṭṭha*), or where all the consonants are unaspirated (*vissaṭṭha*) or nasalized (*niggahīta*), [it would be like the speech] of the Milakkhas—the Damilas, Kirātas, Savaras, and others.
A teaching is called "without phonemes" (*abyañjana*) because it lacks the fullness of phonetic expression, like mere speech. However, the Blessed One said:
“Loose and firm, long and short, heavy and light, nasalized (*niggahīta*), connected and distinct—thus is the tenfold classification according to the cognition of phonemes.”
Having spoken thus, he teaches the Dhamma without omitting any of the tenfold phrasing, but rather making the phrasing complete;
therefore, it is said that "he teaches the Dhamma with its phrasing. Regarding the phrase "entirely complete" (*kevalaparipuṇṇa*):

here, "entirely" (*kevala*) is a designation for the whole, while "complete" (*paripuṇṇa*) refers to speech that is neither deficient nor redundant. This means that he teaches only what is entirely and completely complete, even down to a single portion.
"It is not incomplete" means it should be understood as "entirely complete" because there is nothing to be added or removed.

"Pure" means free from defilement. For if one teaches this Dhamma discourse thinking, "By relying on this teaching, I shall obtain gain or honor," his teaching is impure; however, the Blessed One is indifferent to worldly material things.
With a heart softened by the cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettābhāvanā*) through the radiation of welfare, and with a mind established in the nature of uplifting others, he teaches.
Therefore, it is said that "he teaches the Dhamma that is perfectly pure.
Regarding the phrase "he reveals the holy life" (*brahmacariyaṃ pakāseti*): here, this term *brahmacariya* refers to giving, service, and the virtue of the five training precepts (*pañcasikkhāpada*).

It is seen in these meanings: in the immeasurables (*appamaññā*), in abstinence from sexual intercourse, in contentment with one’s own wife, in energy, in the factors of the Uposatha, in the Noble Path, and in the Dispensation (*sāsana*).
“What is your vow? And what is your holy life (*brahmacariya*)?”
Of what well-performed deed is this the result:
this psychic power, radiance, strength, heroism,
and rebirth— this great celestial mansion of yours, O Naga?
Both my wife and I, in the world of humans,
were both faithful masters of giving;
at that time, my home was like a public well.
And the ascetics and brahmins were satisfied.
That indeed was my vow, that was my holy life;
this is the fruit of that well-practiced conduct.
"Supernormal power, radiance, strength, heroism,
and rebirth— this, O Wise One, is my great celestial mansion.
For in this Puṇṇaka Jātaka, it is stated that "giving is the holy life."
“By what means does the hand become a giver of desires? By what means does the hand become a fountain of honey?
Through what holy life (*brahmacariya*) is merit accomplished in the hand?
By that [holy life], the hand becomes a giver of desires; by that, the hand becomes a fountain of honey.”
“By that holy life of mine, merit succeeds in my hand.
In this *Aṅkurapeta-vatthu*, service is called the holy life (*brahmacariya*). In this *Tittira-jātaka*, it is said:
“Thus, monks, that holy life was known as the ‘Tittiriya’ holy life,” referring to the virtue of the five training precepts (*pañcasikkhāpada-sīla*).

“Brahmacariya” has been mentioned. Furthermore, in this Mahāgovinda Sutta, it is said: “But that brahmacariya of mine, Pañcasikha, was not for disenchantment, nor for dispassion, nor for cessation... [etc. ...but only for rebirth in the Brahma-world.
Here, the four immeasurables (*appamaññā*) are called “brahmacariya. “Others will be non-practitioners of the holy life; we, however, in this regard...”
In this *Sallekha Sutta*, the phrase "we shall be celibate" refers to abstaining from sexual intercourse as celibacy (*brahmacariya*).
[As it says: "We do not transgress against our wives, nor do our wives transgress against us."
"Except for those [wives], we lead the holy life;
therefore, indeed, we do not die young.
In the Mahādhammapāla Jātaka, contentment with one's own wife is called the holy life (*brahmacariya*). "Furthermore, I recall..."
“Sāriputta, having practiced the holy life endowed with four factors, I was indeed an ascetic”—
thus it is said that energy is the holy life in the *Lomahaṃsana Sutta*.
“By a lowly holy life, one is reborn among the Khattiyas;”
“By the middle [practice] one attains the state of the gods, and by the highest, one is purified.
Thus, in the *Nimi Jātaka*, the eightfold Uposatha was described as the holy life (*brahmacariya*) on account of self-taming.
“But this holy life of mine, Pañcasikha, leads exclusively to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation... [and so forth].”
In the Mahāgovinda Sutta itself, the Noble Eightfold Path is called the "Brahmacariya" (the Divine Life), as in the passage: "This indeed is the Noble Eightfold Path.

Furthermore, in the Pāsādika Sutta, the entire teaching comprised of the three trainings is described as: "And this Brahmacariya is successful, flourishing, widespread, popular, and extensive, well-proclaimed as far as gods and humans."
"Brahmacariya" has been mentioned. In this context as well, it is precisely this that is intended by "brahmacariya.
Therefore, "he reveals the brahmacariya" means he teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning... [and so on] ...perfectly pure.
And while teaching in this way, he reveals the entire Dispensation—comprised of the three trainings—as the brahmacariya; thus the meaning should be understood here.

"Brahmacariya" means a way of life that has become sublime (*brahmabhūta*) in the sense of being supreme; or it is said to be the way of life of those who have become sublime, such as the Buddhas and others.
"That Dhamma" refers to the Dhamma possessing the aforementioned excellence. Why was the householder mentioned first? [Because... 191. "The householder hears... etc.

Why does he point out the householder? Because his pride has been humbled and because [the householders] are numerous. For most who have gone forth from kṣatriya families harbor pride based on their birth; those who have gone forth from brahmin families harbor pride based on the mantras;
and those who have gone forth from families of low birth are unable to establish themselves due to their own low status. As for the sons of householders...
However, with sweat pouring from their armpits and salt sprouting on their backs as they ploughed the earth, their pride and arrogance were humbled due to the absence of such [worldly] conceit.
Having gone forth into homelessness, they refrained from pride or arrogance;
by mastering the entire word of the Buddha according to their ability and applying themselves to the work of insight (vipassanā), they were able to establish themselves in Arahatship.
Furthermore, those who have gone forth after leaving other families are not many; householders are indeed numerous.
Thus, because their pride has been humbled and because they are so numerous, he first specifies the householder.
"In another" means in one of the other families. "Reborn" (*paccājāto*) means born again. Regarding the Tathāgata...
"He acquires faith" means that, having heard the perfectly pure Dhamma, he acquires faith in the Tathāgata, the Lord of the Dhamma, thinking:
"That Blessed One is indeed a perfectly enlightened Buddha. "He reflects thus" means he contemplates in this way:
"Household life is crowded," even if there are two husband and wife living in a house sixty cubits wide or a hundred yojanas apart.
Although they dwell [there], nevertheless, for them the household life is indeed a confinement by virtue of its being possessed of belongings and obstacles.

Regarding the "dust-path" (*rajo-patho*), it is stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* that it is the place where the dust of passion (*rāga-raja*) and so forth arises; others also say it is the path by which [the dust] comes.

It is called "open space" (*abbhokāsa*) because it is like the open air in the sense of being unattached. For one who has gone forth [into homelessness] does not [dwell] in gabled houses, jeweled palaces, celestial mansions (*deva-vimāna*), and so on.
Even while dwelling in well-sheltered places with doors and windows closed, one neither clings, nor adheres, nor is bound.
Therefore it is said: “The life of renunciation is open space. Moreover, household life is cramped because there is no opportunity for the performance of wholesome deeds.
It is a path of dust, like an uncovered rubbish heap, because it is a place where dust—in this case, the dust of the defilements—accumulates. It is open space.
The going forth (pabbajjā) exists as an opportunity for the performance of wholesome deeds according to one’s pleasure.
This is not easy... [etc. ... "one should go forth"—herein this is the brief explanation:
that this holy life of the three trainings, having been made unbroken even for a single day, must be practiced in its absolute completeness until it reaches the final consciousness.
And having made it unstained by the impurity of defilements even for a single day, it must be brought to the final moment of consciousness; thus it must be practiced as absolutely pure.
It must be practiced as "scrupulously refined," like a polished conch shell, resembling a clean conch shell.
This is not easy to practice while living the household life, dwelling in the midst of a home—so complete, so perfect... [as before]... What if I were now...?
Having shaved off their hair and beard, and having donned saffron-colored robes— dyed with astringent juice and suitable for those leading the holy life—
they would go forth from the home into homelessness. And here,
since the work such as farming and trade that is beneficial to the household is called "household-ness" (*agāriya*), and that [work] is absent in the going-forth...
It does not exist; therefore, it should be known that going forth is homelessness—that is, *anagāriya*. "One should go forth" means one should practice [the path]. 192–193.
"Small" refers to a mass of wealth below one thousand [pieces]; from one thousand onwards, it is "great.
In the sense of being a bond, relatives themselves are the circle of relatives (*ñātiparivaṭṭa*). That too is called "small" when it consists of fewer than twenty.
From twenty onwards, it is "great. "Restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha" means endowed with the restraint of the Pātimokkha.
"Perfect in conduct and resort" means perfect in both conduct and resort. "In even the slightest" means in those that are very minor.
"Offenses" means unwholesome states. "Seeing fear" means seeing them as fearful. "Having undertaken" means having correctly adopted [the training].
"He trains in the training precepts" means that having undertaken each respective training precept, he trains in them. This is the summary here;
the detailed explanation, however, is stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.

Regarding the phrase "endowed with wholesome bodily and verbal action, one of purified livelihood," by the very mention of "proper conduct and resort" (*ācāra-gocara*), [the meaning is already established].
And although wholesome bodily and verbal actions have already been mentioned, since this so-called virtue of livelihood-purification does not arise in the air or at the tops of trees and such,

but arises only at the doors of body and speech, it is therefore stated as "endowed with wholesome bodily and verbal action" in order to show the doors of its arising. Furthermore, because one is endowed with that [virtue],...
Therefore, he is one whose livelihood is purified. Or rather, it is stated thus by way of the *Samaṇamuṇḍikaputtasutta*. For there it is said:
"And what, carpenter, are wholesome virtues? Wholesome bodily action, wholesome verbal action, and pure livelihood as well—I call this, carpenter, virtue.
Since he is endowed with that [livelihood], [he is called one of purified livelihood].
Therefore, he should be known as one whose livelihood is purified.
"Endowed with virtue" means he is possessed of the threefold virtue as described in the *Brahmajāla Sutta*.

"Guarded in the doors of the sense faculties" means he has closed the doors regarding the six sense faculties, including the mind. "Endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension" [means] in approaching...
In the seven instances beginning with "having returned," he is endowed with both mindfulness and clear comprehension.
"Contented" means he is contented with the threefold contentment regarding the four requisites.
The Shorter Exposition of Virtue.
194–211. Having thus set forth the matrix (mātikā), he spoke the passage beginning with, "And how, Great King, is a bhikkhu accomplished in virtue," while explaining it in successive order.

Therein, the phrase "this too is his virtue in regard to virtue" means that this very abstinence from taking life is one instance of virtue within the virtue of that bhikkhu. Alternatively, this [term] is used in the sense of the reflexive pronoun (*paccatta-vacana*).
*Bhummaṃ*. For in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, this very meaning is stated: "This too is the virtue (*sīla*) of that ascetic.
The remainder should be understood according to the method already explained in the *Brahmajāla Sutta*. "This is his virtue" means "this is his virtue. 212.
"He perceives no fear from any quarter, namely, from the restraint of virtue" refers to those [fears] rooted in non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
Fears arise; among them, he does not perceive this fear—which might otherwise arise from the restraint of virtue—as coming from even a single type of restraint.
Why? Because there is no fear rooted in non-restraint arising from restraint.
"Anointed on the head" means one who has been sprinkled on the head with the consecration of a Khattiya performed according to the prescribed ritual. "That is to say, from an enemy."
He does not perceive any danger from any quarter, even from a single adversary. Why? Because he has humbled his enemies.
"Internally" means within one's own internal sphere; the meaning is: within one's own continuum.

"Blameless happiness" refers to that which is blameless, irreproachable, and wholesome, arising through the factors of non-remorse, gladness, rapture, and tranquility, which have virtue as their proximate cause.
He experiences physical and mental happiness that is fully embraced. "In this way, Great King, a bhikkhu is accomplished in virtue"—
having thus explained in detail by means of the threefold virtue shown in such a continuous sequence,
he concluded the discourse on virtue, stating that a bhikkhu endowed with these is called "accomplished in virtue."
**Discourse on the Restraint of the Faculties** 213.

In the section concerning the guarding of the doors of the faculties, regarding the phrase "with the eye, a visible form," this term *cakkhu* (eye) in some instances refers to the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakkhu*), as it is said:
"He surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye. In other instances, it refers to that which is designated as omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
Regarding "all-seeing eye" (*samantacakkhu*), as it is said: "O Sumedha, having ascended the palace made of Dhamma, you shall become all-seeing.
In some contexts, regarding the "eye of Dhamma" (*dhammacakkhu*), the phrase "the dustless, stainless eye of Dhamma arose" refers here to the wisdom of the three noble paths.
In the passage "the eye arose, knowledge arose," the wisdom consisting of the knowledge of past lives and so forth is called the "eye of wisdom" (*paññācakkhu*).

In passages where it occurs as “with the divine eye” (*dibbena cakkhunā*), it refers to the divine eye. In the passage “dependent on the eye and forms,” it refers to the physical eye (*pasāda-cakkhu*).
However, here this term for the physical eye is used in the sense of eye-consciousness (*cakkhu-viññāṇa*);
therefore, the meaning here is: “having seen a form with eye-consciousness. Regarding what is to be said concerning the remaining phrases:
All of that has been stated in the *Visuddhimagga*. "Unstained happiness" (*abyāsekasukha*):

because it is free from the stain of the defilements (*kilesabyāseka*), one experiences the pure, unmixed, and superior mental happiness (*adhicittasukha*). The Discussion on Mindfulness and Clear Comprehension (*Satisampajañña-kathā*).
214. Regarding the section on mindfulness and clear comprehension (*satisampajañña*), concerning the phrase "when going forward" (*abhikkante*) and "when returning" (*paṭikkante*):
here, first of all, "going forward" refers to advancing, and "returning" refers to turning back; both of these are found within the four postures (*iriyāpatha*).
In the case of walking, one is said to be "going forward" when moving the body forward, and "returning" when turning back.
Even while standing in one place, leaning the body forward is called "approaching," and leaning it backward is called "receding.

In sitting, even while seated, shifting toward the front part of the seat is called "approaching," and shifting back toward the rear part of the seat is called "receding. The same principle applies to lying down as well.
"He acts with full awareness" means he performs all his duties with clear comprehension (*sampajañña*), or rather, he is one who acts only with clear comprehension.
For he indeed exercises clear comprehension regarding "going forth" (*abhikkanta*) and so on; he is never devoid of clear comprehension in any situation.

In this context, clear comprehension is fourfold: clear comprehension of purpose (*sātthaka-sampajañña*), clear comprehension of suitability (*sappāya-sampajañña*), clear comprehension of the field of activity (*gocara-sampajañña*), and clear comprehension of non-delusion (*asammoha-sampajañña*).

In this context, when the intention to go forward has arisen, rather than going merely by the force of that thought, one examines what is beneficial and what is not beneficial, thinking: "Is there any purpose for me in going there, or is there not?
This examination of what is beneficial is *sātthaka-sampajañña* (clear comprehension of the purposeful).

And herein, "what is beneficial" (*attha*) refers to spiritual progress (*dhammato vuḍḍhi*) by way of seeing a shrine (*cetiyadassana*), the Bodhi tree, the Saṅgha, elders, or the meditation on the unattractive (*asubha-dassana*), and so forth.
Indeed, upon seeing a cetiya or the Bodhi tree, one arouses joy with the Buddha as the object; or, by seeing the Saṅgha, one arouses joy with the Saṅgha as the object.
Having done so, by contemplating that very joy in terms of its exhaustion and passing away, one attains Arahatship.

Or, having seen the elders and established oneself in their instruction, or having seen a foul object and aroused the first jhāna therein, by contemplating that very state in terms of its exhaustion and passing away—
One attains arahantship; therefore, it is said that seeing these [benefits] is purposeful.
Some, however, say that even material growth is indeed a benefit, because one has practiced for the sake of supporting the holy life (*brahmacariya*) by depending upon it.
In that regard, having discerned what is suitable and what is unsuitable for that journey, the discernment of the suitable is "clear comprehension of the suitable" (*sappāya-sampajañña*).
For example, visiting a shrine (cetiyadassana) is indeed beneficial;

for if a great festival is held at a shrine, assemblies gather within a radius of ten or twelve leagues. Men and women, adorned and prepared according to their means, move about like figures in a painting.
Therein, greed arises toward a desirable object, aversion toward an undesirable one, and negligence toward that which is neither.
Delusion arises, or one incurs an offense involving physical contact; or there is an obstacle to life or to the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
In such cases, that place is unsuitable. In the absence of the aforementioned obstacles, it is suitable. This same principle applies to the vision of the Buddha. Seeing the Saṅgha is also purposeful.
However, if one has had a great pavilion constructed within a village and [the teaching] lasts throughout the entire night...
When people are engaged in listening to the Dhamma, there occurs both a gathering of people and an obstacle in the very manner already described;
thus, that place is unsuitable. In the absence of such obstacles, it is suitable.
The same principle applies to visiting elders who have large retinues.
The contemplation of the foul is also purposeful; and to illustrate its significance, there is this story:
it is said that a certain young bhikkhu went with a novice to fetch tooth-sticks.
The novice, having left the path and gone ahead, saw a sight of the foul and, having attained the first jhāna, made that very attainment his basis and contemplated conditioned phenomena.
Having realized the three fruits and having taken up a meditation subject for the sake of the higher path, he stood there.
Not seeing him, the youth called out, "Novice! He thought, "From the day I went forth, I have never had two words of conversation with a bhikkhu;
on this other day as well, I shall produce a distinction superior to that."
Having reflected, he gave the reply, “What, venerable sir? When told, “Come,” he came with that single address alone.
Then he said, “Venerable sir, go by this very path; at the place where I am standing, stand for a moment facing the east and look.
He did so, and attained exactly the same distinction as the other. Thus, one foul object [serves] two.
It was born for the welfare of people. Furthermore, although it is thus purposeful, the unattractiveness of women is unsuitable for men, and the unattractiveness of men is unsuitable for women;
only that which is of a similar kind is suitable. Thus, the discernment of what is suitable, which consists in grasping what is suitable, is called "suitability-awareness" (sappāya-sampajañña).
