But for one who has thus taken hold of what is beneficial and suitable, having learned a range of practice called a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) from among the thirty-eight meditation subjects according to his own mental preference, the act of going on the alms-round while taking that very subject with him is called "clear comprehension of the range" (gocara-sampajañña). To explain this, the following tetrad should be understood: 1. “I shall go for alms only within the village boundary. 2. “I shall go for alms only in the direction of the street where such-and-such a family lives. 3. “I shall go for alms only as far as the house where such-and-such a person lives. 4. “I shall go for alms only in the order in which the houses stand. These are the four ways of clear comprehension regarding the range of the alms-round. One should undertake whichever of these suits one’s purpose. However, it is not right to set out on the alms-round without first learning the meditation subject. Therefore, after learning the meditation subject, one should take it with oneself when setting out on the alms-round. This is called clear comprehension of the range. One should undertake whichever of these suits one’s purpose. However, it is not right to set out on the alms-round without first learning the meditation subject. Therefore, after learning the meditation subject, one should take it with oneself when setting out on the alms-round. This is called clear comprehension of the range. In this regard, a certain bhikkhu carries [the meditation subject] forward but does not bring it back; another brings it back but does not carry it forward;
yet another neither carries it forward nor brings it back; and still another both carries it forward and brings it back.
Therein, the bhikkhu who has purified his mind of obstructive states during the day by means of walking and sitting, and likewise during the night...
Having spent the first watch and the middle watch sleeping, and having passed the last watch through sitting and walking meditation,
he performed the duties for the shrine terrace and the Bodhi-tree terrace early in the morning; he sprinkled water on the Bodhi-tree, set out drinking water and water for washing,
and performed all the Khandhaka duties, such as those toward teachers and preceptors.

Having undertaken [the practice], he proceeds. After attending to his bodily needs, he enters his lodging and, having practiced the meditation subject while generating internal heat through two or three cross-legged postures, he rises at the time for the alms-round.
Taking his bowl and robes with the meditation subject foremost, he departs from his lodging and proceeds toward the shrine terrace while keeping the meditation subject in mind.
Having gone there, if his meditation subject is the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*), he enters the shrine courtyard without letting go of it.

If it is another meditation subject, he stands at the foot of the steps, sets it aside like a commodity held in the hand, and taking up rapture with the Buddha as its object, he ascends the shrine courtyard. If it is a large stupa, three times...
Having performed the circumambulation, one should pay homage at four places. If it is a small shrine (*cetiya*), having likewise performed the circumambulation, one should pay homage at eight places.

Having paid homage to the shrine, when one reaches the Bodhi-terrace, one should also pay homage to the Bodhi tree by showing full prostration as if in the very presence of the Blessed Buddha. Thus, he [should pay homage] to both the shrine and...
Having paid homage to the Bodhi tree and returned to the place where he had left it, as if taking up the goods he had deposited, he takes up his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
Near the village, having put on his robe with the meditation subject foremost, he enters the village for alms.
Then, seeing him, people think, "Our noble sir has arrived," and go out to meet him, [offering] the bowl.
Having taken [the visitor] and having had him sit in the assembly hall or in the house, and having given him rice-gruel, they wash his feet with oil and massage them until the meal is finished;
then, sitting before him, they either ask questions or desire to hear the Dhamma.
Even if he does not engage in conversation, one should give a Dhamma talk for the sake of winning over people.
The teachers of the Aṭṭhakathās say, "It is precisely that. For there is no discourse on the Dhamma that is truly divorced from a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*);

therefore, having delivered a discourse on the Dhamma with the meditation subject as its very core, and having partaken of food with the meditation subject as its very core, and having offered a blessing (*anumodanā*), even when followed by people returning [from their work], he should depart from the village and go there.
Having turned back, he sets out on the road.
Then, having departed earlier and finished their meal outside the village, the novice monks and young bhikkhus see him and go out to meet him, taking his bowl and robe.
It is said that the elder bhikkhus think, "He is our preceptor" or "He is our teacher."
They do not perform their duties by looking at one’s face; they perform them simply according to the established limits of their relationship.
They ask him: "Venerable sir, who are these people to you? Are they relatives from your mother’s side or from your father’s side?
"What have you seen that you ask this? "I see that they have affection and great respect for you. "Friends, even more than [what is shown] by one's own mother and father..."
“They perform what is difficult for us; even our very bowls and robes belong to them.
Through their power, we know neither fear in times of danger nor hunger in times of famine. We have no benefactors like these!
Thus he goes along praising their virtues. This is called “he takes away but does not bring back.”
But for one who performs the aforementioned duties and observances even from early morning, the fire element born of karma blazes up;
it releases the non-clung-to and takes hold of the clung-to, and sweat breaks out from the body.

Even though the meditation subject does not yet enter the path, he should take his bowl and robe early and, having hurriedly paid homage at the shrine, depart at the very time when the cattle are leaving.
Having entered a village for alms of rice-gruel and obtained some gruel, he goes to a rest-house and drinks it.
Then, with only two or three swallows, the fire element born of karma releases the clung-to (upādinnaka) matter and takes up the unclung-to (anupādinnaka).

Like one bathed with a hundred jars of water, the fire element attains the quenching of its fever; having thus consumed the gruel under the heading of his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), he proceeds.
Having washed his bowl and face, and having attended to the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) during the interval between meals, he wanders for alms in the remaining areas;

then, having consumed his food while keeping the meditation subject as his primary focus, he returns from there taking up the meditation subject that presents itself in continuous succession. This is called "bringing back but not bringing forth. Such monks are...
Having drunk rice gruel and begun insight meditation (vipassanā), those who attained Arahantship within the Buddha’s dispensation are beyond counting.
Even in the island of Sri Lanka alone, in various villages,
there is no sitting hall where there are not monks who have attained Arahantship after drinking rice gruel.
But he who dwells in negligence, having cast aside his burden and broken all his duties, dwelling with a mind fettered by the five kinds of mental stumps—

entering a village for alms without even the perception that "there is such a thing as a meditation subject," moving about and eating while mingling in unbecoming association with householders, and departing empty-handed— he is called:
“Neither takes away nor brings back.
However, as for that which was described as “both taking away and bringing back,” it should be understood precisely by way of the practice of going and returning.
For sons of good family who desire their own welfare, having gone forth in the Dispensation, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, or even fifty [days],...
Even when living together as a group, they dwell having made a formal agreement: "Friends, you have not gone forth out of debt, nor out of fear, nor because you were driven by a livelihood;
rather, you have gone forth here desiring to be liberated from suffering. Therefore, whatever defilement arises while walking, subdue it right there while walking;
likewise, whatever defilement arises while standing, sitting, or lying down, subdue it right there while lying down."
Having thus made this agreement, when they go on their almsround, there are stones at intervals of half an usabha, one usabha, half a gāvuta, or one gāvuta;
using these as signs, they proceed while attending to their meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
If defilement arises in anyone while walking, he suppresses it right there. If he is unable to do so, he stops, and then [his companion] from behind—
Even one who comes along stands still. Thinking, "This bhikkhu knows the thought that has arisen in you;
this is not suitable for you," he reproaches himself, develops insight, and right there enters the plane of the Noble Ones (ariyabhūmi).
If he is unable to do so, he sits down. Then even one who comes after him also sits down; the same method applies. [Regarding] the plane of the Noble Ones...
Even if he is unable to fall asleep, he goes along suppressing that defilement and attending only to the meditation subject;
he does not lift his foot with a mind dissociated from the meditation subject.
If he should so lift it, he turns back and returns to the very same previous spot, just like the Venerable Mahāphussadeva, who dwelt at the Ālindaka.
It is said that for nineteen years he lived fulfilling the practice of going forth and returning;
people too, while plowing, sowing, threshing, and performing their labors along the road, saw the Elder coming in that manner and thought:
"This Elder goes back again and again; has he perhaps lost his way, or is it because of something else?"

"Have you forgotten? they exclaimed. Disregarding them, he practiced the duties of a recluse with a mind intent on his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), and within twenty years he attained *arahantship*.
On the day he attained *arahantship*, a deity residing at the end of his walking path stood there having lit a lamp with her fingers. The Four Great Kings and Sakka [also appeared].
Sakka, lord of the gods, and Brahmā Sahampati came to wait upon him.
Seeing that radiance, the forest-dwelling Mahātissa Thera asked him on the following day: "Venerable sir, there was a radiance in your presence during the night; what was that radiance?
The elder, wishing to avoid the matter, replied: "Radiance, for instance, can be the radiance of a lamp, or it can be the radiance of a gem."

He spoke these words and others like them. Then, being exhorted with the command, “You must conceal [this],” he acknowledged, saying “Yes,” and reported it—just as the Elder Mahānāga who dwelt in the Black Creeper Arbour did.
It is said that while fulfilling the practice of going forth and returning, he first thought, “I shall honor the Great Struggle of the Blessed One.”
For seven years he resolved upon standing and walking meditation alone. Then, for sixteen years, having fulfilled the practice of going forth and returning, he attained *arahatship*.
Lifting his foot with a mind intent on his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), and returning it when it was lifted by one devoid of that intent, he approached the vicinity of a village.
At a place where suspicion might arise, wondering, "Is it a cow or a renunciant?"...
Standing there and putting on his robe, he washes his bowl with water from inside his waist-cloth and takes a mouthful of water.
For what reason? Lest there be a distraction of the meditation subject for him even by the mere words "May you live long! addressed to people who have come to give alms or pay homage.
Or [he asks], "Venerable sir, what is today's date? regarding the day.
But when asked for the number of monks or questioned about the matter, he swallows water and then speaks.

If there are no inquirers regarding the day or other details, he goes out at the time of departure after spitting it out at the village gate, just like the fifty monks who entered the rains residence at the Kalambatittha monastery. They, it is said, [did so] on the full moon of Āsāḷha.
They made a formal agreement: “Until we have attained arahantship, we shall not speak to one another.
When entering a village for alms, they did so after rinsing their mouths with water. When asked about the day or other such matters, they acted according to the method already described.
There, the people, seeing the spittle, realized: “Today one has come; today two. And they thought thus:
—“Why is it that they do not converse with us alone, or perhaps even among themselves?
If they do not converse even among themselves, they must certainly have fallen into a dispute. Come, let us go and ask for their forgiveness.
Having all gone to the monastery, they did not see even two monks in a single place among the fifty monks. Then he who...
Among them was a man with keen vision who said, "Gentlemen quarrelers, this is not the kind of dwelling place for those who engage in strife;
the shrine courtyard and the Bodhi-tree courtyard have been well-swept, the brooms have been properly set out, and the drinking water and washing water have been well-arranged.
At that, they turned back right there. Those monks, having attained Arahantship within that very rainy season, offered the invitation of purity at the Great Pavāraṇā ceremony.
Thus, like the Elder Mahānāga who dwelt in the Kāḷavallimaṇḍapa, and like the bhikkhus who had entered the rains retreat at Kalambatittha Vihāra,

one should lift the foot with a mind intent solely on the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) and proceed toward the vicinity of the village. Having rinsed one's mouth with water and observed the streets,
one should avoid places where drunkards, gamblers, and other quarrelsome persons reside, as well as places where fierce elephants, horses, and the like are kept.
or if there is none, he enters that street. And while wandering for alms there, he does not go with excessive haste as if in a great hurry;
for there is no such thing as a "speedy" alms-gathering ascetic practice (piṇḍapātika-dhutanga).
Rather, he proceeds like a water-cart that has reached uneven ground, moving steadily and without agitation. And having entered each house, whether [the donor] wishes to give...
Or, having observed that [the donor] is unwilling to give, he waits for a suitable time;
then, having received alms and taken them, he returns either to the village, outside the village, or to the monastery itself.

Sitting in a comfortable and appropriate place, he attends to his meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), establishes the perception of repulsiveness in food by way of the similes of the axle-oil, the wound-ointment, and the son’s flesh, and—
Reflecting thus, he takes food endowed with the eight factors, neither for sport, nor for intoxication, nor for physical beauty, nor for adornment...
[as before] ...and having finished his meal and performed the water-rites, after resting for a moment to allay the fatigue of eating,
just as he did before the meal, so too after the meal— during the first watch and the last watch— he devotes himself solely to the meditation subject.
He brings it to mind; this is called "taking away and bringing back.

Now, while fulfilling this practice of going and returning—known as taking away and bringing back—if he is endowed with the necessary supporting conditions (*upanissaya*), he attains *arahantship* in his very first stage of life.
If he does not attain it in the first stage, then he does so in the middle stage.
If he does not attain it in middle age, then at the time of death; if he does not attain it at the time of death, then having become a son of the gods;
if he does not attain it as a son of the gods, then when a Buddha has not yet appeared, he is reborn and realizes pratyekabodhi.
If he does not realize pratyekabodhi, then in the presence of Buddhas, he becomes one of swift direct knowledge (*kṣiprābhijña*).
He is like the elder Bāhiya Dārucīriya in great wisdom; or like the elder Sāriputta in great psychic power;
or like the elder Mahāmoggallāna in being an advocate of the ascetic practices (dhuta); or like the elder Mahākassapa in possessing the divine eye;
or like the elder Anuruddha in being a master of the Vinaya; or like the elder Upāli.
Or he is a preacher of the Dhamma, such as the Elder Puṇṇa, son of Mantāṇī, who was a forest-dweller;
or such as the Elder Revata, who was one of great learning; or such as the Elder Ānanda, who was desirous of alms; or such as the Elder Rāhula, the Son of the Buddha.
Thus, in this tetrad, for him who both goes out and returns, the clear comprehension of the range of activity reaches its culmination.
Furthermore, non-delusion regarding advancing and so forth is the clear comprehension of non-delusion; this should be understood as follows:

here, when a bhikkhu is advancing or retreating, he does not—as do blind, foolish worldlings—regard advancing and so forth with the thought, "The self advances," or "Advancing has been produced by the self," or "I am advancing," or "Advancing has been produced by me."

Or they are deluded; but one who is not so deluded, when the thought "I am stepping forward" arises, then together with that very thought, the wind-element originating from consciousness arises, producing intimation (*viññatti*).

Thus, by way of the expansion of the wind-element produced by mental activity, this collection of bones designated as the "body" steps forward. As he thus steps forward, with the lifting of each individual foot—
In the two elements—the earth element and the water element—they are deficient and weak, while the other two are excessive and powerful;

likewise in the acts of lifting up and moving away. In the act of letting go, the fire element and the air element are deficient and weak, while the other two are excessive and powerful; likewise in the acts of setting down and stopping.
In that process, the material and immaterial phenomena occurring during the lifting do not reach the carrying forward; likewise, those occurring during the carrying forward do not reach the shifting;
those occurring during the shifting do not reach the releasing; those occurring during the releasing do not reach the placing down;
and those occurring during the placing down do not reach the final resting. In each respective instance, [the movement proceeds] from joint to joint.
Joining with joints and uniting with boundaries, they break apart with a clattering sound like sesame seeds cast into a hot pan.
In that regard, who is it that approaches alone, or for whom is there the approaching of one?
For in the ultimate sense, it is only the elements that go, the elements that stand, the elements that sit, and the elements that lie down—each in its respective part together with material form.
"One consciousness arises, another consciousness ceases;
there is a continuous succession like the flow of a river.
Thus, non-delusion regarding such actions as stepping forward and so forth is called "clear comprehension of non-delusion."
The meaning of the phrase "he acts with clear comprehension when going forward and returning" is thus completed.

Regarding the terms "looking ahead" (*ālokita*) and "looking aside" (*vilokita*): here, "looking ahead" means gazing straight forward; "looking aside" means glancing toward the intermediate directions.
Furthermore, by way of looking downward, upward, and backward, there are also what are called "looking down," "looking up," and "looking behind."
Those [other types of clear comprehension] are not included here. However, these two alone are taken because they are appropriate, or else all of them are indeed included by way of this heading.

In that context, when the thought "I shall look" has arisen, grasping the meaning without looking merely according to the impulse of the mind is clear comprehension of purpose (*sātthaka-sampajañña*).
This should be understood by taking the venerable Nanda as a personal witness. For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Bhikkhus, if it is necessary for Nanda to look toward the eastern direction, having applied his whole mind, Nanda looks toward the eastern direction, thinking:
‘As I look toward the eastern direction in this way, may no covetousness or dejection arise in me.’”
‘Evil, unwholesome states will flow in after me. Thus, in that regard, he is fully aware.
If, monks, Nanda must look toward the western direction... [as before] ...the northern direction... [as before] ...the southern direction... [as before] ...above... [as before] ...below...
[as before] ...or the intermediate directions, Nanda, having applied his whole mind, looks toward the intermediate directions.
—‘As I survey the various directions in this way, covetousness, dejection, and evil unwholesome states will not flow in after me.
Thus, in that regard, he is clearly comprehending.
Furthermore, here too, the purposefulness and suitability [of the practice] should be understood by means of the same previously mentioned visiting of shrines and so forth.

Full awareness of the range of movement (*gocara-sampajañña*), however, is simply the non-abandonment of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). Therefore, in this regard, those whose meditation subjects are the aggregates, elements, and bases should look forward and look around by way of their own respective meditation subjects; or else, those whose meditation subjects are the kasiṇas and so forth should do so by way of the meditation subject as their primary focus.
Internally, there is no such thing as a "self" that looks forward or looks around, nor is there anyone who thinks, "I shall look forward."
But when the mind arises, simultaneously with that very mind, the mind-originated air element arises, producing intimation.

Thus, by means of the expansion of the air element produced by mental activity, the lower eyelid sinks down and the upper one leaps upward. There is no one at all who opens them by means of a machine. Then—
Understanding that "eye-consciousness arises performing the function of seeing" is here called non-delusive clear comprehension (*asammoha-sampajañña*).
Furthermore, non-delusive clear comprehension should be understood here by way of fundamental full understanding (*mūla-pariññā*), adventitiousness, and temporariness.
First, by way of fundamental full understanding:
The life-continuum, adverting, seeing, receiving, investigating, determining, and the impulsion is the seventh.
Therein, the life-continuum proceeds performing the function of a factor for the existence of rebirth; having turned that back—
The functional mind-element (kiriyamanodhātu), accomplishing its function of adverting; following its cessation, the eye-consciousness accomplishing its function of seeing;
following its cessation, the resultant mind-element accomplishing its function of receiving;
following its cessation, the resultant mind-consciousness element accomplishing its function of investigating; and following its cessation, the functional mind-consciousness element.
Accomplishing its function of determining, it impels the impulsion seven times following that [registration].
In this process, even during the first impulsion, there is no such thing as looking forward or looking around by way of lust, hatred, or delusion, thinking, "This is a woman" or "This is a man.
This remains the case for the second impulsion... and so on... up to the seventh impulsion. However, among these, like soldiers on a battlefield, they proceed from the bottom upward.
When [the body] has split and fallen apart, looking and gazing with passion and so forth occurs, thinking, "This is a woman," or "This is a man.
In this way, first of all, non-delusive clear comprehension should be understood here by way of fundamental full understanding (*mūla-pariññā*).
However, when a visible form comes into the range of the eye-door, from the moment the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) vibrates onwards, by way of accomplishing its own function—
When the adverting consciousness and the others have arisen and ceased, the impulsion arises at the very end;
it is like a visitor in the eye-door, which has become the dwelling place for the adverting consciousness and the rest that arose previously.
Just as when a visitor who has entered another's house to beg for something finds the owners of the house remaining silent, he issues his own commands.

It is not fitting; for when the mind does not become lustful, hateful, or deluded even toward the acts of adverting and so forth—which have occurred within the eye-door that is like a dwelling—it is likewise improper for lust, hate, or delusion to arise.
Thus, non-delusive clear comprehension should be understood by way of the adventitious nature [of these mental states].
Furthermore, those consciousnesses that arise in the eye-door, ending with the determining consciousness (*voṭṭhabbana*), together with...
They break apart right there and then along with the associated mental states; they do not see one another, and thus they are fleeting and momentary.

In this regard, just as when all the human inhabitants of a house have died, it is not fitting for the one survivor—who is himself subject to death at that very moment—to take delight in dancing, singing, and the like; even so, [it is the same here].
When, among the mental states associated with consciousness that have a single door— such as adverting and so forth— each has ceased right where it arose,
it is not fitting for the remaining impulsion, which is itself subject to death at that very moment, to find delight through the modes of lust, hatred, or delusion.
Thus should clear comprehension of non-delusion be understood by way of its temporary nature.
Furthermore, this should also be understood by way of reviewing the aggregates (khandha), bases (āyatana), elements (dhātu), and conditions (paccaya).

For herein, the eye and visible forms constitute the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha); seeing is the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha); the feeling associated with that is the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha);
perception is the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha); and contact and so forth are the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha). Thus, of these five aggregates...
In the coming together [of these factors], looking forward and looking around are discerned. In that regard, who is it alone that looks forward and looks around?
Likewise, the eye is the eye-base; visible form is the visible-form base; seeing is the mind-base; and feeling and the other associated mental states are the mental-object base.
Thus, in the coming together of these four bases, looking forward and looking around are discerned.
In that regard, who is it that looks forward and looks around?
Likewise, the eye is the eye-element (*cakkhudhātu*); visible form is the visible-form element (*rūpadhātu*); seeing is the eye-consciousness element (*cakkhuviññāṇadhātu*);

and the mental states associated with that, such as feeling and so forth, are the mental-object element (*dhammadhātu*). Thus, looking forward and looking around occur through the coming together of these four elements.
It is perceived. In that regard, who is it that looks forward and who is it that looks around?

Likewise, the eye is the support-condition (*nissaya-paccaya*); visible forms are the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*); adverting consciousness is the proximity, contiguity, decisive-support, presence, and absence-conditions (*anantara-samanantara-upanissaya-atthi-vigata-paccaya*);

light is the decisive-support-condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*); and feeling and the other mental factors are the co-nascent conditions (*sahajāta-paccaya*). Thus, through the concurrence of these conditions—

Looking forward and looking around are discerned. In that regard, who is it that looks forward, and who is it that looks around? In this way, non-deluded clear comprehension should be understood here by way of reviewing the aggregates, bases, elements, and conditions.
Regarding "in bending and in stretching," this refers to the bending and stretching of the limbs. In that context, the bending and stretching occurs solely through the power of the mind.

Situational awareness of purposefulness (*sātthaka-sampajañña*) is the discernment of what is beneficial and what is not beneficial regarding the bending and stretching of the hands and feet, rather than doing so without reflection.
In this regard, for one who stands with the hands and feet bent or stretched for too long, painful sensations arise from moment to moment;
the mind fails to attain one-pointedness, and the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) falls away.
One does not attain distinction. However, when one bends at the proper time and extends at the proper time, those painful feelings do not arise;

the mind becomes one-pointed, the meditation subject reaches full development, and one attains distinction. In this way, the discernment of what is beneficial and what is harmful should be understood.

Furthermore, even when there is something beneficial, having discerned what is suitable and what is unsuitable, the discernment of what is suitable is "clear comprehension of the suitable. Herein is the method:
It is said that in the courtyard of the Mahācetiya, young bhikkhus were engaged in recitation, while young bhikkhunīs sat behind them listening to the Dhamma.
There, one young man, extending his hand, came into physical contact with a woman; because of that very cause, he was reborn as a householder.
Another bhikkhu, extending his foot, extended it toward a fire; having struck a bone, his foot was consumed by the flames.
Another stretched out his arm on an anthill and was bitten by a venomous snake. Another stretched it out on the crossbar of his robe-shed and was bitten by a gem-bearing serpent.
Therefore, instead of stretching out the arm in such an unsuitable place, one should stretch it out in a suitable place. This is here the clear comprehension of suitability (*sappāya-sampajañña*).

Clear comprehension of the range of action (*gocara-sampajañña*), however, should be illustrated by the story of the Elder Mahā-Tissa: It is said that while the Elder Mahā-Tissa was sitting in his daytime resting place...
While conversing with his pupils, he suddenly bent his hand, then placed it back in its original position and slowly bent it again.

The pupils asked him, "Venerable sir, why did you suddenly bend your hand, then place it back in its original position and slowly bend it again? "Friends, from the time I began my meditation subject..."
"I had begun to attend to it; my hand had never before been withdrawn from my meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna).
But now, while conversing with you, I have withdrawn it. Therefore, please place it back again in its original position.
"Very well, venerable sir; a bhikkhu indeed ought to be like this. Thus it is here as well.
It should be understood that "clear comprehension of the domain" (gocara-sampajañña) is simply the non-abandonment of the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna).
Internally, there is no such thing as a self that bends or stretches;

rather, bending and stretching occur through the expansion of the air-element (vāyodhātu) arising from the aforementioned mental activity, like the movement of the hands and feet of a wooden puppet by means of pulling strings.
In this context, it should be understood that "clear comprehension of non-delusion" (*asammoha-sampajañña*) refers to the thorough understanding [of the process] as it occurs.

Regarding "the wearing of the outer robe, the bowl, and the inner robe": here, "wearing" (*dhāraṇa*) means the use of the outer robe and the inner robe by way of wearing them as undergarments and upper garments, and the use of the bowl by way of receiving alms-food and so forth. Among these, regarding the wearing of the outer robe and the inner robe:

The meaning (*attha*) is precisely that which was described by the Blessed One in such a manner as: "When one has put on or wrapped oneself [in the robe] and wanders for alms, there is the acquisition of material food, and [the robe serves] for the warding off of cold," and so forth. Through this, the clear comprehension of purpose (*sātthaka-sampajañña*) should be understood.
Furthermore, for one whose nature is heat or who is weak, a fine robe is suitable; for one who is sensitive to cold, a thick one is suitable.
A double-layered cloth (*dupaṭṭa*). That which is contrary [to what is needed] is unsuitable (*asappāya*).

Whatever is worn out is indeed unsuitable, for by providing it with door-bolts and so forth, it becomes an obstacle for him. Likewise is a robe made of fine wool, silk, or similar materials that is alluring.
For such a thing creates an obstacle to dwelling alone in the forest and even an obstacle to life itself. But in the absolute sense (*nippariyāyena*), however—

That which arises through wrong livelihood, such as by means of hinting (*nimitta-kamma*) and so forth, and that by the pursuit of which unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline—that is unsuitable. The opposite is suitable.

Herein, "clear comprehension of the suitable" (*sappāya-sampajañña*) refers to this suitability. "Clear comprehension of the domain" (*gocara-sampajañña*) should be understood as occurring precisely through the non-abandonment of the meditation subject.

Internally, there is no such thing as a "self" that puts on the robe; rather, the act of putting on the robe occurs solely through the expansion of the air-element and the activity of consciousness in the manner already described.
In this process, both the robe is insentient and the body is insentient.
The robe does not know, "The body has been clothed by me," nor does the body know, "I have been clothed by the robe. It is merely the elements [that function].
They conceal the collection of elements (dhātusamūha), just as cloth rags or pieces of cotton conceal a physical form.
Therefore, one should feel no joy upon obtaining a beautiful robe, nor any dejection upon obtaining an unattractive one.
For at places such as the Nāgavammika Cetiya or the Bodhi Tree, some people pay honor with garlands, perfumes, incense, and garments, while others do not.
Disrespect consists of blows from sticks and weapons, or being smeared with excrement, urine, and mud.

Just as elephants, anthills, trees, and the like do not experience either joy or dejection because of these things, even so, one should feel no joy upon receiving a beautiful robe, nor dejection upon receiving an ugly one;
it is by means of such reflective contemplation (*paṭisaṅkhāna*) that one should proceed in this matter.
Non-delusive clear comprehension should be understood.

Even when taking up the bowl, one should not grasp it hastily; rather, by reflecting, "Having taken this, while wandering for alms, I shall obtain food," one should understand purposeful clear comprehension in terms of the benefit to be obtained on account of taking up the bowl.
However, for one with a thin and weak body, a heavy bowl is unsuitable, as is any bowl struck with four or five dents.
It is difficult to clean and indeed unsuitable. Even a bowl that is hard to wash is not permitted; it becomes an impediment for one who is washing it.
A bowl with the color of a gem, however, is alluring and—just as in the case described regarding the robe—is unsuitable.
Furthermore, if it is obtained by means of hinting (*nimittakamma*) and so forth, then while one uses it, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline.

This is exclusively unwholesome. The opposite is wholesome. It is by way of this [distinction] that there is "clear comprehension of the suitable" (*sappāya-sampajañña*) here. And "clear comprehension of the domain" (*gocara-sampajañña*) should be understood as occurring precisely through the non-abandonment of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
Internally, there is no such thing as a "self" that takes up the bowl; it occurs solely through the expansion of the air-element of mental activity in the manner already described.
There is what is called the taking up of the bowl. In that case, the bowl is insentient and the hands are also insentient.
The bowl does not know, "I am being held by the hands," nor do the hands know, "The bowl is being held by us.
It is merely elements grasping a collection of elements, like the grasping of a glowing-hot bowl with tongs. It is by way of reflection on such a process that [this is understood].
Non-delusive clear comprehension should be understood.

Furthermore, just as when compassionate persons, seeing destitute people lying in a shelter for the homeless—whose hands and feet are severed, whose wounds are oozing with pus and blood, infested with worms, and swarming with blue flies—provide them with mere rags to cover their wounds; [so too should one act].
And they present medicines with skull-cups and such. In that regard, some receive cloths that are soft, while others receive those that are coarse.
Some receive medicine bowls that are well-shaped, while others receive those that are ill-shaped;
yet they are neither pleased nor displeased by this, for [the bowl] serves merely as a covering for the wound.
Their purpose is served merely by a rag and a bowl for receiving medicine. In the same way,
the bhikkhu who regards his robe as a rag for a wound and his bowl as a vessel for medicine,
and perceives the alms received in the bowl as medicine in that vessel— this is through non-deluded clear comprehension regarding the wearing of the outer cloak and the bowl.
He should be understood as one who acts with supreme clear comprehension (*sampajañña*).

Regarding "eating" and so forth: "eating" refers to the consumption of alms-food; "drinking" refers to the drinking of rice-gruel and the like; "chewing" refers to the chewing of flour-cakes and the like;
"tasting" refers to the tasting of honey, molasses, and the like. Therein, even the eightfold [method] stated by way of the formula beginning with "not for sport" and so forth—
"Meaning" (attha) means purpose. It is by way of that very purpose that "clear comprehension of what is beneficial" (sātthaka-sampajañña) should be understood.
Furthermore, among coarse, refined, bitter, sweet, and other tastes, whatever food does not provide comfort for a particular person is unsuitable for them.
However, that which is obtained through the influence of charms or rituals, and those unwholesome states that arise while one is eating—[these are to be avoided].
Unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline; that is entirely unsuitable, while the opposite is suitable.

It is by way of this [discernment of suitability] that "clear comprehension of suitability" is understood here. Furthermore, "clear comprehension of the domain" should be understood as the non-abandoning of the meditation subject.
Internally, there is no such thing as a "self" who is the eater; it is solely through the expansion of the air-element of mental activity, of the kind already described, [that eating occurs].
There is what is called "receiving with the bowl. There is what is called "placing the hand into the bowl" by means of the diffusion of the air-element produced by mental activity.
By means of the diffusion of the air-element produced by mental activity alone, there is the making of morsels, the lifting of morsels, and the opening of the mouth;
no one opens the jawbones with a key or a mechanical device. It is solely by means of the diffusion of the air-element produced by mental activity that...

There is the placing of a morsel of food in the mouth; the upper teeth perform the function of a pestle, the lower teeth perform the function of a mortar, and the tongue performs the function of a hand.
Thus, there, thin saliva from the tip of the tongue and thick saliva from the root of the tongue smear the food.
That [food], being turned by the hand of the tongue in the mortar of the lower teeth, is moistened with the water of saliva.
Once it has been chewed and ground down by the pestle-like upper teeth, there is no one who puts it inside with a spoon or a ladle;
rather, it enters by means of the air element (*vāyodhātu*). Once it has entered, there is no one who holds it by making a bed of straw;
rather, it remains by means of the air element alone. Once it has stayed [there], there is no one who makes a hearth and [lights] a fire...
There is no such thing as one who "cooks" by kindling a fire; it is cooked by the fire element alone.
There is no one at all who, once it is cooked, takes it out with a stick or a rod; it is the air element alone that carries it out.
Thus, the air element pushes back, pushes forward, holds, turns over, crushes, dries up, and carries away.
The earth element supports, turns about, crushes, and dries up. The water element moistens and maintains its state of moisture.
The fire element digests what has been ingested. The space element provides a clear opening.
The consciousness element, following appropriate application in each respective instance, experiences [the object]. Thus, by way of reflecting on what has thus occurred—
Non-delusive clear comprehension should be understood.
Furthermore, herein, it should be understood through the contemplation of the tenfold nature of repulsiveness:
by way of going, seeking, enjoyment, abode, storage, the unripened, the ripened, the fruit, the outflow, and smearing. Thus, it is here [to be understood] through such contemplation.

Clear comprehension of non-delusion should be understood. A detailed exposition on this point, however, should be taken from the description of the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment in the *Visuddhimagga*.
Regarding "the act of voiding excrement and urine": this refers to the performance of defecation and urination.
In that regard, for one who does not void excrement and urine at the proper time, sweat breaks out from the entire body, the eyes roll, and the mind does not become one-pointed.
Furthermore, other diseases arise; however, for one who acts [properly], none of that occurs—this is the meaning here.
By means of this, clear comprehension of purposefulness (*sātthaka-sampajañña*) is to be understood.
On the other hand, for one who voids excrement or urine in an improper place, there is an offense, infamy increases, and there is a danger to life.
When one performs [the action] in a suitable place, all that [unwholesome result] does not occur;

this is here the "clear comprehension of the suitable" (*sappāya-sampajañña*) by way of that suitability. Furthermore, "clear comprehension of the domain" (*gocara-sampajañña*) should be understood precisely by way of not abandoning the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
Internally, there is no such thing as a "self" performing the act of defecation or urination; it occurs solely through the expansion of the air-element (*vāyodhātu*) consisting of mental activity.
However, there is the business of excrement and urine. Or just as, when an abscess has ripened, pus and blood issue forth involuntarily due to the bursting of the abscess;

and just as water issues involuntarily from a water-vessel that is overfilled—so too, the excrement and urine accumulated in the receptacle for digested food and the bladder, being pressed by the force of the wind, issue forth even against one's will.
They pass out. Now, as he passes out in this way, that excrement and urine belongs neither to the bhikkhu himself nor to another;
it is merely an outflow from the body. How so? Just as when one discards old water from a water-pot, it belongs neither to oneself nor to others; it is merely the act of clearing away.
In this way, clear comprehension through non-delusion (*asammoha-sampajañña*) should be understood by way of reflecting upon what has thus occurred.
Regarding "going" and so forth: "going" refers to the act of walking; "standing" refers to staying; "sitting" refers to the act of sitting; "lying down" refers to sleeping;
"waking" refers to being awake; "speaking" refers to talking; and "remaining silent" refers to not speaking. "When walking, one understands: 'I am walking.'"

In this sutta, "Whether standing, he knows 'I am standing'; whether sitting, he knows 'I am sitting'; whether lying down, he knows 'I am lying down,'" the long-term postures (*addhāna-iriyāpatha*) are described.
In this [other] one, "In advancing, in retreating, in looking ahead, in looking aside, in bending, in stretching," the intermediate [postures] are described.
And in "In going, in standing, in sitting, in sleeping, in waking," [the short-term postures are described].
However, here the minor matters, the fragments, and the postures are discussed. Therefore, in their case too, acting with full awareness should be understood according to the method already stated.
But the Elder Tipiṭaka Mahāsīva said: "When someone, after walking for a long time or after walking meditation, later stands still and reflects thus:
'The material and immaterial phenomena that occurred at the time of walking have ceased right here.'"
This is what is called "acting with clear comprehension when going.
When one who is reciting, answering questions, or attending to a meditation subject stands for a long time and later, while sitting, reflects thus:
"The material and immaterial phenomena that occurred at the time of standing..."
“...have ceased right here. This is called one who acts with clear comprehension while standing.

One who, having sat for a long time merely by way of reciting the scriptures and so forth, later rises and reflects thus: “The material and immaterial phenomena that occurred while sitting have ceased right here”—this is called one who acts with clear comprehension while sitting.
Furthermore, one who, while lying down, either reciting the scriptures or attending to the meditation subject, falls asleep—
Later, having arisen, he reflects thus: “The material and immaterial phenomena that occurred at the time of lying down have ceased right here.
This is what is meant by being one who acts with clear comprehension both while dreaming and while awake.
For sleep is indeed the non-occurrence of functional consciousnesses, while waking is their occurrence.

But when speaking, he speaks mindfully and clearly comprehending, thinking: "This thing called sound arises dependent upon the lips, the teeth, the tongue, and the palate, and dependent upon a corresponding mental application.
Or else, after having recited for a long time, or having explained the Dhamma, or having practiced a meditation subject, [he speaks].
Or, having answered a question, he later reflects while remaining silent: "The material and immaterial phenomena that arose at the time of speaking have ceased right here.
This is one who acts with clear comprehension regarding what has been spoken.
But as for one who, having remained silent for a long time after attending to the Dhamma or a meditation subject, later reflects thus:
“The material and immaterial phenomena occurring at the time one has become silent have ceased right here. For when there is the occurrence of derived materiality, one is said to speak;
when it is absent, one is said to be silent. This is what is meant by being “one who acts with clear comprehension regarding silence.
And this, as stated by the Elder Mahāsīva, is intended in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta as the burden of non-delusion.
In this Fruit of the Ascetic Life, however, all fourfold clear comprehension (sampajañña) is found.
Therefore, in this context, acting with clear comprehension should be understood by way of the four kinds of clear comprehension according to the method already stated.

And in all instances, the meaning of the term "one who acts with clear comprehension" (sampajānakārī) should be understood by way of clear comprehension associated specifically with mindfulness (sati). By means of mindfulness and clear comprehension...

"Endowed with": this is the detailed explanation of that term. However, in the *Vibhaṅga* treatise, these very terms are analyzed as follows: "Mindful and clearly comprehending, he moves forward; mindful and clearly comprehending, he moves backward.
"In this way, O Great King": thus, by means of clear comprehension associated with mindfulness, one carries out the acts of moving forward and so forth.
The meaning is that he is "endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension.
215. Discourse on Contentment:
"In this case, O Great King, a bhikkhu is contented"—here, "contented" means by way of contentment with whatever requisites are available.
He is endowed with this. Furthermore, this contentment is twelvefold, as follows:

regarding robes, there is threefold contentment—contentment with whatever is obtained, contentment with what is sufficient, and contentment with what is suitable. It is the same for alms-food and the other requisites. This is the explanation of its divisions:
Here, a bhikkhu receives a robe, whether it be beautiful or ugly; he makes do with that alone and does not seek another.
He does not even accept it when he obtains it. This is his contentment with whatever robe-cloth is obtained (*yathālābha-santuṣṭi*).

Furthermore, if he is naturally weak, or overcome by illness or old age, and thus fatigues himself when wearing a heavy robe, he exchanges it for a lighter one with a fellow monk who has a similar need;
even while using that lighter one, he remains content. This is his contentment according to his strength (*yathābala-santuṣṭi*).
Another person is one who obtains excellent requisites.
Having obtained a costly bowl or robe—or indeed many bowls and robes—among his alms-bowl, robes, and so forth, he gives them away, thinking, "Let this be for the elders who have long been gone forth;
let this be suitable for those of great learning; let this be for the sick; let this be for those who receive little," and then takes back from them their old robes or other items.
Or, having picked up rags from a heap of refuse and made a *saṅghāṭi* robe from them, even while wearing it, he remains content.
This is his contentment with robes as they happen to be suitable.
Furthermore, in this case, a bhikkhu receives almsfood, whether coarse or refined; he sustains himself with that alone, and not anything else.
He does not long for it, nor does he accept it even when he obtains it. This is his contentment with whatever alms-food is obtained.

However, if he receives alms-food that is contrary to his own nature or contrary to his illness—such that by consuming it he would experience discomfort—he gives that to a fellow monk who is in similar circumstances, and having eaten suitable food from that monk’s hand, [he proceeds].
Even while performing the duties of a recluse, he remains content. This is his contentment with almsfood according to his strength.

Another person receives abundant and exquisite almsfood; yet, like [the one who gives] his robe, he gives that food to elders, those long-ordained, the learned, those of little gain, and the sick, or else eats the leftovers from theirs, or wanders for alms and eats mixed food—yet even so, he remains content.
This is his contentment with almsfood as is appropriate.
Furthermore, when a bhikkhu receives a dwelling—whether pleasing or unpleasing—he gives rise to neither gladness nor dejection;
he is satisfied even with what he has obtained, such as a mere spread of grass. This is his...

Contentment with whatever lodging one obtains is as follows: if, however, one receives a lodging that is naturally unsuitable for oneself or incompatible with one's illness—such that living there causes discomfort—one gives it to a fellow monk of similar standing and remains content even while staying in the suitable lodging belonging to that monk.
This is his contentment regarding the lodging according to his strength.
Another person of great merit obtains many excellent lodgings, such as caves, pavilions, and gabled houses.
Having given these away like robes—to elders, those long ordained, the learned, those of little gain, and the sick—he remains content wherever he dwells.
This is his contentment with a suitable lodging. He who thinks: “The best lodging...”

Reflecting thus: "This is a place for negligence; lethargy and drowsiness descend upon one sitting there, and when one overcome by sleep awakens again, sensual thoughts manifest," he did not accept even such a lodging as it was offered.
Having rejected it, he remained content even while dwelling in the open air, at the foot of trees, and so forth.
This is his contentment with what is appropriate regarding his lodging.
Furthermore, when a bhikkhu receives medicinal requisites—whether coarse or refined—he is satisfied with whatever he receives;
he does not long for another, and even if he were to receive more, he does not accept it. This is his contentment with what is obtained regarding the requisite of medicine.
But if one who needs oil receives molasses, he gives it to a fellow monk, takes oil from his hand,
or seeks out something else entirely, and even while preparing medicine, he remains content.
This is his contentment according to his strength regarding the requisite of medicine.
Another person of great merit receives abundant and excellent medicines, such as oil, honey, and molasses.
Like that [first] monk, he gives these to elders, those who have long been ordained, the learned, those of little gain, and the sick;
even while subsisting on whatever they bring back for him, he remains truly content. But as for one who places bitter gourd in one vessel and the four sweets in another—

When told, "Venerable sir, take whatever you wish," if his illness is cured even by one of those [medicines], he then refuses the "four sweets" (catumadhura)—which are praised by the Buddha and others—calling it "urine-gourd" (muttaharīṭaka), and prepares medicine using only the urine-gourd;
thus he remains supremely content. This is his contentment with what is suitable regarding the requisite of medicine.
However, for a bhikkhu endowed with this twelvefold contentment regarding various requisites, eight articles are permissible:
the three robes, an alms-bowl, a tooth-stick cutter and knife, a single needle, a waist-band, and a water-strainer. And this has been said:
“The three robes and the bowl, the razor, the needle, and the girdle;
together with the water-strainer—these eight belong to the bhikkhu devoted to yoga.
All of these serve both for the maintenance of the body and for the maintenance of the belly. How so? First, having put on the three robes...
When one wears it and moves about, it protects and nourishes the body; thus it is "for the protection of the body.
When one strains water with the hem of the robe and drinks, or when one gathers fruits and other food to eat, it protects and nourishes the belly;
thus it is "for the protection of the belly."

A water pot, too, by being used to draw water, is conducive to the well-being of the body at the time of bathing and when decorating the hut; it is conducive to the well-being of the belly at the time of taking and eating food.

A hatchet, too, by being used for cutting tooth-sticks, and for fashioning the parts and legs of beds and stools, as well as robes and the poles for the hut, is conducive to the well-being of the body; it is conducive to the well-being of the belly at the time of cutting sugarcane, coconuts, and so forth.
Even a needle is for the maintenance of the body at the time of sewing robes; it is for the maintenance of the belly when one eats by piercing cakes or fruits;
a waistband is for the maintenance of the body when one goes about after fastening it; it is for the maintenance of the belly when one gathers sugarcane and the like after binding them;
and a water-strainer is for the purpose of bathing after straining water with it, and for the purpose of cleaning the lodgings.

It is for the maintenance of the body. At the time of straining water, it serves that purpose; and at the time of eating, having taken sesame, rice, parched grain, and so forth with it, it serves for the maintenance of the stomach.
This, then, is the measure of requisites for one who possesses eight requisites.
However, for one who possesses nine requisites, when entering a dwelling, a sitting mat or a key kept there is permissible. For one who possesses ten requisites—
A sitting mat or a piece of hide is permitted for one who possesses eleven requisites;
a walking stick or an oil tube is permitted for one who possesses twelve requisites; and a sunshade or sandals are permitted for one who possesses thirteen requisites.
Among these, only the one with eight requisites is truly contented; the others should not be described as discontented, greedy, or burdened by great possessions.
For these too are indeed few in desire, contented, easy to support, and light in their mode of living.
However, the Blessed One did not speak this sutta with reference to them; he spoke it with reference to one who possesses eight requisites.
For such a person, having placed his small bowl and needle inside his water-strainer and set them within his alms-bowl, hangs the bowl over the shoulder and [carries] the triple robe...
Having made it dependent upon the body, he goes wherever he wishes at ease; there is nothing for him to turn back and take with him.
Thus, demonstrating this bhikkhu’s mode of living in lightness, the Blessed One said:
“He is content with robes that serve to protect the body,” and so forth. In this context, “that which serves to protect the body” means merely that which protects the body.
"By means of what merely sustains the belly" means by that which is sufficient for the maintenance of the stomach.
"He departs having taken [only] this much" means he goes having taken all eight requisites, having made them fastened to his body;
there is no attachment or bond such as, "This is my monastery, my cell, or my attendant. He is like an arrow released from its string, or like a rutting elephant that has strayed from the herd.

And like one who enjoys whatever lodging he desires—whether a forest thicket, the foot of a tree, or a mountain glen—he stands alone and sits alone. In all postures, he is solitary and without a second.
"He is impartial toward the four quarters and free from aversion."
Content with whatever comes by chance,
undaunted by hardships,
one should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros.
Thus described, it attains the state of being like the rhinoceros horn.
Now, establishing that meaning by means of a simile, he says: “Just as,” and so forth. Therein, “a winged bird” (*pakkhī sakuṇo*) means a bird possessed of wings.
“Flies” (*ḍeti*) means it flies up. Here, however, the summary of the meaning is this: birds, it is said, [go] to such-and-such a place...

Knowing that there was a tree in that place with ripened fruit, people came from various directions and, piercing and shaking its fruits with their nails, leaves, beaks, and so forth, they ate them. They had no thought such as, "This is for today; this will be for tomorrow.
But when the fruits were exhausted, they neither appointed a guardian for the tree nor placed a leaf upon it.

They do not place their feet, hands, nails, or beaks upon it. Rather, having become indifferent toward that tree, whichever direction anyone desires, he flies off toward it like one carrying a load of enemies.
In the same way, this bhikkhu, free from attachment and without longing, departs wherever he wishes. Therefore it is said: "Having taken it up, he departs."

The Discourse on the Abandoning of the Hindrances (Nīvaraṇappahānakathā). 216. What does he show by the words "By this and so forth"? He shows the perfection of the requisites for dwelling in the forest.
For one who lacks these four requisites, dwelling in the forest does not succeed—whether due to wild animals or forest-dwelling hunters.
Or he incurs censure from others. Deities dwelling in the forest let out terrifying cries, saying, “What is the use of such an evil bhikkhu living in the forest?
They strike their heads with their hands and make gestures of fleeing.
They spread his ill repute, saying, “So-and-so bhikkhu entered the forest and committed this and that evil deed.”
But for one who possesses these four conditions, dwelling in the forest succeeds.

For he, reflecting upon his own virtue and seeing no blemish or mole whatsoever, generates rapture; then, contemplating that very rapture in terms of its waning and passing away, he enters the plane of the Noble Ones.
The deities inhabiting the forest, being delighted, utter words of praise.
In this way, his fame spreads like a drop of oil cast upon water.
Therein, "secluded" means empty, quiet, and noiseless; this is the meaning. Indeed, with reference to this very point, it is said in the Vibhaṅga:
"Secluded means that even if the lodging is nearby, it is not crowded with householders or those gone forth."
Therefore it is said, "by that it is secluded. One lies down (*seti*) and sits (*āsati*) therein; thus it is called *senāsana* (lodging).

This is a designation for beds, chairs, and so forth. Therefore he said: "Lodging means a bed is lodging, a chair, a mattress, a pillow, a monastery (*vihāra*), a gabled house (*aḍḍhayoga*), a palace (*pāsāda*), a watchtower (*hammiya*), a cave (*guhā*), a tower (*aṭṭa*), a multi-storied building (*māḷa*), a shelter (*leṇa*), or a bamboo thicket (*veḷugumba*)."
“The foot of a tree, a pavilion, a lodging, or wherever else monks return—that is all ‘lodging.
Furthermore: “A vihāra, an aḍḍhayoga, a pāsāda, a hammiya, and a cave”—this is called a *vihāra* lodging.
“A bed, a bench, a mattress, and a pillow”—this is called a bed-and-bench lodging. “A rug, a skin rug, and a grass mat...”
"A leaf-litter" refers to a resting place by way of bedding. "Or where monks withdraw" refers to a resting place by way of location.
Thus there are four kinds of resting places, all of which are indeed included under the term "resting place.
However, here [the author], showing a resting place suitable for a monk who is like a bird and belongs to no particular quarter, says:
He spoke of "the forest, the foot of a tree," and so forth. Therein, "the forest" refers to everything outside the boundary pillar (indakhīla) once one has departed;
this is according to the rule for bhikkhunīs. However, "a forest dwelling (āraññaka) is a resting place at least five hundred bow-lengths distant"—this is appropriate for this bhikkhu.
Its characteristics are described in the *Visuddhimagga* in the section on the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*).
It has been said. "At the foot of a tree" means any secluded spot at the base of a tree providing shade. "A mountain" means a rock formation;

for there, having performed one's water-related duties by the mountain springs, the mind of one sitting in the cool shade of the trees and being fanned by the cool breeze while the various directions are becoming clear becomes one-pointed. "A glen" (kandara): "kaṃ" is what is called...
"Water": a mountain region split by that water, broken open by the water; what they call a "river-pool" (*nadītumba*) or a "river-cove" (*nadīkuñja*).
For there, the sand is like silver plates, the forest thicket at the top is like a canopy of jewels, and the water flows like a mass of jewels.
Having descended into such a cave (*kandara*), having drunk the water, and having refreshed his limbs...
Having made the sand cool, having sprinkled it with water, and having spread out a robe of rags, the mind becomes one-pointed for one who sits performing the duties of a recluse.
"A mountain cave" (*giriguhā*) refers to the space between two mountains, or a single great hollow resembling a mountain pass, characterized as a charnel ground as described in the *Visuddhimagga*.
"A forest retreat" (*vanapattha*) refers to [an area] beyond the village boundary...
Having passed beyond the vicinity of human habitation, where people neither plough nor sow—it is for this reason that it is said:
“‘Forest-thicket’ (vanappattha) is a designation for remote lodgings,” and so forth. ‘Open space’ (abbhokāsa) means uncovered.
However, if one so desires, one may live there having constructed a cloth-tent (cīvarakuṭi). ‘Rice-stubble’ (palālapuñja) means a heap of rice-straw. From a large heap of rice-straw...
For indeed, having cleared away the straw, they make dwellings resembling mountain caves or rock shelters;
even over trees and thickets, they heap straw and sit beneath them to practice the duty of a recluse. It is with reference to this that it was said.
"After the meal" means after the meal. "Having returned from the alms-round" means having returned from the search for almsfood.
*Pallaṅkaṃ* means a cross-legged posture with the thighs bound all around. *Ābhujitvā* means having bound [the legs].
*Ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāyā* means having set the upper body straight, placing the tip of one vertebra against the tip of the next among the eighteen spinal vertebrae.
For when one is seated in this way, the skin, flesh, and sinews do not bend. Then, for him, that which arises due to their bending...
From moment to moment, feelings might arise, but they do not arise [in this case]. When those do not arise, the mind becomes one-pointed;
the meditation subject does not fall away, but attains growth, expansion, and abundance.
"Having established mindfulness facing the nose" means having placed mindfulness directed toward the meditation subject; or, having brought it near to the nose.
This is the meaning. Therefore it is said in the Vibhaṅga: "This mindfulness is established, well-established, either on the tip of the nose or on the sign of the mouth;
therefore it is said: 'having established mindfulness directed to the mouth. Alternatively, *pari* has the sense of embracing (*pariggaha*);
*mukha* has the sense of outlet (*niyyāna*); *sati* has the sense of establishment (*upaṭṭhāna*). Therefore it is called "mindfulness directed to the mouth" (*parimukhaṃ sati*).
The meaning here should be understood according to the method stated in the *Paṭisambhidā*. This is the summary thereof: "Having established mindfulness directed toward the outlet.
Regarding the phrase "covetousness for the world" (*abhijjhāṃ loke*): here, the "world" (*loka*) is the five aggregates of clinging in the sense of breaking up and disintegrating;
therefore, the meaning here is "having abandoned lust for the five aggregates of clinging and having suppressed sensual desire."
"By one free from covetousness" means by one in whom covetousness has departed because it has been abandoned through suppression;
the meaning is that it is not like visual consciousness. "He purifies the mind of covetousness" means he liberates the mind from covetousness.

The meaning is that he acts in such a way that the mind both releases itself from it and, having released it, does not take hold of it again. This same explanation applies to the phrases "having abandoned ill will and hatred," and so forth.
The same method applies here. It is called *byāpāda* because by means of it the mind becomes corrupted, abandoning its former natural state, like spoiled rice;
it is called *padosa* because through the attainment of such a change it becomes defiled, or it defiles and destroys another. Both of these are synonyms for anger (*kodha*).
*Thina* is a sickness of the mind; *middha* is a sickness of the mental factors. Both *thina* and *middha*...

Lethargy and drowsiness (*thinamiddha*). "Perceiving light" (*ālokasaññī*) means being endowed with a perception that is purified and free from hindrances, capable of perceiving the light seen during the day even at night.
"Mindful and clearly comprehending" (*sato sampajāno*) means being endowed with both mindfulness (*sati*) and knowledge (*ñāṇa*).
These two are mentioned because they are supportive of the perception of light. Restlessness and worry (*uddhacca-kukkucca*).
"One who has crossed over doubt" means one who stands having crossed over and transcended doubt.
"One who is without perplexity" means that [doubt] does not occur in the form, "How is this? How is this? Regarding "wholesome states" (kusalesu dhammesu), it refers to blameless states.
One does not doubt in the manner of, "Are these indeed wholesome? How are these wholesome? The meaning is that one does not hesitate. This is the point here.

This is the summary. Furthermore, whatever needs to be said regarding these hindrances (nīvaraṇa) in terms of their etymology, characteristics, and so forth, has all been stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.
218. As for this simile that was spoken, beginning with "Just as if, O Great King," therein "having taken a loan" means having taken wealth on interest.
"Having taken [it]," means: "He should make it end," that is, he should make it such that not even a mere cowrie's worth of its limit remains;
the meaning is that he should discharge it entirely. "From that source" means from the source of debtlessness.
For when he adverts to the thought, "I am debtless," he obtains powerful gladness and attains joy; by that...
It is said: “One may find joy; one may attain gladness.
(219) Because it afflicts by cutting through the four postures with a saw as it were, due to the arising of discordant feelings, it is called *ābādha* (affliction);
one who has this is *ābādhika* (afflicted). Being pained by the suffering that originates from that [affliction], he is *dukkhita* (pained). *Adhimattagilāna* means severely ill.
“Would not delight him” means it would not be pleasing to him because he is overcome by a severe illness. “Strength” means simply strength;
the meaning is that there would be no strength in his body. “On that account” refers to the cause of health. For when one reflects, “I am healthy,” both of those things [health and strength] arise.
Therefore it is said: “He would find joy, he would attain gladness.”

220. "And there would be no loss of any of his wealth" means that there would not be even a loss of a single *kākaṇika* coin's worth of wealth. "On that account" (*tatonidānaṃ*) means on account of imprisonment and release. The rest should be applied to all the phrases in the manner already explained.
221–222. "Not dependent on oneself" (*anattādhīno*) means not dependent on oneself; one does not obtain the freedom to do whatever one pleases.
"Dependent on others" (*parādhīno*) means dependent on others; one acts only according to the will of others. "One who cannot go wherever he wishes" means in whichever direction... [he wishes].
There is a desire to go, a wish arises to travel, yet because of that [bond], he is unable to go.

"From slavery" means from the state of being a slave. "A free man" means one who belongs to himself. "On that account" means on account of his freedom. "A desert road" means a wilderness road; the meaning is a long journey without water. "On that account" means on account of the land of safety (*khemantabhūmi*).

223. Regarding the phrase "these five hindrances being unabandoned," here the Blessed One shows that the hindrance of sensual desire, when unabandoned, is like a debt, while the remaining hindrances are like diseases and so forth.
This is the analogy: for one who, having taken a loan from others, squanders it, is addressed by them as "Pay the debt! even when being spoken to harshly, being bound, or being put to death.
He is unable to ward off anything; he endures it all. For that debt is the very reason for his endurance.

In the same way, whoever is enamored with sensual desire and grasps at an object accompanied by craving, he endures everything—even when being harshly spoken to, bound, or even executed—for that [debt] is the reason for his endurance.
Just as there is a share for those women who are being slain by their household masters, so too should sensual desire be regarded as a debt.

Furthermore, just as one afflicted by a bile disease, even when given honey, sugar, and the like, cannot experience their flavor due to the affliction of that bile disease; [so it is with sensual desire].
He does not perceive it, but simply spits it out, thinking, "It is bitter, it is bitter.
In the same way, one whose mind is corrupted does not accept even the slightest instruction when being exhorted by preceptors and teachers who desire his welfare.
Saying things such as, "You are overstepping your bounds toward me," he abandons the training. Due to a bile disease, that man [rejects] honey, sugar, and so forth...
Just as one who is afflicted by fever does not experience the various flavors of the Teaching, such as the bliss of *jhāna*, so too should ill will (*byāpāda*) be regarded as a disease.
Furthermore, it is like a man bound in prison on the night of a festival; he sees neither the beginning, nor the middle, nor the end of that festival.
Released on the following day, he thinks: "Oh, what a delightful festival there was yesterday! Oh, what wonderful dancing!"
Even after hearing "Oh, what a song! and so forth, he does not give a reply. For what reason? Because he has not experienced the festival.

In the same way, a monk overcome by sloth and torpor, even when a discourse on the Dhamma is being delivered in a manifold manner, knows neither its beginning, nor its middle, nor its end. He too, when the discourse on the Dhamma has concluded, [exclaims]: "Oh, what a discourse on the Dhamma!"
Even when hearing those who praise the listening to the Dhamma, saying, "Oh, what a cause! Oh, what a simile!", he does not give a reply.
Why is that? Because, due to sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*), he has not experienced the discourse on the Dhamma. Thus, sloth and torpor should be regarded as a prison house.
Just as a slave, even while playing at a festival, when told: "There is this urgent task that must be done;
go there quickly! If you do not go, I shall cut off your hand or foot, or your ear or nose," goes immediately and does not get to experience the beginning, middle, or end of the festival—why is that?

Because of dependence on others: in exactly the same way, even for one who has entered the forest for the sake of seclusion while being ignorant of the Vinaya, once the perception that even some allowable meat (kappiyamaṃsa) is unallowable meat arises, he must abandon his seclusion and go to a master of the Vinaya for the purpose of purifying his virtue;
he is unable to experience the bliss of seclusion. Why is this?
"By being overcome by restlessness and remorse": thus, restlessness and remorse should be regarded as a form of slavery.

Just as a person traveling on a long desert road, seeing a place where people have been plundered by bandits and a place where they have been struck, becomes filled with apprehension and suspicion at even the sound of a stick or the cry of a bird, thinking, "The bandits have come."
He goes, he stands, and he turns back; yet the place not yet traversed is far greater than the place already traversed.
With great difficulty and toil, he may reach the land of safety, or he may not.
In the same way, for one in whom doubt has arisen regarding the eight points—such as by way of the thought, "Is he a Buddha, or is he not a Buddha?"—and so forth...
Being full of doubt, one is unable to resolve with confidence and grasp [the truth] through faith. Being unable to do so, one does not attain either the path or the fruit.

Just as on a long journey through a wilderness, the repeated shifting back and forth, the failure to investigate thoroughly, and the arising of trepidation in the mind—thinking "there are robbers" or "there are no robbers"—create an obstacle to reaching a place of safety.
In the same way, doubt—arising as a repeated moving to and fro and revolving about such thoughts as "Is he a Buddha, or is he not a Buddha?
and so forth, producing a state of mental paralysis and vacillation—creates an obstacle to reaching the plane of the Noble Ones;
thus, doubt should be regarded as being like a desert road on a journey.

224. Now, regarding the passage: “Just as, great king, freedom from debt,” here the Blessed One shows that the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*), when abandoned, is like freedom from debt, while the remaining hindrances are like health and so forth. This is the analogy: just as a man who, having taken a loan and applied it to his work, attains success and thinks, “This debt is indeed a root of obstruction,” and then, having paid it back, becomes free from debt and feels secure and happy; even so, great king, when a noble disciple has abandoned the hindrance of sensual desire, he is like one free from debt. This is the analogy. Similarly, just as a man who is ill, suffering, and gravely sick might recover through the power of medicine and become healthy, free from illness, and feel secure and happy; even so, great king, when a noble disciple has abandoned the hindrance of ill will (*vyāpāda*), he is like one who has recovered from illness. This is the analogy. Similarly, just as a man who is imprisoned in a dungeon might escape and find himself free, secure, and happy; even so, great king, when a noble disciple has abandoned the hindrance of sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*), he is like one released from prison. This is the analogy. Similarly, just as a man who is bound with ropes might be freed and find himself unbound, secure, and happy; even so, great king, when a noble disciple has abandoned the hindrance of restlessness and remorse (*uddhaccakukkucca*), he is like one freed from bonds. This is the analogy. Similarly, just as a man who is confused and bewildered might regain his senses and find himself clear-headed, secure, and happy; even so, great king, when a noble disciple has abandoned the hindrance of doubt (*vicikicchā*), he is like one who has regained his senses. This is the analogy. Thus, great king, these five hindrances are like a debt, an illness, imprisonment, bonds, and confusion; and for a noble disciple who has abandoned them, there is this benefit: he gains the joy and happiness of renunciation, which is like the security of one free from debt, the health of one free from illness, the freedom of one released from prison, the liberation of one freed from bonds, and the clarity of one who has regained his senses. Having reflected thus, he should pay back the debt with interest and have the document torn up.
From that time forth, neither anyone would send him a messenger nor a letter. Even when he sees the creditors, if he wishes, he rises from his seat; if he does not wish, he does not rise. Why?
Because of his lack of attachment and non-clinging toward them. In the same way, the bhikkhu—
Thinking, “This so-called sensual desire is the root of impediment,” one abandons the hindrance of sensual desire by developing six qualities.
We shall explain those six qualities in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta.
For one who has thus abandoned sensual desire, just as a man freed from debt feels neither fear nor trepidation upon seeing his creditors, even so...
In another’s dwelling, he is neither attached nor bound. Even when seeing divine forms, no defilement arises in him.
