Therefore, the Blessed One spoke of the abandoning of sensual desire as being like freedom from debt.
Just as that man afflicted with a bile disease, having quelled that illness through medicinal treatment, from that time forth—

One finds the taste of honey, sugar, and so forth. In the same way, a bhikkhu, having developed six qualities [as antidotes] thinking, "This thing called ill-will (*vyāpāda*) is a great cause of harm," abandons the hindrance of ill-will. We shall explain these six qualities among all the hindrances in the *Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna* [Sutta] itself. And it is not only those;
those which are to be developed for the abandoning of sloth-and-torpor (*thinamiddha*) and the rest are also included.

We shall explain all of that in that very place. Thus, having abandoned ill-will, he trains with delight, having received the training rules such as the *Ācāra-pannatti* upon his head, just as a man freed from a bile disease partakes of the taste of honey, sugar, and so forth with relish.
Therefore, the Blessed One spoke of the abandoning of ill-will as being like health.
Just as that man who was imprisoned on a festival day, thinking on another festival day:
"Previously, too, I was bound through the fault of negligence, and because of that I did not enjoy the festival;
now I shall be diligent," becomes heedful so that his enemies find no opportunity, and thus enjoys the festival—so too [should one act].
Having experienced it, he uttered this exclamation: "Oh, what a festival! Oh, what a festival!
In the same way, a bhikkhu, thinking, "This called sloth and torpor is a great cause of harm," develops six qualities and abandons the hindrance of sloth and torpor.
Having thus abandoned sloth and torpor, just as a man released from bondage might wait for seven days for a festival, so too does he wait.
Just as one experiences the beginning, middle, and end [of a festival], even so, experiencing the beginning, middle, and end of the Dhamma-festival,
one attains Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). Therefore, the Blessed One spoke of the abandoning of sloth and torpor as being like liberation from bondage.
Just as a slave, by relying on some friend, might give his master’s wealth away and thereby make himself free, from that time forth doing whatever he wishes;
even so, a bhikkhu—thinking, “This restlessness-and-worry is a great source of harm”—develops six qualities and abandons restlessness-and-worry. He, in this way...

Just as a man who has cast off restlessness and remorse does whatever he wishes, and no one can forcibly turn him back from it, even so he enters upon the way of renunciation according to his pleasure;
restlessness and remorse cannot forcibly turn him back from it. Therefore, the Blessed One [compares him] to one who is free like a slave.
He spoke of the abandoning of restlessness and remorse.
Just as a strong man, taking hold of his sword-hilt, equipped with weapons and accompanied by a retinue, might set out across a wilderness;
and seeing him from afar, the bandits would flee; and he, having safely crossed that wilderness, reaches a place of safety—
He would become joyful and elated. In the same way, a bhikkhu, thinking, "This thing called doubt is a great producer of harm," develops six qualities and abandons doubt.

Having thus abandoned doubt, just as a strong man equipped with weapons and accompanied by a retinue might emerge safely from a place of danger, regarding thieves as no more than blades of grass, he reaches the ground of security.
Just as one reaches [safety], even so the bhikkhu, having crossed the wilderness of misconduct, reaches the supreme land of security, the deathless Great Nibbāna.
Therefore, the Blessed One spoke of the abandoning of doubt as being like the land of security. 225.
"Joy arises" means that a state of satisfaction arises. "In one who is joyful, rapture arises" means that in one who is satisfied, the entire body [is filled with it].

As it is being agitated, rapture arises. "The body of one whose mind is rapturous becomes tranquil" means that for a person whose consciousness is associated with rapture, the mental body becomes tranquil and free from distress.
"He experiences pleasure" means he experiences both bodily and mental pleasure.
"The mind becomes concentrated" means that for one who is made happy by this happiness of renunciation, even by way of access concentration...
The mind is concentrated by way of absorption as well.
Regarding the passage beginning, "Quite secluded from sensual pleasures... he enters and dwells in the first jhāna," this refers to access concentration.

It should be understood that this was said for the purpose of showing the distinction of the mind when concentrated through access-concentration (*appanā-samādhi*), and for the purpose of showing the classification of that concentration when the mind is concentrated. "This very body" refers to this body made of kamma.
"Suffuses" means it moistens and lubricates; it produces the joy and happiness occurring throughout the whole [body]. "Permeates" means it flows all around.
"He fills" means he fills it like a bellows with air. "He suffuses" means he touches it on all sides.

"Of the entire body" means that for this bhikkhu, in every part of the body, there is not even the slightest place—whether within the continuity of the clung-to (upādinnaka) or wherever skin, flesh, and blood may reach—that is not touched by the happiness of the first jhāna.
227. "Dakkha" means one who is clever and capable of preparing, applying, and kneading bath-powders.
"In a bronze vessel" (kaṃsathāle) means in a container made of any metal; however, an earthenware vessel is not durable.
When kneading [the powder] in it, it breaks; therefore, that is not shown. "Sprinkling repeatedly" (paripphosakaṃ paripphosakaṃ) means sprinkling again and again.

"Sanneyya" means that, having taken a bronze bowl with the left hand, one should take a suitable amount of water with the right hand and, sprinkling it again and again while kneading, form a ball. "Snehānugatā" means followed by the moisture of the water.
"Snehaparetā" means embraced by the moisture of the water. "Santarabāhirā" means together with the interior portion.
And by the phrase "on the outside," the meaning is that it is entirely covered with a film of moisture from the water.
"And not dripping" means that the water does not drip drop by drop; it is possible to take it up with the hand, or with two or three fingers, or even to rub it into the palms—this is the meaning.
The Discourse on the Second Jhāna (228–229).

Regarding the simile for the happiness of the second jhāna: "water that has welled up" (*ubbhidodaka*) means water that has burst forth; it does not refer to water that rises up after having broken through from below.
Rather, the meaning is water that wells up from within. "Stream-mouth" (*āyamukha*) refers to the path by which [the water] comes.
"Devoti megho" means a cloud. "Kālena kālaṃ" means from time to time; the meaning is either every half-month or every ten days.
"Dhārā" means rain. "Na anuppaveccheyya" means he would not pour down, that is, he would not let it rain.
"Sītā vāridhārā ubbhijjitvā" means cold streams of water having burst forth, having risen up and filled the lake. For the water rising from below—
The water, rising up again and again, agitates it; the water entering from the four directions agitates the water with old leaves, grass, sticks, poles, and so forth;
the rainwater agitates the water with its falling streams and bubbles.
But when it arises as something already fully established, like that produced by psychic power (iddhi), the water pervades this area and this area...
"There is nothing that does not reach" means there is no place that is not pervaded by it. In this context, the body born of karma is like a lake;
the bliss of the second jhāna is like the water. The rest should be understood in the same manner as before.
This concludes the discussion on the third jhāna.
230–231. *Uppalinī* means "possessing lotuses" because there are lotuses (*uppala*) here, comparable to the bliss of the third jhāna.
The same method applies to the other two terms as well. Furthermore, among the white, red, and blue varieties, any [type] is simply a lotus (*uppala*).

A *puṇḍarīka* has fewer than a hundred petals, while a *paduma* has a hundred petals. Alternatively, even without this restriction on the number of petals, the white variety is called *paduma* and the red variety is called *puṇḍarīka*.
This is the analysis here. "Not emerged from the water" means they have not come up out of the water.

"Growing submerged within the water" means they grow remaining submerged within the surface of the water; the meaning is that they increase. The rest should be understood in the same manner as before.
This concludes the discussion on the fourth jhāna.
232–233. Regarding the phrase “with a mind purified and cleansed,” similar to the bliss of the fourth jhāna:

here, it should be understood that it is *parisuddha* (purified) in the sense of being free from defilements (*nirupakkilesa*), and *pariyodāta* (cleansed) in the sense of being luminous (*pabhassara*). The expression “with a white cloth” is stated for the purpose of providing a cooling effect;
for with a soiled cloth there is no cooling effect, whereas with one that is washed and purified at that very moment, there is a cooling effect.
It becomes powerful. For in this simile, the physical body is like the cloth, and the bliss of the fourth jhāna is like the pervasion of temperature.
Therefore, just as when a well-washed man sits with a pure cloth draped over his head and body, the temperature from his body pervades the entire cloth;
there is no part of the cloth that is not touched by it—so too with the bliss of the fourth jhāna.
"There is no part of the bhikkhu’s body made of primary elements that is not pervaded [by it]. This is how the meaning should be understood here.
Furthermore, the word-by-word commentary on these four jhānas and the method of their development have been explained in the *Visuddhimagga*, and thus are not detailed here.
At this point, one should not conclude that he is only an attainer of the fine-material jhānas and not an attainer of the immaterial jhānas; for among the eight...
Without having attained mastery over the attainments (samāpatti) in fourteen ways, there can be no realization of the higher direct knowledges (abhiññā).
In the Pāḷi, however, only the fine-material jhānas (rūpajjhāna) are mentioned; the immaterial jhānas (arūpajjhāna) must be brought in and explained.
[This concludes] the discussion on insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa).

234. Thus, when his mind is thus concentrated... [pe] ...having attained imperturbability (*āneñjappatta*), this shows that the bhikkhu has mastered the eight attainments (*samāpatti*) in fourteen ways.
The rest here should be understood according to the method explained in the *Visuddhimagga*.

Regarding the phrase "he directs the mind toward knowledge and vision" (*ñāṇadassanāya cittaṃ abhinīharati*): here, "knowledge and vision" refers both to path-knowledge (*maggañāṇa*) and to fruition-knowledge (*phalañāṇa*).

There is the knowledge of omniscience, the knowledge of reviewing, and the knowledge of insight. In the passage, “Friends, for the sake of purification of knowledge and vision, is the holy life lived under the Blessed One? it is the knowledge of the path that is called “knowledge and vision.
In the passage, “This other superhuman state, this distinction of noble knowledge and vision, has been attained as a comfortable dwelling,” it is the knowledge of the fruit.
In the passage, “Knowledge and vision arose in the Blessed One: ‘Āḷāra Kālāma has been dead for seven days,’” it refers to the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
In the passage, “And knowledge and vision arose in me: ‘My deliverance is unshakable; this is my last birth,’” it refers to the knowledge of reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*).
However, here, in the phrase “the mind for the sake of knowledge and vision,” it is the knowledge of insight (*vipassanāñāṇa*) that is called “knowledge and vision.”
"He brings forth" means he makes [the mind] inclined toward, directed toward, and leaning toward that for the purpose of generating insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*).
The meaning of "possessing form" (*rūpī*) and so forth has already been stated. "Accumulated by boiled rice and sour gruel" means increased and grown by both boiled rice and sour gruel.
"Subject to the nature of being impermanent, to being covered, to being rubbed, to breaking, and to disintegrating" means in the sense of non-existence after having existed.
It is of a nature to be impermanent. It is of a nature to be anointed with thin ointments for the purpose of counteracting foul odors.
It is of a nature to be rubbed with light massages for the purpose of dispelling ailments of the limbs and members.

Or, in childhood, it is of a nature to be rubbed by means of stretching, pressing, and so forth, for the purpose of establishing the proper formation of those various limbs and members that were poorly formed due to dwelling in the womb while lying on the thighs.
Even when thus maintained, that which is subject to breaking up and destruction both breaks and scatters; such is its intrinsic nature—this is the meaning.
Therein, in the phrases "possessing form" (*rūpī*) and "composed of the four great elements" (*cātumahābhūtika*), etc., the arising (*samudaya*) is described by six terms.

Together with the term "impermanent" (*anicca*), the passing away (*atthaṅgama*) is described by the final two. "Attached to this, bound to this" refers here to that which is composed of the four great elements.
It is dependent upon and bound to the body.
(235) *Subha* means beautiful. *Jātimant* means arisen from a perfectly pure source.
*Suparikammakata* means well-processed, with stones and gravel removed. *Accha* means transparent skin. *Vippasanna* means perfectly clear.
"Endowed with all qualities" means endowed with all aspects such as washing, piercing, and so forth. By the words "blue," etc., he shows the perfection of color;
for when such [a gem] is strung [on a thread], it becomes clearly visible. "In the same way" is how the application of the simile should be understood here.
For the body born of karma is like the gem; insight-knowledge is like the strung thread; and the man with good eyesight is like the person with vision.
Vipassanā-ñāṇa is like the time when a jewel becomes manifest to a monk who has attained insight and is examining it by holding it in his hand, thinking, "This is indeed a jewel.
It is like the time when the body composed of the four great elements becomes manifest to a monk who has applied his mind and is sitting [in meditation].

Vipassanā-ñāṇa is like the time when a thread becomes manifest to one who has applied his mind, as expressed in this sutta: "In this case, this thread is woven... and so forth. Having applied his mind...

For a seated bhikkhu, it is the time when either the contact and its four concomitants having that as their object, or all consciousness and mental factors, or even insight-knowledge itself, become manifest.
And this insight-knowledge follows immediately after path-knowledge. Even so, since this [section] was commenced in the chapter on the higher knowledges (abhiññā),...
There is no intermediate stage; therefore, it is shown right here.

Furthermore, fear and terror arise in one who has not yet performed the preliminary reflection on impermanence and so forth, when hearing a terrifying sound with the divine ear-element, when recollecting terrifying aggregates through the recollection of past lives, or when seeing even a terrifying form with the divine eye. It does not [arise otherwise].

Therefore, this has been shown right here for the purpose of fulfilling the cause for dispelling fear in one who has attained direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) by means of reflection on impermanence and so forth.
Furthermore, it should be understood that this was shown here from the very beginning because this very bliss of insight (*vipassanāsukha*)—
which brings about the bliss of the path and its fruition— is a distinct, directly visible fruit of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*).

236–237. Discussion of the Knowledge of the Mind-made Power (*manomayiddhiñāṇa*). "Mind-made" (*manomaya*) means produced by the mind. "Complete in all limbs and parts" (*sabbaṅgapaccaṅgi*) means endowed with all major and minor limbs.
"With unimpaired faculties" (*ahīnindriya*) means having faculties that are not deficient in terms of their configuration. For this is the form created by one possessing psychic power (*iddhimat*).
If [the person] possesses supernormal power (*iddhimā*), he is white if she is white; if his ears are unpierced, hers are unpierced—in this way, he is exactly similar to her in every respect.

Indeed, even the triad of similes beginning with "the reed from the *muñja* grass" is stated solely for the purpose of demonstrating their state of similarity. For the reed within him is just like the *muñja* grass; the sword is just like its scabbard, as in the case of a round scabbard.
They throw the wheel right back into the whirlpool; it goes from wide to wider. "Karaṇḍa" is also a name for a snake's slough, not for a basket or a small box.

For a snake's slough is indeed similar to a snake itself. In that context, although it is shown as if a man were pulling a snake out of a *karaṇḍa* with his hand—as in the phrase "a man might pull a snake from its *karaṇḍa*"—it is nevertheless [pulled] by means of the mind alone.
The extraction [of the skin] should be understood. For this snake, remaining within its own species, relies upon a space between logs or between trees;

then, by means of strength characterized as the exertion of drawing its body out from the skin, and as if devouring its own body while loathing the old skin—through these four reasons, it abandons its slough of its own accord.
It cannot be pulled out by anything other than that; therefore, it should be understood that this was said with reference to pulling it out by means of the mind.
Thus, the body of this bhikkhu is like the muñja grass and so forth, while the created form is like the īsikā reed and so forth.

This is the correlation of the simile here. As for the method of creation here and elsewhere, it is discussed in the section on the five higher knowledges, beginning with the supernormal power (iddhividha).

Since this has been explained in detail in every aspect in the *Visuddhimagga*, it should be understood according to the method stated therein. For here, there is only a slight addition by way of similes.

(Discourse on the Knowledge of the Modes of Supernormal Power, etc., §§238–239). In that context, a monk who has attained the knowledge of the modes of supernormal power (*iddhividhañāṇa*) is to be regarded as being like a skilled potter and so forth; the well-prepared clay and so forth [are to be regarded as the bases for his powers].

The supernormal power of transformation (*iddhividhañāṇa*) should be regarded as being like that; the monk’s various transformations (*vikubbana*) should be regarded as being like the fashioning of various vessels and other objects according to one's desire.
240–241. In the simile of the divine ear-element (*dibbasotadhātu*), it is because the road through the wilderness is fraught with danger and peril.
In that case, one who is apprehensive and suspicious would not be able to determine, "This is the sound of a drum," or "This is the sound of a kettle-drum.
Therefore, without mentioning a road through a wilderness, he says "set out on a journey" in order to show a safe path.
For indeed, one who proceeds slowly along a safe path free from fear, having placed a cloth over his head, easily determines sounds of the aforementioned kind.

Just as the time when various sounds become manifest through hearing, so too should the time when divine and human sounds—distinguished by being distant or near—become manifest to the yogi be understood. 242–243.
In the simile for the knowledge of penetration of minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*), "young" means tender; "youthful" means endowed with the bloom of youth; "of a decorative nature" means...

"Though he is young, he is not lazy, nor is his clothing or body soiled; rather, he is by nature fond of adornment"—the meaning is that his habit is to bathe two or three times a day, to put on clean clothes, and to wear ornaments.
"With a blemish" means having some defect such as a black mole, a freckle, a facial blemish, or a pimple. In that regard, just as for him there is a sign of the face...

Just as a fault in the mouth becomes evident when one looks at it, so too it should be understood that for a bhikkhu who has directed his mind toward the knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*) and is seated [in meditation], the sixteenfold states of mind of others become evident.
244–245. In the simile for the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsañāṇa*), it is said that "the actions performed on that day become evident"; thus, on that day...

Only the state of having gone to the three villages is taken [as the example]. In this context, the one who has attained the knowledge of past lives should be regarded as being like the man who has gone to the three villages;

the three existences (bhava) should be regarded as being like the three villages; and just as the actions performed by that man on those three villages on that day become manifest, so too for the bhikkhu seated with his mind directed toward past lives, [the events] within the three existences [become manifest].
The manifestation of the act of speaking should be understood. 246–247.
In the simile of the divine eye, "moving along the street" means moving back and forth. There is also a reading, "moving along the street," which has the same meaning.
In that context, it is like a palace situated at a crossroads in the middle of a city for this bhikkhu.
The body born of karma is to be seen by a monk who has attained the divine eye and stands as if on a palace— just as a man with sight standing on a palace—
watching those entering the womb by way of rebirth-linking like people entering a house,
those emerging from the mother’s womb like people leaving a house, and those wandering back and forth along the streets and lanes.
Wandering beings— beings reborn here and there throughout the three realms of existence, like people sitting in the middle of a crossroads in an open space before them—

become manifest to a bhikkhu who has directed his mind toward the knowledge of the divine eye while sitting [in meditation], just as those people become visible to a man standing on the upper floor of a palace.
The time of its manifestation is to be observed. And this has been stated merely for the sake of ease in teaching. However, in the formless realm, there is no object for the divine eye.
248. Discussion on the Knowledge of the Destruction of the Taints (*Āsavakkhayañāṇakathā*):
"When his mind is thus concentrated"—here, the mind of the fourth jhāna that serves as the basis for insight (*vipassanā*) is to be understood.
“For the sake of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints” means for the purpose of producing the knowledge of the destruction of the taints.

And here, the "destruction of the taints" is spoken of as the path, the fruit, Nibbāna, and even dissolution. For in the passage, “Knowledge of destruction, knowledge of non-arising,” it is the path that is called the destruction of the taints;
whereas in the passage, “Through the destruction of the taints, one becomes a recluse,” it is the fruit.
“For one who observes the faults of others, constantly perceiving grounds for complaint, the taints increase; he is far from the destruction of the taints.

Herein, *nibbāna* is intended. In the passage, “The destruction, passing away, breaking up, impermanence, and disappearance of the taints,” it refers to dissolution (*bhaṅga*). But here, *nibbāna* is what is intended. The path of arahantship is also certainly appropriate.
“He directs the mind” means that insight makes the mind incline toward, lean toward, and tend toward that [object].

The meaning is that, regarding the phrases “this is suffering” and so forth, he understands the entire truth of suffering as it really is—“this much is suffering, there is nothing more than this”—through the penetration of its intrinsic characteristic.
And he understands the craving that produces that suffering as “this is the origin of suffering.”

The meaning is that he understands, through the penetration of their intrinsic characteristics, exactly as they are: that the cessation of both of these at the point where they cease is Nibbāna, which is the non-occurrence of those [defilements], as "this is the cessation of suffering";
and that the Noble Path which brings about that [cessation] is "this is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering."

Having thus shown the truths according to their own nature (*sarūpato*), he spoke the passage beginning with “These are the taints” (*ime āsavā*) in order to show them again by way of the defilements (*kilesavasena*) through a figurative method (*pariyāyato*).
“For one who knows thus, for one who sees thus” (*tassa evaṃ jānato evaṃ passato*):

for that bhikkhu who knows thus and sees thus, he explains the path that has reached its culmination together with insight (*vipassanā*). “From the taint of sensuality” (*kāmāsavā*): from the taint of sensuality (*kāmāsava*). “Is liberated” (*vimuccati*): by means of this...

This shows the moment of the path (*maggakkhaṇa*). By the phrase "it is liberated," the moment of the fruit (*phalakkhaṇa*) is shown. By the phrase "the knowledge arises that it is liberated," the reviewing knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*) is shown.

By the phrases "birth is destroyed" and so forth, its plane is shown. For by means of that knowledge, the one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), while reviewing, understands: "Birth is destroyed," and so forth.
But what is the birth of this person that has been exhausted? And how does one understand it? First of all, his past birth has not been exhausted, because it was already exhausted previously.
Nor has the future [birth] been exhausted, because there is no effort directed toward the future. Nor has the present [birth] been exhausted, because it still exists.
However, that which would have arisen due to the non-cultivation of the Path—distinguished by the various aggregates within the single, fourfold, or fivefold realms of existence—is [now exhausted].
Birth has been exhausted because the Path has been cultivated, having reached the state of non-arising in the future.

Having reviewed the defilements abandoned through the cultivation of the Path, he understands— knowing that "in the absence of defilements, even existing karma will not lead to rebirth in the future."
"Vusitaṃ" means lived, fully lived. "Brahmacariyaṃ" refers to the holy life of the path.
For, together with the virtuous worldling, the seven types of trainees are said to be "living the holy life," whereas one whose taints are destroyed has "lived it.
Therefore, when he reviews his own dwelling in the holy life, he understands: "The holy life has been lived. It has been accomplished.

"Karaṇīya" (what is to be done) refers to the sixteenfold task accomplished by means of the four paths through the modes of full understanding, abandoning, realizing, and developing with respect to the four truths.
By each respective path, the defilements to be abandoned have been abandoned; the meaning is that the root of suffering has been cut off.
For while those such as the "virtuous worldlings" perform that task, the one whose taints are destroyed has completed what was to be done.
Therefore, reviewing what was to be done by himself, he understands: "What was to be done has been done. Regarding the phrase "there is nothing further of this nature":

he understands that there is no further task of cultivating the path for him to perform—whether for the sake of this present state, for the sixteen functions, or for the destruction of the defilements.
Alternatively, "of this nature" (*itthattāya*) means from this state of being, from this [existence].
Such is the manner [of his understanding]. Now he understands: "I have no further continuity of aggregates beyond this present continuity of aggregates.

These five aggregates, however, remain with their roots cut like trees, and with the cessation of the final consciousness, they will go out like a fire without fuel, passing into a state of non-designation."
249. *Pabbatasaṅkhepe* means on the summit of a mountain. *Anāvila* means free from mud. *Sippiyo ca sambukā ca* is *sippisambukaṃ*.
*Sakkharā ca kathalāni ca* is *sakkharakathalaṃ*. *Macchānaṃ gumbā ghaṭā* is *macchagumbaṃ*.
Regarding the phrase "whether standing still or moving," here the gravel and pebbles remain stationary, while the others...

"They are walking and they are standing": just as, even when some cows are standing or sitting while others are present, one says "these cows are walking" by referring to those that are walking, and thus the others are also said to be "walking";
so too, by referring to the pebbles and gravel which are actually standing, the other two [the cows] are also said to be "standing. And the other two are indeed walking.
It is said that "he moves even over pebbles and gravel" by way of having taken them as a basis. In this context,

the time when the four truths become manifest to a monk who has directed his mind toward the destruction of the taints (*āsava*) should be understood as being like the time when a man with sight, standing on the shore and looking out, clearly perceives the small shells, snails, and so forth.

Up to this point, ten kinds of knowledge have been demonstrated: insight-knowledge, mind-made-knowledge, the knowledge of the various supernormal powers, the knowledge of the divine ear, the knowledge of penetration of minds, the knowledge of past lives, the two types of knowledge—the knowledge of future existences and the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings—accomplished by means of the divine eye, the knowledge of the divine eye itself, and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. The analysis of their objects is as follows:
It should be understood as follows: therein, insight-knowledge has seven kinds of objects by way of being limited (*paritta*), exalted (*mahaggata*), past, future, present, internal, and external.
Mind-made knowledge takes as its object only the form-base (*rūpāyatana*) to be created;
thus, it has a limited, present, and external object. Knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya-ñāṇa*) has an immeasurable, external, and indeterminate object.

The classification of the objects of the remaining [fruits] is stated in the *Visuddhimagga*. With the words "superior" or "more excellent," the Blessed One concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of Arahantship, meaning that there is no fruit of recluseship whatsoever more excellent than this by any method.
This concludes the discourse on King Ajātasattu’s declaration of his status as a lay follower (*upāsaka*).
250. The king, applauding here and there, listened attentively from beginning to middle to the end, and thought:
"Alas, for a long time I have been questioning various recluses and brahmins on these questions; like one threshing chaff, I have obtained no essence.
Oh, how perfect is the Blessed One’s excellence of qualities, he who, as it were, has lit a thousand lamps for me!"
Having created a great light, he answered these questions.

Thinking, "For a very long time indeed I have been deceived, not knowing the power of the qualities of the One Possessing Ten Powers," his body was suffused with the fivefold joy born of recollecting the Buddha’s virtues.
Manifesting his own faith, he declared himself a lay follower (*upāsaka*). To demonstrate this, the passage beginning with "When this was said, the king... was commenced.

In this context, regarding the phrase "It is excellent, venerable sir" (*abhikkantaṃ, bhante*), this word *abhikkanta* is seen to be used in the senses of destruction (*khaya*), beautiful (*sundara*), handsome (*abhirūpa*), and rejoicing (*abbhanumodana*).

For instance, in such passages as, "The night is excellent, venerable sir; the first watch has passed; the community of monks has been sitting for a long time," it is seen in the sense of destruction.
[And in the passage: "This person is pleasing to me; among these four types of persons, he is more excellent... it is seen in the sense of being beautiful.
In such passages as "and more excellent," it means beautiful.
[As in: "Who is worshipping my feet, shining with supernatural power and glory, illuminating all directions with most radiant beauty?"

In such contexts as these, it means "beautiful. In phrases such as "Excellent, Master Gotama," it signifies approval. Here too, it is used specifically for approval. And because it is used for approval, it should be understood that the words "Well said, well said, venerable sir" have been spoken.
The wise employ repetition (āmreḍita) in cases of fear, anger, praise, haste, curiosity, joy, sorrow, and faith.

And by this characteristic, it should be understood that this [word] is stated twice here: once by way of confidence (*pasāda*) and once by way of praise (*pasaṃsā*). Alternatively, "excellent" (*abhikkanta*) means exceedingly desirable, exceedingly agreeable, or exceedingly beautiful.
Here, he praises the teaching with one word "excellent" and his own confidence with the other.
This is the intended meaning here: "Excellent, venerable sir, is this Dhamma-teaching of the Blessed One; 'excellent' is this [teaching] of the Blessed One."
"My confidence [arose] by means of the teaching of the Dhamma. Or rather, this is the Blessed One’s own speech, praising [himself] with reference to two pairs of meanings:
the Blessed One’s word is "excellent" because it destroys faults, and it is "excellent" because it brings about the attainment of virtues.

Likewise, it is excellent because it generates faith, because it generates wisdom, because it possesses meaning, because it possesses phrasing, because its words are clear, and because its meaning is profound.

It should be connected with such qualities as: being pleasant to the ear, heart-stirring, not exalting oneself, not disparaging others, cool with compassion, bright with wisdom, delightful upon first encounter, capable of withstanding scrutiny, pleasant while being heard, and beneficial when investigated.
Beyond that, he further praises the teaching itself by means of four similes. In this context, "upturned" (*nikkujjita*) means placed face-downward.
"Or one that has grown face-downward. "He should turn it upright" means he should make it face upward. "Covered" means covered with grass, leaves, and so forth.

"He should uncover" means he should remove [the covering]. "Or for one who is lost" means for one who is confused about the directions. "He should point out the way" means taking him by the hand, he should say, "This is the way.
"In the dark" refers to the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, at midnight, amidst thick forests and masses of clouds.

"In this darkness possessing four factors. This, first of all, is the explanation of the literal meaning of the words. This, however, is the interpretation according to the intended purpose (*sādhippāyayojanā*).

Just as someone might turn upright what has been overturned, so [the Buddha] raises me up from unrighteousness (*asaddhamma*), having turned me away from the true Dharma and fallen into unrighteousness.
Just as one might uncover what is concealed, so [he reveals it] following the disappearance of the Blessed One Kassapa’s dispensation (*sāsana*).
From that time forth, by revealing the Teaching that had been concealed by the thicket of wrong views—
just as one might point out the path to one who is lost— and by disclosing to me, who had set out upon a bypath and a false path,

the path to heaven and liberation; and just as one might hold up an oil lamp in the darkness, [you revealed] to me, who was submerged in the darkness of delusion, the forms of the Jewels, beginning with the Buddha.
"Because the Blessed One, my Lord, who holds aloft the lamp of the teaching that destroys the darkness of delusion which conceals what is not seen,
has proclaimed the Dhamma through these various methods, the Dhamma has been proclaimed in many ways.
Having thus praised the teaching, he manifested his state of serene confidence toward the Triple Gem with a mind purified by this teaching.
He said, "Esāham... and so forth. Therein, "esāham" means "this I. "I go for refuge to the Blessed One" means:
"The Blessed One is my refuge, my ultimate resort, the protector from suffering, and the provider of welfare.
With this intention, I go to, resort to, serve, and attend upon the Blessed One; or rather, I know and understand him thus. For of those verbal roots...
The meaning is "going," and "understanding" is also their meaning. Therefore, for the phrase "I go," the meaning "I know" and "I understand" is also stated.

Regarding the words "the Dhamma and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus": herein, it is called "Dhamma" because it sustains (dhāreti) those who have attained the path, realized cessation, and are practicing according to the instructions, preventing them from falling into the four states of misery; as for its meaning:

The Noble Path and Nibbāna. And this has been said in detail: “Bhikkhus, to whatever extent there are conditioned phenomena, the Noble Eightfold Path is declared to be the foremost among them. Moreover, it is not only the Noble Path and Nibbāna;
rather, the Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyatti) is also included along with the Noble Fruits. For this has been said in the *Chattamāṇavaka-vimāna*:
“The fading of lust, unshakable, sorrowless, the Dhamma that is unconditioned and not repulsive;
this sweet, skillful, well-expounded Dhamma—approach it for the sake of refuge.
For here, “the fading of lust” refers to the Path. “Unshakable, sorrowless” refers to the Fruit. “The Dhamma that is unconditioned” refers to Nibbāna.
"Non-repulsive, sweet, proficient, and well-analyzed"—thus are the aggregates of Dhamma analyzed by means of the Three Piṭakas.
"United by way of view and virtue" is the Saṅgha; in its actual sense, it is the assembly of the eight noble persons (ariyapuggala). For this has been said in that very same *Vimānavatthu*:
"And where they say a gift yields great fruit, among the four pure pairs of persons..."
"And those eight persons who see the Dhamma—go for refuge to this Saṅgha.
Here, "the Saṅgha of bhikkhus" means the community of bhikkhus. At this point, the king has declared the three goings for refuge.
This concludes the discourse on going for refuge.

Now, for the sake of proficiency regarding those goings for refuge, this method should be understood: namely, refuge, the going for refuge, he who goes for refuge, the classification of the going for refuge, the fruit of the going for refuge, the defilement, and the analysis. To begin with, as to the meaning of "refuge":
it is called *saraṇa* because it destroys (*harati*) suffering. For those who have gone for refuge, by that very act of going for refuge—
The meaning is that it "strikes down" (hanati) and destroys fear, terror, suffering, and the defilements of miserable rebirths; this is a synonym for the Triple Gem itself.
Alternatively, the Buddha strikes away (hiṃsati) the fear of sentient beings by engaging them in what is beneficial and turning them away from what is harmful.

The Dhamma [does so] by delivering them from the wilderness of existence and by bestowing consolation. [The Saṅgha does so] by causing even small acts of service to yield the attainment of vast fruits.
The Saṅgha. Therefore, by this method as well, the Triple Gem is the refuge.

The arising of consciousness that proceeds in the mode of taking them as its ultimate resort—having dispelled defilements through faith in and reverence for them—is "going for refuge. A sentient being endowed with that [consciousness] goes for refuge.
By means of the aforementioned type of mental arising, one thinks: "These three Gems are my refuge; these are my ultimate resort. Thus...
The meaning is "he approaches. Thus, first of all, the refuge, the act of going for refuge, and the one who goes for refuge—these three should be understood.
As for the classification of the act of going for refuge, there are two kinds: supramundane and mundane.
Therein, the supramundane occurs at the moment of the path for those who have seen the Truths; by way of the total eradication of the defilements of going for refuge, it has Nibbāna as its object.
Having performed it as a duty, it succeeds in its entirety toward the Triple Gem.
For worldlings, the mundane going for refuge succeeds by way of its object through the suppression of the defilements, having the qualities of the Buddha and so forth as its object.
In terms of meaning, this is the acquisition of faith in the bases such as the Buddha, and right view rooted in faith; among the ten bases of meritorious action, it is called "rectification of view."
That [taking of refuge] functions in four ways: by the surrendering of oneself, by making that one’s supreme resort, by entering into the state of a disciple, and by prostration.
Therein, "surrendering of oneself" means the relinquishing of oneself to the Buddha and the others, thinking:
"From this day forward, I surrender myself to the Buddha, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha. "Making that one’s supreme resort" means: "From this day forward..."

"Having made [this resolve]: 'I am one who has the Buddha as my ultimate resort, the Dhamma as my ultimate resort, and the Saṅgha as my ultimate resort,' you should hold me as such"—this is the state of having them as one's ultimate resort.

As for "entering into discipleship": "Starting from today, 'I am a resident pupil of the Buddha, a resident pupil of the Dhamma, and a resident pupil of the Saṅgha'—you should hold me as such"—this is the entry into discipleship. Prostration...

By name: “From this day forward, may you remember me as one who performs only the three acts of homage—prostration, rising to greet, joining the palms, and respectful conduct—toward the Buddha and the other two [the Dhamma and the Saṅgha]. Such is the supreme act of veneration toward the Buddha and the others.
For by performing even one of these four modes, the taking of refuge is indeed accomplished.
Moreover, I surrender myself to the Blessed One; I surrender myself to the Dhamma;
I surrender myself to the Saṅgha; I surrender my life. My self is indeed surrendered, my life is indeed surrendered.
For as long as life lasts, I go for refuge to the Buddha; the Buddha is my refuge, my shelter, my protection. This too is the surrendering of oneself.
It should be understood thus: "May I indeed see the Teacher; may I see the Blessed One himself; may I indeed see the Sugata;
may I see the Blessed One himself; may I indeed see the Perfectly Enlightened One; may I see the Blessed One himself.
In this way, Mahākassapa’s entry into discipleship should be understood as being like his going for refuge.
“Thus shall I wander from village to village, from town to town, paying homage to the Fully Awakened One and to the sublime nature of the Dhamma.
In this way, one’s taking of refuge should be understood as having that as one’s ultimate goal, just as was the case for Āḷavaka and others. Then Brahmāyu...

The brahmin rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, prostrated with his head at the Blessed One’s feet, kissed the Blessed One’s feet with his mouth, stroked them with his hands, and announced his name:
“I am Brahmāyu, O Gotama, a brahmin; I am Brahmāyu, O Gotama, a brahmin. In this way, too, the prostration by falling flat is to be understood.

Furthermore, this [refuge] is fourfold by way of relatives, fear, teachers, and those worthy of offerings (*dakṣiṇīya*). Among these, going for refuge occurs through prostration to one worthy of offerings, and not through the others.
For one takes refuge by way of what is supreme, and one breaks [the refuge] by way of what is supreme.
Therefore, if a Sākiyan or a Koliyan pays homage thinking, "The Buddha is our relative," that [refuge] is simply not taken.
It becomes a refuge. Or, if one pays homage out of fear, thinking, "The ascetic Gotama is honored by kings and possesses great power;

if he were not saluted, he might even do me harm," that refuge is not truly taken. Or, if one remembers something learned in the presence of the Blessed One during his time as a Bodhisatta, or at the time of his Buddhahood—
“A wise person living in a household should divide their wealth into four parts:
with one part they should enjoy their wealth; with two parts they should engage in business;
and the fourth part they should set aside as a reserve for times of misfortune.”

Having received such instruction, one pays homage [to the Teacher] thinking, "He is my teacher," and the taking of refuge is thereby accomplished. However, for one who pays homage thinking, "He is the foremost person worthy of offerings in the world," by that very act the taking of refuge is accomplished.

For a lay follower—male or female—who has thus taken refuge, even if they pay homage to a relative who has gone forth among other sects, thinking, "This is my kinsman," their going for refuge is not broken; how much less so for one who has not gone forth. Likewise...
This is because one who bows to a king out of fear might even cause harm if he is not honored for being revered by the kingdom.
Likewise, even if one bows to a teacher of any craft or to a sectarian teacher, thinking, "He is my preceptor," the refuge does not break;
thus should the various types of going for refuge be understood.

And herein, regarding the supramundane going for refuge, the four fruits of recluseship are the fruit of ripening (*vipākaphala*), while the destruction of all suffering is the fruit of benefit (*ānisaṃsaphala*). For it has been said:
"But whoever has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, He sees the Four Noble Truths with right wisdom."
Suffering, the origin of suffering, the transcendence of suffering,
and the Noble Eightfold Path leading to the cessation of suffering—
this indeed is the secure refuge, this is the supreme refuge.
“By coming to this refuge, one is liberated from all suffering.
Furthermore, the fruit of its benefits should be understood by way of not approaching [the world] as permanent and so forth. For it has been said:
“It is impossible, it is out of the question, that a person endowed with right view should approach any conditioned phenomenon as permanent... [and so on].”
"It is impossible for anyone to regard any conditioned phenomenon as pleasant... or to regard any phenomenon as a self...
or to deprive one's mother of life... or one's father... or an arahant... or, with a malicious mind, to draw blood from a Tathāgata...
or to cause a schism in the Saṅgha... or to acknowledge another teacher; such a thing cannot happen. This is the worldly [view].
Furthermore, both the attainment of existence and the attainment of wealth are indeed the fruits of going for refuge. For this has been said:
"Whoever has gone for refuge to the Buddha, they shall not go to the plane of misery;
having abandoned the human body, they will fulfill the host of devas."
Furthermore, it is said: “Then Sakka, lord of the devas, together with eighty thousand deities, approached the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna...
[omitted] ...As Sakka, lord of the devas, was standing to one side, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this to him:
‘It is good, lord of the devas, to go for refuge to the Buddha. To the Buddha—’”

"By reason of going for refuge, Lord of Devas, some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world... they surpass other devas in ten respects:
in divine lifespan, in divine beauty, in divine happiness, in divine fame, in divine sovereignty, and in divine..."
“By means of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles. This same method applies to the Dhamma and the Saṅgha as well.
Furthermore, the specific fruits of going for refuge should be understood by way of the Velāma Sutta and others. Thus should the fruit of going for refuge be understood.
And therein, mundane going for refuge is defiled by ignorance, doubt, wrong knowledge, and so forth, regarding the three objects.
It is not of great radiance, nor does it have great extension. There is no defilement in the supramundane [going for refuge].
As for the mundane going for refuge, there is a twofold division: blameworthy and blameless.
Among these, the blameworthy occurs through surrendering oneself to another teacher and so forth; that results in an undesirable fruit. The blameless occurs through death; that—
Because it is without karmic ripening, it is fruitless. However, for that which is supramundane, there is no breach at all;
for even in another existence, a noble disciple does not designate another teacher. Thus, the defilement and the breach of going for refuge should be understood.
"May the Blessed One, O Lord, remember me as a lay follower" means: may the Blessed One remember me thus, "This one is a lay follower."

The meaning is "let him know. However, for the sake of proficiency regarding the rules for a lay follower (*upāsaka*), the following miscellaneous points should be understood here: Who is a lay follower? Why is he called a lay follower?
What is his virtue? What is his livelihood? What is failure? What is success? In this regard, who is a lay follower?
Any householder who has gone for refuge. For this has been said: "From the moment, Mahānāma..."
“He has gone for refuge to the Buddha, he has gone for refuge to the Dhamma, he has gone for refuge to the Saṅgha.
To this extent, Mahānāma, one is a lay follower (upāsaka). Why is he called a *upāsaka*?
Because of his attendance (*upāsana*) upon the Three Jewels. For he attends upon the Buddha, thus he is an *upāsaka*; likewise, he attends upon the Dhamma and the Saṅgha.

What is his virtue? It is the five abstinences. As it is said: “Insofar, Mahānāma, as a lay follower abstains from the destruction of life, from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, and from liquor, wine, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence—to this extent, Mahānāma, a lay follower is virtuous.”
What is right livelihood? It is the maintenance of life by means that are lawful and righteous, having abandoned the five kinds of wrong trade. For this has been said:
“Monks, there are these five trades that should not be practiced by a lay follower. Which five?
Trade in weapons, trade in living beings, trade in meat, trade in intoxicants, and trade in poisons. These, monks, are the five...”
“Trade is not to be practiced by a lay follower.
What is failure? Any failure of that very virtue and livelihood is his failure.
Furthermore, it should be understood that whatever makes him an outcaste, as well as being stained and loathsome, is also his failure. These...
And in terms of meaning, there are five factors, beginning with lack of faith. As it is said:
"Bhikkhus, endowed with five qualities, a lay follower is a lay outcaste, a stain upon the laity, and a reproach to the laity.
With which five? He is faithless, he is immoral, he is a superstitious omens-seeker, he believes in auspicious signs..."
He performs no work, and seeks outside of this [community] those worthy of offerings, and there he performs acts of merit.
What is his accomplishment? It is that accomplishment which consists both in his perfection of virtue (*sīlasampadā*) and his perfection of livelihood (*ājīvasampadā*);
and it consists of the five qualities beginning with faith (*saddhā*), which produce the state of being a jewel and so forth. As it is said: “Bhikkhus, an upāsaka endowed with five qualities...”
There is the lay follower who is a jewel, the lay follower who is a lotus, and the lay follower who is a white lotus. By what five qualities? He is endowed with faith; he is virtuous;
he does not rely on superstitious omens; he has confidence in kamma, not in omens;
he does not seek those worthy of offerings outside this [Sāsana]; and he performs meritorious deeds here first.”
Regarding the phrase *ajjatagge*: here, this word *agga* is seen in the senses of beginning, limit, portion, and best.
For instance, in such passages as “From this day forward (*ajjatagge*), my dear gatekeeper, I shut the door against the Nigaṇṭhas and Nigaṇṭhīs,” it is seen in the sense of a beginning.

In such passages as “He should touch that fingertip (*aṅgulagga*) with that very fingertip; the tip of a sugarcane (*ucchagga*), the tip of a bamboo (*veḷagga*),” it is seen in the sense of a limit. [And in] “the sour tip (*ambilagga”)…” [it is seen in the sense of a portion].

In such passages as, "Let him divide [the food] into portions according to the sweetest, or the bitterest, or according to the size of the dwelling, or the size of the courtyard," it means a *portion*.
In such passages as, "Bhikkhus, however many beings there are—whether footless... [etc. ...the Tathāgata is declared the foremost among them," it means the *best*.

But here, it should be understood in the sense of a *beginning*. Therefore, "from this day forward" (*ajjatagge*) means "making today the beginning" (*ajjataṃ ādiṃ katvā*); such is the meaning in this context.

It is to be understood as follows: *ajjatam* means "the state of being today. Alternatively, the reading is *ajjadagghe*, where the letter *da* serves to facilitate the euphonic junction (*padasandhi*) between words;
the meaning is "today as the beginning" (*ajja agga*). *Pāṇupetam* means "endowed with life" (*pāṇehi upetam*).

"May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower (*upāsaka*) who has gone for refuge through the threefold going-for-refuge, who has no other teacher, and who is endowed [with this refuge] for as long as my life lasts—may he know me to be such a one who makes things allowable (*kappiyakāraka*)."

"For even if someone were to cut off my head with a sharp sword, I would never say of the Buddha, 'He is not the Buddha,' or of the Dhamma, 'It is not the Dhamma,' or of the Saṅgha, 'It is not the Saṅgha.
Having thus gone for refuge by surrendering myself, I confess my transgression: *accayo maṃ*..."
He said, "Venerable sir," and so forth. In that context, *accaya* means an offense. *Accagā maṃ* means it occurred having passed over me and overcome me.
Regarding the phrase *dhammikaṃ dhammarājānaṃ*: one who practices the Dhamma is called *dhammika*.
One who has become a king through the Dhamma alone, and not through unrighteousness such as patricide, is a *dhammarāja*. *Jīvitā voropesiṃ* means I deprived him of life.
"May he accept" means may he forgive. "For restraint in the future" means for the sake of restraint in what is to come;
that is, for the purpose of not committing such an offense, fault, or transgression again. 251.
"Taggha" is an emphatic particle. "You make amends according to the Dhamma" means exactly as the Dhamma stands, so you act.
"You do" means "you ask for forgiveness. "We accept that from you" means we forgive that offense of yours.
"This, Great King, is growth in the Noble One’s Discipline" means, Great King, this is what is called growth in the Noble One’s Discipline, in the teaching of the Buddha, the Blessed One.
What is it? It is when one, having seen a transgression as a transgression, makes amends according to the Dhamma.

Regarding the future restraint to be undertaken, the Blessed One, however, speaking with reference to the individual, said: "He who, having seen a transgression as a transgression, makes amends according to the Dhamma, undertakes restraint for the future.
(252) "When this was said" means when it was thus spoken by the Blessed One. Regarding the phrase "Come now, venerable sir," here *handā* means...

The word *vacasā* is a locative particle (*nipāta*). For he spoke thus after having made this a matter of speech regarding the departure. "Having many duties" (*bahukicca*) means having weighty duties.
"Having much to do" (*bahukaraṇīya*) is a synonym for that same term. "Whose time now you [deem]" (*yassadāni tvaṃ*) means:
O Great King, as for the time of departure which you now deem or know, it is said that you alone know its time. Having performed a circumambulation (*padakkhiṇaṃ katvā*).
"He departed" means that after circumambulating three times keeping the Blessed One to his right, placing his hands joined with ten fingers together in brilliant *añjali* upon his head,
and walking back while facing the Blessed One as long as he remained within the range of vision,
he departed after prostrating himself with the fivefold contact at the spot where he lost sight of him.
253. "O monks, this king is wounded; indeed, O monks, this king is wounded. He is struck down; indeed, he is struck down. This is what is meant:
"O monks, this king has become wounded, struck down, and deprived of his foundation;
for he himself has wounded himself in such a way that no foundation remains for him. "Free from dust" means free from the dust of passion and so forth.

It is "stainless" (*vītamaḷa*) because of the departure of passion, impurity, and so forth. "The eye of Dhamma" (*dhammacakkhu*) means either the eye regarding phenomena, or an eye consisting of Dhamma;
in other contexts this is a designation for the three [higher] paths, but here it refers specifically to the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*).
This is what is meant: if his father had not been killed by him, he would have attained the path of stream-entry while sitting right here on this very seat.
He would have attained [the goal], but an obstacle arose for him through association with evil friends. Nevertheless,
because he approached the Tathāgata and went for refuge to the Triple Gem, by the greatness of my teaching,
just as if someone had committed a murder yet were released with a punishment of merely a handful of flowers, even so—
"Having been reborn in an iron cauldron, falling for thirty thousand years until reaching the bottom,
and then rising for thirty thousand years until reaching the top again— only then will one be released. This, it is said, was indeed spoken by the Blessed One,
though it has not been included in the canonical text (Pāḷi).
But did the king obtain some benefit from hearing this discourse? He obtained a great benefit.
For from the time his father was killed, he could find no sleep by night or by day;
but from the moment he approached the Teacher and heard this sweet and nourishing teaching of the Dhamma, he found sleep. Of the three...
He rendered great honor to the jewels. There was no one possessed of ordinary faith equal to this king.
Furthermore, in the future, he will become a Paccekabuddha named Vijitāvī and attain final Nibbāna.
Thus spoke the Blessed One. Delighted, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
Thus ends the commentary on the Sāmaññaphala Sutta in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the commentary on the Dīghanikāya. 3.
Commentary on the Ambaṭṭha Sutta.
Commentary on the Journey: 254. "Thus have I heard... among the Kosalans" refers to the Ambaṭṭha Sutta. Herein, this is the commentary on the hitherto unexplained words. "Among the Kosalans":
the Kosalans are royal princes belonging to a particular province; the name "Kosala" is applied by conventional usage (*rūḷhisadda*) to the entire country where they dwell.
It is said [to have been] in that Kosala country. However, the ancients say:

because in the past, having heard that Prince Mahāpanāda did not even so much as smile after seeing various theatrical performances and the like, the king said, "Whoever makes my son laugh, him I shall adorn with every ornament.
Thereupon, even the ploughs were abandoned, and a great multitude of people assembled.
Even after displaying various performances for more than seven years, the people were unable to make him laugh;
thereupon Sakka, the king of the gods, sent a troupe of actors, who made him laugh by displaying celestial performances.
Then those people departed toward their respective dwellings. On the way back, they encountered friends, kinsmen, and others.
While offering hospitality, they said, “Is it well with you, sir? Is it well with you, sir?
Therefore, because of that word “well” (*kusala*), that region is called Kosala.
As for the phrase “wandering on a journey,” he was traveling along a road. Now, this wandering of the Blessed One is of two kinds.

—There is the hurried journey and the unhurried journey. In this context, seeing a person capable of being awakened even from afar and going there immediately for the sake of awakening them is called a hurried journey; this is to be seen in such instances as the Elder Mahākassapa’s going out to meet [the Buddha].
For the Blessed One, while going out to meet the Elder Mahākassapa, covered a road of three *gāvutas* in a single moment.
He went for the sake of Āḷavaka thirty yojanas; likewise for Aṅgulimāla. For Pakkusāti, however, he went forty-five yojanas.
For Mahākappina, one hundred and twenty yojanas. For the sake of Dhaniya, he went seven hundred yojanas.
For the novice Vanavāsī Tissa, the co-resident disciple of the General of the Dhamma, he went one hundred and two hundred and ninety-three yojanas.
One day, it is said, the Elder said, "Venerable Sir, I shall go to the presence of the novice Tissa.
The Blessed One replied, "I too will go," and addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"Ānanda, announce to the twenty thousand who possess the six super-knowledges: 'The Blessed One, it is said, will go to the presence of the forest-dwelling novice Tissa.'"

Then, on the second day, surrounded by a retinue of twenty thousand arahants whose taints were exhausted, he rose into the air and descended at a distance of two hundred yojanas at the gate of his alms-village.
There he put on his robe. Seeing him as he was going toward the place of work, the people said, "The Teacher has come;
do not go to work," and having prepared seats and given him rice-gruel, they [honored him].
While preparing their morning meal, they asked the young bhikkhus, "Where is the Blessed One going, venerable sirs?
The lay followers replied, "The Blessed One does not go elsewhere; he has come right here for the purpose of seeing the novice Tissa.
They thought, "It seems the Teacher has come to see our own preceptor, the Elder! Alas, we have not seen the Elder!"
“...or so little,” they said, and were filled with joy.
Then, at the conclusion of the Blessed One’s meal, the novice, having wandered for alms in the village, asked:
“Lay followers, has the great Saṅgha of bhikkhus arrived? They replied to him: “Venerable sir, the Teacher has arrived. He [then approached] the Blessed One.
Having approached, he requested almsfood. The Teacher took his bowl with his hand and said, "Enough, Tissa;
the meal is finished. Then, having asked leave of his preceptor, he sat down on his own seat and performed the meal-rite.
At the conclusion of his meal-rite, the Teacher pronounced a blessing over him.
Having gone out and stood at the village gate, he asked, "Tissa, which way is the path that leads to your dwelling?
"This one, Blessed One. "Go ahead, Tissa, and show me the way," he said.

It is said that although the Blessed One was himself the guide of the entire world including the devas, he acted as a guide for that path for three *gāvutas* so that he might have the opportunity to see the novice.
So, having gone to his own dwelling place, he performed the duties toward the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One asked him, "Tissa, which is your walking path?
and having gone there, sat down on the stone seat where the novice used to sit and asked, "Tissa, did you dwell happily in this place?
He replied, "Yes, venerable sir, I dwelt happily in this place."
As Vāsava heard the sounds of lions, tigers, elephants, deer, wild boars, and other creatures, the perception of the forest arose in him, and he thought, "I dwell happily here.
Then the Blessed One said to him, "Tissa, assemble the community of monks; I shall give you the inheritance of a Buddha.
When the community of monks had assembled, the Blessed One conferred full ordination upon him and [returned] to his own dwelling place.

"He has come"—this is called a hurried journey (*turitacārikā*). However, the traveling of one who supports the world through alms-gathering and other means, day by day, following the sequence of villages and market towns at a pace of one or two *yojanas* per day, is called an unhurried journey (*aturitacārikā*).
While wandering on this [latter] journey, the Blessed One [traversed] the great circuit (*mahāmaṇḍala*), the middle circuit (*majjhimamaṇḍala*), and the inner circuit (*antomaṇḍala*).
He wanders about in one of these three circles. Therein, the great circle is eight hundred yojanas, the middle circle is six hundred yojanas, and the inner circle is three hundred yojanas.
When he desires to wander on the great circle, having performed the Great Invitation (Mahāpavāraṇā), on the first day of the lunar fortnight, surrounded by a great community of monks...
He sets out. Within a radius of one hundred yojanas, there is a single great clamor. Those who arrive first are permitted to receive invitations.
The honor intended for the other two circles descends upon the Great Circle.
Therein, the Blessed One, staying for one or two days in various villages and market towns, favors the great masses by accepting material offerings.
Increasing his wholesome merit connected with the turning away from saṃsāra through the gift of the Dhamma, he brings his wandering tour to an end after nine months. However,
if during the rains retreat the monks' serenity and insight are still immature, then after not holding the *pavāraṇā* at the Great *Pavāraṇā*, but instead granting a *pavāraṇā-saṅgaha*,
and then holding the *pavāraṇā* on the full moon day of Kattika, [he concludes it] on the first day of the month of Migasira.
Accompanied by a great assembly of bhikkhus, he departed and descended into the Middle Region.
For other reasons as well, when desiring to wander through the Middle Region, he would depart only after having resided there for four months.

In the same manner as previously described, the veneration [of the people] from the other two regions descends into the Middle Region. The Blessed One, in the same manner as before, [surveyed] the world...
While bestowing his favor, he brought his wandering tour to an end after eight months. However,
if even for the Blessed One who had completed the three-month rains retreat there were beings to be converted whose faculties were not yet mature, he would wait for the ripening of those faculties,
remaining in that very place for another month, or two, three, or four months, surrounded by a great community of monks.
He departs. In the same manner as previously described, the honor paid in the other two circles descends into the inner circle.
The Blessed One, favoring the world in the same way as before, concludes his wandering tour after seven, six, five, or four months.
Thus, while wandering on tour anywhere within these three circles, he does not—
[He thinks: "He wanders for the sake of robes and such things. But as for those who are poor, foolish, aged, or sick, when will they come and see the Tathāgata?
However, while I am wandering on tour, the great multitude will obtain a vision of the Tathāgata;
therein some will clarify their minds, some will honor him with garlands and the like, and some will offer alms from their ladles."
Some will see; some, having abandoned wrong view, will become those possessed of right view.
That will be for their long-term welfare and happiness. Thus he wanders on tour out of compassion for the world.
Furthermore, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, wander on tour for four reasons: by means of walking about, for the sake of physical well-being; [and so forth].
For the purpose of desiring to obtain the occasion for a significant event (*atthuppatti*); for the purpose of laying down the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) for the monks;
and for the purpose of awakening those beings capable of being awakened whose faculties have reached maturity in various places.
Furthermore, for four other reasons, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, go on tour: thinking, "They will go for refuge to the Buddha," or [to] the Dhamma, or to the Saṅgha.
Or thinking, "They will go," or "I shall satisfy the four assemblies with a great rain of Dhamma.
Furthermore, for five other reasons the Blessed Buddhas wander on tour:

thinking, "They will abstain from taking life," or "They will abstain from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, and from the use of intoxicants such as liquor, spirits, and fermented liquors which cause heedlessness."
Or, for eight other reasons, the Blessed Buddhas go on tour:
thinking, "They will attain the first jhāna," or "they will attain the second jhāna," and so on, up to "they will attain the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
For eight other reasons as well, the Blessed Buddhas go on tour: [thinking], "They will attain the path of stream-entry..."
"Or they will attain," or "they will realize the fruit of stream-entry... up to ... the fruit of arhatship. This is the unhurried journey;
here, it is intended as "journeying. Furthermore, this is twofold: the unattached journey and the attached journey.
Among these, that which proceeds by way of a sequence of villages, market towns, and cities is the unattached journey.
...so it is called. However, that which proceeds for the sake of a single being who is to be awakened is called "the fixed wandering. This is what is intended here.

At that time, it is said, when the Blessed One had spread the net of knowledge over the ten-thousandfold world system at the conclusion of his duties during the last watch of the night and was surveying those kinsmen among beings who were to be awakened, the brahmin Pokkharasāti [fell within] the net of omniscient knowledge.
He had entered within. Then the Blessed One considered: "This brahmin appears within the net of my knowledge;
does he perhaps possess the necessary potential (upanissaya)? Examining him, and seeing that he possessed the potential for the path of stream-entry, [the Blessed One reflected]:
"When I have gone to this district, he will send his pupil Ambaṭṭha to seek out my physical marks; he will engage in debate with me."
Having uttered various kinds of unseemly speech, he will say [this]; I shall subdue him and render him harmless. He will tell it to his teacher;
then, having heard that report, the teacher will come and seek out my physical marks.
I shall teach the Dhamma to him. At the conclusion of that teaching, he will be established in the fruit of stream-entry. The Teaching.
“...it will be fruitful for the great multitude,” he thought, and set out for that district accompanied by a retinue of five hundred bhikkhus.
Therefore it is said: “While wandering on tour among the Kosalans together with a great Saṅgha of bhikkhus, numbering about five hundred.
“To where Icchānaṅgala was”: in whichever direction or region one must enter to reach Icchānaṅgala. Or, in whatever place...
*Ichchhānaṅgalaṃ*. There is also a reading, *ijjhānaṅgalaṃ*. *Tadavasari*: he went by means of that;
or, he entered it. The meaning is: he went in that direction, or he went to that place. "He dwells at Ichchhānaṅgala in the forest grove of Ichchhānaṅgala" means:

having relied upon Ichchhānaṅgala, having established the camp of the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakhandhāvāra*) in the forest grove of Ichchhānaṅgala, [he dwells] with the banner of concentration (*samādhikonta*).
Having raised [the banner], the Dhamma King, revolving the essence of omniscient knowledge, dwells in whatever dwelling he pleases. 255.
"Now at that time": at the time when the Blessed One was dwelling there, at that time.
"At that time" is the meaning of this phrase. One who "utters the brahma" (brahmāṇati) is a *brāhmaṇa*; the meaning is that he recites the mantras.

For this indeed is the etymological definition (*niruttivacana*) of those who are *brāhmaṇas* by birth. However, the Noble Ones (*ariya*) are called *brāhmaṇas* because they have banished evil (*bāhitapāpa*).
"Pokkharasāti" is his name. Why is he called "Pokkharasāti"? It is said that his body was like a white lotus (*pokkhara*).
It shines like a silver arch erected in the city of the gods. Its head, however, is black in color, as if made of sapphire.
His hair appears like a streak of dark clouds against the lunar disc. His eyes resemble blue lotuses.
His nose is perfectly rounded and utterly pure, like a tube of silver. And so too are the palms of his hands, the soles of his feet, and the gateway of his mouth.
His appearance shone as if it had been treated with the juice of the *kata-lākha* plant; the Brahmin’s physical form had reached the pinnacle of beauty.
"It is fitting to appoint this Brahmin as king in a place that is currently without a ruler. Thus he was resplendent.
Because his face resembled a lotus (*pokkhara*), they knew him by the name Pokkharasāti.
Furthermore, during the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa, he became a master of the three Vedas;
having given alms to the One of Ten Powers and heard his teaching of the Dhamma, he was reborn in the world of the gods.
When he subsequently returned to the human world, loathing dwelling in a mother’s womb, he was born within the calyx of a lotus in a great lake in the Himalayan region. And not far from that lake...
The ascetic lived in a leaf-hut. Standing on the bank, he saw that lotus and thought: "This lotus is larger than all the other lotuses.
I shall take it when it has blossomed. Yet, even after seven days, it did not bloom.
The ascetic wondered, "Why indeed does this not bloom even after seven days? Come now, I shall take it," and so he descended [into the water].
He took it. As soon as it was severed from its stalk by him, it blossomed.
Then, within it, he saw a white-colored boy, tawny with lotus pollen, like a silver image gilded with gold dust. "This one must be possessed of great merit;
come now, I shall raise him," he thought, and having led him to a leaf-hut, he looked after him until he reached the age of seven years.
From that time on, he had him study the three Vedas. Having mastered the three Vedas, the boy became a learned and skilled man, the foremost Brahmin in Jambudīpa.
On another occasion, he displayed his craft to King Kosala.
The king, being pleased with his skill, granted him the great city named Ukkaṭṭhā as a royal gift (brahmadeyya). Thus it was for him.
Because he used to lie upon a lotus, they knew him as "Pokkharasāti.
He "dwelt in Ukkaṭṭha," meaning he lived in the city named Ukkaṭṭha; or alternatively, he dwelt there having overcome [all opposition].
Having become the master of that city, he lived within the boundaries prescribed for where one ought to dwell. Of him...
It is said that they took possession of the site of the city after setting up torches; while the torches were burning, they seized it, and therefore it is called Ukkaṭṭhā.
*Okkaṭṭhaṃ* is also a reading, with the same meaning. However, here, due to the influence of the prefix (*upasagga*), the accusative case should be understood as having the sense of the locative;
this is because the [prefix] is not an object (*anupayoga*) in the remaining words. In this regard, the grammatical rule (*lakkhaṇa*) should be sought from the treatise on grammar (*saddasattha*).

"Sattussadaṃ" means crowded with beings (*sattehi ussadaṃ*); it is densely populated, filled with many people, and thronged by humans. The meaning is that it is also filled with various creatures such as elephants, horses, peacocks, and deer used for nourishment.

Furthermore, because this city is endowed with fodder-grass for the elephants, horses, and so forth grown in its outskirts, as well as with grass for roofing houses; likewise, it is endowed with timber and wood for the construction of houses.
And because within it there were many lotus ponds of circular, square, and other shapes, variegated with water-born flowers,
as well as numerous large reservoirs always filled with water, it is therefore said to be "with grass, wood, and water.
"Together with grain" (*sadhañña*) means containing a great accumulation of grain, distinguished by the various types of early and late harvests.
The meaning is as follows. Up to this point, the prosperity and success of that brahmin who dwells in the city with the white parasol raised, sporting like a king, has been illustrated.
"Royal domain" (rājabhogga) means a territory granted by the king. If one asks by whom it was given: it was given by King Pasenadi of Kosala.
*Rājadāyaṃ* means that which has become the inheritance of the king; the meaning is "an heirloom.
*Brahmadeyyaṃ* means a gift for the best [the brahmins]; the meaning is that it should be enjoyed under the designation of "king" after raising the white parasol.

Alternatively, *rājabhoggaṃ* refers to [land] governed by the king as he administers all judicial matters and collects taxes from river-fords, mountains, and so forth, while raising the white parasol.

Having offered it, one should eat it. Regarding the phrase "given by King Pasenadi of Kosala as a royal gift" (*rājadāya*): because that city was given by the king, it is called a "royal gift. However, the words "given by King Pasenadi of Kosala" are stated here in order to indicate the donor, the king.
"Brahmadeyya" means a gift for the noble ones (*seṭṭha*). Just as it has been given, it must not be taken back again.
It exists; it has been relinquished and abandoned. Such is the meaning of "given.

"He heard" means he listened and apprehended; he understood by following the sound of the speech that had reached the door of his hearing. *Kho* is a particle used for emphasis or merely to fill out the verse.
Therein, in the sense of emphasis, it means "he indeed heard," and there was no obstacle whatsoever to his hearing.
The meaning should be understood as "there was. However, by means of the filler word (*padapūraṇa*), it serves merely to provide smoothness to the phrasing of the sentence.
Now, in order to clarify the matter that the brahmin Pokkharasāti heard, he said: "The ascetic Gotama, indeed, sir," and so forth.
In this context, he should be understood as an "ascetic" (*samaṇa*) because he has stilled evil. For it has been said: "His evil, unwholesome states have been stilled..."
“Dhammas,” and so forth. And the Blessed One has stilled evil by means of the unsurpassed Noble Path.
Therefore, this name—namely, “ascetic” (*samaṇa*)—is acquired by him through his qualities as they truly are. The particle *khalu* is a fixed expression used for the purpose of recitation.
*Bho* is a mere form of address derived from the brahmin caste; for it is said: “He is called a ‘bho-vādin’ if he possesses something [worldly]. *Gotama*...
He describes the Blessed One by way of his clan (*gotta*). Therefore, in the phrase "O sir, the ascetic Gotama," the meaning should be understood as: "The ascetic, O sir, belongs to the Gotama clan.
