"Son of the Sakyas" (*Sakyaputta*) is an indication of the Blessed One’s high birth. "One who has gone forth from the Sakya clan" (*Sakyakulā pabbajito*) is an indication of the state of having gone forth out of faith (*saddhā-pabbajita*).
It is said that he has gone forth out of faith, having abandoned that very family which was not overcome by any misfortune and whose wealth was undiminished.
What follows thereafter is of the same meaning already stated. "But as for that," etc., is exactly as it was stated in the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta*.
"Excellent indeed" means beautiful indeed; it is said to be conducive to welfare and conducive to happiness. Of such [persons]...
"Arahants" means those who have attained the qualities of reality as they truly are, such that the world has gained faith in them and bestowed upon them the title "Arahant.
"There is a sight [of them]" means: having opened eyes that are serene with confidence, thinking "even a mere sight is good," one forms this aspiration.
Regarding the term "Ajjhāyaka" (Reciter):
"‘They do not meditate now, they do not meditate now,’ Vāseṭṭha—thus, ‘Ajjhāyaka, Ajjhāyaka’ was the third word coined in the time of the first cosmic age. Thus it was at the beginning of the eon.
This is a term of reproach for Brahmins who are devoid of *jhāna*. However, one who now studies that [Veda] is an *ajjhāyaka* (reciter).
They employ this as a term of praise, in the sense of "one who recites the mantras. One who retains the mantras is a *mantadhara*.
"Of the three Vedas" refers to the *Ṛgveda*, *Yajurveda*, and *Sāmaveda*. One who has gone to the further shore (*pāragū*) by means of the practice of lip-striking [the syllables].
One who has reached the further shore (*pāragū*). Together with the *nighaṇḍu* and the *keṭubha*, [he is one] "together with the *nighaṇḍu* and *keṭubha*" (*sanighaṇḍukeṭubhānaṃ*).
*Nighaṇḍu* is the science that elucidates synonyms for trees and so forth. *Keṭubha* is the science that provides assistance to poets through various rules and applications of composition.

Together with the analysis of phonemes (*akkharappabheda*), [he is one] "together with the analysis of phonemes" (*sākkharappabhedānaṃ*). The "analysis of phonemes" (*akkharappabheda*) consists of both phonetics (*sikkhā*) and etymology (*nirutti*).

"Those for whom the *itihāsa* is the fifth": having made the *Atharvaveda* the fourth, that which is connected with such expressions as "thus it was," "thus it was"—namely, the ancient narratives known as *itihāsa*—is the fifth of these; thus they are "those for whom the *itihāsa* is the fifth.
Of those Vedas, one who studies and knows the *pada* (word-text) and the remainder, namely the *vyākaraṇa* (grammar), is a *padaka* and a *veyyākaraṇa*. [And] the *Lokāyata*.

The *Vitaṇḍavādasattha* (the treatise on sophistry) is so called. The *Mahāpurisalakkhaṇa* (the Treatise on the Marks of a Great Man) is a work twelve thousand verses in length that elucidates the marks of great men such as the Buddhas;

therein were the so-called "Buddha-mantras" consisting of sixteen thousand stanzas, by virtue of which those endowed with these marks are called Buddhas, and by virtue of which others are called Paccekabuddhas.

By this, the distinction is recognized: the two chief disciples, the eighty great disciples, the mother of the Buddha, the father of the Buddha, the chief attendant, the chief female attendant, and the wheel-turning monarch.
"Anavaya" means one who is not deficient in these worldly arts and the marks of a Great Man, but is a fulfiller of them; that is, one who is not lacking (avayo).
This is what is meant. One who is called "inferior" (avaya) is one who is unable to retain those [teachings] both in meaning and in text.

"One who has been authorized and acknowledged" (anuññātapaṭiññāta) means both authorized and acknowledged. He is authorized by the teacher through such statements as, "What I know, you know too," and so forth.
He is acknowledged by his giving an affirmative reply to the teacher, saying, "Yes, teacher"—this is the meaning.
"In regard to what authority? In his own traditional teaching, the word of the Three Vedas. It is said that this brahmin thought:
"In this world, many people wander about taking the name of one who is renowned as 'I am a Buddha, I am a Buddha.
Therefore, it is not proper for me to approach him based on mere hearsay alone; for if one approaches someone [without certainty], there may even be a retreat."
"It would be a great burden; even harm might arise. Suppose I were to send my pupil and have him find out whether he is a Buddha or not, and only then approach him.
Thinking thus, he addressed the young man, saying, "My dear, this one...

and so forth. "Taṃ bhavantaṃ" means "that venerable Gotama. "Tathā santaṃ yeva" means "while he is truly such. For here too, the accusative case is used in the sense of describing a state of being (itthambhūtākhyāna).
258. "But how, sir, shall I know him?"—the meaning here is: "Sir, tell me how I may know that venerable Gotama, in such a way that he can be known. Alternatively, *yathā* is merely a particle.
*Kathaṃ* is an interrogative regarding manner; the meaning is: "In what manner shall I know that venerable Gotama?"
When this was said, his preceptor replied to him, "My dear, do you speak as if you were standing on the earth yet could not see the earth,
or as if you were standing in the radiance of the moon and sun yet could not see the moon and sun?
Having spoken thus, he demonstrated the manner of knowing by saying, "My dear, they have indeed come," and so forth.

In this context, "in the mantras" means in the Vedas. It is said that even before the Tathāgata was to arise, the Suddhāvāsa deities inserted the marks into the Vedas and named them "Buddha-mantras," teaching the Vedas in the guise of brahmins, thinking:
"By following these, beings of great influence will come to know the Tathāgata. Therefore, previously, the marks of a Great Man were [contained] in the Vedas.
They come; but when the Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna, they gradually disappear. Therefore, at present, they do not exist.

"Of the Great Being" (mahāpurisassa) means of that person who is great through qualities such as his vow, the undertaking of knowledge, and compassion. "Only two destinations" (dve yeva gatiyo) means only two ultimate ends.
Now, although this word *gati*—as in "Sāriputta, there are these five destinations"—refers to different types of existence (*bhava*), here it refers to the ultimate goal.

The word *gati* occurs [in various senses]: in such passages as "the forest is the *gati* of deer," it refers to a dwelling place; in "thus they possess supreme *gati*," it refers to wisdom (*paññā*);
and in "gone to its *gati*," it refers to a state of diffusion. However, here it should be understood that it occurs in the sense of finality (*niṭṭhā*).

In this regard, although a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*) possesses certain characteristics by virtue of which he becomes a wheel-turning monarch, the Buddha does not become so by those very same characteristics.
They exist; however, because they share the commonality of being born, they are said to be "those very same things.
Therefore it was said: "endowed with which... If he dwells in a house, that is, if he lives in a household. He becomes a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*):

he is called a king because he gladdens (*rañjeti*) the world through four wonderful qualities and the bases of sympathy; he sets the wheel-jewel in motion, [possessing] the four wheels of prosperity.
He turns [the wheel], he causes others to turn it beyond himself, and because there exists in him the turning of the wheels of postures for the benefit of others, he is a *cakkavattī*.
Here, "king" (*rājā*) is the general term; "wheel-turner" (*cakkavattī*) is the specific one. He acts according to the Dhamma, thus he is "righteous" (*dhammika*);

the meaning is that he conducts himself by way of the proper method and equity. Having obtained the kingdom through the Dhamma, he has become a king, thus he is a "Dhamma-king" (*dhammarājā*). This is by virtue of performing the Dhamma for the benefit of others.

Or he is righteous (*dhammika*). He is a Dharma-king (*dhammarāja*) because he practices the Dharma for his own welfare. He is "one who has conquered the four quarters" (*cāturanta*) because he is the lord of the earth bounded by the four oceans, adorned with the four kinds of islands;
this is the meaning. He is a "conqueror" (*vijitāvī*) because he has conquered internal enemies such as anger and external kings.
He has "attained stability in his realm" (*janapadatthāvariyappatta*) because he has attained permanence within his kingdom.

Having attained stability, it cannot be moved by anyone. Or, a country that has attained stability therein—being devoted, intent on its own work, immovable, and unshakable—is called "one that has attained the stability of a country.
*Seyyathidaṃ* is a particle; its meaning is, "What are these? In the passage beginning with *cakkaratanaṃ*, there is the wheel-treasure (*cakkaratanaṃ*) and so forth.
Because it produces delight, it is a "jewel" (*ratana*); thus it is the "Wheel-Jewel" (*cakkaratana*). This principle applies to all [the jewels] alike.

Among these jewels, however, this Wheel-turning Monarch (*cakravattirāja*) conquers what is unconquered by means of the Wheel-Jewel; he traverses the conquered realm at his pleasure by means of the Elephant and Horse Jewels;
he protects the conquered realm by means of the Counsellor-Jewel (*pariṇāyakaratana*); and he experiences the pleasure of enjoyment through the remaining [jewels].
By the first [jewel], his application of the power of energy (*ussāha-satti*) is perfected; by the last, his application of the power of counsel (*manta-satti*);

and by the jewels of the elephant, the horse, and the householder, his application of the power of lordship (*pabhu-satti*) is perfectly complete. Through the jewels of the woman and the gem, he experiences the happiness of wealth (*bhoga-sukha*);

through the remaining [jewels], the happiness of sovereignty (*issariya-sukha*). Specifically, these first three [jewels] arise through the influence of kamma produced by the wholesome root of non-hatred (*adosa-kusalamūla*).

It should be understood that the middle [forty-nine] arise through the power of kamma produced by the wholesome root of non-greed (*alobha*), and the final one arises through the power of kamma produced by the wholesome root of non-delusion (*amoha*).
This is the summary here. For the detailed explanation, however, it should be taken from the teaching on the *Ratana-sutta* in the *Bojjhaṅga-saṃyutta*.
"More than a thousand" means exceeding one thousand. "Brave" means those of a fearless nature. "Heroic in form" means having bodies like those of the sons of the gods.
Thus, first of all, some explain it. But this is the true meaning here: "Vīra" refers to supreme heroes;
the "vīraṅga" of heroes means the cause of heroism, which is to say, vigor (*vīriya*). Those who have the form of a vīraṅga are called "vīraṅgarūpā";
it is said that they are as if their very bodies consist of vigor. "Crushers of enemy armies" means if [the enemy] should stand facing them.
The intention is that the enemy army is capable of crushing him. "By the Dhamma" means by the Dhamma of the five precepts, beginning with "A living being must not be killed.
Regarding the phrase "He is an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, whose veil is removed from the world":

here, having removed that veil from the world—which is shrouded in the darkness of defilements by the seven veils of lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, views, ignorance, and misconduct—he has brought forth light on all sides.
"Having offered and standing" means "with the covering opened. Herein, it should be understood that by the first word, his worthiness for worship is expressed;

by the second, the cause thereof, because he is a Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha); and by the third, the state of having the covering opened, which is the cause of his Buddhahood, is stated.
Alternatively, "vivaṭṭacchado" means both "opened" (vivaṭṭa) and "without covering" (vicchada); thus it is said to be devoid of the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) and devoid of concealment (chadana).
Thus, by means of that [third vesārajja], he is an *arhat* due to the absence of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*), and a *sammāsambuddha* due to the absence of concealment (*chadana*).

In this way, two causes have been stated for the first two terms; herein, the first [vesārajja] establishes the first [term], the first [vesārajja] establishes the second, and the third and fourth establish the third.
Furthermore, the first is the *dhammacakkhu*, and the second is the *buddhacakkhu*.
It should be understood that he accomplishes the third [type of] universal eye (*samantacakkhu*). By saying, "You are a receiver of the mantras," he produces in him confidence regarding the mantras.
259. Through that discourse of the teacher, he too becomes free from delusion regarding the characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*), as if the Buddha-mantras had become unified in appearance.
"Perceiving thus, he said: 'So be it. The meaning of this is: 'Sir, as you say, so shall I do.
"Having mounted a chariot drawn by mares" means having ascended a chariot yoked with mares.
It is said that the brahmin sent the young man away, giving him the very same chariot that he himself used for his travels. The young men, too, were indeed the pupils of Pokkharasāti.
It is said that he gave them the instruction: "Go together with Ambaṭṭha.

"As far as the ground for the vehicle" means as much distance as it is possible to travel by vehicle; this is what is called "the ground for the vehicle. "Having descended from the vehicle" means having gone to the vicinity of the gate-tower, which is the non-vehicle ground, and having stepped down from the vehicle.
"And at that time" refers to the time when Ambaṭṭha entered the monastery. And at that time...
It was at the time of midday. But why were they walking at that time?
It was for the purpose of dispelling the lethargy and drowsiness caused by their excellent meal, or because they were practitioners of daytime exertion (*divāpadhānika*).

For when such people walk after the meal, bathe, allow their bodies to take on the natural temperature, and then sit down to practice the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*), their minds become one-pointed.
"Where those bhikkhus were": it is said that he, thinking "Where is the ascetic Gotama?
and not going from one dwelling to another, resolved, "I will enter only after asking," and while looking about, saw two bhikkhus clad in rag-robes walking on the great walkway like forest elephants;
he then went into their presence. It is with reference to this that "where those bhikkhus were," and so forth, was said. "For the purpose of seeing" means:
"To see" means having a desire to behold. 260.
"Born of a well-known clan" (*abhiññātakolañño*) means born into a famous family. It is said that at that time in Jambudīpa, there was a famous family known as the Ambaṭṭha clan.

"Of one who is well-known" (*abhiññātassa*) means of one who is renowned by reason of his physical appearance, lineage, and status. "Not heavy" (*agarū*) means not burdensome. For he [who spoke thus] to Ambaṭṭha...
He would not be able to make himself understood, and his conversation with him would be difficult;

however, thinking that even when questioned by a hundred or a thousand such young brahmins, the Blessed One has no hesitation in answering, they thought, "It will not be troublesome. By "vihāra," they meant the Perfumed Chamber (gandhakuṭi).

*Ataramāno* means not hurried; it means placing the foot slowly at the place where the foot-measure falls, performing the proper action so as not to disturb the well-swept sand, which resembles a carpet of pearls, *muttāda*, and *sinduvāra* flowers. *Āḷinda* means the porch (*pamukha*).
*Ukkāsitvā* means having made the sound of clearing the throat. *Aggaḷa* means the door-panel. *Ākoṭehi* means [strike] gently with the tips of the fingernails.
"It means: 'Strike it near the keyhole. It is said that non-humans strike the door too high, while long-nosed creatures (dīghajātikā) strike it too low.
Without striking it in those ways, one should strike it in the middle, near the keyhole; thus they speak when explaining this practice of knocking on the door.
"The Blessed One opened the door" does not mean that the Blessed One rose up and opened the door. Rather, [it means] "let it be opened. However—
He extended his hand. Then, thinking, "For many millions of eons while you were giving gifts, the Blessed One has never personally performed the task of opening a door," the door opened by itself.
However, since it was opened by the mind of the Blessed One, it is appropriate to say that the Blessed One opened the door.
“They exchanged greetings with the Blessed One” means that just as the Blessed One asked them about their health and well-being, so too they were of a like-minded joy with the Blessed One.
They reached a state of unity, like cold water mingled with warm water.
And by which [greeting]—“I hope, Master Gotama, you are faring well; I hope you are getting by; I hope for you, Master... [and so forth].
They exchanged greetings with such talk as, “May there be little illness for Gotama and his disciples; may there be little affliction, lightness, strength, and well-being.
This [talk] is called *sammodanīya* (conducive to greeting) because it generates a greeting consisting of joy and gladness, and because it is appropriate for greeting.

It is [called] *sāttham* (meaningful) and *sabyañjanam* (well-phrased) because, due to the sweetness of its meaning and expression, it can be sustained and maintained continuously even for a very long time.

It is "conducive to remembrance" (*sāraṇīya*) because it pertains to the state of an *arahant* and because it is something to be remembered. It is "conducive to amity" (*sammodanīya*) because it is pleasant while being heard, and "conducive to remembrance" because it is pleasant when being recollected.
Likewise, it is "conducive to amity" due to the purity of its phrasing (*byañjana*), and "conducive to remembrance" due to the purity of its meaning (*attha*).
Having thus exchanged such greetings—conducive to amity and conducive to remembrance—in many ways, having brought them to a conclusion and finalized them...
They sat down to one side.
But as for the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha, it is said that he did not feel even a slight glimmer of confidence in the Blessed One’s physical perfection;
thinking instead, "I shall discredit the One of Ten Powers," he loosened the upper garment tied around his belly, let it hang from his neck, and with one hand—
Taking hold of the hem of his robe and ascending the walkway, he showed his arm at one time, his belly at another, and his back at another;
at one time he made a gesture with his hand, and at another he made a movement with his eyebrows, saying: "I hope, Master Gotama, that your elements are in balance;
I hope you do not suffer from lack of alms-food; for your appearance shows that you are indeed free from fatigue."
For your limbs and members are large, and you are beautiful wherever you go.
Because many people have conceived great respect for you, thinking, "He is a king who has gone forth," and "He is a Buddha," they give you choice, nutritious food. Look, sir, at this house;
it is like a painted hall, like a celestial palace. Look at this couch; look at this pillow. What [more could there be]?
“It is difficult for one dwelling in such a place to practice the duty of a recluse.
Thus he spoke such mocking words, which were intended to remind [the Buddha] of his improper conduct. Therefore it is said:

“But the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha, while walking, exchanged various polite greetings with the Blessed One who was sitting; while standing, he also exchanged various polite greetings with the Blessed One who was sitting...”
“How can he engage in any conversation that is worth remembering?
Then the Blessed One thought: “This young brahmin is like one who, stretching out his hand, wishes to grasp the peak of existence;
like one who, stretching out his foot, wishes to wander in Avīci; like one who wishes to cross the great ocean; like one who [wishes to climb] Sineru...”
"Like one wishing to climb up, he exerts himself in the wrong place; come, let me consult with him. Thus he spoke to the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha.
"By teachers and their teachers" means by the teachers and by their teachers as well.
The commentary on the first charge of pride.
263. Regarding the phrase "walking, he may speak": here, a brahmin is permitted to converse with a teacher-brahmin while in any of the three postures.

However, this young man, because of his arrogance and stubbornness, thinking, "I shall engage in conversation while employing all four postures," said, "Or, Master Gotama, lying down, one may speak with one who is lying down."

Then, it is said, the Blessed One said to him: "Ambaṭṭha, a conversation with a teacher—whether while walking with one who is walking, standing with one who is standing, or sitting with one who is sitting—is indeed found among all teachers.
But you are conversing with your teacher while lying down; is your teacher a cow, or are you?"
Thus, having become angry, he said: "And as for those shavelings, Master Gotama," and so forth.
In this context, it would have been appropriate to say "shavelings, shavelings" regarding the ascetics, or "ascetics, ascetics. However, speaking with contempt, he said "shaveling-ascetics.
"Ibbhas" means householders. "Kaṇhas" means dark-skinned; that is, black. Regarding the term "bandhupādāpacca": here, "bandhu" refers to Brahmā.
This is what is intended. For brahmins refer to him as "the Grandfather" (*pitāmaha*). "Pādāpaccā" means those who are not descended from feet;
the intention is that they were born from the back-foot of Brahmā. It is said that his view was this:
"Brahmins emerged from the mouth of Brahmā, kṣatriyas from his chest, vaiśyas from his navel, śūdras from his thighs, and ascetics from his back-feet. Thus...
And although he spoke thus without making a specific restriction, he nevertheless said, "I am speaking only to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One thought: "From the moment Ambaṭṭha arrived, in speaking with me he has spoken out of sheer pride, like one seizing a venomous snake by the neck, like one embracing a mass of fire, like one [approaching] a rutting elephant..."
Thinking, "Like one who touches with his trunk, he does not know his own measure;

come now, I shall make him know it," he said, "But you, Ambaṭṭha, are indeed one who has need [of this]," and so forth. In that context, *attha* refers to the purpose consisting of the duties to be performed upon arrival;
that which possesses this is *atthika*, meaning the mind of that young brahmin. One who has such a need is *atthikavā*.
The meaning is: "Your coming here was for that very purpose.
*Kho pana* is merely an expletive particle (*nipātamattaṃ*). *Yāyeva kho panatthāya* means "for whatever purpose indeed.

*Āgaccheyyātha* means "you might come"—that is, you might come to me or to others at any time whatsoever. *Tameva atthaṃ* (that very purpose) refers specifically to the masculine gender (*purisaliṅgavasena*).
It was said: "You should attend to it" means you should keep it in mind. This is what is meant:
"You have been sent by your teacher for his own business, not for the sake of our disparagement; therefore, attend to that very task.

Having thus shown the proper conduct for those who have come into the presence of others, [the text continues] for the purpose of subduing pride: "He is indeed one who has not yet lived the holy life..."

He then spoke the words beginning with "But indeed... The meaning of this is: "Behold, sirs, this young man Ambaṭṭha, who, having lived improperly in the teacher's family, being untrained and of little learning, yet fancies himself as one who has lived properly—thinking, 'I have lived properly, I am trained, I am well-learned.
For what else could be the cause for his such harsh speech toward me, other than his failure to live properly in the teacher's family?"
"For they speak thus because they are unawakened, untrained, and of little learning.
(264) "Enraged" means angry. "Displeased" means not having his own way; but did the Blessed One say this after knowing the state of his anger, or without knowing it?
He said it after knowing it. Why did he say it after knowing it? For the purpose of crushing his pride.
For the Blessed One knew: “When this has been said by me, he will become angry and revile my kinsmen.

Then, just as a skilled physician draws out and removes a morbid humor, even so shall I uproot clan by clan and family by family, and having cut down his banner of pride—which stands raised as high as the peak of existence—I shall cause it to fall.”
"Grumbling" means rubbing [against others]. "Despising" means treating with contempt. "Will be brought low" means he will be brought to the fault of a fierce disposition and so forth.
"Fierce" means possessed of anger based on pride. "Harsh" means rough. "Frivolous" means light;
they are satisfied or provoked by even a little, like a gourd-bowl floating on the surface of water, which rises up with only a small amount [of water]. "Garrulous" means those who speak much.
He speaks with the intention that when the Śākyas have their mouths open, there is no opportunity for another to speak.
"Samānā" (equal) is a synonym for the preceding word "santā" (being). "Na sakkaronti" means they do not treat the brahmins in a beautiful manner.
"Na garuṃ karonti" means they do not show respect toward the brahmins. "Na mānenti" means they do not honor them with esteem.
They do not honor them; that is, they do not perform worship for them with garlands and the like. They do not show them respect;
that is, they do not display acts of reverence or humble conduct toward them through salutations and the like. "Tayidaṃ" means "this indeed.
"Yadime Sakyā" means "since these Sakyans do not honor the brahmins... [and so on] ...do not show them respect," all of this—namely, their failure to honor them and so forth—is what is referred to.
"It is not fitting, it is not in accordance"—this is the meaning.
265. Commentary on the second *ibbha* (outcaste) verse:
"They have offended" means they have committed an offense. In the phrase "one has said this," *idaṃ* here is a mere particle; [the sense is] "one has said."
*Attha*: meaning. *Sandhāgāra*: the hall for royal administration. *Sakyā*: consecrated kings. *Sakyakumārā*: those not yet consecrated. *Uccesu*:
on various types of seats such as couches, stools, cane chairs, wooden benches, and spread rugs, according to their respective rank.
*Sañjagghantā*: laughing with loud laughter by way of derision. *Saṅkīḷantā*: performing mere laughter, such as clapping fingers, striking hands, and so forth.
"Doing so, they think only of me; thus do I perceive it: they laugh only at me, not at anyone else.
But why did they act in this way? It is said that they knew Ambaṭṭha’s family lineage.
And at that time, he was wearing his lower garment tucked down as far as his ankles, holding the hem of the cloth with one hand.
Having had his shoulder-bone rubbed, he came along as if intoxicated by pride and arrogance.
Then, saying, "Behold, sirs, the reason for the arrival of our slave Ambaṭṭha of the Kaṇhāyana clan," they acted in this manner.
He too knew his own family lineage; therefore, he reasoned, "He thinks it is only me."
"By means of a seat": an invitation by means of a seat is one such as "This is a seat; sit here. No one did so.
266. *Laṭukikā*: a small bird living among clods of earth in a field. *Kulāvake*: in its dwelling place.
“Kāmalāpinī” means one who speaks as she pleases; whatever she desires, that she utters.
No swan, crane, or peacock comes along and restrains her by saying, “Why are you prattling? “Abhisajjituṃ” means to seize [her] out of anger.

When this was said, the young man, thinking, “This ascetic Gotama, having treated his own kinsmen like little quails, now treats us like swans, cranes, and peacocks—he has become arrogant,” displayed four further colors.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Son of a Slave Girl: 267.
*Nimmādeti* means he humbles, he causes to lose pride, he makes him devoid of conceit. *“Yaṃnūnāhaṃ”* means “if, however, I were to say.
It is said that Ambaṭṭha uttered these words—“I am a Kaṇhāyana, O Gotama”—three times with a loud voice. Why did he say it?
“Does he not know his impure state? “Yes, he knows it. Even though he knows, this cause is concealed by existence (*bhava*);
therefore, he has not seen it. Thinking, “What will the Great Ascetic say when he does not see it? he spoke out of arrogance and stubbornness.
“Mātāpettika” means belonging to one’s mother and father. “Nāmagotta” refers to the name by way of designation (*paṇṇatti*) and the lineage by way of tradition (*paveṇī*).
"Lineage": "Recalling" means while recollecting and purifying the ancestral lineages. "Sons of masters" means sons of lords.

"Son of a slave-girl" means a son of a domestic slave-girl. Therefore, this shows that when the Sakyans saw him not approaching them—as one who ought to approach his masters like a slave—they mocked him.

From this point on, having declared his own status as a slave and the Sakyan’s status as a master, and bringing forward the family lineage of both himself and Ambaṭṭha, he said, "The Sakyans indeed... and so forth. Therein, "they hold" means they establish;
"Okkāka is our forefather"—the meaning is that they act in this way. It is said that at the time of that king's speaking, [a light] like a torch issued from his mouth.
"Light issued forth; therefore they named him Okkāka. "He caused [them] to go forth" means he led them out.
Now, showing them by way of their names, he said: "Okkāmukha," and so forth. Herein, this is the sequential account:
it is said that King Mahāsammata, the first of the world-age, had a son named Roja. Roja’s son was Vararoja; Vararoja’s son was Kalyāṇa.
From Kalyāṇa came Varakalyāṇa; from Varakalyāṇa, Mandhātā; from Mandhātā, Varamandhātā;
from Varamandhātā, Uposatha; from Uposatha, Vara; from Vara, Upavara; from Upavara, Makhādeva;
and from Makhādeva, there were eighty-four thousand kṣatriyas in successive lineage. Following them, there were three Okkāka lineages. Among them—
King Okkāka had five chief queens— Hatthā, Cittā, Jantu, Jālinī, and Visākhā—
and each was accompanied by a retinue of five hundred women. The eldest queen had four sons— Okkāmukha, Karakaṇḍu,
Hatthinika, and Sinisūra— and five daughters— Piyā, Suppiyā, Ānandā, Vijitā, and Vijitasenā.
Thus, having given birth to nine sons, she passed away.
Then the king brought another young and beautiful princess and established her in the position of chief queen.
She gave birth to a son named Jantu. On the fifth day, having adorned him, they presented him to the king. The king—
Pleased, he granted her a boon. She consulted with her kinsmen and requested the kingdom for her son.
The king rebuked her, saying, "Begone, you outcaste! You seek to create an obstacle for my sons.
Yet she repeatedly gratified the king in private and continued to entreat him, saying such things as, "Great King, it is not right to speak falsehoods."
Then the king addressed his sons: "My dear sons, when I saw your youngest brother Jantukumāra, I rashly granted a boon to his mother; she now wishes to divert the kingdom to her son.
With the exception of you, [I grant] as many auspicious elephants, horses, and chariots as you desire."
“Take him and go; after my passing, you may come and rule the kingdom. With these words, he dispatched them along with eight ministers.
Having wept and wailed in various ways, they asked the king and the royal women for forgiveness, saying, “Father, forgive our fault.
Then, asking the king’s permission, saying, “We too shall go with our brothers,” they departed from the city.
Taking their sisters and surrounded by a fourfold army, they departed from the city.
Thinking, "The princes will come and rule the kingdom upon the passing of their father; let us go and attend upon them," many people followed after them.
On the first day, the army was about one *yojana* in length; on the second, it was about two *yojanas*; on the third, it was about three *yojanas*.
The princes deliberated: "This is a great army; if we were to crush some neighboring king and seize his territory, even he would not withstand us.
What is the use of inflicting suffering upon others? This Jambudīpa is vast;
let us build a city in the forest. Having spoken thus, they set out toward the Himālayas and searched for a site for a city.
And at that time, our Bodhisatta, having been reborn in a family of great brahmin landowners and having become known as the brahmin Kapila, went forth and took the ascetic’s renunciation.
He lived on the slope of the Himalayas, having constructed a leaf-hut on the bank of a lotus pond within a grove of plantain trees.
It is said that he possessed a knowledge called *bhūmijāla*, by which [he could see] upwards eighty cubits.
In the sky, as well as below on the ground, he perceives both virtues and faults.

In this place, grass, shrubs, and creepers grow turning to the right and facing the east. When lions, tigers, and other wild beasts, deer, pigs, snakes, cats, frogs, and mice pursue them, upon reaching that place they are unable to continue their chase; rather, being utterly terrified by it, they simply turn back.
Thus, having recognized, "This is the foremost spot on earth," he had a leaf-hut constructed there.

Then, seeing those princes who had come to his own dwelling place while searching for a site for a city, and having questioned them and learned of their situation, he felt compassion for them and said: "In this very place where the leaf-hut was built..."
"This city shall become the foremost city in Jambudīpa. Every single man born here will be capable of overcoming even a hundred men or a thousand men.
Build the city here; construct the king’s palace on the site of the leaf-hut.
For standing in this very place, even the son of a caṇḍāla would be superior by the power of a wheel-turning monarch."
“Venerable sir, is this not a dwelling place for the noble one? “Do not worry about it as ‘my dwelling place.
Build a leaf-hut on one side of mine, establish a city, and give it the name Kapilavatthu.
They did so and made their home there.
Then the ministers thought, "These children have reached maturity; had their father been present, he would have arranged their marriages.
Now, however, the responsibility falls upon us. Having reflected thus, they consulted with the princes.
The princes said, "We see no daughters of kṣatriyas who are our equals, nor do we see any kṣatriya youths who are the equals of our sisters."
"In our union with those of unequal status, the sons born to us will be impure by reason of their mother or father and will fall into a confusion of castes.

Therefore, we prefer to live only with our sisters. Out of fear of such a confusion of castes, they placed their eldest sister in the position of a mother and established a household with the remaining sisters.
As they grew with sons and daughters, at a later time, leprosy broke out on the eldest sister;

her limbs became like *koviḷāra* flowers. Even as the princes sat, stood, and ate together with her, they thought, "This disease may spread upon us," and one day, while going for a pleasure excursion to the park—
Having placed him upon a vehicle as if he were a corpse, they entered the forest, had a lotus pond dug in the ground,
and having thrown him into it along with various kinds of food, they covered the opening with a stone slab as if it were part of a house, spread earth over it, and departed. At that time,
the King of Bārāṇasī named Rāma was being shunned by his dancing women and palace attendants because of a leprosy affliction.
Driven by that sense of spiritual urgency, he gave the kingdom to his eldest son, entered the forest, and there constructed a leaf-hut.
Living there on roots and fruits, before long he became healthy and golden-hued.
As he wandered here and there, he saw a large hollow tree; having cleared out a space inside it measuring sixteen cubits, he took up residence there.
Having fitted a door and a window and fastened a ladder, he made his dwelling there.
Having kindled a fire in a charcoal pit, he would sleep at night listening for the sounds of deer, wild boars, and other animals. Observing, "In such-and-such a place a lion made a sound;
in such-and-such a place a tiger," he would go there at dawn and [take] the meat of the remains.
Having taken it and cooked it, he ate it.

Then one day, while he was sitting there having kindled a fire at dawn, a tiger, drawn by the scent of the princess's body, came to that place and, shaking up the dust, made a breach in the embankment; and through that breach—

Seeing a tiger, she was terrified and let out a cry. Hearing that sound and perceiving, "This is the voice of a woman," he went there early in the morning and asked, "Who is here? "It is a woman, my lord. "What is her caste?
"She is the daughter of the great king Okkāka, my lord. "Is she able to leave? "She cannot, my lord. "For what reason? "Because of a skin disease."

"I have [a remedy] for you. Having inquired about her entire condition, and because she would not come out due to her pride as a kshatriya, he made known his own status as a kshatriya, saying, "I too am a kshatriya.

He provided a ladder, helped her up, led her to his own dwelling place, gave her only the medicines he himself had used, and before long restored her to health and a golden complexion. Then, by her...
He lived together with her. Through that very first cohabitation, she conceived and gave birth to two sons;
again another two, and so on, until she had given birth sixteen times. Thus, there were thirty-two brothers.
When they had gradually reached maturity, their father instructed them in all the various arts and crafts.
Then one day, a forest-dweller living in the city of King Rāma, while searching for gems on the mountain, saw the king;
recognizing him, he said, “I know you, O Lord. Thereupon, the king questioned him about all that had transpired.
At that very moment, those two boys arrived. Seeing them, he asked, “Who are these? [The man replied,] “They are your sons.”
When this was said, he asked them about their lineage and thought, "I have now received my inheritance.
He went to the city and informed the king. The king, thinking, "I shall bring my father back," went there with a fourfold army.
Having paid homage to his father, he entreated him, saying, "O Lord, accept the kingdom. He replied, "Enough, dear son; it is not for me there."
“I am going; remove this tree right here and build a city for me,” he said.

Having done so, and because he had removed the *kola* tree from that city, it was given the name Kolanagara; and because it was built on the path of the tiger (*byaggha*), it was given the name Byagghapatha.
Thus, having bestowed these two names upon it, he paid homage to his father and departed for his own city.
Then, when the princes had reached maturity, their mother said: "Dear ones, you have Sakyas living in Kapilavatthu who are your maternal uncles.
Regarding the daughters of your uncles, there is such a thing as seizing them by the hair and such a thing as seizing them by the garment.
When they come to the bathing place, you should go there and let whoever pleases you take whichever one."
They went there accordingly, bathed in those waters, and while their heads were drying, they took whatever they desired, called out their names, and departed.
When the Śākya kings heard this, they said, "Let it be so, friend; they are indeed our own kinsmen," and remained silent.
This is the origin of the Śākyas and Koliyas. Thus did the Śākyas and Koliyas establish mutual marriage alliances with one another.
For those who performed [these deeds], the lineage has come down uninterrupted until the time of the Buddha. In that context, the Blessed One, in order to show the Sakyan lineage, said:
"They were banished from the kingdom and lived on the bank of a lotus pond on the slopes of the Himalayas," and so forth. Therein, *sammanti* means they dwell.
Indeed, O sir, these Sakyans, though banished from the kingdom and dwelling in the forest, did not allow any confusion of their caste.
They are capable, able, and competent to protect the family lineage—this is the meaning. "From that as the foremost" means taking him as the first, starting from him;
this is the meaning. "And he was their ancestor" means that King Okkāka was their forefather.
There is not even a mere trace of intermixture with the householder lineage among them.
Having thus explained the lineage of the Sakyans, he now explains the lineage of Ambaṭṭha, saying: “Now as for the king’s...,” and so forth.
“He begot one named Kaṇha” means that he gave birth to a son of dark complexion who had teeth already grown within the womb, with a full beard and mustache.
“He cried out” means that when [the attendants], fearing that a *yakkha* had been born, fled and closed the door, [he cried].
Wandering here and there among the household dependents, saying things such as "wash [your feet]," he made a loud noise.
Those young brahmin students said this to the Blessed One in order to clear themselves of reproach:
"Do not say this, sir," and so forth. It seems they thought to themselves: "Ambaṭṭha is the senior pupil of our teacher."

"If we do not say even a single word or two in such a situation, this man will cause a rift between us and our teacher," they said thus solely for the sake of escaping blame. However, they desired his state of being free from pride in their hearts;
for it is said that he was even disliked by them because of his reliance on pride. "Of beautiful speech" means one whose words are sweet.
"In this speech" means in the speech of the three Vedas which he himself has mastered. "To respond" means to give a reply to the question asked;
the sense is to answer it. Or, [it refers to] "in this speech of the slave’s son. "To respond" means to state a rejoinder. 269.
Then the Blessed One—[thinking], "If these young brahmins were sitting here in this way... [the text continues].
“They will make a loud noise, and this discussion will not reach its conclusion. Come now, let me silence them and speak only with Ambaṭṭha.
He said this to those young men. In that context, *mantavho* means “you should deliberate.
*Mayā saddhiṃ paṭimantetū* means “let him converse with me. When this was said, the young men thought: “Ambaṭṭha...”
When he was told, "You are the son of a slave-girl," he was unable to lift his head again. "This thing called birth is indeed difficult to discern;
if the ascetic Gotama were to say anything else such as 'you are a slave,' who would dare to dispute with him?
Let Ambaṭṭha himself untie the knot he has tied for himself. Having thus freed himself, [he spoke] over him.
Throwing [the challenge], they said: “Well-born indeed, O Gotama,” and so forth.

(270) *Sahadhammiko* means with reason, having a cause. *Akāmā byākātabbo* means that even if one does not wish to do so oneself, one must still provide an answer; the meaning is that it must necessarily be resolved. *Aññena vā aññaṃ paṭicarissasi* means you will evade [the question] with some other statement.
"Paṭicarissasi" means you will evade, cover over, or conceal [the truth].
For when one who is asked, "What is your clan? replies, "I know the three Vedas," and so forth, this is called evading with something else.
"Pakkamissasi vā" means that even though you know the answer to the question asked, you will rise from your seat and depart out of a desire not to speak.
"He remains silent," [she thought], "the ascetic Gotama wishes to have me confess my status as the son of a slave myself;
once it is confessed by oneself, one is indeed born a slave. But after he has urged me two or three times, he will become silent;
then I shall turn around and depart. Having thought this, she remained silent.
271. "Vajirapāṇi" means one who has a thunderbolt (*vajira*) in his hand. "Yakkha" does not refer to just any random spirit; it should be understood as Sakka, the king of the gods.
"Blazing" (*āditta*) means having the color of fire. "Flaming up" (*sampajjalita*) means burning intensely.

"Become a mass of flames" (*sajotibhūta*) means become luminous on all sides; the meaning is that it has become a single web of fire. "He stands there" [referring to] a great head, resembling a *kandala* flower bud.
Having manifested such various and hideous forms—such as fearsome fangs, eyes, and noses—he stood there.
But why did he come? It was for the purpose of eliciting a view [from the Buddha].
Furthermore, it was because the Blessed One had fallen into a state of indifference toward teaching the Dhamma, thinking: "If I were to teach the Dhamma, others would not understand me."
When Sakka came to the Blessed One together with Mahābrahmā, he made this promise: “Blessed One, teach the Dhamma;
if we do not abide by your command, we shall cause others to abide by it. Let there be the Wheel of Dhamma for you, and the Wheel of Authority for us.
Therefore, [Sakka] has come thinking: “Today, having terrified Ambaṭṭha, I will cause him to answer the question.”
“The Blessed One alone sees and Ambaṭṭha too”—for if others had also seen it, that matter would have been a source of concern;
they might have said, “This ascetic Gotama, knowing that Ambaṭṭha was not entering into his own doctrine, summoned a *yakkha* and showed him to him;
then Ambaṭṭha spoke out of fear. Therefore, [he said], “The Blessed One alone sees and Ambaṭṭha too.”
As soon as he saw it, sweat broke out over his entire body. As it writhed inside his belly, he let out a great cry.
Looking around to see if anyone else was watching, he did not perceive even the bristling of another's hair.
Then he thought: "This fear has arisen for me alone; if I say, 'I am a *yakkha*, what will they think? "Are your eyes [the only ones that see]?"

"There is; you yourself see the spirit, but having not seen the first spirit, you see it only because you have been cast into a debate with the ascetic Gotama"—thinking thus, and considering, "Now I have no other refuge here except for the ascetic Gotama," the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha... [and so on] ...said this to the Blessed One.

272. *Tāṇaṃ gavesī* means seeking refuge. *Leṇaṃ gavesī* means seeking a hiding place. *Saraṇaṃ gavesī* means seeking a shelter. Herein, it is called *tāṇaṃ* because it protects (*tāyati*) and guards.
It is called *leṇaṃ* because beings hide (*nilīyanti*) therein. It is called *saraṇaṃ* because one goes to it for safety (*sarati*);
the meaning is that it destroys or shatters fear. *Upanisīditvā* means having approached and sat down on a lower seat.
Having sat down. "Let him speak" means let him say.
Regarding the *Ambaṭṭha-vamśa-kathā* (273–274):
"The southern country" (*dakkhiṇa-janapada*) is well known as the Southern Road (*dakkhiṇāpatha*). It refers to the well-known country to the south of the Ganges.
At that time, it seems, there were many brahmin ascetics in the southern region. He went there and won the favor of one ascetic through his observance of proper conduct.
Seeing his service, the ascetic said to him, "O man, I shall give you a mantra;
take whichever mantra you desire. He replied, "I have no need for any other mantra, teacher."
“There is a task for which there is no weapon that can prevail; give me that spell.
He replied, “Very well, sir,” and gave him the spell called Ambaṭṭha, which travels with the bow.
Having received that spell and tested it right then and there, he thought, “Now I shall fulfill my desire,” and took on the guise of a seer.
He went into the presence of Okkāka. Therefore it was said: “Having gone to the southern country and studied the *brahmamanta* spells, he approached King Okkāka.
Here, “*brahmamanta*” refers to the most excellent spells because they are endowed with majestic power (*ānubhāva*). [Okkāka asked: “Who is this? Is he my son by a slave woman?”
"Who indeed, O friend, is this son of my slave-woman? [Thinking thus,] he drew that arrow—meaning the king, desiring to kill him, having equipped it with a sharp point;
yet by the power of the man's spell, the king was unable either to shoot it or to withdraw it, and stood there for that very moment with sweat breaking out over his entire body, trembling with fear.
“Ministers” means great ministers. “Counsellors” means others who move within the assembly. They said this:
“The entire kingdom was destroyed by a rain of weapons because King Daṇḍakī offended the ascetic Kisavaccha.
And Nāḷikera, having offended Ajjuna among the five hundred ascetics and Aṅgīrasa, split the earth and entered hell.”
Thinking thus out of fear, they spoke these words beginning with, "May it be well, venerable sir.
When Kaṇha remained silent for a long time after hearing the words, "It shall be well with the king," he was then entreated in many ways:
"It was a grave deed on the part of your king, when he aimed a razor-headed arrow at a seer such as myself."
Having said "He will speak," etc., he later spoke as follows: "Undriyissati" means it will break apart; it will be scattered like a handful of husks.
This he speaks falsely, thinking, "I shall save the people.
For the power of his magic spell (vijjā) extends only as far as the stiffening of the body, and not beyond that. This same principle applies to the subsequent statements as well.
His hair stood on end; he would not even experience a single thrill of horripilation.
It is said that he spoke thus after having made the king give his promise: "If the king will give that maiden to me. He fixed a razor-sharp arrow upon the prince;
by means of the incantation "Let the arrow descend," he fixed it upon the prince’s navel. [He gave] his daughter.
Thinking, "She is not a slave," he washed her head, made her a free woman, gave her to him as a daughter, and established her in a position of high honor.

As for the words, "But you, young man, do not [think so]," the Blessed One spoke this in order to reassure Ambaṭṭha by making it clear that "Ambaṭṭha is a kinsman of the Sakyans on one side. Thereafter, Ambaṭṭha was consecrated with a hundred jars of water.

Having become calm and composed as if relieved of his distress, he thought: "The ascetic Gotama intends to win me over by making me a kinsman through one side [of the argument], thinking, 'I am indeed a kshatriya.
This is the description of his status as the most excellent of kshatriyas.
275. Then the Blessed One, thinking, “This Ambaṭṭha perceives himself as ‘I am a khattiya,’ yet he does not know his own lack of khattiya status;
well then, I shall make him know it,” spoke the words beginning with “What do you think, Ambaṭṭha? in order to show the lineage of the khattiyas, thereby extending the subsequent instruction.
In that context, *idha* means “in this world. *Brāhmaṇesu* means “among the brahmins.”
In between. "A seat or water" means either the first seat or the first water. "At a funeral feast" refers to a meal prepared specifically for the deceased.

"At a *thālipāka*" refers to a meal such as one for an auspicious occasion. "At a sacrifice" refers to a sacrificial meal. "At a guest-meal" refers to a meal prepared for guests or a meal consisting of gifts.
"Would it be so? means: would it be so for that son of a kṣatriya? Or "obstructed"?
"His [desire] blows unobstructed" means that regarding Brahmin girls, there may or may not be any restraint;
the sense is that he may or may not obtain a Brahmin maiden. "Not having attained" means not having reached the status of a Khattiya; the sense is that he is impure.
"Having made a woman into a woman" means having sought out a woman. "In some particular matter."
"In some fault" means in an improper act that should not have been done by the brahmins. "With a bag of ashes" means with a bag of ash;
the meaning is that they scattered ashes on their heads.
"In the progeny" (*janetasmim*) means in the offspring; the meaning is "in the people. "Those who follow their lineage" refers to those among the people...
They refer to their clan, saying, "I am a Gotama, I am a Kassapa. Among those in the world who refer to their clans, the Khattiya is the best.
"Authorized by me" means that having been compared with my omniscient knowledge, they were taught and authorized by me.
The commentary on the first section for recitation is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on Knowledge and Conduct (Vijjācaraṇakathāvaṇṇanā) 278.
Now, upon hearing the phrase "one endowed with knowledge and conduct" (*vijjācaraṇasampanno*) in this verse, Ambaṭṭha thought:
"Knowledge (*vijjā*) refers to the three Vedas, and conduct (*caraṇa*) refers to the five precepts; this we alone possess. Thus, [I am] one endowed with knowledge and conduct."
Having reached the conclusion, "He is the best, we alone are the best," he asked about knowledge and conduct:

"But what, Master Gotama, is that conduct, and what is that knowledge? Then the Blessed One, having rejected the definition of knowledge and conduct associated with birth and other such views established in the brahminical tradition, [taught] the unsurpassed knowledge and conduct.
Wishing to demonstrate this, he said, “Indeed not, Ambaṭṭha,” and so forth. In that context, “discourse on birth” (*jātivāda*) means a discourse concerning birth;
the meaning is that such statements as “this is appropriate only for a brahmin, not for a *sudda*,” and so on, apply everywhere. The same method applies in all instances.
“Bound by the discourse on birth” (*jātivādavinibaddhā*) means bound within the discourse on birth. This same method applies in all instances.
Then Ambaṭṭha thought: “Where we thought we would get stuck, the ascetic Gotama has cast us far away, like winnowing chaff in a great wind.
But where we could not get stuck, there he has directed us. It is right that this perfection of our knowledge and conduct be known.
Having thought this, [he spoke again regarding] the perfection of knowledge and conduct.
He asked. Then the Blessed One, in order to show the knowledge and conduct (*vijjācaraṇa*) starting from its origin, said to him: "In this case, Ambaṭṭha, the Tathāgata...
and so forth. And here, the Blessed One, analyzing the threefold virtue (*sīla*) included within conduct, said: "This is his [virtue]... and so on.
Instead of releasing him on the grounds of "conduct," he released him on the grounds of "virtue" alone, thinking, "This too belongs to his virtue. Why?

Because that person also possessed some degree of virtue; therefore, if he had been released on the grounds of conduct, he might have become attached right there, thinking, "We too are endowed with conduct.
But it was on account of that which he had never before seen even in a dream that he was released.
"Entrusting [the practice], he enters and dwells in the first jhāna. This too is his conduct... pe ...he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna;
this too is his conduct," it is said. Up to this point, all eight attainments have been presented as "conduct.
However, from the starting point of insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*), there are eight kinds [of knowledge].
Wisdom is presented as true knowledge (*vijjā*).
Commentary on the Discourse on the Four Gateways to the Lower Realms (280):
"Gateways to the lower realms" means gateways to destruction. "Unable to overcome" means not attaining, or being unable to withstand.

"Or: 'Taking a khārī-measure of various items'—here, *khārī* refers to the requisites of an ascetic, such as the fire-drills (*araṇī*), a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), a bamboo staff (*sujā*), and so forth.
*Vidha* means a basket (*kāja*). Therefore, the meaning is: 'taking a basket filled with these [requisites].
As for those who read it as *khārivividhaṃ*, they explain: '*Khārī* is a name for a basket; *vividhaṃ* means many requisites, such as water-pots and the like. 'One who subsists on fallen fruit'..."
"Subsisting on fallen fruit": he is an attendant (*paricāraka*) by way of performing duties such as making things allowable, receiving the alms-bowl, and washing the feet.

Granted that even a novice monk (*sāmaṇera*) who has destroyed the taints (*khīṇāsava*), though superior in virtue, may act as an attendant to an ordinary monk (*puthujjana bhikkhu*) according to the method described;
yet this one was not like that, being inferior both in terms of virtue and in terms of performing services.
But why is it said that the ascetic renunciation (*tāpasapabbajjā*) is a door to the destruction of the Dispensation (*sāsana*)?
Because, as the Dispensation progresses, it will decline through the influence of the ascetic renunciation.

For in this Dispensation, those who are modest and desirous of training, having gone forth but being unable to fulfill the three trainings, [will think]: "There is no Uposatha or Pavāraṇā ceremony with you."
Having felt disgust, they avoided it, thinking, "Whether it be the training or the formal act of the Saṅgha.
He thought, "The fulfillment of the practice in the Teaching is difficult, like walking on the edge of a razor; but the life of a forest ascetic is easy and is approved by many people.
Having thus left the order, he became an ascetic. When others saw him, they asked, "What have you done? He replied, "It was a heavy burden for you..."
"In the Dispensation [of the Buddha] there is true work, but here we are those who act according to our own whims," he says.

If he thinks, "If it is thus, I too shall go forth right here," and follows his example, he becomes an ascetic (*tāpasa*). In this way, one after another, more and more people gradually become ascetics.
When they have arisen, the Dispensation is said to have declined. Such a person as this is called a "Buddha" in the world.

It will be merely a matter of hearing that such a teaching as this arose for him. With reference to this, the Blessed One said that the ascetic’s renunciation was a gateway to the destruction of the Teaching (*sāsana*).
"A spade and a basket" means both a spade and a basket for the purpose of gathering bulbs, roots, and fruits. "Or near a village" means...
Failing to achieve the perfection of true knowledge and conduct (*vijjācaraṇasampadā*) and considering it difficult to sustain his life through such means as agriculture,
he builds a fire-hall on the outskirts of a village or a town for the purpose of deceiving the many people; there he remains,
tending the sacrificial fire by performing oblations with ghee, oil, curds, honey, molasses, sesame seeds, rice, and various types of wood.
"Having made a four-doored house" means having built a four-faced tavern, having constructed a pavilion at its entrance,
and having provided drinking water there, he invites all who come with water. Whatever travelers,
exhausted from their journey, give him— whether a bowl of rice or grains of rice— after they have drunk the water and are satisfied, he accepts it all.
Having performed acts such as taking loans, he gives food to some for the sake of receiving more material goods, and to others, cooking vessels and the like.
He takes the material goods or grain and so forth given by them and employs them for the purpose of increasing his wealth.
Thus, with his prosperity growing, he acquires cattle, buffalo, female and male slaves, and attendants, and establishes a large household. It is with reference to this that it was said:
It is said: “Having built a house with four doors, he dwells therein. “I shall honor him according to my ability and according to my strength”—this, however, is the gateway to his practice;
for by means of this gateway, he practices in this way.
And by this much, all forms of the ascetic’s renunciation have been demonstrated by the Blessed One.
How so? There are eight kinds of ascetics: those who live with their wives and children; those who live by gleaning; those who do not cook over a fire; those who do not cook food themselves;
those who eat only what is gathered in the hollow of their hands; those who eat only from the tooth-prints [left by animals]; those who eat only fallen fruit; and those who eat only withered leaves.
Among these, those who live having established a household, like Keṇiya the matted-hair ascetic, are called "those who live with their wives and children."

However, those who, thinking "the state of having sons and wives is unsuitable for one who has gone forth," gather rice, mung beans, māsa beans, sesame seeds, and so forth from threshing floors and pounding grounds, cook them, and consume them, are called *uñchācariya* (gleaners).

Those who, thinking "it is improper to wander from threshing floor to threshing floor, bring back rice, and pound it before consuming it," collect alms of husked rice in villages and market towns, cook it, and consume it, are called *anaggipakkika* (those who do not cook over fire).

Those who, thinking, "What is the use of food cooked by oneself for one who has gone forth? enter the village and take only food that has been cooked by others, are called *asāmapāka* (those who do not cook for themselves).

Those who, thinking, "Day after day, the search for alms is indeed painful for one who has gone forth," peel the bark from mango trees and other such trees using a stone held in their fist and eat it, are called *asmamuṭṭhika* (those who use stones as mortars).

But those who, thinking, "Wandering about peeling bark with a stone is indeed painful," extract the bark with their teeth alone and eat it, are called *dantavakkalika* (those who use their teeth as mortars).

Those who, thinking, "For one gone forth, eating what has been plucked by hand with the teeth is suffering," eat fruits that have fallen after being struck by clods, sticks, and the like, are called "those who eat fallen fruit" (*pavattaphalabhojana*).

However, those who, thinking, "To consume [fruit] after having it knocked down by clods, sticks, and the like is unbecoming for one gone forth," sustain themselves by eating only flowers, fruits, withered leaves, and so on, that have fallen of their own accord, are called "those who eat withered leaves" (*paṇḍupalāsika*).
They are of three kinds—superior, middling, and inferior. Among them, those who do not rise from their sitting place and [take fruit] with their hand...
Those who take and eat what has fallen within their reach are the superior ones (*ukkaṭṭhā*).
Those who do not go from one tree to another are the middling ones (*majjhimā*). Those who go to various roots of trees, search for food, and eat it are the inferior ones (*mudukā*).
Furthermore, these eight types of ascetic renunciation are all included within these four categories. How so? Among them—
For indeed, those who live with their wives and children resort to the household life by means of gleaning;

those who do not cook with fire and do not cook with a pot resort to the hearth-room; those who eat handfuls of stone and those who wear garments of teeth resort to a diet of bulbs, roots, and fruits;
and those who eat fallen fruit and those who eat only withered leaves resort to a diet of fallen fruit. Therefore it was said:
—“And by this much, all forms of the ascetic life have been demonstrated by the Blessed One.

Now, in order to show Ambaṭṭha, together with his teacher, that they had not even reached the gateway to the perfection of knowledge and conduct (*vijjācaraṇasampadā*), the Blessed One said, “What do you think, Ambaṭṭha? and so forth. The meaning of this is already clear. By himself...

"Even one belonging to the states of misery (āpāyika), being incomplete"—this means by one who belongs to the states of misery and is incomplete through the perfection of true knowledge and conduct (vijjācaraṇasampadā).
283. Regarding the commentary on the practice of the former seers (pubbakaisibhāva):
"Dattika" means that which has been given. "He does not even grant his presence"—why does he not grant it? It is said that he [does not do so] in person...
He knows a spell called *āvaṭṭanī*. Whenever the king is adorned with magnificent ornaments, he stands near the king and recites the names of those ornaments.
Once the king’s names have been recited, the king is unable to say, "I will not give them.
Having given them, on a subsequent festival day, when [the king] says, "Bring the ornaments back," [he replies], "They are gone, Your Majesty."
When he was told, "It was given by you to the brahmin," he asked, "Why was it given to me?
Those ministers said, "That brahmin knows the art of enticement (*āvaṭṭanimāya*) face-to-face; having enticed you with that, he takes [the wealth] and departs.
Others, unable to endure his excessive intimacy with the king, said, "Your Majesty, in this brahmin’s body..."
“There is a disease called *saṅkhaphalita-kuṭṭha*. Upon seeing this, you should embrace it and touch it;
however, this disease known as *kuṭṭha* spreads through physical contact, so do not act in such a way.
From that time forth, the king did not grant him his presence.
However, because that brahmin was wise and skilled in the science of statecraft (*khattavijjā*), an action performed after consulting with him would not be contradictory;
therefore, standing inside the hempen wall, he consulted with him while standing outside.
It is with reference to this that it is said: “he consults through the cloth. In that context, *tirodussantena* means *tirodussena*.
Or rather, this is the reading: *dhammikaṃ* means blameless; *payātaṃ* means brought forward and given.

"How could that king [be such]?"—referring to the king for whose sake the brahmin would accept such alms, how could that king not even grant him an audience? But this [brahmin] takes what is not given through deceit; therefore, for him...
“The intended meaning here is that one must reach the conclusion: ‘The king does not grant him an audience.
However, apart from this reason, no one other than the king and the brahmin knows [the truth].
Even though this is thus secret and concealed, they will certainly reach the conclusion: ‘The ascetic Gotama is omniscient,’ so the Blessed One declared.”

284. Now, since this Ambaṭṭha and his teacher were excessively conceited on account of their mastery of the mantras, the Blessed One, in order to humble that pride based upon their knowledge of the mantras, extended the teaching further by saying: "What do you think, Ambaṭṭha, suppose here a king... and so forth.
In this context, *rathūpatthare* means a place prepared and spread out for the king to stand upon in his chariot. *Uggehī vā* means by those who have risen high or are of high birth.
"By ministers. "By khattiyas" means by princes who have not yet been consecrated. "They deliberate on some matter" refers to such public deliberations as:
"It is fitting to construct a pond or a reservoir in such-and-such a place," or "We should establish a village, a market town, or a city in such-and-such a place.
"That very same deliberation" means that which was deliberated upon by the king is indeed that very same [deliberation]. "By those very same [ministers]."
One might deliberate by means of modes such as the tossing of the head or the tossing of the eyebrows. "Spoken by the king" means as it was spoken by the king;
the meaning is that he speaks what is capable of establishing that very purpose. 285. "Proponents" means those who cause [the matter] to proceed.
"Of whom" means belonging to whom. "Mantra-word" refers to that which is designated as the Veda.
"Mantra" alone [is the subject]. "Chanted" (*gīta*) means recited by the ten ancient Brahmins, such as Aṭṭhaka and others, by way of perfecting the melody.
"Proclaimed" (*pavutta*) means spoken by others; the meaning is "recited. "Collected" (*samihita*) means gathered together, heaped up, or established as a single mass;
the meaning is "placed together in a heap. "They chant after that" means that nowadays Brahmins chant that which was previously chanted by them.
They sing along and recite along. "They repeat after that" means they repeat after that; this is a synonym for the preceding term.

"They repeat what has been spoken" means they recite along with what was spoken and recited by them. "They cause others to recite what has been read" means they cause others to recite what was read by them.
"Namely, what are they?"—this is what he asks. "Aṭṭhaka" and so forth are their names.

It is said that they, having observed with the divine eye (*dibba-cakkhu*) and without causing harm to others, compiled the mantras in accordance with the word of the Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened Kassapa Buddha.
However, other brahmins, having introduced [teachings on] the taking of life and so forth, split the three Vedas apart.
They made it contradictory to the word of the Buddha. "This possibility does not exist" means that the reason by which you might become a seer (*isi*)—that cause does not exist.

Here, the Blessed One, because he knew—"Even though he is being questioned, having recognized his own obstinate nature, he will not give an answer"—therefore, without even seeking a formal admission, he rejected that state of being a seer.

286. Now, because those ten ancient brahmins lived in forest regions at the foot of mountains, free from the scent of raw flesh, free from the scent of women, wearing dust and dirt, practicing celibacy, and subsisting on forest roots and fruits;
and whenever they wished to go anywhere, they traveled through the air by means of psychic power (*iddhi*), having no need for a vehicle—[this applies] in all directions.
And for them, the cultivation of the divine abodes such as loving-kindness constitutes their protection;
they have no need for walls or guards. Since Ambaṭṭha had previously heard of their practice, the Blessed One said, "What do you think, Ambaṭṭha?
and so forth, in order to show that this teacher of his is far removed from their practice.
In this context, "with the black hair removed" means having the black hair searched out and taken away.

"With the flanks bent by head-ornaments" means with the sides of the body bent by head-coverings such as cloth bands, silk ribbons, and the like. "With manes trimmed" means with manes trimmed in the appropriate places for the sake of beauty;
and here, it is specifically the manes of the mares that are trimmed, not those of the chariots, because they are yoked to the mares.
Furthermore, even chariots are called "kuttavāla. In the phrase *ukkiṇṇaparikhāsu*, it means in moats that have been dug out.
In *okkhittapalighāsu*, it means in places where obstacles (*paligha*) have been set up. Regarding *nagarūpakārikāsu*:
here, "upakārikā" refers to the plastering work done all around the base of a city wall for the purpose of preventing others from climbing over it. However, in this context, by those "upakārikās,"...
“Fortified cities” refers specifically to those that serve as strongholds for a city.

“They cause themselves to be protected” means that even while living in such cities, they cause themselves to be guarded. “Doubt” (*kaṅkhā*) is a state of uncertainty, such as “Is he omniscient, or is he not?
“Perplexity” (*vimati*) is a synonym for that same state; it means a distorted understanding, or an inability to reach a definitive conclusion. Regarding this, the Blessed One [said] to Ambaṭṭha...
"In this present state of existence, there is no manifestation of the Path; only the day passes away.
Yet he has come for the purpose of seeking the marks, and even that task he forgets. Well then, I shall give him a method so that mindfulness may be aroused," he said.
*Commentary on the Seeing of the Two Marks*
287. Having spoken thus, [the Blessed One] rose from his seat and went outside for the purpose of undertaking a walking meditation (caṅkama-adhiṭṭhāna).
For no one is able to seek out the marks (lakkhaṇa) of the Buddhas when they are sitting or reclining; however, they can do so when they are standing or walking.

Moreover, it is the custom of the Buddhas that, upon knowing someone has come to seek their marks, they rise from their seats and undertake a walking meditation. Therefore, the Blessed One rose from his seat and went outside.
He had set out. Therefore, the passage beginning with "Then the Blessed One" was spoken.
*Samannesī* means he searched for; he gathered them together while counting them one by one or two by two. *Yebhuyyena* means for the most part;
the meaning is that he saw many and did not see few. Then, in order to illustrate those which he did not see, it was said:
"Except for two": "He doubts" means he arouses a longing, thinking, "O, may I see him!

"He is perplexed" means that while searching for them here and there, he is distressed and unable to see them. "He does not resolve" means that because of that perplexity, he does not reach a definitive conclusion.
"He does not gain confidence" means that regarding the Blessed One—[thinking], "This one possesses the complete marks"—he does not attain serene faith.

He does not attain confidence (*pasāda*). By "doubt" (*kaṅkhā*), weak perplexity is meant; by "wavering" (*vicikicchā*), middling [perplexity]; by "lack of resolve" (*anadhimuccanatā*), strong [perplexity];
and by "lack of serene confidence" (*asampasāda*), the state of turbidity of the mind due to those three factors is expressed.

"Sheathed" (*kosohita*) means covered by the sheath of the lower garment. "The private parts" (*vatthaguyha*) refers to the male organ; for the Blessed One’s private parts were sheathed like those of a noble elephant.
It was golden-colored, resembling the interior of a lotus. Because it was covered by his robe, he did not see it;
and because his tongue had gone inside his mouth, he did not perceive its great extent. Thus, regarding those two characteristics, he became doubtful and perplexed.
"Of such a kind" refers to that form. What else need be said here? This has been stated by the Elder Nāgasena himself.
When questioned by King Milinda: "Venerable Nāgasena, it was difficult for the Blessed One to do. Why so, Great King?

[The Elder replied: "Because, Great King, he created occasions for shame in the minds of the great multitude, as well as for the Brahmin Brahmāyu, his pupil Uttara, the sixteen Brahmins who were pupils of Bāvari, and the three hundred young men who were pupils of the Brahmin Sela."
"He showed him, venerable sir. "The Blessed One did not show the king his secret form, great king. The Blessed One showed him a shadow.
Having fashioned it by means of psychic power, he showed the king a mere shadow-form, clad in an undergarment, girt with a waist-band, and draped in a robe.
"If a shadow is seen, is that not indeed what was seen, venerable sir? "Let that be, great king."
“If there were a being capable of awakening upon seeing the form of the heart, the Perfectly Enlightened One would have extracted the flesh of the heart and shown it to him.
“You are skillful, venerable Nāgasena.
“*Ninnāmetvā* means having extracted. *Anumasi* means he rubbed it, having made it like a stiff needle; by doing so...”

And herein, it should be understood that softness is indicated by the touching of the ear-lobes, length by the touching of the nostrils, thinness by the touching of the nose-tip, and breadth by the covering of the forehead.
"Waiting" means expecting; the meaning is that he is looking forward to his arrival, longing for his coming.
290. *Kathāsallāpo* means both talk (*kathā*) and conversation (*sallāpa*), the sense being speaking and replying.
291. *Aho vata* is an expression of reproach. *Re* is an address used in a sense of contempt. *Paṇḍitakā*—he said this while feeling disgust for that very person.
The same method applies to the other two phrases as well. "By such a man, it is said, who acts as a companion for profit..."

He says this with reference to the following meaning: "If such a person as you were to exist—one who acts for the welfare of others and brings about their benefit—a man would go only to hell and nowhere else. *Āsajja āsajja* means having struck, having struck.
"One might lead even us in this way, one might lead us in this way"—having said these words, beginning with "Ambaṭṭha, Pokkharasāti the brahmin," and so forth... thus [he spoke].
Having brought him back again and again, having exposed his hidden conduct, and having firmly established his status as a slave and so forth, he said:
"The intention was that you were making us revile [him]. "He set him in motion on foot" means that he struck him with his foot and cast him down upon the ground.
And as for how he previously went along as a charioteer, having mounted the chariot together with his teacher—that too...
Having cleared a space, he proceeded on foot right in front of the chariot.
[Commentary on Pokkharasāti’s Approach to the Buddha, §§ 292–296] "Ativikālo" means it was very late;
there was not even time for a conversation of friendly greeting. "Āgamā nu khvidha" means...
"Is it not so, sir?"—this is a question. "May he consent"—that is, may he accept.
"For today"—that is, for the sake of whatever merit, joy, and gladness shall arise for me today from performing this service for you.
"The Blessed One consented by silence"—the Blessed One, without moving either body or speech, maintained his acceptance within himself.
He consented by remaining silent. This means that for the sake of favoring the brahmin, he accepted [the invitation] with his mind alone.
297. “With excellent” means with the highest. “With his own hand” means with his own hand. “Satisfied” means he thoroughly satisfied him, making him full, well-fed, and as much as he required.
“Entertained” means he thoroughly entertained him, using hand gestures such as “enough, enough.”
He caused [him] to refuse [further food]. "One who has eaten" (*bhuttāvī*) means one who has finished eating.

"One who has removed the hand from the bowl" (*onītapattapāṇi*) means one whose hand has been withdrawn from the bowl; that is what is meant. There is also a reading *onittapattapāṇi*. Its meaning is as follows:
"one whose hand is separated from, or devoid of, the bowl" is *onittapattapāṇi*; he is such a one. Having washed both the hands and the bowl—

The meaning is that he sat down after setting aside his bowl to one side. "He sat down to one side" means that, having understood the Blessed One to be in such a state, he sat down in a certain place.
(298) "Graduated discourse" (*anupubbiṃ kathaṃ*) means a discourse in successive order. A graduated discourse is as follows: immediately after giving comes virtue;...
This is a discourse illuminating these matters: that heaven follows immediately after virtue, and the Path follows immediately after heaven.
For this very reason, he said: "That is to say, a talk on giving," and so forth. "Okāraṃ" means "avakāraṃ," which is to say, a state of inferiority.
"Sāmukkaṃsikā" means "sāmaṃ ukkaṃsikā"—drawn out by oneself, grasped by one's own self, seen through self-existent knowledge (*sayambhūñāṇa*), and not shared with others; such is the meaning.
What, then, is that? It is the teaching on the Noble Truths. For this very reason it was said: "Suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Here, by the term "Dhamma-eye," the path of stream-entry is intended.
