To show the manner of its arising, he said: "Whatever is subject to origination, all that is subject to cessation. For that [eye] has cessation as its object.
Thus, by performing what is to be done, it arises for one who penetrates all conditioned phenomena in this way.
Commentary on the Declaration of Lay-Faith by the Upāsaka Pokkharasāti (299):

"Diṭṭhadhamma" means that by him the Dhamma of the Noble Truths has been seen (*diṭṭha*). This same method applies to the remaining terms as well. "Tiṇṇavicikiccha" means that doubt has been crossed over.
"By this [he is] one whose doubts have been crossed. "One whose perplexity has departed" means one for whom uncertainty (*kathaṃkathā*) has vanished.

"Attained to intrepidity" means having reached a state of confidence (*visāradabhāva*). Where? In the Teacher’s dispensation. "Not dependent on another" means that he does not rely on another as a condition here, nor does he proceed by means of another's faith.
The rest is self-evident, as it follows the method already explained everywhere and its meaning is clear.
Thus ends the commentary on the Ambaṭṭha Sutta in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the commentary on the Dīghanikāya. 4.
Commentary on the Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta.
300. Thus have I heard... [etc. ...In Aṅga: this is the Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta. Herein, this is the commentary on the words not previously explained.
"In Aṅga" (*Aṅgesu*): those known as the Aṅgas are royal princes from the countryside who received that designation because of their physical beauty;
the territory inhabited by them, though it is but a single province, is called "Aṅga" by way of conventional usage (*rūḷhi-sadda*). "In that province of Aṅga. "On a journey" (*cārikaṃ*): here too...

Both itinerant wandering and settled wandering are intended here. At that time, it is said, as the Blessed One was surveying the ten-thousandfold world system, the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa appeared within the net of his knowledge.
Then the Blessed One thought, "This brahmin appears within the net of my knowledge;
does he perhaps possess the necessary spiritual potential? Investigating thus, he saw: "In me..."
When he has gone there, the disciples of that [teacher] will speak in praise of the brahmin in twelve ways and will not allow him to come into my presence.
But he, having refuted their argument, will speak in praise of me in twenty-nine ways;
having approached me, he will ask a question. At the conclusion of the answer to his question, he will take refuge.
"he will go," and having seen this, he set out for that country accompanied by a retinue of five hundred bhikkhus. Therefore it is said:
"While wandering on tour among the Aṅgas... he arrived at Campā.
On the bank of the Gaggarā lotus pond—that is, not far from the city of Campā—[belonging to] the king's chief queen named Gaggarā.

There was a lotus pond known by the name Gaggarā because it had been dug out. On its banks, all around, was a vast grove of *campaka* trees adorned with flowers of five colors, such as blue and others.
In that *campaka* grove, fragrant with the scent of blossoms, the Blessed One was dwelling.
It is with reference to this that it is said: "on the bank of the Gaggarā lotus pond. [The phrase] "by Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha" [is used].
In this context, he is called Māgadha because he is the lord of the Magadhas. He is called Seniya because he is endowed with a great army.
*Bimbi* means gold; therefore, because his complexion resembles the color of excellent gold, he is called Bimbisāra.
(Verses 301–302) They are called *saṅghā* because they have become many and are gathered together. They are [called] *saṅghī* because a *saṅgha* exists for them in each direction.
*Saṅghī*: Previously, having been without a group inside the city, they went outside and attained the state of a group; thus they became "group-leaders" (*gaṇī*).
"He addressed the *khattā*" means that the *khattā* is called a high official capable of answering questions when asked;
he addressed him, saying, "Let them wait," meaning "let them wait a moment, let them not go."
The Discourse on the Qualities of Soṇadaṇḍa.
303. "From various kingdoms" (*nānāverajjaka*): those born in various kinds of kingdoms—namely, in various different kingdoms such as Kāsī, Kosala, and so forth;
or those whose dwellings are in those places; or those who have come from them—these are the "people from various kingdoms. Of those people from various kingdoms.

"Because of some business or other": it is said that in that city, Brahmins would assemble for two purposes—either for the sake of witnessing a sacrifice or for the sake of reciting the mantras. At that time, however, there was no other sacrifice in that city;
these men had assembled in the presence of Soṇadaṇḍa for the purpose of reciting the mantras. It is with reference to this that it was said.
—“On account of some business or other. When they heard of his departure, they thought:
“This Soṇadaṇḍa is a prominent brahmin, and most of the other brahmins have gone for refuge to the ascetic Gotama; he alone has not gone.
Now, if he goes there, he will surely be ensnared by the ensnaring magic of the ascetic Gotama.”
“He will go for refuge; consequently, there will no longer be an assembly of brahmins at his house door.
Having deliberated, “Come now, let us create an obstacle to his departure,” they went there. It was with reference to this that it was said:
“Then those brahmins,” and so forth.
In this context, "by this factor" means by this reason as well. Having stated that reason in this way, they further thought:
"There is no being who does not rejoice when his own praise is being spoken; let us stop his departure by reciting his praises.
Thinking thus, they spoke the reasons beginning with, "For the venerable Soṇadaṇḍa is well-born on both sides," and so forth.
"From both sides" means from two lineages. "On the mother’s side and on the father’s side": your mother is a brahmin, your mother’s mother is a brahmin, and her mother too is a brahmin;

your father is a brahmin, your father’s father is a brahmin, and his father too is a brahmin—in this way, you, sir, are well-born on both sides, on the mother’s side and on the father’s side. "Of pure descent" means your maternal lineage is pure.
The meaning is "the womb. Regarding the phrase "of a stomach that digests evenly," here the karma-born fire element is called the "stomach" (*gahaṇī*).

As for the expression "as far as the seventh generation of ancestors": here, the father's father is the "grandfather" (*pitāmaha*); the generation of the grandfather is the "grandfather-generation" (*pitāmahayuga*).
"Generation" (*yuga*) refers to the measure of a lifespan; however, this is merely a verbal designation. In actual fact, the grandfather himself is the "grandfather-generation."
Beyond that, all his ancestors are included by the mention of the grandfather alone. Thus, he is one whose lineage is pure back as far as the seventh generation.
Alternatively, they show him to be "uncensured and unreviled in respect of birth.
"Uncensured" means not censured or reviled with such words as, "Take this man away! What is the use of him? "Unreviled" means not reviled.
He had never before experienced abuse or censure. For what reason? Because of his birth. The meaning is:
by such words as, "He is of low birth. "Wealthy" means a lord.
"Possessed of great riches" means endowed with vast wealth. Indeed, in your house, on the earth...
They show that while he possesses great wealth like a heap of dust and sand, the ascetic Gotama is actually destitute, sustaining himself by filling his belly with alms.

"One of great enjoyment" means one who has great enjoyment by way of the five strands of sensual pleasure. Thus, thinking that they would demonstrate the Blessed One’s lack of virtue by way of the opposite of whatever virtue they mention, they speak in this manner.

"Handsome" (*abhirūpa*) means more handsome, more excellent in form than other men. "Beautiful to behold" (*dassanīya*) means worthy of being seen because those who look upon him are never satiated even after looking for a whole day.
"Gracious" (*pāsādika*) means that he generates clarity of mind by his very appearance. "Lotus-like quality" (*pokkharatā*) refers to the state of being beautiful;
"lotus-like quality of complexion" (*vaṇṇa-pokkharatā*) is the excellence of complexion, and he is endowed with that perfection of complexion.
This is the meaning. However, the Ancients said: "They call the body *pokkhara*, and *vaṇṇa* is simply complexion.
According to their opinion, *vaṇṇapokkharāni* means both complexion and the body. The state of these two is *vaṇṇapokkharatā*.

Thus, "by supreme *vaṇṇapokkharatā*" means by means of an exceedingly pure complexion as well as by the perfection of bodily form; such is the meaning. "Possessing a Brahma-like complexion" (*brahmavaṇṇī*)...
"Of excellent complexion": even among those with pure complexions, the meaning is that he is endowed with the most excellent, golden complexion.
"Possessing a body like that of Brahmā": he is endowed with a body exactly resembling the body of Mahābrahmā. "A field not small for seeing":
the opportunity for seeing the Blessed One’s body is not small, but great; all his limbs and members are indeed beautiful to behold.
And they illuminate those very same [qualities] as being great.

One who possesses virtue is "virtuous" (sīlavā). One whose virtue is grown and increased is "one of grown virtue" (vuddhasīlī). By "with grown virtue" (vuddhasīlena) is meant by virtue that is grown and increased.
"Endowed with" (samannāgato) means joined with it. This is a synonym for the term "one of grown virtue."
All of this is said with reference solely to the five precepts (*pañcasīla*).

Regarding the phrases "one of beautiful speech" (*kalyāṇavāca*) and so forth: one whose speech is beautiful, excellent, and characterized by well-rounded words and syllables is "one of beautiful speech.
One whose vocal expression is beautiful and sweet is "one of beautiful vocal expression. "Vocal expression" (*vākkaraṇa*) refers to the sound of utterance.
"Porī" means "urban" because it exists in a city (*pura*) due to its perfection of qualities; or, it is "urban" because it exists in a city.

It is called "porī" because it resembles an urban woman (*porī*) in its delicacy; [the word] "by that urban [speech]" refers to this. "Vissaṭṭhāya" means unobstructed, being free from faults such as stammering or excessive slowness.
"Anelagalāya" means devoid of *elagala*. For when anyone speaks, *elā* (saliva) trickles out (*gaḷanti*), which is spittle.
Or they trickle away, or drops of saliva issue forth; his speech is called "slurred" (*elagala*), meaning it is the opposite of that [clear speech].
"Capable of making the meaning known" means capable of making known the meaning of what has been spoken by making the beginning, middle, and end clear.
"Old" (*jiṇṇa*) means old through the state of being worn out by aging. "Aged" (*vuddha*) means having reached the limit of the growth of the limbs and members of the body.
"Mahallaka" means endowed with great age; it is said to mean one who has long been born. "Addhagata" means one who has traversed the path;
the intention is that he has passed through two or three royal successions. "Vayo-anuppatta" means having reached the final stage of life;
the "final stage of life" refers to the last third of a hundred-year lifespan.

Moreover, "aged" (*jiṇṇo*) means ancient; it is said to refer to one belonging to a lineage that has existed for a long time. "Venerable" (*vuḍḍho*) means endowed with growth in virtues such as moral conduct and behavior.

"Elderly" (*mahallako*) means possessed of great wealth or status. "One who has reached the journey's end" (*addhagato*) refers to one who has set out upon the path, whose nature it is to proceed without transgressing the boundaries of the Brahmins' vows and practices.
"One who has attained old age" (*vayo-anuppatto*) refers even to the state of being advanced in years by birth.
He has reached his final age. 304. Regarding the phrase "when this was said":
when this had been spoken by those brahmins, Soṇadaṇḍa—[thinking] "these brahmins [are distinguished] by birth and so forth"—
“They are speaking in praise of me, yet it is not proper for me to take pleasure in my own praise.
Come now, I shall shatter their argument, make known the greatness of the ascetic Gotama, and cause them to go there,” he thought, and then said:
“Therefore, sirs, listen to me as well,” and so forth. In that context, the phrases beginning with “those who are well-born on both sides” and so on—

They possess qualities similar to his own qualities. Thinking, "Who am I, and who are the qualities such as the excellence of birth belonging to the ascetic Gotama?", he considers them to be far superior to his own qualities;

yet he proclaims the others solely for the purpose of illustrating the greatness of the Blessed One. By thus restricting [the claim] with the words, "We alone are worthy," he demonstrates this: "If one is to be approached because of the greatness of one's qualities..."

It is called "name" because it is insignificant and inferior. For just as a mustard seed compared to Mount Sineru, a cow’s footprint compared to the great ocean, or a drop of dew compared to the water in the seven great lakes is limited and inferior, even so, when our own virtues are compared to the virtues of the ascetic Gotama—beginning with his perfection of birth—our virtues are limited and inferior. Therefore...
"We ourselves ought to approach the venerable Gotama for the purpose of seeing him.

"Leaving behind a great multitude of kinsmen" means that he went forth having left behind six million families—eighty thousand families on his mother's side and eighty thousand families on his father's side.
"Both those on the ground and those in the air" refers here to the lotus ponds plastered with lime in the royal court and in the pleasure groves.
Wealth that has been filled with the seven treasures and placed in the ground is called "buried wealth.
Wealth that has been filled and placed in the towers and other structures of a palace is called "aerial wealth. This, first of all, is what comes down by way of family inheritance.
However, on the very day the Tathāgata was born, four treasures—Saṅkha, Eḷa, Uppala, and Puṇḍarīka—emerged. Among these:
The *saṅkha* [lotus] is four *gāvutas* in size; the *elo* is half a *yojana*; the *uppala* is three *gāvutas*;
and the *puṇḍarīka* is one *yojana*. Even among these, as each is taken, it remains full; thus it should be understood that the Blessed One went forth, having renounced abundant gold and silver.
"Being young" means being in the prime of youth. "With very black hair" means having hair that is perfectly black, with hair resembling the color of collyrium.

"Having offered," is the meaning. "With the auspicious" means with what is beneficial. "With the first stage of life" means with the first of the three stages of life. "Of those who do not desire" means of those who are unwilling;
here the genitive case is used in the sense of disregard (*anādara*). "Tear-faced" (*assumukha*) means those whose faces have tears upon them;
"of those tear-faced ones" means of those whose faces are moistened by tears. "Weeping" means crying out and lamenting.
"Of no small scope": here it should be understood that for the Blessed One, the scope for being seen is indeed immeasurable.

On this matter, there is this story: it is said that in Rājagaha, a certain brahmin, having heard that he was unable to grasp the measure of the ascetic Gotama, took a sixty-cubit bamboo pole and [stood] at the city gate at the time when the Blessed One was entering for alms.
When the Blessed One arrived, he stood outside holding a bamboo pole and remained nearby. The bamboo reached only as high as the Blessed One’s knees.
On the following day, he joined two bamboos together and stood nearby. The Blessed One, appearing only as high as the waist above the two bamboos, said:
“Brāhmaṇa, what are you doing? “I am taking your measure,” he replied.
“Brahmin, even if you were to come after joining together the bamboos that fill the entire interior of the world-system, you would still not be able to grasp my measure.
For I have fulfilled the perfections for four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons in such a way that another could not grasp my measure; incomparable, Brahmin, is the Tathāgata.”
Having said, "He is immeasurable," he spoke this verse from the *Dhammapada*:
"For one who honors such as these— those who have attained Nibbāna and are free from fear—
it is not possible for anyone to calculate even this much merit."
At the conclusion of the verses, eighty-four thousand beings drank the Deathless.
There is another account: Rāhu, it is said, was the lord of the Asuras; he was four thousand eight hundred yojanas in height.
The distance between his arms was twelve hundred yojanas, and the thickness between them was six hundred yojanas. [The same applies to] the palms of his hands and the soles of his feet.
In width it was three hundred yojanas. His fingers were fifty yojanas long; the space between his eyebrows was fifty yojanas.
His mouth was two hundred yojanas wide and three hundred yojanas deep, with a circumference of three hundred yojanas.
His neck was three hundred yojanas, his forehead three hundred yojanas, and his head nine hundred yojanas. "I am so tall that, having bent down to the Teacher—"
Thinking, "I shall not be able to look upon him," he did not come. One day, having heard the Blessed One’s praise, he thought, "By whatever means possible I shall look upon him," and so he arrived.
Then the Blessed One, knowing his intention, considered: "In which of the four postures shall I show myself to him?"
Having reflected, [the Blessed One thought], "Even one who is lowly, when standing, appears as if high; I shall show myself to him while lying down.
He said, "Ānanda, prepare a couch in the courtyard of the Perfumed Chamber," and there he assumed the lion’s posture.
When Rāhu arrived, he saw the Blessed One lying down and, raising his neck, looked up at him like the full moon in the midst of the sky.
When it was asked, "What is this, O Lord of Asuras? he replied, "The Blessed One will not come because he thinks, 'I shall not be able to look down.
It was not with my face turned downwards, O Lord of Asuras, that the perfections were fulfilled; rather, giving was performed by directing [the mind] upwards.
On that day, Rāhu went for refuge. Thus, the Blessed One is no small opportunity to behold.
He is virtuous by virtue of the fourfold purification; that virtue, moreover, is noble, supreme, and utterly pure. Therefore he said: "One who possesses noble virtue" (*ariyasīlī*).
This very virtue is wholesome in the sense of being blameless. Therefore he said: "One who possesses wholesome virtue" (*kusalasīlī*). "By means of wholesome virtue" is a synonym for this.
"Teacher of many teachers" refers to the Blessed One, for at each single teaching of the Dhamma, eighty-four thousand living beings [attain realization].
Although immeasurable gods and humans drink the nectar of the path and its fruits, he is therefore the teacher of many; yet among those disciples who are to be trained, he is the preceptor.
Regarding the phrase "one whose sensual lust is destroyed": while it is true that all defilements have been destroyed in the Blessed One, the brahmin does not know this.
He speaks of the virtue only in respect of what he himself knows. As for "free from deceit": "adornment with the bowl, adornment with the robe..."
He is free from the frivolity described as "the adorning of this putrid body... the fondling and petting of it.
He is one who "places no evil before him," meaning he conducts himself having placed the nine supramundane states (navalokuttaradhamma) foremost.
He has "respect for the brahmin folk," that is, for the community of brahmins consisting of Sāriputta, Moggallāna, Mahākassapa, and others, and for this very community.
The meaning is: "For this generation moves about placing the ascetic Gotama before them. Furthermore, *apāpapurekkhāro* means one for whom evil is not a priority;
it means he does not move about having placed evil before him, nor does he desire evil.

Of what [generation]? Of the brahminical generation. What is meant is that even toward the brahminical generation with whom he is in conflict, he remains without hostility and seeks only their welfare and happiness.
“From another kingdom” (tiroraṭṭhā) means from another kingdom. “From another district” (tirojanapadā) means from another district.
“Come to ask a question” means that wise kṣatriyas and others, as well as devas, brahmās, nāgas, gandhabbas, and so forth, come having prepared questions [with the thought]:
“We shall ask a question. In this regard, some [criticize] either the fault in the question or the acceptance of the answer.
Or, perceiving their own incapacity, they remain silent without even asking questions. Some do ask;
for some, the Blessed One, having inspired them with the zeal to inquire, provides the answer.
Thus, the doubts of all of them reach their resolution upon reaching the Blessed One, just as waves break upon reaching the great ocean.
“Ehi svāgatavādī” means that he addresses each person—whether a god, a human, one gone forth, or a householder—who has come into his presence, saying, “Come, welcome.
Regarding “sakhila”: what is gentleness (*sākhalya*)?
It means being endowed with gentleness as described by the method beginning with, “That speech which is not harsh, pleasant to the ear,” and so on; the meaning is that he possesses soft words.

"Sammodaka" means one skilled in welcoming; the meaning is that he should be the first to engage in friendly conversation with the four assemblies as they arrive, using such methods as "Is it bearable, monks?
Is it sustainable?"—thereby appearing to pacify all the weariness of their journey.
"Abbhākuṭiko" means as some [people] might [behave toward] an assembly...
Having reached [a state of fear], their faces become stiff and contracted; it is not like this.
Rather, upon seeing the assembly, his lotus-face blossoms like a lotus touched by the morning sun and becomes as beautiful as the full moon.
"With an open face" means that, unlike some who do not say anything at all when an assembly has gathered—as if their faces were turned downward—his speech is exceedingly rare and precious.
He is not like that. Rather, the ascetic Gotama is easy to speak with;
he shows that no regret arises in those who come into his presence as to why they have come here, for upon hearing the Dhamma, they become truly glad at heart.
"One who speaks first" means that when speaking, he speaks first, and that indeed at the appropriate time and in the appropriate measure.
He speaks only that which is based on the goal, not idle talk.
"In that village" refers to where the Blessed One dwelt; it is said that there, powerful deities take up their protection, and by virtue of that, no calamity befalls the people.
For it is the dust-demons (*paṃsupisācaka*) and the like who [otherwise] afflict humans.
They harass [them], but by the power of those [monks], they flee far away. Moreover, by the power of the Blessed One’s loving-kindness (*mettā*), non-human beings do not harass human beings.

One who possesses a *saṅgha*—meaning a *saṅgha* that has been instructed in the *Saṅgīti* and so forth, or one that he himself has established—is "one who has a *saṅgha*" (*saṅghī*). And such a person as this...
One who has a *gaṇa* (a group) is a *gaṇin*. Alternatively, this is a synonym for the preceding term.
One who is a teacher (*ācariya*) of a *gaṇa* by way of teaching proper conduct is a *gaṇācariya*. "Of many founders of sects" (*puthutitthakarānaṃ*) means of numerous founders of sects.

"In whatever way" (*yathā vā tathā vā*) means by whatever means whatsoever, even merely by such things as being naked (*acelaka*). "He comes together" (*samudāgacchati*) means he approaches from all sides; he increases.
"They are our guests" means they are our visitors, newcomers, and hospitable guests; this is the meaning. "I master" means I know.
"Of immeasurable praise" means that even by an omniscient one such as he, his praise would be immeasurable—let alone by someone like me;
thus it is shown. And this has also been said:
“Even if a Buddha were to speak the praise of another Buddha for an entire eon,
without speaking of anything else,
that eon would be exhausted in its long duration.”
“The praise of the Tathāgata would never come to an end.
But having heard this discourse on the Teacher’s virtues, those brahmins reflected:
“Just as the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa speaks in praise of the ascetic Gotama, that worthy Gotama must possess extraordinary qualities; for one who knows his qualities thus…”
But because the teacher had waited for too long, they thought, "Come now, let us follow him," and so they followed.
Therefore, when this was said, the words beginning with "those brahmins" were spoken. In that context, *alam eva* means "it is indeed appropriate.
*Api puṭosena*: *puṭosa* refers to provisions for a journey; the meaning is that it is indeed appropriate to approach even while taking those provisions. *Puṭasena* is also [a variant].
"Reading," its "meaning," and "a bundle on the shoulder"—thus it is "shoulder-bundle" (*puṭaṃsa*); by that "shoulder-bundle.
What is meant is: even by one carrying a bundle of provisions on the shoulder.
Commentary on the Reflections of Soṇadaṇḍa.
306–308. *Tirovanasaṇḍagatassa*: having gone beyond the forest grove; the meaning is, having entered the interior of the monastery.
*Añjaliṃ paṇāmetvā*: those belonging to both sides [of the dispute] thought thus:
"If those of wrong view should reproach us, saying, 'Why did you pay homage to the ascetic Gotama?'—to them [we shall say], 'What is there in merely making the gesture of añjali?'"
"We shall say: 'Veneration is indeed required. If those of right view should reprove us, saying, 'Why did you not pay homage to the Blessed One?', we shall reply:
'Is veneration accomplished merely by striking the ground with the head?
Is not the act of joining the palms likewise veneration? Regarding name and clan: 'O Gotama, I am Datta, the son of so-and-so.'"

Those who say, "I am named so-and-so; I am a friend; I have come here," are announcing their names. Those who say, "Sir Gotama, I am Vāseṭṭha by name, Kaccāna by name; I have come here," are announcing their clan.
It is said that these impoverished, aged sons of good family did this thinking, "We shall become well-known in the midst of the assembly by way of our names and clans. But as for those...
They sat in silence—those who were like crows and those who were blind fools. Therein, the "crows" (kerāṭikā) think:
"Even by engaging in one or two conversations, one becomes trustworthy; once trust has been established, it is not proper not to give one or two alms.
Having thus freed themselves from [the obligation], they sit in silence. The "blind fools" (andhabālā), due to their very ignorance, are like a lump of clay that has been cast away.
They sit silently wherever they are, as if [possessed by something].
Regarding the description of the brahmin’s state of mind (Brāhmaṇapaññattivaṇṇanā):
"With his own mind, he discerned the reflection in the other's mind," said the Blessed One—"From the moment this brahmin arrived..."
“With his face cast down and his body stiff, what is he thinking as he sits? What indeed is he contemplating?
Thus reflecting, he knew the other’s mind with his own mind. Therefore it is said: “Having known the deliberation of his mind with his own mind. He is tormented means he falls into distress.
Having surveyed the assembly, [he thought] regarding the Blessed One’s own doctrine: “By asking questions in the water...”
Being measured, as if lifted up and set upon dry land, with his body and mind completely calmed, he looked around the assembly as if saying,
"May the honorable sirs examine my words," solely through the perception of [wrong] views; then, having surveyed the assembly,
he said this to the Blessed One.

311–313. "Of those taking up the ladle" (*sujam paggaṇhantānam*): the meaning is, among the brahmins who take up the ladle for the purpose of performing a sacrifice, [he was] either the first or the second.
The ancient masters (*porāṇā*) say: "Of those receiving the great sacrifice being given at the ladle.
Thus, the brahmin answered the question correctly according to his own system. But the Blessed One [responded] specifically as the supreme brahmin.
For the sake of showing [this], he said, "But as for these," and so forth. They said this thinking:
"If one endowed with birth, appearance, and mantras is not a brahmin, then who indeed will be a brahmin in the world?
This Soṇadaṇḍa is destroying us; come now, we shall refute his argument. Thus they spoke. "He disparages" means he rejects. "He intrudes" means...
He enters. This was said with the intention: "If you wish to go for refuge to the ascetic Gotama out of faith, then go;
do not break the agreement with the brahmin. 314. *Etadavoca* ("He said this"):
while these brahmins were thus shouting all at once, [he thought], "This discussion has reached its conclusion..."
Thinking, "He will not go; well then, let me silence them and speak only with Soṇadaṇḍa," he spoke the words beginning with, "If this is indeed yours.
(315–316) "Sahadhammena" means with reason. "Samasamo" means equal by way of parity, setting aside partial equality.
“Equal” means equal in every respect. “I know his parents”—why would she not know the parents of her sister’s son?
She says this specifically with reference to the indication of their lineage. “She might even speak a falsehood” means she might utter a falsehood that destroys one’s welfare.
“What will appearance avail? means: if there are no internal virtues, what will it do? What will his...?
The meaning is that he will be able to preserve his status as a brahmin. Furthermore, if it should be argued:

"It is natural virtue (*pakatisīla*) that accomplishes the status of a brahmin for one established in virtue"—even in this case, it is virtue alone that accomplishes it; for in its absence, the status of a brahmin does not exist. Thus, [the mention of] caste and so forth is merely a delusion.
Having heard this, those brahmins [realized]: "The Teacher has spoken of the true nature (*sabhāva*)."
He said, “We have criticized you without cause,” and they became silent.

Then the Blessed One thought, “The question has been posed by the brahmin; but what will be able to establish itself in this matter? *Commentary on the Discourse on Virtue and Wisdom (Sīlapaññākathā)* 317. Thereafter, the Blessed One [reflected]: “The question has been stated by the brahmin; however, what here will be able to find a firm footing?”
"Will he not be able [to answer]? For the purpose of testing him, he said: "But among these brahmins... and so forth.
"Purified by virtue" means cleansed by virtue. "Where there is virtue, there is wisdom": in whatever person there is virtue, in that very person there is wisdom;
how could there be wisdom in one who is immoral? Or, in one who lacks wisdom—a dullard or a fool—how could there be virtue? "Virtue and wisdom" refers to both virtue and...
"And the mark of wisdom is the mark of virtue. "Mark" means wisdom itself. Thus, O Brahmin, the Blessed One spoke, assenting to the words of the Brahmin.
In this context, "wisdom cleansed by virtue" means cleansed by the fourfold purification of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*).
But how does one cleanse wisdom through virtue? It is in the case of an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) whose virtue has lasted for sixty-eight years.

It is unbroken; thus, even at the time of death, having destroyed all defilements and washed away [the stains] with virtue, one attains Arahantship—just like the Elder Mahāsaṭṭhivassa in the Kandarasāla Pariveṇa.
It is said that while the Elder was lying on his deathbed, groaning from intense pain, King Tissa went to the door of the pariveṇa, thinking, "I shall see the Elder."
Standing there, he heard that sound and asked, "Whose sound is this? It was the sound of the elder’s groaning.
[The visitor thought,] "Even after sixty years of the life of renunciation, he has not performed so much as a single act of discerning feelings; I will not pay him homage now.
Having turned back, he went to pay homage to the Great Bodhi tree. Then the young attendant said to the elder, "Venerable sir, why is this?"
“Be ashamed! Even King Saddha, having become remorseful, will not pay homage,” he thought as he departed.
“Why, friend? [the youth asked]. “Because I heard the sound of your sighing. “In that case, grant me the opportunity,” he said;
then, suppressing his pain and attaining Arahatship, he gave the young man a sign: “Go, friend, and now have the king pay homage to us.”
Having gone there, the boy said, “Now indeed, pay homage to the Elder.

As the king was paying homage to the Elder while falling like a crocodile, he said, “I do not pay homage to the noble one’s state of Arahantship; rather, standing on the level of an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), I pay homage only to his protected virtue (*sīla*).
In this way, it is said that wisdom is purified by virtue. Now, for one who possesses internal restraint of virtue...

There is none [who does so]. However, by means of *ugghāṭitaññutā* (the state of one who understands through a condensed teaching), at the conclusion of a four-line verse, one washes away one’s defilements with wisdom and attains *arahantship* together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*). This is what is meant by "washing away defilements with wisdom.
It is just like the case of the minister Santati. But why did he say, "Which one, O Brahmin"? It seems the Blessed One thought: "The Brahmins, in their own tradition..."
“They designate the five precepts as ‘virtue,’ and the wisdom that grasps the three Vedas as ‘wisdom. They do not know the higher distinction.

Suppose I were to show the brahmin the path-virtue, the fruition-virtue, the path-wisdom, and the fruition-wisdom—which constitute the higher distinction—and conclude my teaching with the pinnacle of Arahantship. Then, out of a desire to speak to him...
He asked: “But what, brahmin, is that virtue? And what is that wisdom? Then the brahmin thought:
“I have answered the question according to my own system. But the ascetic Gotama has turned back to ask me again;
now, will I be able to satisfy his mind and answer him, or not? If I am unable…”
“Even though shame has arisen in me first, it will break; however, for one who is unable [to fulfill his duty], there is no fault in saying ‘I am not able.
Having thus turned back and placing the burden upon the Blessed One himself, he said, “We are limited to this much,” and so forth.
In that context, “limited to this much” means that the mere statement, “This much is our virtue and wisdom,” is the limit.
"Our knowledge is limited to this much; beyond this, we do not know the meaning of what has been said"—this is the sense.

Then, in order to demonstrate the range of his virtue and wisdom from the very moment of the Tathāgata’s arising—the foundation of virtue and wisdom—the Blessed One said, "In this case, O Brahmin, the Tathāgata," and so forth.
The meaning of that [passage] is exactly as explained in the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta*.
This, however, is the distinction: here, all three kinds of virtue are presented simply as "virtue" by the phrase, "And this is his virtue";
whereas the four jhānas, beginning with the first, are in actual fact the perfection of wisdom (*paññāsampadā*).
Thus, instead of presenting them under the heading of wisdom, they are shown merely as the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for insight-wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*).
"Wisdom has been brought forth starting from insight-wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*).
This concludes the discourse on the declaration of the lay follower status by Soṇadaṇḍa (Sūtras 319–322).
As for the meaning of the word *svātanāya*, it should be understood in the same manner as explained previously under the word *ajjatanāya*. By that...
"Lest that assembly should despise me. Therefore, when they see you from afar and rise from their seats, that assembly will think:

"This Soṇadaṇḍa is standing in his final stage of life, an old man; but Gotama is young, a youth, not even old enough to be his grandson, yet he rises from his seat for one who has not even attained the status of his own grandson!"
"He might despise me. [The thought: "There is no lack of rising from my seat for the sake of disrespect toward the venerable Gotama;
rather, I shall not rise out of fear of losing my wealth and position. It is fitting that both you and I should know this.
Therefore, let the venerable Gotama accept this rising from my seat as such"—it is said that by this [he meant]:
A hypocrite such as this is rare; however, he has no lack of respect for the Blessed One.
Therefore, out of fear of losing his gains, he speaks thus by way of hypocrisy. The same principle applies to the other cases as well.

Regarding the phrase "with a talk on the Dhamma," etc., it means that after instructing him in the welfare pertaining to the present life and the future life with a Dhamma talk appropriate to that moment, and having encouraged him toward wholesome states...
Having had him take it, the Blessed One there encouraged him, made him zealous, and having gladdened him with that zeal and by pointing out his other existing virtues,
he rained down the rain of the Dhamma jewel and rose from his seat and departed. But because of his own deceitfulness,
even though the Blessed One had thus rained down the rain of the Dhamma, the brahmin was unable to produce any distinction [in his realization].

He was not able [to refute it]. All his previous and subsequent discourse was solely for the sake of his future attainment of Nibbāna and for the development of the impression (vāsanā) conducive to it.
Thus ends the commentary on the Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya.
5. Commentary on the Kūṭadanta Sutta 323.
"Thus have I heard... in Magadha": this is the Kūṭadanta Sutta. Herein, this is the commentary on the words not previously explained.
"In Magadha": the Magadhans were royal princes of a certain province; even that single province where they dwelt is called "Magadha" by way of conventional usage (*rūḷhisadda*).
...so it is said, in that district of Magadha. From here on, the method is exactly as stated in the two previous suttas.
Ambalaṭṭhikā is just as described in the Brahmajāla Sutta. "Kūṭadanta" is the name of that brahmin. "Upakkhaṭo" means prepared.
"Vacchatarasatāni" means hundreds of calves. "Urabbhā" refers to young rams. These, first of all, are in the text.

They had indeed arrived. However, it should be understood that even though they are not mentioned in the canonical text (Pāḷi), many hundreds of animals and birds—seven hundred of each—are included therein.

It is said that he desired to perform a sacrifice of all seven hundred beings. "Brought to the sacrificial post" (thūṇūpanītāni) means they were brought to the post known as a *yūpa* for the purpose of being tied and kept there.

328. Here, "threefold" (*tividha*) refers to the manner of establishing (*vidhā*); thus, the meaning is "threefold establishment" (*tiṭṭhapana*). "The sixteen requisites" (*soḷasaparikkhāra*) means accompanied by a retinue of sixteen. 330–336.
"They dwell" (*paṭivasantī*) means they dwell for the purpose of experiencing the sacrifice. "In the past" (*bhūtapubba*):
the Blessed One, as if lifting up a treasure buried in the earth and making it into a heap before him, [revealed] his former conduct hidden by existence.
He spoke while pointing [to him]. "Mahāvijita" (Great Conqueror): it is said that he conquered the great circle of the earth bounded by the ocean;
thus, because he possessed a great conquest (*vijita*), he came to be known as Mahāvijita. Regarding "wealthy" (*aḍḍha*) and so forth:
anyone who is wealthy by means of his own possessions is "wealthy," but this one was not merely wealthy; he was one of great riches (*mahaddhana*).
He was endowed with great wealth of immeasurable number. He was one of "great possessions" (mahābhoga) because he possessed vast and sublime enjoyments by way of the five strands of sensual pleasure.

He was one who had "abundant gold and silver" (pahūtajātarūparajata) due to the abundance of gold and silver both in terms of lump-sum wealth and in terms of gold and silver coins such as the *māsaka*, [possessing] gold and silver numbering many tens of millions (*koṭi*).
The meaning is "endowed with. *Vitti* means satisfaction; *vittūpakaraṇa* means an instrument of satisfaction, which is to say, a cause for satisfaction.

One who possesses abundant instruments of satisfaction—consisting of various kinds of ornaments, vessels of gold and silver, and so forth—is called "one possessing abundant instruments of satisfaction.
This refers to wealth consisting of the seven treasures, as well as all types of staple and non-staple food that have been stored away.

"Abounding in grain and possessing abundant wealth and grain. Alternatively, this is stated by way of his daily expenditure, gifts, receipts, and so forth, in terms of the circulation of his wealth and grain.
"With full treasuries and storehouses": a treasury (kosa) is called a storehouse; it is one whose treasury is filled with wealth kept stored away.
The meaning is: "one whose storehouses are filled with grain. Alternatively, there are four kinds of treasuries (kosa):
elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry. There are three kinds of storehouses (koṭṭhāgāra): a storehouse for wealth, a storehouse for clothing, and a storehouse for grain.
Since all of these were full for him, he was one whose treasury and storehouses were full (paripuṇṇakosakoṭṭhāgāra). "Arose" (udapādi) means it came into being. It is said that this...
One day, the king set out on a tour called the "Jewels Inspection. He asked his treasurer: "Dear son, by whom was this vast wealth accumulated?
"By your father, grandfather, and so forth, down to the seventh generation of the family line.
"But having accumulated this wealth, where did they all go? "They have all gone, O King."
"She has fallen under the power of death. "Father, did she go without taking her own wealth? "My lord, what are you saying?
This thing called wealth is something to be abandoned when one goes; it is not something to be taken along when one goes. Then the king turned back and, sitting in the chamber of glory, thought:
"I have indeed attained [my goal]," and so forth. Therefore it is said: "Thus a reflection arose in his mind."
337. "Having addressed the brahmin": why did he address him? It is said that he thought thus:
"When giving a gift, it is proper to give after consulting with at least one wise person; for an action performed without consultation leads to later regret.
Therefore, he addressed him. Then the brahmin thought: "This king wishes to give a great gift..."

Furthermore, there will be many thieves in his realm; while he is giving gifts, those who bring the requisites for the offering—such as milk, curd, and rice—will find their houses plundered by thieves in the absence of men.
The entire realm will fall into a state of clamor due to the fear of thieves, and consequently, the king’s giving will not continue for long, nor will his mind remain one-pointed.
“Come now, I shall convince him of this matter. Then, in order to convince him of that matter, he said, “Of the venerable king,” and so forth.
In that context, *sakaṇṭako* means having thorns in the form of thieves. *Panthaduhanā* means those who plunder the road; the meaning is “highwaymen.
*Akiccakārī assa* means he would be a doer of what should not be done, a doer of what is contrary to the Dhamma. *Dassukhīlaṃ* means a thief’s stake.
“By killing” means by slaying or by beating. “By binding” means by means of shackles and the like.
“By seizure” means by loss; the meaning is: by punishment inflicted such as “Seize a hundred! Seize a thousand!

“By censure” means by causing one to incur reproach through having the five locks of hair shaved off, being smeared with cow dung, having a wooden staff bound around the neck, and so forth. “By banishment” means...
"By removal from the kingdom. "I shall uproot" means I shall thoroughly remove by means of the correct cause, method, and reason.

"The survivors of those slain" means the survivors of those who have died. "Exerting themselves" means making an effort. "Let him provide" means let him give again even more seed, food, and all the implements and tools for plowing, since what was previously given was insufficient; this is the meaning. "Let him provide what has been brought" means...
The meaning is: "Without making a witness and without recording it on a leaf, let him give the price of the goods by way of cutting off the root.
For "pābhata" is a name for the price of goods (bhaṇḍamūla). As it is said:
"Even with a small amount of merchandise, a wise and discerning person..."
"He raises himself up like a tiny spark that is being fanned.

"Food and wages" means: let him give daily food as well as monthly and other provisions for maintenance, together with grants of positions, villages, market towns, and so forth, in accordance with his proficiency in various wholesome deeds (*kusalakamma*). "Devoted to their own work" refers to [work] such as agriculture, trade, and so on.
They were engaged and occupied with their respective duties. "A hoarder" means one who accumulates wealth and grain.

"Established in safety" means they stood in security, free from fear. "Thornless" means devoid of the thorns of thieves. "With joy, rejoicing" means with joy, they were joyful. Or rather, this is the reading:
"with hearts mutually delighted"—this is the intended meaning. "With doors thrown open" means that due to the absence of thieves, the doors [were left open].

"Not having restrained [them], with the doors wide open"—this is the meaning. "He said this" means that, having understood the entire extent of the country's prosperity and flourishing state, he spoke these words.
339. Commentary on the Four Requisites:
"Therefore, let your lordship..."—the brahmin, it is said, thought: "This king is exceedingly intent on giving a great almsgiving."
“Having become inspired, if he were to give without first consulting his own followers—the kṣatriyas and others—they would not be pleased.
I shall act in such a way that they will be pleased with the gift. Therefore, he said, “In that case, sir,” and so forth.
In this context, *negama* means those who dwell in towns (*nigama*); *jānapada* means those who dwell in the countryside (*janapada*). *Āmantayantaṃ* means...
"Let him invite and let him inform. "Whatever may be mine" means whatever authorization of yours might belong to me.
"Ministers" refers to dear companions; "councilors" refers to the rest who carry out orders. "May your majesty sacrifice" means "may your majesty perform the sacrifice," for they thought:
"This king, instead of giving gifts by force while thinking 'I am the lord,' has invited us; therefore, it is well done by him."
Saying “So be it,” they spoke thus with joyful minds. Otherwise, if not invited, they would not even go to see the place of sacrifice.
By saying, “It is time for the sacrifice, Great King,” they speak while indicating that such a gift cannot be given when there is no property to be given or when one is advanced in age;
but you are both very wealthy and young, and therefore this is your time for sacrifice.
“Anumatipakkhā” means those who give their consent; the meaning is “givers of consent. “Parikkhārā bhavanti” means they become attendants or retinues.
However, in the passage, “The chariot has virtue as its equipment, meditation as its axle, and energy as its wheels,” the word *parikkhāra* is used in the sense of an ornament.
This concludes the commentary on the eight requisites (*aṭṭhaparikkhāra*).
340. "By eight factors" means by the eight factors beginning with being well-born on both sides.
"By fame" means by virtue of possessing the capacity to issue commands. "Faithful" means he has faith that there is a fruit for giving.

"A giver" means one who is brave in giving. It does not mean he remains merely faithful; the meaning is that he is also capable of renouncing. "A master of giving" means being the master of whatever gift he gives.
He gives; he is neither a slave nor a companion. For he who enjoys sweet things himself but gives what is not sweet to others gives as a slave to the gift-property known as "giving.
He who gives exactly what he himself eats gives as a companion. But he who sustains himself with anything at all and gives what is sweet to others—
The meaning is: "This [person] is like that," referring to one who, having become a husband or a master, gives.

Regarding the phrase "to ascetics, brahmins, the poor, the wretched, the beggars, and the supplicants": here, *samita-pāpā* (those who have stilled evil) are the ascetics (*samaṇā*), and *bāhita-pāpā* (those who have cast out evil) are the brahmins (*brāhmaṇā*). The "poor" (*kapaṇā*) are unfortunate, destitute people. The "wayfarers" (*addhikā*) are those traveling on a road.
The "beggars" (*vaṇibbakā*) are those for whom it is said: "What is given is desirable, lovely, pleasing, timely, and blameless."
They wander about praising the virtue of giving in such a manner as: "One should gladden this mind;

may your honor go to the Brahma-world," and so forth. "Beggars" are those who wander about begging, saying things such as, "Give even a handful! Give even a bowlful! "Opānabhūta" means become like a well. It is a common resource for all to enjoy.
The meaning is: "being like a lotus pond dug out at a crossroads. Regarding the phrase *sutajātassa*: here, "that which has arisen from hearing" (*sutajāta*) refers simply to what has been heard.

Regarding the phrase "to contemplate matters of the past, future, and present": one who contemplates thus—"This prosperity of mine is due solely to merit performed in the past"—is indeed called capable of contemplating a matter of the past. "Now, merit..."
Thinking, "Having performed [this], it will be possible to attain prosperity in the future," one becomes capable of contemplating the future.
Thinking, "This meritorious deed is the practice of the virtuous; I possess wealth as well, and I have the intention of a donor;
come now, let me perform meritorious deeds," one contemplates the present.
"He is called capable" is how it should be understood. "Thus these" means these very things as they have been described.
It is said that when one is endowed with these eight factors, the great multitude approaches from all directions to give gifts.
[They do not approach] thinking such things as: "This ill-born man, how long will he last? Now, having become remorseful, he will cut off [the supply]," and so forth.
No one thinks that anyone else should approach him. Therefore, it is said that these eight factors are "requisites.
(Commentary on the Four Requisites, etc., 341).
"Of those holding up the ladle" means of those holding up the offering-spoon at the place where a great sacrifice is being received.

“By these four” means by Sujātā and the others. For if they were not present, people would not approach [the monk], saying things such as, “How long will the gift given through the arrangements of one so ill-born continue?
However, because there is no reason for reproach, they do indeed approach. Therefore, these too are said to be requisites.
"342. He taught the three methods": he taught the three points for establishing [the mind]. It is said that he thought:
"When people give a gift, they waver at one of three points; well then, let me first of all make this king steady regarding those points.
Therefore it is said, "He taught the three methods. In the phrase "of your majesty the king," the word "of" (*bhoto*) is used in the sense of the instrumental case.
This is a term of address. Alternatively, the reading is *bhotā raññā* (“by you, O King”). “Regret should not be made” means: “One should not harbor subsequent remorse caused by the loss of wealth;
rather, one’s prior intention should be established as unwavering, for in this way the gift becomes of great fruit.
This same principle applies to the other two instances as well. For even the intention of relinquishment is [strengthened] by the subsequent recollection of it.

And they must be kept steady. For one who does not do so, the gift does not bear great fruit, nor does the mind incline toward magnificent wealth, as was the case with the merchant householder who was reborn in the Mahāroruva hell. 343.
"In ten ways" means by ten reasons. It is said that this thought occurred to him: "If this king [were to give] to those of immoral conduct..."
Seeing this, he will think, "Alas, my gift is lost, for such immoral people are eating it," and he will give rise to remorse even toward those who are virtuous;

thus his gift will not be of great fruit. Since remorse in donors arises precisely because of the recipients, [the Buddha thought], "Come now, I shall dispel that remorse for him right at the outset. Therefore...
"It is appropriate for it to be cut off in ten ways; he also dispels the remorse in those who have received [the gift].
By the phrase "for them alone by that," he shows: "By that evil, an undesirable result will come to them alone, not to others.
"Yajataṃ bhava" means "May you give. "Sajjataṃ" means "may you relinquish. "Antaraṃ" means "internally."
344. “He instructed the mind in sixteen ways”: here, the brahmin began what is called the King’s expression of gratitude for the great gift.
In this context, “he instructed” means he spoke by repeatedly showing: “A donor who gives such a gift obtains such-and-such prosperity.
“He incited” means he spoke after having incited him toward that same purpose. “He inspired” means [he spoke] by dispelling his remorse.
He purified his mind. "He gladdened him" means he spoke after offering praise, saying, "Well done by you, Great King, in giving this gift.
"There was no one to speak according to the Dhamma" means there was no one to speak with justice and reason.
"345. Trees were not cut down for the sake of sacrificial posts (yūpa), nor was grass mown for the sake of the sacrificial strew (barhis)" refers to those [trees] known as sacrificial posts.
Having hoisted great pillars, they would write and set up the names:
“Such-and-such a king, such-and-such a minister, or such-and-such a brahmin is performing such a great sacrifice.

And as for the *dabbha* grasses they cut and use to encircle the sacrificial hall with a garland-like arrangement or spread upon the ground—even these, neither the trees nor the blades of grass were cut down.
They were driven away. He shows that neither cows nor goats and the like will be slaughtered. "Slaves" refers to those who are domestic slaves and so forth.
"Servants" refers to those who perform work after first receiving wages. "Laborers" refers to those who work for food and hire.
Those "threatened with sticks" means those who, having been seized with sticks, clubs, mallets, and the like, are told: "Perform your work!"
"Perform [the service]," thus were they urged. "Urged by fear" means: "If you perform the work, it is well;
if you do not perform it, we shall cut you, bind you, or kill you"—thus urged by fear.

But these did not perform the preliminary services because they were urged by punishment, nor because they were urged by fear, nor while weeping with tearful faces; rather, they did so solely through affectionate conduct.
They treated them with courtesy. For there they did not address a slave as "slave," a messenger as "messenger," or a laborer as "laborer.
Rather, addressing them with affectionate courtesy according to their names, they assigned work appropriate to each—whether they were women or men, strong or weak—and said, "Do this and that.
And they themselves performed their own tasks according to their own preference.
They performed it. Therefore it was said: “Those who wished did so; those who did not wish did not do so.
What they wished, that they did; what they did not wish, that they did not do. That sacrifice reached completion with ghee, oil, fresh butter, curds, honey, and molasses.
It is said that the king [placed] at the four gates outside the city and within the city...
And he celebrated [the festival] by having great halls for almsgiving constructed at five locations; having spent one hundred thousand [pieces of gold] for each hall,
he distributed five hundred thousand [pieces] day after day, starting from sunrise,
with his own hand taking a golden spoon and offering exquisite food mixed with ghee, oil, and other ingredients, according to the requirements of each specific time.
He satisfied the great multitude with rice gruel, solid food, meals, condiments, drinks, and so forth.

He had these given out exactly as requested to those who came wishing to take them away in their vessels. At the time of evening, however, he honored them with garments, perfumes, garlands, and other offerings.
Then, having filled large jars with ghee and other substances, he said: "Whoever wishes to consume whatever [is desired], let him consume it," and [he provided] many hundreds...
He had them stationed in their respective places. With reference to this, it was said: “That sacrifice reached its conclusion with ghee, oil, fresh butter, curds, honey, and molasses. 346.
“Taking abundant wealth” means having taken much property. It is said that they thought: “This king...”
Without having the ghee, oil, and other provisions brought from the countryside, he gives a great almsgiving by taking only what belongs to himself.
However, it is not right for us to remain silent, thinking, "The king is not having anything brought.
For the wealth in the king's house is not inexhaustible; and if we do not give, who else will give to the king? Come now, let us give him our wealth.

"Let us bring it together. Thus, having gathered wealth from the portions of the villages, the portions of the market towns, and the portions of the cities, they filled their wagons and presented it to the king.
It was with reference to this that he said, "Abundant wealth," and so forth. 347.
"To the east of the sacrificial enclosure" means to the eastern part of the hall of giving at the city gate to the east.

Just as those coming from the eastern direction would drink rice-gruel at the alms-hall for the kṣatriyas and eat at the king’s alms-hall before entering the city, they established [resting places] in such locations.

To the south of the sacrificial enclosure means that, by the same method described for the alms-hall at the southern city gate, they established them on the southern side. The same method applies to the western and northern directions as well.

348. "Oh, what a sacrifice! Oh, what a perfection of sacrifice!"—thus the brahmins spoke with delighted minds while praising [the Buddha], having heard that he had brought the sacrifice to completion with ghee and other offerings, thinking:
"Whatever is sweet in the world, that alone the ascetic Gotama speaks of; come now, let us praise his sacrifice.
He sat there in silence, reflecting on the matter that was to be explained further below.
He remained seated in silence. However, when the brahmin said, "Does the venerable Gotama recall this?", he spoke by way of an indirect inquiry.
For otherwise, had he asked directly—“But were you, Master Gotama, the king at that time, or were you the brahmin chaplain?”—he would have appeared as if lacking respect.
349. Regarding the description of the sacrifice of perpetual giving:

"But there is, Master Gotama," said the brahmin—this was because he thought, "It is a heavy burden for all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa to rise up again and again to give gifts; and if the entire country does not perform its own duties, it will perish. There is...
"Is there now another sacrifice for us that requires less effort and yields greater fruit than this sacrifice?"—asking this matter, he said.
"Constant gifts" (*niccadānāni*) means regular gifts, such as daily meals.
"Family sacrifices" (*anukulayaññāni*) refers to those performed by one's ancestors, such as fathers and grandfathers, which are continued even by poor people through the succession of generations.
Sacrifices must be performed; indeed, such regular offerings made for the sake of virtuous ones are not discontinued even by poor families in that household.
Here is an illustration: it is said that in the house of Anāthapiṇḍika, five hundred regular meals were given. [There were] tooth-sticks made of ivory.
There were five hundred [voters]. Then, that family was gradually overcome by poverty, and one girl in that family was unable to give more than a single voting-stick (*salāka*).

Later, after she had entered King Setavāhana’s service and cleared the threshing floor, she gave that voting-stick using the grain she had obtained. A certain elder informed the king. The king [sent for her].
Having brought her back, he appointed her to the position of chief queen. From that time forward, she again provided five hundred sets of meals by ticket.
As for the "strokes of the rod": having said, "Stand in order! Stand in order! and "Take them, take them!
as they were being distributed while walking straight ahead, strokes of the rod and throat-seizures were seen being inflicted. This, O Brahmin, is—

"Because of the cause... pe ...and because it is of greater benefit. Herein, since there is no need for many attendants or requisites in this distribution of tickets (salākabhatta) as there is in a great sacrifice (mahāyañña), it is therefore "less troublesome" (appaṭṭhatara).
And since there is no undertaking here consisting of oppression through the interruption of the work of many people, it is therefore "less laborious" (appasamārambhatara).
And because this has been offered and relinquished to the Saṅgha, it is called a "sacrifice" (yañña).

Furthermore, because it is not easy to measure the overflow of merit from an offering endowed with six factors—even as much as the water in the great ocean—and because this [offering] is of such a kind, it should be understood as having even greater fruit and greater benefit. Having heard this...
The brahmin thought: "Even this constant meal, while giving it day after day as one rises up again and again, causes the work of one person to perish each day.
A fresh effort must be exerted anew every time.
Is there perhaps another sacrifice than this that requires less trouble and involves less exertion? Therefore, he said, "But is there, Master Gotama... and so forth.

In this regard, because there is no conclusion to the duties in the case of a meal by ticket (*salākabhatta*), one must simply provide for it by rising again and again without performing any other work.
However, in the case of a gift of a monastery (*vihāradāna*), there is a conclusion to the duties;
for whether one builds a leaf-hut or a great monastery after expending a hundred million coins, once the expenditure of wealth has been performed, [the duty is fulfilled].
Once it has been built, even seven or eight years, a hundred years, or a thousand years pass by;

one need only perform the necessary repairs where it has become worn or fallen into disrepair. Therefore, this gift of a monastery is less troublesome and involves less labor than the gift of daily alms-food (*salākabhatta*).
Furthermore, according to the method of the Suttantas, it is for the purpose of warding off cold, and so forth.
Nine benefits have been stated [for the forest life] according to the Khandhaka method:
"It wards off cold and heat, as well as wild beasts,
snakes, mosquitoes, and gadflies, and even the frosts and rains."
Then, when fierce wind and heat arise, one is protected from them;
for the sake of shelter, for the sake of comfort, and for the purpose of meditating and practicing insight.
The gift of a monastery to the Saṅgha is praised as supreme by the Buddha.
Therefore, indeed, a wise person, seeing his own welfare,
should have delightful monasteries built and cause those learned in the Dhamma to dwell therein.
Therefore, [he should provide] food and drink, as well as clothing and lodgings.
One should give with a serene mind to those who have become upright.
They teach him the Dhamma that dispels all suffering,
by knowing which Dhamma here, he attains final Nibbāna, free from taints.
Seventeen benefits have been stated. Therefore, it should be understood that this [offering] is more fruitful and brings greater benefit than even a ticket-meal (*salākabhatta*).
Yet, because it is dedicated to the Sangha, it is called a "sacrifice" (*yañña*). Having heard this as well, the brahmin thought:
"To give a monastery after having renounced wealth is indeed difficult; for even a single *kākaṇika* coin belonging to oneself..."
“Since it is difficult for others to give away, let me ask about a sacrifice that requires even less standing and even less exertion.
Then, asking him about this, he said: “But is there, sir,” and so forth. 350–351.
In this context, because even when a monastery has been given once, there is still the need for repeated repairs such as roofing, patching, and mending; and—
The duty [of giving] certainly exists; however, as for taking refuge, once it has been taken in the presence of a single bhikkhu, or of the Saṅgha, or of a group, it remains taken forever.
There is no need to perform it again and again. Therefore, compared to the gift of a monastery, it is of less consequence and involves less effort.
And because what is called "taking refuge" pertains to the Three Jewels—
The meritorious deed consisting of the sacrifice of one’s life bestows the attainment of heaven; therefore, it should be understood as having even greater fruit and greater benefit.
Furthermore, a sacrifice by way of the sacrifice of one’s life for the sake of the Three Jewels is so called.
Having heard this, the brahmin thought: “It is indeed difficult to sacrifice one’s own life for another.”
“Is there perhaps a sacrifice even more excellent than this?”—asking this, he spoke again, beginning with “But is there, Master Gotama? and so forth.

In that context, regarding the phrases such as “abstention from taking life,” *veramaṇī* means abstention (*virati*). That is threefold: abstention by attainment, abstention by undertaking, and abstention by the destruction of the bridge.
Among these, [the first] is that which occurs even without having taken up the training precepts (*sikkhāpada*).
When one refrains from killing living beings and so forth— not because of recollecting one’s own birth, clan, family lineage, and so on, but thinking,
“This is not fitting for me”— and thus avoids the occasion for success, that abstention is to be understood as *sampattavirati* (abstention by reason of opportunity).

However, for one who takes up the training precepts by saying, “From this day forward, even for the sake of my life, I shall not kill a living being,” or “I abstain from killing living beings,” or “I undertake the restraint [from killing],” that abstention is to be understood as *samādānavirati* (abstention by undertaking).
For noble disciples (*ariyasāvaka*), however, the abstinence associated with the Path is called "the bridge-breaking abstinence" (*setughāta-virati*).
In this context, the first two types of abstinence proceed by taking as their object that basis—such as the life-faculty—that is to be transgressed through acts like killing.
The latter [abstinences] have Nibbāna alone as their object. And herein, those who [keep] the five training rules together...
When one takes [all] together, if one part is broken, all are broken. But for one who takes each separately, only that which he transgresses is broken.
However, there is no such thing as a "breaking" of the abstinence consisting in the destruction of the bridge;
for even in another existence, a noble disciple does not kill a living being nor drink fermented liquor, even for the sake of his life. Even if fermented liquor and milk were mixed together and...

If they place it in the mouth, only the milk enters, not the liquor. How is this so? Just as when water mixed with milk is poured into the mouths of herons, only the milk enters and not the water. If it is asked, "Is this established by nature (*yonisiddha*)? it should be understood that this is established by the very nature of things (*dhammatāsiddha*).
For, in the act of going for refuge, the straightening of one's view is what is weighty; whereas in the undertaking of the training precepts (*sikkhāpada*), [the observance of the rules is weighty].

It is, however, merely a matter of abstention. Therefore, whether one undertakes it in this way or that, and whether one undertakes it thoroughly or not, it is less difficult to practice and involves less exertion.
Yet, because there is no gift equal to the five precepts, its great fruitfulness and great benefit should be understood here. For this has been said:

“Monks, there are these five gifts, great gifts, ancient, long-standing, traditional, old, unadulterated, never before adulterated, not being adulterated now, nor to be adulterated in the future, unreproached by wise recluses and brahmins.
What are the five? Here, monks, a noble disciple, having abandoned the taking of life...”
He abstains from taking life. By abstaining from taking life, monks, a noble disciple gives fearlessness to immeasurable beings;

he gives freedom from enmity; he gives freedom from ill will. Having given fearlessness, freedom from enmity, and freedom from ill will to immeasurable beings, [he himself partakes] in immeasurable fearlessness, freedom from enmity, and freedom from ill will.
...he becomes a partaker. This, monks, is the first gift, a great gift... [as before] ...by the wise.
Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple, having abandoned taking what is not given... [as before] ...having abandoned sexual misconduct... [as before] ...having abandoned false speech...
[as before] ...having abandoned the basis for negligence consisting in fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants... [as before] ...These, monks, are...
"The five gifts, the great gifts, are the foremost... [etc. ...by the wise.
Furthermore, this pentad of virtue is called a "sacrifice" because it is undertaken with the thought:
"I shall protect it by relinquishing attachment to self and attachment to life. In that regard, although going for refuge alone is the most senior of the five precepts,
But this [practice] is said to be of great fruit by virtue of the morality protected through being established in the very act of going for refuge.
Having heard this as well, the brahmin thought: "It is difficult to protect what is called the five precepts;
is there perhaps something else that is just like this, yet easier than this and of even greater fruit? Then he...
Questioning again, he said, "But is there, Master Gotama," and so forth.

Then the Blessed One, wishing to show that for one established in the fulfillment of the threefold morality, the sacrifices beginning with the first jhāna are more excellent and yield greater fruit, began his teaching starting from the appearance of a Buddha, saying, "In this case, O Brahmins," and so forth. Therein, because [the previous section] below...
Endowed with the qualities already mentioned, one who is established in the first jhāna does not become weary when producing the second jhāna and so forth;
therefore, those [higher jhānas] require little effort and little exertion.
Furthermore, because the first jhāna here bestows a lifespan of one *kappa* in the Brahma-world, the second eight *kappas*, the third sixty-four *kappas*, and the fourth...

It lasts for five hundred eons. When that same [meditation] is cultivated by way of the attainments of the base of infinite space and so forth, it bestows a lifespan of twenty, forty, sixty, and eighty-four thousand eons; therefore, it is more fruitful and more beneficial.
Furthermore, because opposing states such as the hindrances have been abandoned, it should be understood as a sacrifice (*yañña*).

Insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) is of little effort and little exertion because it does not weary one while producing its results by being established in the qualities at the conclusion of the fourth jhāna;
yet it is of great fruit because there is no happiness equal to the happiness of insight.
It is called a "sacrifice" (*yañña*) because of its relinquishing of the opposing defilements. As for the mind-made psychic power (*manomaya-iddhi*), since it is [established] in insight-knowledge...
Establishing oneself [in these], one brings them forth without fatigue; therefore, they require little effort and little exertion.
Because of the capacity to create forms resembling oneself, they are of great fruit. Because it involves the relinquishing of one's own adverse defilements, it is a sacrifice (*yañña*).

As for the knowledge of the supernormal powers (*iddhividha-ñāṇa*) and so forth, since one who brings them forth by establishing oneself in the knowledge of the mind-made body (*manomaya-ñāṇa*) and others does not become fatigued, they likewise require little effort and little exertion. Each of them...

It is a sacrifice because it abandons the opposing defilements. Furthermore, the supernormal power of transformation (*iddhividha*) is included here because of its capacity to display various kinds of transformations;

the divine ear (*dibbasota*) because of its capacity to hear the sounds of gods and humans; the knowledge of the penetration of minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*) because of its capacity to know the sixteen types of minds of others;
the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa*) because of its capacity to recollect whatever place one desires; and the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*).
It should be understood that the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhayañāṇa*) is of great fruit because it is capable of producing the most exquisite supramundane bliss of the Path.

Furthermore, since there is no sacrifice more distinguished than that of Arahantship, the Teacher concluded his teaching with the pinnacle of Arahantship, saying: "This too, O brahmins," and so forth.
Commentary on the Declaration of Kūṭadanta’s Status as a Lay Disciple (354–358).

When this had been said—meaning, when the Blessed One had spoken thus—the brahmin Kūṭadanta, having gained confidence in the teaching and desiring to go for refuge, spoke these words beginning with, “Excellent, Master Gotama! *Upavāyatu* means “having approached.”
“May a breeze blow, cool to the body, to extinguish the fever of my frame. Having said this, the brahmin dispatched a man, saying:
“Go, dear sir, enter the sacrificial enclosure and release all those living beings from their bonds.
He replied, “Very well,” and having done so, returned and reported: “Sir, those living beings have been released. Until—
The brahmin did not hear of that occurrence, and so the Blessed One did not yet teach the Dhamma. Why? Because "there was a state of agitation in the brahmin’s mind.
But upon hearing [the news], his mental disposition became serene, thinking, "Alas, many living beings have been liberated by me!
Knowing his mind to be serene, the Blessed One began the teaching of the Dhamma. With reference to this, it is said: "Then..."

The passage beginning with “Then the Blessed One... was spoken. Furthermore, the passage beginning with “a malleable mind” was spoken with reference to the suppression of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) by means of the power of the gradual discourse (*ānupubbikathā*). The remainder is of plain meaning.
Thus [ends] the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, the commentary on the *Dīghanikāya*.
The commentary on the Kūṭadantasutta is finished.
6. The commentary on the Mahālisutta:
The exposition of the occasion concerning the brahmin messenger.
359. Thus have I heard—on one occasion the Blessed One was at Vesālī; this is the *Mahāli Sutta*. Herein is the commentary on the previously unexplained terms.
"Vesālī" refers to the city so named because it repeatedly attained a state of vastness (*visāla*). "In the Great Wood" (*mahāvana*):
outside the city there is a natural grove that stands as a single expanse connected to the Himalayas. This...
It is called "Mahāvana" (Great Forest) because of its great extent; [it was] in that Mahāvana.
"In the gabled hall" (*kūṭāgārasālā*): they established a monastic park (*saṅghārāma*) within that forest grove.

There, having joined the rafters and constructed upon the pillars a palace resembling a celestial mansion in the form of a gabled hall, the entire monastic park came to be designated as the "gabled hall."
It was so stated. The Blessed One was dwelling in dependence on Vesālī in that Saṅghārāma monastery.
Therefore it is said: "He was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Forest in the Gabled Hall. "Kosalans" means inhabitants of the kingdom of Kosala.
"Māgadhas" means inhabitants of the kingdom of Magadha. "On account of business" means on account of a task that must necessarily be performed; for that which ought not to be left undone...
What is appropriate is called "a duty" (*kicca*); that which must necessarily be done is called "what ought to be done" (*karaṇīya*).
360. "The Blessed One was in seclusion" means that having withdrawn from wandering among various objects, he has gone into seclusion and hidden himself;
the meaning is that, having attained solitude, he experiences the delight of meditative absorption (*jhāna*) upon a single object. "Right there" means in that very monastery.
"To one side" means that having moved away from that place, they sat down in the shade of various trees.
Regarding the description of Oṭṭhaddha the Licchavi:
"Oṭṭhaddha" is the name he received because of his protruding lips. "With a great assembly of Licchavis" refers to [the time] before the meal.
Having given alms to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, having undertaken the observance factors (uposathaṅga) in the presence of the Blessed One,
and having had perfumes, garlands, and other offerings brought, he caused a great assembly of Licchavi kings to gather through a public proclamation;
that great assembly, adorned with garments, ornaments, and ointments of blue, yellow, and other colors, was like the retinue of the Tāvatiṃsa devas.
He approached together with the assembly of Licchavis. "It is not the right time, Mahāli"—for Mahāli was the original name of that Oṭṭhaddha;
it was by means of that original name alone that the Elder addressed him as "Mahāli.
"He sat down to one side" means he sat down together with that assembly of Licchavis in suitable shade of trees, speaking in praise of the Triple Gem.
362. The novice Sīha was the nephew of the Venerable Nāgita; having gone forth at the age of seven, he applied himself diligently to the Teaching and was a novice monk named Sīha.
It is said that upon seeing that great assembly—this vast multitude seated filling the entire monastery—he thought:
"This assembly is immense; it has filled the whole monastery. Surely today the Blessed One [will address] this assembly..."
"He will teach the Dhamma with great enthusiasm; what if I were to inform my preceptor and have him announce to the Blessed One that a great assembly has gathered?
Having thought this, he approached the Venerable Nāgita.
