"Venerable Kassapa," he said, addressing the Elder by his clan name. "This multitude" means this collection of people.
“You yourself should inform the Blessed One. It is said that Sīha was a trusted confidant of the Blessed One;
for this elder had a stout body, and because of the weight of his body, his slothfulness in rising, sitting, and so forth seemed as though it were not entirely abandoned.
Now, this novice performed his duties for the Blessed One from time to time. Therefore, the elder [said to him], “You too, for the Ten-Powered One...”
Having said, "I am trustworthy," he replied, "Go, you yourself announce it. "In the shadow of the monastery" means in the shade of the monastery;
the meaning is that the area was covered by the shadow of the peaked-roofed great hall. It is said that this peaked-roofed hall was long from south to north and faced east;
therefore, a great shadow spread out before it, and there the lion prepared a seat for the Blessed One.

363. Then the Blessed One, having emerged through the doorways and the window openings, his departure signaled by the six-colored Buddha-rays streaming forth and spreading out, went out from the peaked-roofed hall like the full moon emerging from the midst of clouds and sat down on the excellent Buddha-seat that had been prepared. Thus it was said: “Then...”
Then the Blessed One, having emerged from his dwelling, sat down on the seat prepared in the shade of the dwelling.

“Regarding the phrases ‘in former days, O Bhante,’ and ‘in even earlier days’: here, the day before yesterday is called ‘former’ (*purima*), and the day prior to that is ‘even earlier’ (*purimatara*).
From that point onward, however, all [preceding days] are both ‘former’ and ‘even earlier.’”
[The words] "honti" [are understood]. Regarding "yadagge": starting from the initial day, the meaning is "on whichever day I dwell having made it the limit and the peak";
thus, "as far as my dwelling" is what is meant. Now, showing its duration, he said, "not long—three years.
Alternatively, "yadagge" may mean: "starting from whichever day I have made the limit, I dwell for not long—three years."
The meaning is as follows: "From the day I began, not long ago, I have dwelt [here]; that is to say, for exactly three years.
This was said with reference to him who, taking up the Blessed One’s bowl and robes, attended upon the Blessed One for three years;

it is in relation to him that he speaks thus. "Pleasant things" means things born of what is dear, things born of what is sweet. "Connected with sensual desire" means things associated with the gratification of sensual pleasure.
"Delightful" means things that give rise to passion. But why does Sunakkhatta not hear the divine sounds?
It is said that he approached the Blessed One and requested the practice for the divine eye;
the Blessed One explained it to him, and having practiced according to the instructions, he developed the divine eye and saw the forms of the deities.
He thought, "In this physical form, there must be a sweet sound; how indeed might one hear it?
Having approached the Blessed One, he asked about the preparatory exercise for the divine ear (*dibbasota*).
Furthermore, in the past, he had made a virtuous bhikkhu deaf by striking him on the ear with a stone. Therefore, even while performing the preparatory exercise, [he was unable to hear].
He was incapable of attaining the divine ear. Therefore, the Blessed One did not explain the preliminary practice to him.
At that point, having harbored resentment toward the Blessed One, he thought: "Surely this thought occurs to the ascetic Gotama:
'I am a kshatriya and he too is a kshatriya; if his knowledge increases, he too will become omniscient. This is out of envy."
“He did not tell me. Having gradually returned to the state of a householder, while explaining that matter to Mahāli the Licchavi, he spoke as follows:

“Developed in one direction” means developed toward one side or one portion; the meaning is that it was developed for the purpose of seeing divine forms or for the purpose of hearing divine sounds. “Tiriyan” means across the intermediate directions. “Developed in both directions”...

The meaning is: "It has been developed for both sides, for both portions. "This, Mahāli, is the cause" means that this concentration, developed one-sidedly for the very purpose of seeing divine forms, is the cause. Having heard this matter, that Licchavi thought:
"I consider this hearing of sounds with the divine ear to be the supreme goal within this teaching; surely for him..."
“For the sake of this purpose these bhikkhus have practiced the unerring holy life for fifty-five years;
what if I were now to ask the One of Ten Powers about this matter?
Then, asking about that matter, he said, “Surely, Bhante, of these...,” and so forth. [He spoke] regarding the development of concentration.
In this context, "development of concentration" refers to concentration itself; the meaning is "of those concentrations developed in both ways.

Now, because these developments of concentration are external to the Teaching and not internal, the Blessed One rejected them and spoke the words beginning with "Not so, Mahāli," in order to show the purpose for which bhikkhus lead the holy life.
Commentary on the Three Noble Fruits (Catuariyaphalavaṇṇanā) 373. "Of the three fetters" refers to the three bonds, namely, personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) and the others.

For they fetter sentient beings to the chariot of the suffering of the round of existence; therefore, they are called "fetters" (*saṃyojana*). "He becomes a stream-enterer" means he enters the stream of the Path.
He has entered [the path]. "One whose nature is not to fall into the states of misery" means one whose nature is not to fall into the four lower realms (*apāya*).

"One who is fixed" means fixed by the fixedness of the Dhamma. "One who has enlightenment as his final goal" means that enlightenment—consisting of the three higher paths—is his supreme destination (*parāyaṇa*), or that it is to be attained by him;
thus he is "one who has enlightenment as his final goal."
*Tanuttā* means "slightness" due to the weakness of the obsessions (*pariyuṭṭhāna*) and because they arise only occasionally.
*Orambhāgiyānaṃ* means "belonging to the lower part," for one who is bound by these is unable to be reborn in the higher Pure Abode realms (*suddhāvāsabhūmi*).
*Opapātiko* is a term that excludes the other modes of birth (*yoni*). In this context, *parinibbāyī* refers to one whose nature is to attain final Nibbāna in that very same subsequent existence.
"Subject to non-returning" (*anāvattidhamma*) means that from that Brahma-world, one is of a nature not to return again by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).

"Liberation of mind" (*cetovimutti*) refers to purity of consciousness; it is a designation for the fruit-of-Arahantship consciousness which is liberated from all fetters of the defilements (*kilesa*).
"Liberation by wisdom" (*paññāvimutti*): here too, it is specifically the wisdom of the fruit-of-Arahantship, liberated from all fetters of the defilements, that is called liberation by wisdom.

It should be understood. "In this very life" (*diṭṭheva dhamme*) means in this very personal existence (*attabhāve*). "By oneself" (*sayaṃ*) means by one's own self. "Through direct knowledge" (*abhiññā*) means having fully known.

"Having realized" (*sacchikatvā*) means having made it manifest before one's eyes. Alternatively, "having realized through direct knowledge" (*abhiññā sacchikatvā*) also has the meaning of having realized by means of direct knowledge, that is, by means of particularly distinguished wisdom (*abhivisiṭṭhena ñāṇena*).
"Attaining" (*upasampajja*) means having reached and having acquired. Having heard this, the Licchavi king...
He thought: "This Dhamma cannot be penetrated by flying up like a bird, nor by crawling on the chest like a lizard;
surely there must be a preliminary practice for one who penetrates it.
I shall first ask him about it."
Commentary on the Noble Eightfold Path (Ariya-aṭṭhaṅgika-magga): 374–375.
Then, asking the Blessed One, he said, “But is there, venerable sir,” and so forth.
It is called “eightfold” because it consists of eight factors alone, like a five-fold musical ensemble or an eight-village district; it is not so called because of its constituent parts.
There is indeed another path; for this very reason it was said: "That is to say, right view... pe ...right concentration.
Therein, right view has the characteristic of seeing rightly. Right intention has the characteristic of directing [the mind] rightly.
Right speech has the characteristic of encompassing rightly. Right action has the characteristic of originating rightly. Right...
Right livelihood has the characteristic of purification. Right effort has the characteristic of right exertion. Right mindfulness has the characteristic of establishing.
Right concentration has the characteristic of right composure. Each of these has three functions. To wit:
first, right view abandons wrong view along with its own opposing defilements.
It abandons [defilements], takes cessation as its object, and perceives the associated states through non-delusion by way of dispelling the delusion that conceals them.
Right intention and the other factors likewise abandon wrong intention and so forth, and take cessation as their object;
however, in this context, right intention specifically directs the co-nascent states. Right speech...
Right view correctly discerns; right action correctly originates; right livelihood correctly purifies;
right effort correctly exerts; right mindfulness correctly establishes; and right concentration correctly strives.
Furthermore, while this so-called right view consists of various moments and various objects in its preliminary stage, at the moment of the path it is of a single moment.
They have a single object. However, in terms of their function, they receive four names, beginning with "knowledge regarding suffering.
Right intention and the others also have different moments and different objects during the preliminary stage; at the moment of the Path, they have the same moment and the same object.

Among them, right intention receives three names in terms of its function, beginning with "intention of renunciation. Right speech and the other three abstinences [also receive their respective names].
There are [the factors] such as volition (cetanā) and so forth; however, at the moment of the Path (maggakkhaṇa), there is only abstinence (virati).

As for right effort (sammāvāyāma) and right mindfulness (sammāsati), this pair also receives four names according to their functions by way of the right exertions (sammappadhāna) and the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna).
Right concentration (sammāsamādhi), however, is simply right concentration both in the preliminary stage and at the moment of the Path.

Thus, among these eight states, right view was taught by the Blessed One first because it is of great benefit to the yogi practicing for the attainment of Nibbāna. For this has been called "the lamp of wisdom" and "the sword of wisdom.
Therefore, having dispelled the darkness of ignorance through this right view—which in the preliminary stage is termed insight-knowledge—
Slaying the thieves of the defilements, the practitioner of yoga reaches Nibbāna by means of safety. Therefore it was said:
"Right view is taught first because it is highly beneficial to the yogi who has set out for the attainment of Nibbāna.
Right intention, however, is beneficial to that [right view], and therefore it is mentioned immediately after it. For just as a money-changer, with his hand—
Just as one who turns over a kahāpaṇa coin again and again with his eye perceives, "This is genuine;

this is counterfeit," so too the practitioner of yoga, having reflected with initial application (vitakka) in the preliminary stage, perceives through the wisdom of insight (vipassanā-paññā), "These phenomena belong to the sense sphere (kāmāvacara);
these phenomena belong to the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), and so forth. Or, just as by a man...

Just as a carpenter, having grasped a great tree at its base and turned it over and over again, fells it with an axe and brings it to his work, so too the practitioner of yoga, having reflected upon the states presented by reflection, delimits them with wisdom according to the method:
"These belong to the sense-sphere, these to the fine-material sphere," and so forth, and brings them to his work. By that...
It is said: "Right intention, however, is of great assistance to it; therefore, it is mentioned immediately after that.
This [right intention] is helpful to right speech just as it is to right view. As it was said:
"First, Visākha, having thought and deliberated, one subsequently utters speech"; therefore, right speech is mentioned immediately after that.
However, because people in the world first make verbal agreements, saying, "We shall do this and that," and then engage in their various tasks, speech is thus an aid to bodily action;
therefore, right action is mentioned immediately after right speech.
Having abandoned the fourfold misconduct of speech and the threefold misconduct of body, both—
Because one who fulfills good conduct alone fulfills the virtue of the eightfold livelihood, whereas another does not, right livelihood is taught immediately after both of those.
Furthermore, it is not proper for one whose livelihood is thus purified to dwell with negligence, thinking, "My livelihood is completely pure," and thereby becoming satisfied with that much alone;
rather, [one must maintain] this energy in all postures...
Immediately following that, right effort (*sammāvāyāma*) was taught in order to show that [effort] must be undertaken.

Next, right mindfulness (*sammāsati*) was taught in order to show that even for one who has initiated energy, mindfulness must be well-established with respect to the four bases, beginning with the body.
Furthermore, because mindfulness thus well-established [discerns] the courses of those phenomena that are either conducive or non-conducive to concentration (*samādhi*),...
Having investigated, one is able to settle the mind on a single object; therefore, it should be understood that right concentration is taught immediately after right mindfulness.
"For the realization of these states" means for the purpose of making manifest these [fruits], such as the fruit of stream-entry and so forth.

Why was this [discourse] begun with the words, "Once upon a time..."? It is said that this king held the view, "Form is the self";
therefore, his mind did not find conviction in the teaching. Thus, the Blessed One began it for the purpose of revealing that man's view.
This was undertaken to bring forward a single reason. Herein, this is the summary of the meaning: “At one time I was dwelling at Ghosita’s Monastery;
while I was staying there, those two renunciants questioned me thus.
Then, having shown them the arising of a Buddha and speaking on what is called the ‘Thread of Dhamma,’ I said this: ‘Friends, a clansman endowed with faith...’”

“Having gone forth in the teaching of such a Teacher, having fulfilled the threefold morality and established himself by attaining the first jhāna and the others, if he were to say ‘that soul’ and so forth—would that be appropriate for him? When they replied, “It would be appropriate,” [the Blessed One said]:
“But, friends, I know this and I see this, yet I do not speak thus.”
Having rejected that argument and demonstrated one who was further along toward the destruction of the taints, I said, "It is not proper for him to speak thus.
When they heard my words, they became glad at heart. When this was said, he too became glad at heart.
Therefore it was said: "The Blessed One said this. Oṭṭhaddha the Licchavi, glad at heart, rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words."
Thus ends the commentary on the Mahālisutta in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the commentary on the Dīghanikāya. 7.
The commentary on the Jāliyasutta.

Thus have I heard... [as before] ...at Kosambī: this is the Jāliya Sutta. Herein, this is the commentary on the words not previously explained.
"In the Ghosita Monastery" means in the monastery built by the merchant Ghosita. Formerly, it is said, there was a kingdom named Allakappa. From there, a curious man...
A man named Dalidda, fleeing toward the kingdom of Avanti with his wife and children out of fear of famine, was unable to carry his son;
he left him behind and continued on. The mother turned back, took the child, and they went on until they entered a village of cowherds.
At that time, the cowherd had prepared a great deal of milk-rice (pāyāsa), and having obtained some from him, they ate it.

Then that man, having eaten a large quantity of gruel and being unable to digest it, passed away during the night and took rebirth right there in the womb of a female dog, becoming a dog. He became dear to the cowherd.
And the cowherd attended upon a paccekabuddha. At the conclusion of his meal, the paccekabuddha [gave a portion] to the dog...
He gave a single morsel of food to each one. Having conceived affection for the Paccekabuddhas, he went with the cowherd even to the leaf-hut.
When the cowherd was not present, he would go there himself at mealtime and bark at the door of the leaf-hut to announce the time;
and on the way, upon seeing fierce wild beasts, he would bark to drive them away. He [served] the Paccekabuddhas with gentleness...
Having passed away with that thought, he was reborn in the world of the devas. There, his name became Ghosaka-devaputta.
After falling from the world of the devas, he was reborn in the house of a certain family in Kosambī.
A wealthy merchant who had no sons gave him wealth to the boy’s parents and adopted him as his own son. Then, when his own children were born, [the merchant] seven times...
He set about having him killed. Due to his merit, however, he did not meet death in any of those seven places;
finally, having regained his life through the ingenuity of a merchant’s daughter, he later attained the position of a merchant upon his father’s passing and became known as the merchant Ghosaka.
There were others as well in Kosambī, such as the merchant Kukkuṭa and the merchant Pāvāriya.
There were two merchants; with him, there were three.
At that time, five hundred ascetics from the Himalayas used to come to Kosambī from time to time for the purpose of warming their bodies;
these three merchants, having built leaf huts in their respective gardens, attended upon them.
They were doing so. Then one day, as those ascetics were coming from the Himalayas, exhausted and parched by thirst in a great wilderness, they reached a large banyan tree.
Seeking favor from the deity dwelling there, they sat down. The deity extended a hand adorned with all manner of ornaments and [offered] them water for drinking and other provisions.
Having given it, he dispelled his fatigue. Amazed by the power of the deity, they asked:
"Deity, what deed did you perform to obtain this success? The deity replied:
"In the world, a Blessed One named Buddha has appeared; he is currently staying at Sāvatthī, and the householder Anāthapiṇḍika [is supporting] him..."
He attended to them. On the Uposatha days, after giving his own hired laborers their regular food and wages, he had them observe the Uposatha.
Then one day, having arrived at midday for my morning meal, I saw that no one was performing any labor;
so I asked, “Why are the people not working today? He [the householder] told me the reason for that matter.
They informed me. Then I said, "Now half a day has passed;
is it possible to perform half a Uposatha? Thereupon, having informed the merchant, he replied, "It is possible.
So, having undertaken half a day of the half-Uposatha, I died on that very day and obtained this prosperity."

Then those ascetics, having heard that "the Buddha has indeed appeared," were filled with joy and gladness. Although they wished to go from there to Sāvatthī, they thought, "Our chief patrons have been very helpful to us;

we shall inform them of this matter as well. Having gone to Kosambī and received the hospitality and great respect of the merchants, they said, "We shall depart this very day. [The merchants asked: "Why so, venerable sirs?"
When he said, "Turitāttha, did you not previously stay for four or five months before departing?
they reported what had happened. When they said, "In that case, Venerable Sir, let us go together," he replied, "We are going;
you may come slowly. Having gone to Sāvatthī and gone forth in the presence of the Blessed One, they attained arahantship.

They arrived. Those three merchants, each accompanied by five hundred carts, went to Sāvatthī, performed acts of giving and other meritorious deeds, and requested the Blessed One to come to Kosambī. Upon their return, they had three monasteries built.
Among them, the one built by the merchant Kukkuṭa was called the Kukkuṭārāma, and the one built by the merchant Pāvāriya was the Pāvārikambavana.
It was called Ghosita’s Monastery because it was built by the merchant Ghosita; it was with reference to this that it was said:
“He dwells at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Monastery.
*Muṇḍiya* is his name, and *Jāliya* is likewise the other’s name. However, because his preceptor—
He wanders for alms with a wooden bowl; therefore, he is called "the wooden-bowl disciple.
They said this: having become desirous of leveling a charge with the intent of finding fault, they said this. Thus, it seems, was their thought:
"If the ascetic Gotama says, 'The soul is that same as the body,' then we shall level this charge against him."
—“Master Gotama, according to your doctrine, it is right here that the being perishes; therefore, your doctrine is one of annihilationism.
But if he should say, “The soul is one thing, the body is another,” then we shall attribute this doctrine to him:
“In your doctrine, it is the form (rūpa) that perishes, not the being; thus, in your doctrine, the being becomes eternal.”

Then the Blessed One thought, "These people ask this question for the sake of engaging in debate; they do not know that within my teaching there is a Middle Way that does not fall into these two extremes.
Well then, instead of answering their question directly, I shall teach the Dhamma in order to reveal that very Middle Way.
Having thus reflected, he said, "In that case, friends," and so forth.
379–380. "Is it proper for him to say this? means: Is it appropriate for one who has gone forth out of faith, having fulfilled the threefold virtue and attained the first jhāna, to speak thus?
Having heard that, the wanderers [thought]: "Since an ordinary person (puthujjana) is not free from doubt, he might occasionally speak in such a manner."
Thinking, "He should speak," they said, "It is fitting for him to say this. But when I said, "And yet, I do not say so," I meant:

"I know it to be thus, but I do not say so; rather, having performed the preliminary work of the kasiṇa, as one develops it, through the power of wisdom, a sublime state of mind arises—this is what I designated by that name. It is not fitting for him to say that.

The wanderers say this, thinking: "Since he is one whose taints are exhausted, who is free from delusion, and has crossed over doubt, it is not fitting for him to say this. The rest here is of plain meaning.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, the commentary on the *Dīghanikāya*.
The commentary on the Jāliya Sutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta:
The account of Acela Kassapa.
381. Thus have I heard... [as before] ...dwelling at Uruññā; this is the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta.
Herein is the commentary on the previously unexplained terms. "At Uruññā": both the kingdom and the city bear this very name;
the Blessed One was dwelling in dependence upon the city of Uruññā. "In the Deer Park at Kaṇṇakatthala": Kaṇṇakatthala is not far from that city.
There was a certain delightful stretch of land called the Deer Park (Migadāya), so named because it had been granted as a sanctuary for deer;
it was there, in that Deer Park at Kaṇṇakatthala. "Acela" means a naked wanderer. "Kassapa" is his name. "Tapassin" means one who relies on asceticism.
"Lūkhājīvin" refers to a life of austerity by way of practices such as being naked and going without a rag-robe.
"Ascetic" means one who lives a coarse life; "him," meaning that one who lives a coarse life. "He reviles" means he mocks. "He reproaches" means he insults or derides.
"Explaining the Dhamma and what is in accordance with the Dhamma" means they speak a reason that conforms to the reason stated by Master Gotama.
"A legitimate discussion and counter-discussion" means that, being accompanied by reasons, it is either a discussion or a counter-discussion regarding what has been stated by others.
Or, what reason—even if it were merely trifling—would not come to be censured by the wise? This is what is meant:
"Is there not, in every respect, a censurable reason in your doctrine? "Not wishing to misrepresent" means not wishing to speak with what is untrue.

382. Regarding the passage beginning with "A certain ascetic living a harsh life," etc.: here, a certain person is an "ascetic" (tapassin) because he relies on austerities such as the renunciation of nakedness;
thinking, "I shall maintain my life by means of what is coarse," he torments himself in various ways, such as by consuming grass, cow dung, and so forth.
Due to his lack of merit, he does not even obtain a comfortable way of life. He [commits] the three types of misconduct.
Having filled [the bowl], he is reborn in hell.
Another person, though likewise dependent on such torment, is meritorious and receives gain and honor.
Thinking, "Now there is no one equal to me," he exalts himself in a high position and resolves, "I shall produce even greater gain."
Having fulfilled the three types of misconduct by way of improper seeking, one is reborn in hell. It is with reference to these two that the first method was stated.
Another person, dependent on austerity and living a harsh life, possesses little merit; he does not obtain a livelihood through ease. He thinks:
"Because of my past failure to perform meritorious deeds, a pleasant livelihood has not arisen for me; come now, let me perform meritorious deeds."
Having fulfilled the three types of good conduct, one is reborn in heaven.
Another person, though living a coarse life, becomes meritorious and easily obtains the means for his livelihood.

He reflects: "In the past as well, it was through my performance of merit that a happy livelihood arose for me. Thinking thus, he abandons wrong means of livelihood and fulfills the three types of good conduct.
He is reborn in heaven. It is with reference to these two that the second method was stated.

However, there is one ascetic who dwells without suffering, yet is associated with external practices—whether he be an ascetic or a covered wanderer—and due to his lack of merit, he does not obtain agreeable requisites.
By means of improper search, he engages in the three types of misconduct.
Having filled himself with merit and established himself in happiness, he is nevertheless reborn in hell.
Another person possesses merit; thinking, "Now there is no one equal to me," he gives rise to conceit.
Seeking gain and honor through improper means, and holding wrong views, he thinks: "Happy is this young female wanderer..."
Having reflected on such things as, "The touch of soft, hairy [skin]," one who falls into a state of craving for sensual pleasures fulfills the three types of misconduct and is reborn in hell.
It is with reference to these two that the third method was stated.

Furthermore, another person dwells in little suffering and possesses little merit; thinking, "Even in the past, because I failed to perform meritorious deeds, I did not obtain a livelihood through happiness," he fulfills the three types of good conduct and is reborn in heaven.
Another person is meritorious; thinking, "In the past, through having performed merit, I obtained happiness;
now I shall perform further merits," he fulfills the three types of good conduct and is reborn in heaven. It is with reference to these two that the fourth method is stated.
This has been presented according to the perspective of the non-Buddhist sects (tīrthikas), but it is also found within the Buddha's teaching (sāsana).

For one person lives a coarse life by undertaking the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), or due to a lack of merit, he fails to obtain enough food to fill his belly even after wandering through the entire village.

Thinking, "I shall procure the requisites," he either engages in wrong livelihood such as practicing medicine and the like, or falsely claims to have attained Arahantship, or indulges in the three bases of hypocrisy; thus, he is reborn in hell.

Another person is likewise possessed of merit. Having given rise to conceit because of that attainment of merit, and desiring to make his acquired gain stable, he fulfills the three types of misconduct through improper search and is reborn in hell.
Another person has undertaken the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) but possesses little merit; he does not obtain a livelihood easily. He thinks:
“Previously, due to my lack of merit, I obtained nothing at all. If I were to engage in improper search now, even in the future I would find happiness difficult to obtain.”
Thinking, "I shall become [an arahant]," one fulfills the three types of good conduct; yet, being unable to attain arahantship, one is reborn in the heavenly realms.

Another person is meritorious; thinking, "In the past, through my merit, I am now happy; now too I shall perform merit," he abandons wrong livelihood, fulfills the three types of good conduct, and—being unable to attain arahantship—is reborn in the heavenly realms.
383. *Āgatiñca* means: "These have come from such-and-such a place"—thus, their coming (*āgati*). *Gatiñca* means: now...
"And the place to be gone to. "And passing away" means passing away from there. "And rebirth" means the rebirth of those who have passed away from there.
"Why shall I criticize all austerity?"—by what reason shall I criticize it?
For we indeed criticize only that which is to be criticized and praise that which is to be praised; we do not act like a great washerman who, while washing, [destroys] what has been washed.
He shows this by saying, "And let us wash it on one side. Now, explaining that meaning, he said: "There are, Kassapa, certain recluses and brahmins," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "whatever they [consider] partial":
this refers to the fivefold morality, for no one in the world would say of it, "It is not good."
Furthermore, as for "some of them," that refers to the fivefold enmity, which no one says is "good.
Again, as for "some of them," that refers to non-restraint in the five doors; they, it is said, say: "The eye should not be shut off;
agreeable forms should be seen with the eye"—and this same method applies to the ear and the other sense-doors. Again, as for "some of them," that refers to restraint in the five doors.

Having thus demonstrated the similarity and dissimilarity of his own doctrine with that of others, he now says, beginning with "That which we...", in order to demonstrate the similarity and dissimilarity of the doctrines of others with his own.
In this context as well, the meaning should be understood by way of the five precepts and so forth.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion concerning the application of inquiry.
385. *Samanuyuñjantu*: let them cross-examine. In this context, one who asks about a tenet (*laddhi*) is said to "cross-examine" (*samanuyuñjati*);
one who asks about the reason (*kāraṇa*) is said to "probe" (*samanugāhati*); one who asks about both is said to "interrogate" (*samanubhāsati*).
Or, regarding "with the Teacher, with the Teacher": having associated the Teacher with [the opponent] by means of the Teacher—[asking], "What does your Teacher say of those teachings..."
“Does he proceed having abandoned them entirely, or does the ascetic Gotama [proceed]? The same method applies to the second phrase as well.
Now, showing that meaning by applying it, he said: “Those which, for these venerable ones...
and so forth. Therein, “unwholesome, reckoned as unwholesome” means they are both unwholesome and reckoned—known—as “unwholesome,” or they are established by being made into a category.
This is the meaning. This same method applies to all the following phrases. Furthermore, in this context, "blameworthy" (*sāvajja*) means accompanied by hatred (*sadosa*).
"Not fit for noble ones" (*na alamariya*) means they are not capable, not able, to become noble ones in the sense of being faultless.
386–392. "That which the wise, when investigating... means that because of which the wise, when questioning us and others, would speak thus.
"That possibility exists" means that such a cause exists. Or alternatively:
"Whatever those venerable group-teachers may do," the meaning is that those venerable group-teachers proceed by abandoning even the slightest [fault].
"In that regard, they would for the most part praise us alone"—this the Blessed One said even while cross-examining a teacher with respect to a teacher.
—Also when the Sangha investigates the Sangha. Why? Because even in the praise of the Sangha, the praise of the Teacher himself is established.

For those who gain confidence in the Sangha through the excellence of the Buddha, and in the Buddha through the excellence of the Sangha, likewise, having seen the excellence of the Blessed One’s physical form or having heard his teaching of the Dhamma, they become speakers thus: “It is a gain... [for the Sangha].”
"O, how wonderful are the disciples who dwell in the presence of such a Teacher! In this way, they gain confidence in the Saṅgha through the excellence of the Buddha.
Furthermore, having observed the conduct and sphere of activity of the bhikkhus—their advancing, retreating, and so forth—people will say:
"If such is the quality of tranquility in those disciples who dwell in his presence, what must the Teacher himself be like?"
Thus, through the excellence of the Saṅgha, they have confidence in the Buddha. Therefore, whatever praise is for the Teacher is for the Saṅgha;
and whatever praise is for the Saṅgha is for the Teacher. Since the praise of the Teacher is established even through the praise of the Saṅgha, the Blessed One said in both methods:
"They would mostly praise us alone in that regard. The ascetic Gotama [has taught] these teachings without remainder...
It proceeds by abandoning; or rather, regarding the passage beginning "But as for those venerable ones who are teachers of a group," this is the intended meaning here:

the three abstinences exist by way of both undertaking what is attained and the destruction of the bridge. Among these, others possess only the abstinence consisting in the undertaking of what is attained, but the abstinence consisting in the destruction of the bridge does not exist at all for them.
However, among the five types of abandoning—namely, abandoning by factor, by suppression, by eradication, by subsiding, and by escape—[the former two apply].

For others, there is only the abandonment by way of substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga*) and suppression (*vikkhambhana*), by means of the eight attainments and bare insight (*vipassanāmatta*) respectively;
the other three types of abandonment do not exist at all for them.

Likewise, regarding the fivefold restraint—namely, restraint of virtue (*sīla-saṃvara*), restraint of patience (*khanti-saṃvara*), restraint of knowledge (*ñāṇa-saṃvara*), restraint of mindfulness (*sati-saṃvara*), and restraint of energy (*vīriya-saṃvara*)—in their case, there is only the mere fivefold precept (*pañcasīlamatta*).
Others possess only the patience of endurance (*adhivāsanakhanti*); they lack everything else entirely.

Furthermore, there are five recitations of the *uposatha*; among these, others possess only the five precepts (*pañcasīla*), while the morality of restraint according to the *pātimokkha* (*pātimokkhasaṃvarasīla*) is entirely absent.
Thus, regarding the abandoning of the unwholesome and the undertaking of the wholesome, in the three abstentions and the five [precepts]...

Regarding the abandonments, the fivefold restraints, and the fivefold summaries—the Blessed One roars his lion’s roar thus: “I alone and my Saṅgha of disciples are renowned in the world; for there is no teacher equal to me, nor is there any Saṅgha equal to my Saṅgha of disciples.”
The Exposition of the Noble Eightfold Path (Ariya-aṭṭhaṅgika-magga-vaṇṇanā) 393.
Having thus let out the lion’s roar, in order to make known the unerring nature of that roar, he said:

“There is, Kassapa, a path,” and so forth. Therein, “the path” (maggo) refers to the supramundane path (lokuttara-maggo). “The way of practice” (paṭipadā) refers to the preliminary stage of practice (pubbabhāga-paṭipadā).

The terms beginning with "one who speaks of time" (*kālavādī*) have been explained in the *Brahmajāla Sutta*. Now, presenting both that twofold path and the way of practice (*paṭipadā*) together, he said:
"This very Noble [Path]," and so forth. Upon hearing this, the naked ascetic thought:
"The ascetic Gotama thinks, 'The path and the way of practice belong to me alone; they do not exist for others. Come now, I shall..."
“I shall explain the path to us as well. Thereupon, he explained the practice of the naked ascetics (acelaka). Thus it was said:
“When this was said, the naked ascetic Kassapa said this to the Blessed One... [omitted] ...he dwells devoted to the practice of bathing in water.
This concludes the commentary on the discourse concerning the undertaking of austerities.
394. In this context, *tapopakkamā* means undertakings of austerity; the meaning is "austere practices. *Sāmaññasaṅkhātā* means reckoned as the duties of a recluse (*samaṇa*).
*Brahmaññasaṅkhātā* means reckoned as the duties of a brahmin (*brāhmaṇa*). *Acelako* means one who is naked; the meaning is "bare. *Muttācāro* means one of loose conduct;
he is devoid of the conduct of a worldly gentleman regarding such acts as defecation, for he performs his excretion while standing.
He urinates, chews, and eats. "Wiping the hands" means that while the alms-food is still in his hand, he wipes the hand with his tongue;
or, having voided excrement, perceiving it as a stick, he wipes it away with his hand.
He is not one who says "Come, Venerable Sir" when told, "Come for the sake of receiving alms. "In that case, stay," [he says].
"Venerable sir," though thus addressed, he does not stop; therefore, he is called *natiṭṭhabhaddantika*.
It is said that he does neither of these two things [stopping or accepting] thinking, "I must carry out his word. *Abhihaṭa* refers to almsfood brought and received beforehand.
*Uddissakata* refers to almsfood announced as, "This was prepared specifically for you. *Na nimantana* means no invitation.
He does not consent to, nor does he accept, even a monk who has been invited with the words, “You may enter such-and-such a family, street, or village.
He does not accept alms-food being given after it has been taken out from a jar (*kumbhi*).
He does not accept it from the mouth of a *kaḷopī*—where *kaḷopī* means either a cooking pot or a basket; he does not accept it from there either. Why?
“The *kumbhika* insects, too, receive a blow from the ladle by depending on me. “Not with a sheep between”:
he does not accept [food] being given while placing a threshold-block (*ummāra*) in between. Why? “This [sheep] is receiving the role of an intermediary by depending on me.
The same principle applies to the staff and the pestle as well.
"Of two" means that when two people are eating, he does not accept [food] if one person rises to give it. Why? Because "it would cause an obstruction to the other's mouthful.
Regarding "not from a pregnant woman," and so forth: he does not accept [from them] because "the child in the womb of a pregnant woman suffers;
for a nursing woman, it causes an obstruction to the child’s milk; for a woman who has gone to another man, it causes an obstruction to her pleasure. "In crowds" means...

Having announced [the meal] and when the food had been prepared—at that time of famine, it is said, the disciples of the naked ascetics (acelaka) would collect rice and other provisions from here and there for the sake of the naked ascetics and cook the meal. Even from such [sources], the strict naked ascetic did not accept anything.
Nor where there was a dog—where a dog stood waiting with the thought, “I shall obtain alms”—there he [did not accept].
He does not accept what has been brought without it being given. Why? Because that would be an obstacle to his alms-round.

"Moving in groups" means moving in crowds; for if people, seeing a naked ascetic, enter a meal-house thinking, "We will give alms to him," and while they are entering, flies that were hidden in the openings of baskets and such fly up and move about in swarms.
He did not accept alms brought from there. Why? Because, he thought, "By depending on me, an obstacle to the flies' range of activity has arisen.

*Thusodaka* refers to sour gruel (*sovīraka*) made from all kinds of grain ingredients. In this context, while the drinking of fermented liquor (*surā*) alone is blameworthy, this person, however, perceives it as blameworthy even in the case of all [the aforementioned substances].
An *ekāgārika* is one who, having obtained alms in only a single house...
He returns. "One who subsists on a single mouthful" means one who maintains himself with only a single morsel of food.

The same method applies to those who eat every two days, and so forth. "With a single gift" means with one offering. A "gift" (datti) is a small bowl in which they place the first portion of almsfood.
"Daily" means with an interval of one day. "Fortnightly" means with an interval of half a month. "Eating meals by turn" means...
"Eating food on specific days" means eating food that arrives according to a schedule of days—such as every other day, every two days, every seven days, or every half-month.
395. "One who eats greens" means one who eats fresh greens.
"One who eats millet" means one who eats the grain of millet. Regarding *nīvāra* and so forth...
*Nīvāra* is a species of wild rice that grows spontaneously in the forest. *Daddula* is the husk discarded by leather-workers after they have scraped the hide.
*Haṭa* refers to both slime and moss. *Kaṇa* is the bran. *Ācāma* is the scorched rice stuck to the bottom of the cooking pot;
he takes it from where it was discarded and eats it. Some also call it "rice-gruel."
*Piññāka* and the other items are well known. "One who eats fallen fruit" means one who eats fruit that has fallen [from the tree].
396. *Sāṇāni* refers to garments made of hemp or bark-fiber. *Masāṇāni* refers to garments made of mixed fibers.
*Chavadussāni* refers to rags discarded from a corpse, or lower garments made by weaving together *eraka* grass and the like. *Paṃsukūlāni* refers to [rags] on the ground...
"Cast-off rags. *Tirīṭāni* means garments made from tree bark. *Ajina* is the hide of the antelope (*ajina-miga*).
*Ajinakkhipa* is that same hide split in the middle. *Kusacīra* is a garment made by weaving *kusa* grass.
The same method applies to garments made of *vāka* grass or wooden boards. *Kesakambala* is a blanket made from human hair, with reference to which it was said:
“Monks, just as among all woven garments, a hair-cloth is declared to be the most inferior.
A hair-cloth, monks, is cold in the cold, hot in the heat, of little value, ugly, foul-smelling, and unpleasant to the touch.
“Horse-hair blanket” means a blanket made from horse-hair. “Owl-feathered” means having sewn together the feathers of owls.
"Clad in a garment of bark. "Devoted to the exertion of squatting" means he is devoted to the energy of squatting;
even when walking, he does so by repeatedly springing up while remaining in a squatting position.

"One who uses a bed of thorns" means that having dug iron thorns or natural thorns into the ground, he spreads a hide over them and performs standing, walking, and other postures there. "As for lying down," even when lying down...
He makes his bed right there. "A bed on a wooden plank" means a bed on a tree-branch board.
"A bed on the bare ground" means a bed on the bare ground, on a high place. "Sleeping on one side" means he sleeps only on one side.
"Wearing dust and dirt" means that after anointing his body with oil, he stands in a dusty place; then dust and dirt adhere to his body, and that—

He maintains [these practices]. "One who accepts whatever seat is offered" (yathāsaṃthātiko) is one whose habit is to sit down exactly where he finds a seat, without displacing what has been provided.

"One who eats scraps" (vekaṭiko) is one whose habit is to eat discarded food. "Scrap" (vekaṭaṃ) refers to excrement. "One who abstains from drinking" (apānako) is one who has renounced the drinking of cold water.
"Three times in the evening" (sāyaṃ tatiyakaṃ): morning, midday, and evening—thus three times a day.
"He dwells devoted to the practice of descending into water, thinking, 'I shall wash away evil.
This is the commentary on the pointlessness of undertaking such ascetic practices (397).
Then the Blessed One, demonstrating that those ascetic practices are useless without the perfection of virtue and the other [qualities], said:
—“Even if he is naked, Kassapa,” and so forth, he said. Therein, *ārakā va* means “far indeed. *Averaṃ* means free from the enmity of hatred.
*Abyāpajjaṃ* means free from the affliction of mental distress.

“It is difficult, Master Gotama,” [said Kassapa]; this was because Kassapa thought, “We previously considered only this much to be the state of a recluse (*sāmañña*) and the state of a brahmin (*brahmañña*).”
"Let us deliberate; you, however, speak of something entirely different regarding asceticism and brahminhood," he said, pointing this out.

"This is indeed the natural state" means this is a discussion concerning the ordinary nature of things. And by this measure, Kassapa—meaning, "Kassapa, if by such a limited extent of practice as this, asceticism or brahminhood were called difficult or very difficult"—he spoke.
“If this had not been so, it would not have been right to say that the state of a recluse is difficult to achieve.
This is the meaning here in connection with the sequence of words. In this manner, the connection between the words is to be understood throughout.
399. Regarding the term *dujjāno* (difficult to know): he [the Blessed One] thought, “Previously we wandered about thinking, ‘By this much one becomes a recluse or a brahmin.’”

He said this with reference to the fact that you, however, speak otherwise. Then the Blessed One, having rejected that theory of his and revealing how it is difficult to understand by its very nature, spoke again:
"Nature, indeed," and so forth. There too, the meaning should be understood by connecting the words in the same manner as previously stated.
Commentary on the Perfection of Virtue, Concentration, and Wisdom (Sīla-samādhi-paññā-sampadā): 400–401.
But why does he ask, “But what, Master Gotama, is that? It is said that this wise man had grasped the discourse even as the Blessed One was speaking;
then, realizing that his own practice had become useless, [he thought], “Is this ascetic...”
Gotama said: “If this perfection of virtue, perfection of mind, and perfection of wisdom have not been developed and realized by him, then he is indeed far from true asceticism,” and so forth.
“Now, let me question him regarding those attainments,” he thought, and thus he asked in order to ascertain his possession of the perfection of virtue and the other qualities.
Then the Blessed One, having shown the arising of a Buddha and teaching the Dhamma of the lineage, [described] those attainments.

To demonstrate this, he said, “In this regard, Kassapa,” and so forth. And the phrase “by this perfection of virtue, Kassapa” is stated specifically with reference to the fruit of arahantship alone; for the teaching of the Blessed One culminates in the fruit of arahantship.
Therefore, he said that there is no perfection of virtue, mind, or wisdom superior or more sublime than the perfections of virtue, mind, and wisdom associated with the fruit of arahantship.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Lion’s Roar: 402.
Having spoken thus, he now uttered the unsurpassed Great Lion’s Roar, saying: “There are, Kassapa, some recluses and brahmins,” and so forth.
In this context, *ariya* means free from defilement and supremely pure. *Parama* means...
"Supreme": beginning with the five precepts up to the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha, these are simply virtue;
however, that which is associated with the supramundane path and fruit is called "supreme virtue. "In that regard, I see no one equal to myself":
the meaning is that regarding both that [ordinary] virtue and supreme virtue, I do not see any person equal to myself, possessing virtue equal to my own. "I alone am superior in that regard."
"I alone am supreme in that virtue. In what respect? That is to say, "in higher virtue" (*adhisīla*);
the meaning is, "in that which is the supreme virtue. Thus he roars this first lion's roar.

"Those who speak of austerity and self-disgust" (*tapojigucchavādā*) refers to those who advocate austerity and self-disgust. In that context, "austerity" (*tapas*) means it "burns" (*tapati*); it is a term for the energy that burns away the defilements.

"Name" (*nāma*): that very thing by which one loathes the defilements is "loathing" (*jigucchā*). Regarding the phrase "the noble ones are supreme": here, they are "noble" (*ariya*) because they are free from fault;

furthermore, the austerity and loathing (*tapojigucchā*) consisting of insight-effort (*vipassanāvīriya*) arising by way of the eight bases for exertion (*aṭṭha-ārambhavatthu*) is merely "austerity and loathing," whereas that associated with the paths and fruits is called "supreme.
"They train in loathing" (*adhijegucchanti*): here, the state of loathing is "loathing" (*jeguccha*), and it is "supreme" (*uttama*).
"Disgust and further disgust": therefore, regarding this "further disgust," the meaning here should be understood as "I alone am superior in this regard.
Even in the context of wisdom (*paññā*), both the wisdom of the ownership of one's actions (*kammassakatā-paññā*) and the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*) are called wisdom;
however, that which is associated with the Path and its Fruits is called supreme wisdom. In the term *adhipañña*, a change of grammatical gender (*liṅga-vipallāsa*) should be understood.

This, however, is the meaning here: regarding what is called "higher wisdom" (*adhipaññā*), one should understand that in the section on liberation, the liberations consisting in "partial relinquishment" (*tadaṅga-vimutti*) and "suppression" (*vikkhambhana-vimutti*) are merely "liberation," whereas the liberations consisting in "complete eradication" (*samuccheda-vimutti*), "tranquillization" (*paṭippassaddhi-vimutti*), and "escape" (*nissaraṇa-vimutti*) are the "supreme liberation.
And here too, as for this "super-liberation" (*adhivimutti*), the meaning is: "I alone am superior in this regard."
403. "In an empty place" means in an empty house; the intention is that he sits all alone. "And among the assemblies" means among the eight kinds of assemblies. And this has also been said:

"Sāriputta, there are these four grounds of self-confidence belonging to the Tathāgata. Endowed with these grounds of self-confidence, the Tathāgata claims his place as a leader and roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies. This sutta should be quoted in detail.
"And they ask him questions" means that wise gods and humans, having prepared a question, ask him about it.
"He explains" means he answers at that very moment. "He satisfies the mind" means he indeed gladdens the minds of the great multitude by answering the question.
"But they do not think it worth hearing" means that even though he speaks while satisfying their minds, others do not consider his words worth hearing;
and so they would say—this is the meaning. "And they think it worth hearing" means...
Both gods and humans consider it worth hearing with great enthusiasm. "They have confidence" means they become well-pleased, with minds that are clear and gentle.

"They manifest their confidence" does not mean they are merely pleased in mind; rather, by relinquishing excellent robes and so forth, as well as great monasteries such as the Veḷuvana Vihāra, they manifest their confidence. "For the sake of becoming such [as they are]"—
The meaning is that they practice the Dhamma he teaches for the sake of becoming such [as it is], for the purpose of fulfilling the practice in accordance with the Dhamma (*dhammānudhammapaṭipatti*).
And "they practice for the state of being such" means they practice for the sake of becoming such;
for having heard the Dhamma of that Blessed One, some establish themselves in the refuges, some in the five precepts, and others, having gone forth...
They go forth. And as for "those who have entered the path succeed": those who have entered that practice are able to fulfill it;
indeed, they fulfill it in every way. It should be said that by the fulfillment of their practice, they satisfy the mind of that Blessed One Gotama.
Standing in this context, the lion’s roars should be brought together: [the roar] that a certain ascetic was reborn in hell.
"I see," this is one lion’s roar of the Blessed One. "I see another reborn in heaven," this is another.
"In the abandoning of unwholesome states, I alone am supreme," this is another. "In the undertaking of wholesome states, I alone am supreme," this is another.
"In the abandoning of unwholesome states, my Saṅgha of disciples alone is supreme," this is another. "In the undertaking of wholesome states, my Saṅgha of disciples alone..."
"One thinks: 'I am the best. Another thinks: 'There is no one equal to me in virtue. Another thinks: 'There is no one equal to me in energy.
[The same applies to] wisdom... liberation... Another thinks: 'Seated in the midst of the assembly, I roar the lion's roar.
Another thinks: 'I roar with confidence. Another thinks: 'They ask me a question. Another thinks: 'When asked a question, I provide the answer.'"
One [thought]: "I please the mind of another by my answer. One [thought]: "Having heard [me], they think it worth hearing. One [thought]: "Having heard, they have confidence in me.
One [thought]: "They manifest an attitude of confidence. One [thought]: "They practice according to the way of practice I teach.
One [thought]: "And having practiced, they please me. Thus, for each of the preceding ten [statements].
“*And he roars amidst the assemblies*,” and so forth—these are ten sets of ten attendants.
Thus, by way of being the attendants for the preceding ten, there are one hundred of the former and the ten themselves; thus there are one hundred and ten lion-roars.
In other suttas besides this one, such lion-roars are rare; therefore, this sutta is called the *Mahāsīhanāda* (The Great Lion’s Roar). Thus.
The Blessed One, having thus refuted the dispute that "the ascetic Gotama roars the lion’s roar, yet he roars it only in empty places," now spoke the passage beginning with "Once, indeed...
in order to demonstrate the lion’s roar he had previously roared within an assembly. *Commentary on the Discussion of the Probationary Period for Heretics* (Titthiyaparivāsakathāvaṇṇanā)

404. Therein, "a certain ascetic practitioner of the holy life" refers to a certain wanderer named Nigrodha, an ascetic practitioner of the holy life, who questioned me while I was dwelling there on Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagaha.
He asked a question regarding the mastery of loathing for evil through energy (*adhijegucche*). This [was asked] when the Blessed One was at the Mahāvihāra on Vulture Peak.
Sitting in the royal park of Queen Udumbarikā, having heard with his divine ear-element the conversation between the wanderer Nigrodha and the lay follower Sandhāna, he came through the air,
sat down on a seat prepared near them, and answered the question asked by Nigrodha regarding higher refinement; it was with reference to this [that the Blessed One said].
It was said. "By a measure like that of another" means by a supreme measure; the meaning is, by an exceedingly great standard.

"Who indeed, venerable sir?"—except for a foolish person of blind views, who else of a wise nature would say, "Who indeed, having heard the Blessed One’s Dhamma, would not be satisfied? "May I obtain..."—this he [said] thinking, "For a long time indeed have I..."
Having applied himself to what is not conducive to deliverance, he has only exhausted himself;

like one who rolls about thinking, “I shall bathe on the bank of a dry river,” or like one who threshes husks, no purpose whatsoever has been accomplished. “Come now, I shall apply myself to the yoga,” he thought, and so he spoke.

Then the Blessed One [considered] that probation for former members of other sects which had been prescribed by him in the Khandhaka, and that [rule] concerning those who were formerly members of other sects...

Standing on the level of a novice, he undertakes the practice according to this method: “Venerable sir, I, named so-and-so, formerly belonging to another sect, desire the full admission (upasampadā) into this Dhamma and Vinaya;
therefore, venerable sir, I request a four-month probation from the Saṅgha.
It is with reference to such a person that the Blessed One said: “Kassapa, whoever was formerly belonging to another sect,” and so forth.
405. In this context, the word "going forth" (*pabbajjā*) is used merely for the sake of euphony; for one receives the going forth even without having completed the probationary period.
However, one who desires full ordination (*upasampadā*) must complete the probation by fulfilling the eight duties, such as entering the village at the proper time and so forth.
"With a mind resolved" (*āraddhacittā*) means with a mind satisfied by the fulfillment of the eight duties; this is the summary meaning here.

In detail, however, this *tīṭṭhiyaparivāsa* (probation for those belonging to other sects) is to be understood according to the method explained in the commentary on the *Pabbajjā-khandhaka* in the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya.
Furthermore, "api ca me'ttha" means "and moreover, in this matter.
"Puggalavemattatā viditā" means "the diversity of persons is known"—namely, that "this person is worthy of probation; this one is not worthy of probation. This...

He shows that [the meaning] is clear to him. Then Kassapa thought: “Oh, how wonderful is the Buddha’s teaching, wherein they take only what is appropriate after thus heating and pounding it, while discarding what is inappropriate!
Thereupon, his zeal for the going-forth being greatly increased, he said, “If, venerable sir,” and so forth.
Then the Blessed One, perceiving Kassapa’s intense aspiration, thought, "Kassapa does not deserve probation," and addressed a certain bhikkhu:
"Go, bhikkhu, bathe Kassapa, give him the going-forth, and bring him back.
Having done so, that bhikkhu gave him the going-forth and returned to the presence of the Blessed One. In the midst of the assembly, the Blessed One—
Having had him sit down, he conferred full ordination upon him. Therefore it was said: “The naked ascetic Kassapa received the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One;
he received full ordination. “Not long after his full ordination” means having become fully ordained, not long thereafter.
“Withdrawn” means withdrawn from both sensual objects and the defilements of sensual desire, both in body and in mind. “Diligent” means...
"Not abandoning mindfulness regarding the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). "Ardent" (*ātāpī*) means ardent through the ardor of energy (*vīriya*) known as both physical and mental.
"With mind sent forth" (*pahitatta*) means one whose mind is directed toward, or who has relinquished attachment to, both body and life due to lack of regard for them.

"For whatever purpose" (*yassatthāya*) means for whichever purpose. "Noble sons" (*kulaputtā*) refers to those of noble conduct. "In the right way" (*sammadeva*) means precisely by way of the cause or reason. "That unsurpassed" (*tadanuttaraṃ*).
That unsurpassed goal: "the consummation of the holy life" (*brahmacariyapariyosāna*) refers to the fruit of arhatship, which constitutes the culmination of the holy life of the path.
It is for the sake of this that sons of noble family go forth into homelessness. "In this very life" (*diṭṭheva dhamme*) means in this very personal existence.
"Having realized it through direct higher knowledge" (*sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā*) means having made it personally manifest through one's own wisdom, having made it independent of others.
The meaning is: "Having attained and having dwelt," he dwelt having reached and accomplished [it]. And while dwelling thus, "birth was exhausted...
[etc. ...he directly knew.
Having thus shown the stage of his reviewing, [the Buddha] concludes the teaching with the pinnacle of Arahantship: "A certain one..."
"But indeed, the Venerable Kassapa became one of the Arahants"—so it is said. In this context, "one" (*aññatara*) means a single individual.
"One of the Arahants" (*arahantaṃ*) means he was among the Arahants who were disciples of the Blessed One; this is the intended meaning here.
Furthermore, whatever has not been stated at intervals [in this passage] is already evident, as it has been explained in its respective places.
Thus ends the commentary on the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya. 9.
Commentary on the Poṭṭhapāda Sutta.
The Exposition of the Poṭṭhapāda Paribbājaka Vatthu: 406.
"Thus have I heard... at Sāvatthī" refers to the Poṭṭhapāda Sutta. Herein, this is the commentary on the words not previously explained:
"He was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park" means that, depending upon Sāvatthī, he who belonged to Jeta’s...
In the forest of Kumāra, a monastery was established by the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, and [the Buddha] dwelt there.
As for the wanderer named Poṭṭhapāda—he was a covered-wanderer (channa-paribbājaka) called Poṭṭhapāda.

It is said that in his time as a layman, he was a wealthy brahmin who, having seen the danger in sensual pleasures, renounced a mass of wealth amounting to four hundred million and went forth among the sectarians.
He became a teacher of a school (gaṇācariya). It is called *samayappavādaka* because they propound their own doctrines (*samaya*) there;

for it is said that at that place, brahmins such as Caṅkī, Tārukkha, and Pokkharasāti, as well as renunciants such as the Nigaṇṭhas, Acelakas, and Paribbājakas, gathered together and spoke, discussed, and expounded their respective doctrines.
Therefore, that monastery is called *Samayappavādaka*. And that very [monastery] was known by the name Tindukācīra...
Because it was surrounded by rows of *timbaru* trees, it was called the Tinduka-orchard (*tindukācīra*).

However, since there was originally only one hall there, but later many halls were built thanks to the wandering ascetic Mahāpuñña, it is called "Ekasālaka" (the Single-Hall) based on the name derived from that original single hall. As for Mallikā, she was the queen of King Pasenadi.
Being like a pleasure grove and endowed with flowers and fruits, it was designated as "Mallikā’s Grove" (*ārāma*) because of Mallikā.
At that time, [the Blessed One] was dwelling in Mallikā’s Grove, which had single-sālā trees, *tinduka* wood, and *acīra* cloth, and was a place of worldly discourse.
"Dwells" (*paṭivasati*) means he dwells in the comfort of his residence. Then, one day at the time of dawn, the Blessed One [attained] the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
Having spread out his net of knowledge and surveying the world, he saw the wanderer Poṭṭhapāda caught within that net of knowledge and thought:
"This Poṭṭhapāda appears in my net of knowledge; what indeed will become of him? Examining him closely, he saw:
"I shall go there today, and then Poṭṭhapāda will ask me about cessation and emergence from cessation."
He will ask me a question; having reconciled both [answers] with the knowledge of all the Buddhas, I shall explain them to him.
Then, after a few days have passed, Citta will come into my presence bringing Hatthi Sāriputta;
I shall teach them the Dhamma, and at the conclusion of that teaching, Poṭṭhapāda will go for refuge to me, as will Citta Hatthi Sāriputta.
“Having gone forth in my presence, he will attain arahantship.

Then, early in the morning, having attended to his physical needs, he donned a well-dyed inner robe, fastened a waist-belt resembling a flash of lightning, and placed his rag-robe—colored like a cloud and standing as vast as a great rain-cloud encompassing Mount Yugandhara—over one shoulder. It was of priceless value.
Having hung a crystal bowl from his left shoulder, thinking, "I shall enter Sāvatthī for alms," he emerged from the monastery like a lion from the foothills of the Himālaya.
With reference to this matter, it was said: "Then the Blessed One," and so forth.
407. *Etadahosi* (this occurred to him): having gone near the city gate and looking at the sun according to his own preference, [he perceived] that it was indeed too early.
Having seen this, it occurred to him. The particle *yaṃ-nūnāhaṃ* is like an expression indicating doubt;
however, there is no such thing as doubt for the Buddhas—such as "we shall do this," "we shall not do this," "we shall teach the Dhamma to this person," or "we shall not teach it to this person.
Nevertheless, this preliminary stage of reflection is found in all Buddhas. Therefore he said:
—“*Yaṃ nūnāhaṃ*”: the meaning is “if, however, I were to speak.

408. *Unnādiniyā*: of one crying out loudly; and because she was crying out in this manner, her sound was high due to its upward movement, and great due to its spreading in all directions—thus it is “of one making a loud noise and a great noise. For those wanderers, from early morning...

There is no duty to be performed upon rising, such as the service to a shrine (*cetiyavatta*), the service to the Bodhi tree (*bodhivatta*), the service to teachers and preceptors (*ācariyupajjhāyavatta*), or wise attention (*yoniso manasikāra*).

Therefore, having risen early in the morning and sitting in the morning sun, they engage one another in conversation concerning the hands, feet, and so forth of women, men, boys, girls, and others, saying, "This hand is beautiful; this foot [is beautiful]."

Or, having initiated a conversation concerning physical beauty, or other objects such as the gratification of sensual pleasures (*kāmassāda*) and the gratification of existence (*bhavassāda*), they gradually engage in various kinds of "animal talk" (*tiracchānakathā*), such as talk about kings and so forth.
Therefore it is said: "of one who is noisy, making a loud noise and a great clamor, speaking various kinds of animal talk."
Then the wanderer Poṭṭhapāda, having observed those wanderers, thought: "These wanderers show extreme lack of respect for one another;

and since the appearance of the ascetic Gotama, we have become like glow-worms in the rising of the sun, and our gains and honor have diminished. But if the ascetic Gotama were to come to this place..."
"If a disciple or a lay supporter were to come upon him, it would be extremely embarrassing;
moreover, the fault of the assembly falls upon the leader of the assembly. Looking here and there, he saw the Blessed One.
Thus it is said: "Then the wanderer Poṭṭhapāda... [they all became silent]."
409. "He established her there" means he instructed her; he concealed her fault. He established her in such a way that she became well-composed.

Just as a man entering the midst of an assembly might adjust his lower garment, adjust his upper robe, and wipe away spots of dust for the purpose of concealing a fault, so too did he act for the purpose of concealing her fault.
“‘Be quiet, sirs,’ he says, training them; the meaning is that he establishes them in such a way that they become well-composed.
‘One who desires little noise’ means he wishes for little noise; he sits alone, he stands alone, and he does not subsist by the company of crowds.
‘He would think it right to approach’ means he would think it right to come here. But why did he [approach] the Blessed One?”
"Does he expect a visit? "He is longing for his own advancement. It is said that when wanderers see Buddhas or disciples of the Buddha coming into their presence, they think:
"Today the ascetic Gotama has come to us, Sāriputta has come; yet they do not go to the presence of this one or that one. Look!"
Thinking, "This is our supreme status," they exalt themselves in the presence of their own attendants and place themselves in a high position;
they even strive to win over the Blessed One’s attendants. Indeed, upon seeing the Blessed One’s attendants, they say:
"Even your teacher, Master Gotama, and the disciples of Gotama come into our presence."
“We are all in harmony with one another. Yet you do not wish to even look at us with your eyes, nor do you perform the proper duties of respect toward us.
What wrong have we done? Then some people thought, “Even the Buddhas go to them; what need have we?
From that time on, whenever they saw them, they did not neglect them. They remained silent—thus [it was said] regarding Poṭṭhapāda.
Having surrounded him, they sat down silently.
"Welcome, venerable sir! means: "The arrival of the Blessed One is most welcome, venerable sir";
for it indicates that when the Blessed One comes there is joy, and when he departs there is sorrow. Why did he say, "It has been a long time, venerable sir"? Was the Blessed One here before as well?
"Has he been there before? "No, he has not been there before. However, for people, such friendly greetings as "Where are you going?
Where have you come from? Are you lost? Have you been gone for a long time? are customary; therefore, he spoke thus.
And having spoken in this way, he did not remain sitting stiff with pride, but rose from his seat and went out to meet the Blessed One.
Indeed, it is rare to find one who, upon seeing the Blessed One approach, does not invite him to a seat or show him due honor.
Why? Because of his high birth. This wanderer, too, having cleared away the seat where he himself was sitting, invited the Blessed One to sit, saying:
"Venerable sir, let the Blessed One sit; this seat is prepared. (The intervening conversation)
"Unfinished" means: "From the time you first sat down until my arrival, what conversation was left unfinished during this interval?
On account of my arrival, which discussion has not reached its conclusion? Speak it; I shall bring it to its end and then give [the gift].
Thus he made his invitation for the Omniscient One. Then the wanderer said: "A conversation that is useless..."

Pointing out that "this [discourse] is indeed substanceless and dependent on the cycle of existence; it does not deserve to be spoken in your presence," he said, "Let this stand aside, venerable sir," and so forth.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Cessation of Perception (Abhisaññānirodhakathā):
"Let this stand aside, venerable sir": if the Blessed One should wish to hear it, this discourse will not be difficult to obtain later on.
"It will happen; however, there is no need for us to engage in this discussion. Having obtained the arrival of the Blessed One, we shall ask about some other important matter," he indicates.
Then, asking him, he said: "Venerable sir, those former [events]," and so forth.
In that context, as for the phrase "in the Hall of Wonders" (*kotūhalasālā*), there was no separate hall named "Hall of Wonders. Rather, it was where various sectarian teachers...
Ascetics and brahmins engage in various kinds of talk; because this is a source of curiosity for many, such as "What does this one say?
What does that one say?", it is called the "Hall of Curiosity. Regarding the phrase "the cessation of perception" (*abhisaññānirodhe*):
here, *abhi* is merely an intensifying prefix (*upasagga*). The discussion arises concerning the cessation of consciousness (*cittanirodhe*), that is, momentary cessation (*khaṇikanirodhe*).

This is the meaning. Now, this is the cause for its arising: When the Blessed One, it is said, tells a Jātaka tale or proclaims a training rule (sikkhāpada), the fame of the Blessed One spreads throughout the whole of Jambudīpa.
Hearing this, the sectarians (titthiyā) think, "The venerable Gotama, they say, speaks of his former conduct; why should we not be able to speak something similar?"
Acting as a counterpart to the Blessed One, they would discuss one occasion from a previous life, saying, "Master Gotama laid down a training rule;
why should we not be able to lay one down too? and thus they would lay down some minor training rule for their own disciples.
At that time, however, the Blessed One, seated in the midst of the eightfold assembly, was delivering a discourse on cessation (*nirodha*).
He spoke. When the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) heard this, they thought, "It seems Master Gotama speaks of what is called 'cessation' (nirodha);
we too shall speak of it. Having assembled, they spoke. Therefore it is said: "A discussion concerning the cessation of perception arose.

In that context, "some among them" refers to certain individuals. And here, the "former" refers to one who has gone forth in an external religious order (titthāyatana), regarding the activity of the mind.

Having seen the fault [in perception] and having developed the attainment, perceiving the state of being without consciousness to be peace, he passed away from here and remained for five hundred eons in the non-percipient realm (*asaññībhava*).
Upon returning and arising here again, seeing no cause for the arising and cessation of perception, he said:
"Without cause, without condition."
The second [deity] restrained him; perceiving that the ascetic Migasiṅga was unconscious, he said, "He has come, and he has gone.
It is said that the ascetic Migasiṅga was one who practiced self-mortification and fierce austerities, possessing supreme mastery over his faculties.
By the power of his virtue, the palace of Sakka became hot. Sakka, the king of the gods, thought, "Does this ascetic perhaps aspire to the position of Sakka?"
He sent a celestial maiden named Alambusā, saying, "Come, and break this ascetic’s penance.
She went there. On the first day, as soon as the ascetic saw her, he fled and entered his leaf-hut.
On the second day, overcome by the hindrance of sensual desire, he seized her by the hand; touched by that divine contact, he lost consciousness for three years.
After three years had passed, he regained consciousness. That theorist, thinking that he had emerged from cessation after the passing of three years, spoke thus.
The third [theorist] refuted him, referring to the practice of *āthabbana* (sorcery), saying: "They draw him near and they draw him away."
He said: "It seems that the practitioners of *āthabbaṇa* (sorcery), having employed their arts, show a being as if its head were cut off, its hands were severed, or as if it were dead.
Seeing that being return to its normal state, that proponent of a speculative view, thinking 'this one has emerged from cessation,' spoke thus."
The fourth [teacher], having refuted him, spoke the passage beginning with "For there are, sir, deities" with reference to the intoxicating sleep of the female *yakkhas*.
It is said that the female *yakkhas*, performing offerings to the deities throughout the entire night by dancing and singing, would drink a bowl of liquor at dawn, roll over, and fall asleep;
they would then wake up during the day. Seeing this, that proponent of a wrong view—
—“Thinking that ‘they had entered cessation at the time of sleep and emerged from cessation upon waking,’ he spoke thus.
But this wanderer Poṭṭhapāda was of an intelligent nature; therefore, upon hearing that discourse, remorse arose in him:
‘The talk of these men is like the chatter of a ram; for they describe four kinds of cessation, whereas by this [teaching]...’”
"And there must be only one cessation, not many. That one must be distinct from others;
moreover, it cannot be known by anyone other than the Omniscient One.
Had the Blessed One been present here, he would have made it manifest this very day, illuminating it like a thousand lamps, saying: 'This is cessation; this is not cessation.'"

He recollected only the One Possessed of the Ten Powers. Therefore he said, "To me, venerable sir," and so forth. In that context, *aho* and *nūna* are two particles used in the sense of recollection;
by means of them, as he was recollecting the Blessed One, this thought occurred to him: "Oh, how wonderful is the Blessed One! Oh, how wonderful is the Sugata!
"Whoever among these" means whoever is well-skilled, subtle, and expert regarding these things subject to cessation.
The Blessed One [thought], "Oh, he would surely speak! Oh, the Sugata would surely speak!"—this is the intended meaning here.
"One who knows the natural state" (*pakataññū*) means one who knows the natural condition or inherent nature due to mastery in practice; thus, he is "one who knows the natural state.
"How indeed?"—the wanderer says this while entreating, "Blessed One, we do not know; you know, so please tell us. Then the Blessed One...
While speaking, he said, "In that regard, Poṭṭhapāda," and so forth.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Arising and Cessation of Consciousness Without Cause (Ahetuka-saññuppāda-nirodha-kathā-vaṇṇanā): 412.

Therein, "in that regard" (*tattha tatra*) means among those recluses and brahmins. "From the very beginning they have failed" (*āditova tesaṃ aparaddhaṃ*) means from the very start of their discourse.
"Transgressed" indicates that one has stumbled right in the middle of the house.

Regarding the phrase "with cause and with condition," here both "cause" (*hetu*) and "condition" (*paccaya*) are synonyms for "reason"; the meaning is "with reason. Showing that reason, he said, "A single training.
In that context, "a single perception arises through the training" means that certain perceptions are born from the training.
413. "And what is training? the Blessed One said. By way of asking what that training is, the Blessed One spoke with the desire to explain it in detail.

Now, since there are three trainings—training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*), training in higher mind (*adhicitta-sikkhā*), and training in higher wisdom (*adhipaññā-sikkhā*)—the Blessed One, in order to show them, [proceeded] from the arising of a Buddha to illustrate the arising and cessation of perception together with its cause.
Beginning with the establishment of the doctrine of the Thread (*tantidhamma*), he said: "In this case, Poṭṭhapāda, the Tathāgata appears in the world," and so forth.

Therein, only two trainings—the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*) and the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-sikkhā*)—are presented in their own form; however, the third is found in the passage:
"But this, Poṭṭhapāda, is the path leading to the cessation of suffering; it is the categorical Dhamma taught by me."
