It should be understood that they have come [into this context] because they are included by way of right view and right intention. "Perception of sensual desire" (*kāmasaññā*) refers both to lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure and to unarisen sensual conduct.
Among these, lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure is eradicated by the path of the non-returner (*anāgāmimagga*);
however, unarisen sensual conduct is what is relevant in this instance. Therefore, its preceding "perception of sensual desire" [is what is meant here].
For one possessing the first jhāna, that which is called "prior sensual perception"—so named because it resembles the sensual perceptions previously arisen—is ceased;
the meaning is that what had not yet arisen does not arise.
At that time, in that moment of the first jhāna, he possesses only the subtle and true perception of the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.
The subtle perception (saññā) designated as the joy and happiness born of seclusion (vivekaja-pīti-sukha) is "true" (sacca), meaning it is real (bhūtā).

Alternatively, because it is subtle through the abandoning of the gross factors such as sensual desire (kāmacchanda) and so forth, and is true by virtue of its reality, it is called "subtle-true-perception" (sukhumasaccasaññā).

Since he possesses this subtle-true-perception associated with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, he is described as "one who has the subtle-true-perception associated with the joy and happiness born of seclusion."
"Perceiving the subtle reality of the joy and happiness born of seclusion"—this is how the meaning should be understood here. This same method applies everywhere.

Regarding the phrase "thus it is training": since one trains while entering, resolving upon, and emerging from the first jhāna, it is called "training" because it is to be trained in thus. By that which is reckoned as training...
By means of the first jhāna, thus a single subtle and true perception of rapture and pleasure born of seclusion arises. The meaning is that, in this way, a single perception of sensual desire ceases.

"This is the training," the Blessed One said; that is, "this single training, consisting of the first jhāna," the Blessed One spoke. By this same method, the meaning is to be understood in all instances.
However, since contemplation of the factors (*aṅga*) of the eighth attainment belongs to the Buddhas alone— and even among disciples, not even those like Sāriputta possess it—
while disciples possess only contemplation of the aggregates (*kalāpa*), this [passage] has extracted the contemplation of the factors by stating,
"perception, perception. Therefore, after showing only the perception culminating in the base of nothingness, it further...
In order to show that this very state is the "summit of perception" (*saññagga*), he said: "From the time, Poṭṭhapāda... [etc. ...he touches the summit of perception.
(414) Therein, "Poṭṭhapāda, as for the bhikkhu": this refers to whichever bhikkhu named Poṭṭhapāda. "He has the perception of 'here'":
in this teaching, he has the perception of "here"; or rather, this is the reading: by means of his own perception of the first jhāna.

The meaning is that he possesses perception. "From there to there, from there to there" means that the bhikkhu, from the first jhāna to the second jhāna, and from that too to the third jhāna—thus, by means of each respective perception of the jhānas, being possessed of his own perception after his own perception—he successively touches the peak of perception.
"The peak of perception" refers to the base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana).
Why? Because it is the foremost of the mundane attainments that perform functions.
For, standing in the attainment of the base of nothingness, one enters even the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and cessation.
Thus, because it is the foremost of the mundane attainments that perform functions, it is called the "summit of perception"; the meaning is that one touches or reaches it.
Now, in order to show the cessation of perception (*saññā-nirodha*), he said: "Of him who stands at the peak of perception," and so forth.

Therein, regarding the two terms "he would intend" (*ceteyya*) and "he would form" (*abhisaṅkhareyya*): when entering into jhāna, one is said to "intend"; the meaning is that one repeatedly prepares the mind.
When forming an attachment for the sake of a higher attainment, one is said to "form. And these perceptions of mine...
"Would they cease" means these perceptions of the base of nothingness would cease. "And other gross [perceptions]" means that other gross life-continuum (bhavaṅga) perceptions would arise.
"He neither intends nor forms [an intention]"—here, although he is indeed intending, he does not intend;
although he is indeed forming [an intention], he does not form one. For this bhikkhu, from the base of nothingness...

Having emerged from that state and entered the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*), there is no mental application or directed attention (*ābhogasamannāhāra*) with the thought, "I shall remain for one or two mental moments.
However, there is indeed mental application and directed attention solely for the sake of attaining the higher cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
This point can be illustrated by the example of the son's house.

It is said that his son’s house was located behind his father’s house; therefore, when the young man returned to the dining hall carrying excellent food from there, the Elder asked him, “The alms-food is delightful; where was it brought from?
He pointed out the very house from which he had received it, saying, “From such-and-such a house. However, even though he had passed by his father’s house on the way, [he did not mention it].

Even when he has arrived there, there is no mental engagement (*ābhoga*) with it. In this context, the attainment of the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana-samāpatti*) is to be seen as the assembly hall;

the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana-samāpatti*) as the father’s house; and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) as the son’s house.
It is like standing in the assembly hall, not attending to the father’s house, and pointing out the son’s house from the base of nothingness.

Having emerged from that state and attained the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he does not attend to his father’s house even for "one or two mental moments," but rather attends to it for the sake of attaining the higher cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). Thus, while intending, he does not intend;
while forming volitional formations, he does not form them. Those very perceptions—namely, the perceptions of the jhānas—cease. Other...
And other coarse perceptions of the life-continuum do not arise. "He touches cessation":
that monk who has practiced in this way touches, finds, and attains the cessation of perception and feeling.

Regarding the phrase "the attainment of the successive cessation of perceptions with full awareness" (*anupubbābhisaññānirodhasampajānasamāpatti*): here, *abhi-* is merely an intensifying prefix (*upasagga*), and the term *sampajāna* refers to full awareness.

It is stated with the word "cessation" (nirodha) placed in between. Regarding the sequence, the meaning here is "the attainment of the cessation of perception through full awareness" (*sampajañña-saññā-nirodha-samāpatti*).

Furthermore, in that context, "the attainment of the cessation of perception through full awareness" means either the attainment of the cessation of perception at the end for one who is fully aware, or the attainment of the cessation of perception for a wise monk who possesses full awareness; this is the specific sense.

Now, having stood here, the discussion on the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) must be told. However, this has been explained in its entirety in the *Visuddhimagga* within the section on the benefits of developing wisdom; therefore, it should be understood exactly as it is stated there.
Thus, after the Blessed One had delivered this discourse on cessation to the wanderer Poṭṭhapāda, he said, "What do you think?
and so forth, in order to make him acknowledge that such a discourse does not exist elsewhere. And the wanderer...
Claiming, “Blessed One, today, apart from your discourse, I have never before heard such talk,” he replied, “Certainly not, Bhante.
Then, showing that he had carefully mastered the Blessed One’s discourse, he said, “In this way indeed, Bhante,” and so forth.
Thereupon, the Blessed One, granting him permission, said, “You have grasped it well.”
“Thus it is, Poṭṭhapāda,” he said.
Then the wanderer, thinking, “The Blessed One has stated that the base of nothingness is the pinnacle of perception.
Is this alone the pinnacle of perception, or is there a pinnacle of perception even in the remaining attainments? asked about that matter:
He said, “Is it only one? and so forth. The Blessed One answered him as well. In that context, *puthūpi* means “even many.
“In whatever way, Poṭṭhapāda, he touches cessation” means by whichever kasiṇa among the earth-kasiṇa and others, or by whichever jhāna among the first jhāna and others.
This is what is meant: if, by means of the earth-kasiṇa acting as the instrument, he attains the earth-kasiṇa absorption...
Entering [the attainment] once, one touches the cessation of the previous perception, which is one peak of perception (*saññagga*).
Then, entering it two times, three times, a hundred times, a thousand times, or a hundred thousand times, one touches the cessation of the previous perception—a hundred thousand peaks of perception.
This same method applies to the remaining kasiṇas. Regarding the jhānas as well, if by means of the first jhāna...
By means of that [attainment] acting as the instrument, one touches the cessation of the previous perception once; this is one "peak of perception" (*saññagga*).
Then, if one touches the cessation of the previous perception two times, three times, a hundred times, a thousand times, or a hundred thousand times, there are a hundred thousand peaks of perception.
This same method applies to the remaining meditative attainments (*jhāna-samāpatti*) as well. Thus, by way of entering [them] once...
Or, grouping all [perceptions] together under the characteristic of perceiving, there is one "summit of perception" (*saññagga*); yet there are many, by way of entering into successive attainments.
"Venerable sir, is it perception?"—thus he asks the Blessed One regarding a monk who has entered the attainment of cessation:
"Does perception arise first? To him, the Blessed One replied: "Perception, Poṭṭhapāda."
In this context, "perception" (saññā) refers to the perception of jhāna; "knowledge" (ñāṇa) refers to insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa).

According to another method, "perception" refers to the perception of insight; "knowledge" refers to path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa). According to yet another method, "perception" refers to the perception of the path; "knowledge" refers to fruition-knowledge (phala-ñāṇa). However, the Elder Tipiṭaka Mahāsīva said: "What are these monks saying?
Previously, Poṭṭhapāda asked the Blessed One about cessation (nirodha); now [he asks] about cessation..."
Questioning about emergence (*vuṭṭhāna*), he says: "When one emerges from cessation, does the perception of the fruit of arahantship arise first, or rather the knowledge of reviewing?
Then the Blessed One said, "Perception indeed, Poṭṭhapāda," because the perception of the fruit arises first, and subsequently the knowledge of reviewing. In that context:

"With the arising of perception" means with the arising of the perception of the fruit of arahantship; subsequently, there occurs the arising of the knowledge of reviewing, thinking, "This is the fruit of arahantship.
"Indeed, it is through this condition for me" means: "Indeed, through the condition of the perception of the fruition-concentration, the knowledge of reviewing has arisen for me.
Commentary on the Discussion of Perception as Self.

417. Now, just as a village pig, even if bathed in scented water, anointed with perfumes, adorned with garlands of flowers, and placed upon a royal couch, finds no pleasure but instead rushes back to the dung heap to find happiness;
even so, by means of the Blessed One’s teaching—which is struck through with the most subtle and delicate characteristics—[the wanderer found no peace].
Even though he was bathed, anointed, and adorned, and even though he was placed upon the noble bed of Nirodha, he found no happiness therein.
Taking his own view to be like a place of excrement, he questioned him alone, saying: "Venerable sir, is perception the self of a person?
and so forth. Then, having obtained his consent and wishing to explain, the Blessed One said: "But who..."
He said, "It is gross," and so forth. Then, although he held the view that "the self is formless," he thought, "The Blessed One is skilled in teaching;
let him not shatter my view from the very beginning," and thus, preserving his own position, he said, "It is gross," and so forth.
Thereupon, the Blessed One, pointing out the fault in that [view], said, "For it is gross for you," and so forth.
In this context, *evaṃ santaṃ* means "in such a state. This is an accusative case used in the sense of a locative.
Alternatively, the meaning here is: "to you who return to a self existing in such a state.
Because the four aggregates arise and cease simultaneously, although whatever perception arises is the very same that ceases, yet, by way of successive succession, "another perception... [arises].
“...other perceptions arise and other perceptions cease.
Having thus spoken, and after the fault in that [position] was pointed out, he stated, “I [am], venerable sir, mind-made,” and so forth;
yet even there, when the fault was given, just as one who is insane might grasp at something else as long as his own perception has not been established, so too did he proceed.
He answers one question while, at the time of establishing his perception, he speaks only what ought to be said;
in this very way, having grasped one thing and answered another, now speaking only according to his own tenet, he says, "Indeed, [the self] is formless," and so forth.
Even there, because he desires the arising and cessation of perception, yet conceives of the self as eternal, therefore for him it is just so.
Pointing out the fault, the Blessed One said, "Even though this is so," and so forth.

Then, because he was overcome by wrong view, the wanderer—failing to understand that diversity even as it was being explained by the Blessed One—said, "But is it possible for me, venerable sir," and so forth.
Thereupon, the Blessed One [spoke] to him because, although he was seeing the arising and ceasing of perception, he was still composed of perception (*saññāmaya*).
He conceives of himself as permanent. Therefore, he said, "It is indeed difficult to know," and so forth.
Herein, this is the summary of the meaning: Your view is one thing, your inclination is another, your preference is another;

your way of seeing has proceeded in one way alone, yet what is acceptable to you and what pleases you is quite different; your application is directed elsewhere, and [your conviction] is indeed toward something else.
“Being devoted to and engaged in the practice; and having that as your teacher’s instruction, and being a teacher in another sectarian fold.

Therefore, by you—who hold a different view, who have different inclinations, who have different preferences, who apply yourself differently, and who have a different teacher’s instruction—this is difficult to understand.
Then the wanderer said: “Whether perception is the self of a person, or whether perception is one thing and the self another...”
Thinking, "I shall ask him about such states as eternalism," he spoke again, beginning with, "But what, venerable sir?

and so forth. Therein, "the world" refers to the self. "For this, Poṭṭhapāda, is not conducive to welfare" means that this speculative view, Poṭṭhapāda, is not based on the welfare of this world or the next world, nor is it based on one's own welfare or the welfare of others. Not...

"Connected with the Dhamma" means not dependent on the nine supramundane states (*navalokuttaradhamma*). "Not pertaining to the beginning of the holy life" means it is not even the mere beginning of the holy life of the Dispensation, which consists of the three trainings;
it does not even amount to the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*).

"Not leading to disenchantment" means it does not conduce to disenchantment with the round of existence (*saṃsāra-vaṭṭa*). "Not leading to dispassion" means it does not conduce to dispassion toward the round of existence.

"Not for cessation" means it does not lead to the bringing about of the cessation of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*). "Not for peace" means it does not lead to the pacification of the round of existence.
"Not for direct knowledge" means it does not lead to the act of direct realization through the thorough understanding of the round of existence.
"Not for enlightenment" means it does not lead to the awakening to the round of existence. "Not for Nibbāna" means...
It does not lead to the direct realization of the deathless, great Nibbāna.
Regarding the passages beginning with "This is suffering": with the exception of craving, the five aggregates of the three planes are suffering;
because it is the source of that very suffering, craving together with its conditions is the origin of suffering. The non-occurrence of both is the cessation of suffering.
"The meaning is: 'The Noble Eightfold Path is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering,' thus have I declared.

Having spoken thus, the Blessed One thought, "There is neither the manifestation of the path nor the realization of the fruit for this wanderer, and it is my time for the alms-round," and he became silent. The wanderer, too, [perceived] that manner...
As if announcing the Blessed One’s time for departure, he said, "It is even so," and so forth.
(421) *Vācāsannitodakena* means by the goad of speech. *Sañjhabbharimakaṃsu* means they made it filled with joints, i.e., touched continuously;
it is said that they pierced it from above. *Bhūtaṃ* means existing by way of its own nature (*sabhāvato*). *Tacchaṃ*.
*Ta-tha* is a synonym for that very same thing. *Dhammaṭṭhitatā* refers to the established nature within the nine supramundane states.
*Dhammaniyāmatā* refers to the fixed order of the supramundane states. For there is no discourse of the Buddhas whatsoever that is divorced from the Four Noble Truths;
therefore, it is of such a nature.
Commentary on the Cases of Citta, Hatthisāriputta, and Poṭṭhapāda (422).
Regarding "Citta and Hatthisāriputta": it is said that he was the son of an elephant trainer in Sāvatthī.
Having gone forth in the presence of the Blessed One and mastered the Three Piṭakas, he became skilled in subtle points of meaning. Previously...
However, due to the commission of evil karma, he fell away seven times and was born as a householder.
It is said that during the dispensation of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa, there were two friends who were harmonious with one another and studied together.

One of them, becoming dissatisfied, conceived a desire for the life of a householder and informed the other. The latter [described] the disadvantage of the householder’s life and the excellence of the going-forth...
Having shown him the benefits, he instructed him. Having heard this and being delighted, on another day when a similar thought arose, he said to him:
"Friend, such a thought arises in me: 'I shall give these bowl and robes to you.
Out of greed for the bowl and robes, [the other] showed him the advantages of the householder's life and [dissuaded him] from the going-forth.
He spoke of the dangers [of the household life]. Upon hearing this, his mind became dispassionate toward the state of a householder and he took delight only in the going forth.

Thus, because the talk concerning the advantages of the household life had been spoken by a virtuous bhikkhu at that time, he has now gone forth on his seventh attempt after having fallen away six times. [This was] regarding Mahāmoggallāna and the Elder Mahākoṭṭhika.
And while they were discussing the Abhidhamma, he would interrupt their talk from time to time.
Then the Elder Mahākoṭṭhika rebuked him. Being unable to establish himself in what had been taught by the Great Disciple, he left the order and became a householder.
Now this man was a lay friend of Poṭṭhapāda; therefore, after he had left the order and two or three days had passed, [he went to] Poṭṭhapāda.
He went into his presence. Then, seeing him, [the Buddha] said, “Friend, what have you done? You have turned away from the teaching of such a Teacher as this!
Come now, it is fitting for you to go forth. Taking him with him, he went into the presence of the Blessed One.
Therefore it is said: “Citta Hatthisāriputta and the wanderer Poṭṭhapāda.”
423. "Blind" means they are blind because of the absence of the eye of wisdom (*paññācakkhu*); they are sightless due to its non-existence.
You alone among them are "possessed of eyes," being possessed of the eye of wisdom merely by virtue of knowing what is well-spoken and what is ill-spoken.
"One-sided" means having a single portion. "Established" means set forth. "Not one-sided" means not having a single portion; [they are] not by way of a single portion alone.
The meaning is that it was not stated whether [the world] is eternal or non-eternal.
Regarding the commentary on the categorical teachings (ekaṃsika-dhamma), verses 424–425:
Why did the Blessed One begin with the words, "There are, Poṭṭhapāda"? [It was] because of the goal (niṭṭhā) established by the outsiders.

It is for the purpose of showing that [their systems] do not lead to liberation. For all the various sectarians, just as the Blessed One does with regard to the deathless Nibbāna, likewise prescribe their own respective final goals by way of a "world-pinnacle" and so forth; yet that [goal] does not lead to liberation.
Having been prescribed in such a manner, it does not lead out or proceed; on the contrary, it is rejected by the wise and turns back.

To demonstrate this, the Blessed One spoke as follows: "In that regard, knowing and seeing the world of absolute happiness in the eastern direction, or in the western, or in any other direction—abide thus, knowing and seeing in this way.
For in that world, the bodily forms and other characteristics of human beings have been seen before. [The term] *appaṭihīraka* means...
"Without a basis for confidence" (*appaṭihīrakataṃ*) means devoid of a foundation; it is said to be "not leading to liberation.
426–427. "The most beautiful woman in the land" (*janapadakalyāṇī*) means one who is peerless among the women of the country in terms of complexion, physical form, grace, deportment, and so forth.
Commentary on the Three Attainments of Self (Tayo-attapaṭilābha-vaṇṇanā)

428. Thus, having shown that the final goal of others is not conducive to liberation, the Blessed One said, “There are three, Poṭṭhapāda,” and so forth, in order to show that his own final goal is indeed conducive to liberation.
In this context, “acquisition of a self” (*attapaṭilābha*) means the acquisition of a personal existence (*attabhāvapaṭilābha*).
And here, the Blessed One demonstrated the three realms of existence (*bhava*) by means of three acquisitions of personal existence. By the acquisition of a gross personal existence...
He showed the realm of sensual existence (*kāmadhātu*), beginning from the Avīci hell and ending with the Paranimmitavasavatti heaven.
By means of obtaining a mind-made body (*manomayakāya*), he showed the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), beginning from the level of the first jhāna and ending with the Akaniṭṭha Brahmā-world.
By means of obtaining an immaterial body (*arūpakāya*), [he showed] beginning from the Ākāsānañcāyatana Brahmā-world and ending with the Nevasaññānāsaññāyatana Brahmā-world.

He showed the formless existence (*arūpabhava*). "Defiled phenomena" (*saṃkilesikā dhammā*) refers to the twelve unwholesome types of consciousness. "Purifying phenomena" (*vodāniyā dhammā*) refers to serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).

"The fulfillment and abundance of wisdom" (*paññāpāripūriṃ vepullattaṃ*) means both the fulfillment and the vastness of the wisdom of the path (*magga-paññā*) and the wisdom of the fruit (*phala-paññā*).
*Pāmujjanti* means youthful joy (*taruṇapīti*). *Pīti* means powerful gladness (*balavatuṭṭhi*). What is meant [by this]?

Regarding what we said—“having realized it for himself through direct knowledge, he enters and dwells in it”—for one dwelling thus, there will be that very joy (*pāmojja*) and rapture (*pīti*), as well as tranquility of the mental body (*nāmakāyapassaddhi*), mindfulness well-established (*sati sūpaṭṭhitā*), supreme knowledge (*uttamajāṇa*), and bliss (*sukha*).
This is a dwelling. And among all dwellings, it alone is rightly called "blissful," for it is "peaceful and supremely sweet.
In that regard, in the first jhāna, all six factors beginning with joy (pāmojja) are obtained;
in the second jhāna, joy in the sense of weak rapture (pīti) ceases, while the remaining five are obtained; in the third, rapture (pīti) ceases, while the remaining four are obtained.
Likewise in the fourth [jhāna]. Among these four jhānas, in the *Sampasādanīya Sutta*, only pure insight (*suddhavipassanā*) together with the foundational jhāna (*pādakajjhāna*) is mentioned.
In the *Pāsādika Sutta*, insight is mentioned along with the four paths (*magga*).

In the *Dasuttara Sutta*, the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) belonging to the fourth jhāna is mentioned. In this *Poṭṭhapāda Sutta*, "gladness" (*pāmojja*) is indeed a synonym for "rapture" (*pīti*).
It should be understood that this is called the attainment of fruition belonging to the second jhāna.
432–437. Regarding the phrase "or this is it": here the word *vā* has the sense of "clarifying" (*vibhāvana*).
Having thus clarified and made manifest, we would declare: "Is it as others say: 'Perceive the self as exclusively happy'? To which they reply, "No."
"They say"—the meaning is "I do not speak thus. "Possessing a miracle" (*sappāṭihīraka*) means having a demonstration;
the meaning is "leading to liberation. "It becomes vain" means it becomes empty; the intention is that on that occasion, such [a person] does not exist. "It becomes true" means it becomes real;
the meaning is that on that occasion, only he [who speaks thus] is true. Here, however, this Citta [says this] because of his own lack of omniscience.

Having explained the three kinds of acquisition of a self (*attapaṭilābha*), he was unable to extract the point that what is called "acquisition of a self" is merely a conceptual designation (*paññattimatta*);

rather, he concluded by teaching it simply as "acquisition of a self. Then the Blessed One, wishing to show him that here the phenomena are form and so forth, while "acquisition of a self" is a mere name, and that such conventional expressions arise when those respective forms and so forth exist, [spoke] to him...
Having grasped [the meaning] by way of designation (*nāmapaññatti*), he spoke the words beginning with "At whatever time, O Citta," for the purpose of handing it over.
And having spoken thus, for the purpose of instructing by means of a counter-question, he spoke again the words beginning with "If they were to ask you this, Citta.
Therein, that acquisition of a self (*attapaṭilābha*) which was mine in the past—that very acquisition of a self was mine at that time; it was real.
Regarding the statement, "The past was vain, the future is vain, the present is vain," this is what is shown here:
because those past phenomena do not exist now, but have gone by the name of "they were," therefore that acquisition of a self of mine was real at that very time.
However, because future and present phenomena did not exist then, at that [time]...
At that time, [he said], "The future is vain, the present is vain," thus he acknowledges the acquisition of a self as being merely a name in terms of its meaning.
The same method applies to the future and the present as well.
Then the Blessed One, in order to reconcile his own explanation with that person's explanation, said: "In this very way..."
Having spoken thus with the words "O Citta," and so forth, he spoke again—"Just as, O Citta, from a cow comes milk"—and so on, establishing that meaning by means of a simile.
Herein, this is the summary of the meaning: just as milk comes from a cow, and curds and so forth come from milk and the rest;
therein, at whatever time there is milk, at that time there is neither curd nor any one of the others, such as butter.
It comes to be reckoned as a number, a term, a name, and a designation. Why? Because of the absence of those factors upon which the designations "curd" and so forth depend.
Rather, at that time, it is only milk that comes to be reckoned as such. Why?
Because of the presence of those factors upon which the number, term, name, and designation "milk" depends. This is the same [for all].
This principle applies everywhere. These, O Citta, are called the gross acquisition of self, the mind-made acquisition of self, and the formless acquisition of self.
These, O Citta, are merely worldly designations, mere worldly conventions, and mere acknowledgments.
Likewise, they are merely worldly expressions, merely paths of speech, and merely modes of common usage.
"These are merely designations by name. Thus, having previously explained the three ways of acquiring a self, the Blessed One now states that all this is merely conventional usage.
Why? Because, in the ultimate sense, there is no such thing as a "being";
this world is empty and void.

The Buddhas’ discourse, however, is twofold: conventional discourse (*sammuti-kathā*) and ultimate discourse (*paramattha-kathā*). Therein, such expressions as “a being,” “a person,” “a god,” and “a Brahmā” are called conventional discourse.

Such expressions as “impermanence, suffering, non-self,” “the aggregates, elements, bases,” and “the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts” are called ultimate discourse. Among these, that which belongs to the teaching of convention...
When one says "a being," or "a person," or "a god," or "Brahmā," [the listener] is able to understand, penetrate, proceed toward,

and attain the victory of Arahantship; for such a person, the Blessed One speaks from the very beginning as "a being," or "a person," or "a god," or "Brahmā," whereas for one who is [ready] for the teaching of the ultimate truth, he speaks of it as "impermanent" or "suffering."

Having heard one of the teachings beginning with "impermanence" (vāti-ādi), if a person is able to understand, penetrate, proceed toward, and attain the victory of Arahantship, [the teacher] speaks to him only of one of those things such as "impermanence" or "suffering.

Likewise, for a being who awakens through conventional discourse (sammutikathā), he does not first speak of the ultimate truth (paramatthakathā). Rather, having awakened them through conventional discourse, [he subsequently teaches the ultimate truth].
Afterwards, he speaks on the ultimate truth (*paramattha*). Even for a being who is to be awakened by a discourse on the ultimate truth, he does not first speak on conventional truth (*sammuti*).
Rather, having awakened them through a discourse on the ultimate truth, he subsequently speaks on conventional truth.
However, for one who would naturally speak on the ultimate truth first, the teaching becomes harsh in its manner; therefore—
The Buddhas first speak discourses on conventional reality and afterwards speak discourses on ultimate reality.

Even when speaking discourses on conventional reality, they speak only what is true, only what is factual, and only what is not false. Even when speaking discourses on ultimate reality, they speak only what is true, only what is factual, and only what is not false.
The Fully Awakened One, the best among speakers, has proclaimed two truths:
the conventional and the ultimate; a third is not found.
Conventional speech is true by reason of worldly consensus.
"The ultimate meaning (paramatthavacana) is the truth, the actual characteristic of phenomena.

Having turned back the teaching by means of those worldly conventions and worldly designations through which the Tathāgata speaks— speaking without misapprehending because he is free from the misapprehensions of craving,
conceit, and views— he brought it to its conclusion with the pinnacle of Arahantship.
The remainder is clear in meaning throughout.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Poṭṭhapāda-sutta* in the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, the commentary on the *Dīgha Nikāya*.
10. Commentary on the Subha Sutta:
Commentary on the Case of the Young Man Subha 444.
“Thus have I heard... at Sāvatthī” is the Subha Sutta. Herein, this is the commentary on the words not [previously] explained. Not long after he had attained final Nibbāna...
"Bhagavatī" refers to the time when the Blessed One had recently attained final nibbāna, at a period of only one month after his passing.

This was said with reference to the day he sat in the monastery after having come bringing the Blessed One’s bowl and robes, and having drunk a milk-purgative, according to the method described in the *Nidānavaṇṇanā*.
"Todeyyaputta" means the son of the brahmin Todeyya; it is said that he...
Not far from Sāvatthī there was a village named Tudigāma; because he was its chief, he came to be known as Todeyya.
He was very wealthy, possessing a fortune of four hundred and fifty million, yet he was extremely stingy.
Thinking, "There is no such thing as an inexhaustible store of wealth for one who gives," he gave nothing to anyone. Even to his own son, he said:
“Having seen the exhaustion of collyrium, the accumulation of anthills,
and the gathering of honey, the wise man should dwell at home.
Having thus instructed him in non-giving alone, [the deity] was reborn as a dog in that very house upon the dissolution of his body.
Subha cherished that dog exceedingly. He fed it with the very food he himself ate and, lifting it up, had it lie upon his excellent couch.
Then one day, when the young brahmin had gone out, the Blessed One entered that house for alms.
Seeing the Blessed One, the dog went toward him, making a "bhukkāra" sound. Then—
The Blessed One said to him, "Todeyya, because you previously insulted me by calling me 'Ho! Ho!', you were reborn as a dog;
now too, by making this sound of 'bhuk', you shall go to Avīci. Hearing these words, the dog became remorseful and lay down upon the ashes inside the hearth.
When people tried to lift him up and place him on a bed, they were unable to do so.
Subha arrived and asked, "By whom was this dog removed from its bed? The people replied, "By no one," and reported what had happened.
Upon hearing this, the young man became angry, thinking, "My father has been reborn in the Brahma-world, yet the ascetic Gotama treats my father like a dog;
whatever comes to his mouth, he speaks. And so he addressed the Blessed One.
Desiring to reproach him with false speech, he went to the monastery and asked about that matter. Having told him exactly as it was, the Blessed One said, for the sake of not being deceptive:
"But, young man, is there any wealth that was not mentioned by your father?
"There is, Master Gotama: a golden garland worth a hundred thousand, golden sandals worth a hundred thousand, and [a parasol] worth a hundred thousand."
"A golden bowl and a hundred thousand kahāpaṇas. "Go, feed that dog with honeyed milk-rice mixed with little water, place him on his bed, and question him when he has fallen into a slight sleep;
he will tell you everything, and then you will know: 'This is my father. He did exactly so. The dog told him everything, and then—
Having understood, "He is my father," and with a mind full of faith toward the Blessed One, he went to the Blessed One and asked fourteen questions;
at the conclusion of the answers, he went for refuge to the Blessed One. It was with reference to him that it was said, "The young brahmin Subha, son of Todeyya.
"He dwells in Sāvatthī" means he lives there after having come from his own village of wealth.

445–446. He addressed a certain young man: having heard that after the Teacher had attained final nibbāna, "the Elder Ānanda has indeed come taking his bowl and robes, and the great multitude is approaching to see him," [he thought], "Now, having gone to the monastery in the midst of the great multitude, it will not be possible to easily perform a friendly greeting or deliver a discourse on the Dhamma."
Thinking, “When he comes to my house to hear [the Dhamma], I shall welcome him with ease;
furthermore, I have a certain doubt, and I will ask him about it,” he addressed a certain young brahmin. Regarding the words beginning with *appābādha*:
*ābādha* refers to discordant sensations (*visabhāga-vedanā*) which, having arisen in one part of the body, [restrain] the four postures as if with an iron band.
He says: "As if having bound it, he takes hold of it; ask about its absence. "Free from affliction" (*appātaṅka*) refers to a disease that makes life difficult;
he says: "Ask about the absence of even that. For one who is ill, rising up is indeed heavy;
there is no strength in the body. Therefore, he says: "Ask about the state of being free from illness and about strength. "Living at ease" (*phāsuvihāra*)—
He says, "He asks about his dwelling in comfort during the four postures: walking, standing, sitting, and lying down.
Then, showing the manner in which he should be questioned, [the Blessed One] said, "Subho," and so forth.
"Having taken into account the time and the occasion" means having grasped and reflected upon the time and the occasion through wisdom.
The meaning is this: "If it should be our time to go tomorrow, strength will pervade our bodies and there will be no other discomfort on account of the journey;
therefore, having considered both the time and the occasion—which is the convergence of the causes for going—[we thought], 'Perhaps we might indeed come tomorrow. This is what was said.
448. By the bhikkhu Cetiya: because he was born in the kingdom of Ceti, he was thus named Cetiya. "A conversation conducive to amity and recollection":
"O Ānanda, what indeed was the illness of the One Possessed of the Ten Powers? What did the Blessed One consume?
Moreover, sorrow has arisen in you all because of the Teacher’s final nibbāna; for the Teacher is not merely yours alone."
"He has attained final Nibbāna, a great loss for the world with its devas! Who now shall be released from death?
Where that Supreme Person among the world with its devas has attained final Nibbāna, whom else will the King of Death now look upon with shame?
Having thus concluded this pleasant and memorable conversation connected with death, he [addressed] the Elder...
Having given food appropriate to the medicine he had drunk the previous day, he sat down to one side at the conclusion of his meal.
"An attendant who stays near" means being an attendant and remaining in close proximity, not seeking out faults.

"Not with the intention of investigation" means not with the purpose of testing him. "One who moves about nearby" is a synonym for the preceding phrase. Why does he ask, "For whom is that venerable Gotama [staying]?"?

It is said that this thought occurred to him: "Regarding those teachings upon which Master Gotama established this world, have they perished in his absence, or do they still endure? If they endure, Ānanda will know;
let me ask him. Therefore, he asked.
449. Then the Elder, presenting the three Piṭakas by grouping them into three aggregates, spoke the words beginning with “Of the three.
Not perceiving what had been stated in brief, the young man thought, “I shall ask for details,” and spoke the words beginning with “Of which three?
Commentary on the Aggregate of Virtue (Sīlakkhandha)

450–453. Then, when the Elder had pointed them out with the words, "The noble aggregate of virtue," the other asked again regarding each one: "But what, Master Ānanda, is that noble aggregate of virtue?
The Elder, showing him the arising of the Buddha and teaching the Dhamma of the lineage, answered everything in due order according to the method spoken by the Blessed One. Therein—
"There is indeed more to be done here": herein, in the Blessed One’s teaching, it is not virtue alone that is the essence;
rather, this is merely the foundation. He showed that there is indeed something else to be accomplished beyond this.
"Outside of this" means outside of the Buddha's teaching.
The Exposition of the Aggregate of Concentration (Samādhikkhandhavaṇṇanā). 454.

And as for the passage, "How, young man, is a bhikkhu one who guards the doors of the sense-faculties?", this was said by the Venerable Ānanda even when he was asked about the aggregate of concentration, [the young man] having asked: "But what, Master Ānanda, is that noble aggregate of concentration? regarding those [faculties] which...

“Endowed with virtue, guarding the doors of the sense faculties, possessed of mindfulness and clear comprehension, and contented”—thus, immediately after virtue, the factors beginning with restraint of the sense faculties were listed as qualities that assist both virtue and concentration in their interval.

Having explained those, [the author], wishing to demonstrate the aggregate of concentration (*samādhikkhandha*), began [this section]. And here, only the fine-material jhānas (*rūpajjhāna*) [are intended].
They have not been included; rather, the formless attainments (*arūpa-jhāna*) must be brought forward and explained.
For there is no such thing as a formless attainment that is not comprised within the fourth jhāna. 471–480.
Regarding the phrase "there is still more to be done," herein, in the Blessed One’s teaching, one does not [attain the goal] by mere one-pointedness of mind alone.
There is indeed such a thing as reaching the conclusion; however, this shows that there is still something else to be done beyond this.

By the phrase "there is nothing further to be done here," he shows that within the Blessed One’s dispensation, there is truly nothing more to be accomplished, for the Blessed One’s dispensation culminates in Arahantship. The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
Thus ends the commentary on the Subha Sutta in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya. 11.
Commentary on the Kevaṭṭa Sutta.
Commentary on the Discourse to Kevaṭṭa the Householder’s Son 481.
“Thus have I heard... at Nāḷandā” refers to the Kevaṭṭa Sutta. Herein, this is the commentary on the words not previously explained.

“In the mango grove of the robe-dealer” means in the mango grove belonging to a robe-dealer. “Kevaṭṭa” is the name of that householder’s son; it is said that he possessed a fortune of four hundred million.
The wealthy householder was exceedingly faithful and confident. Because his faith was so predominant, he thought:

"If even a single bhikkhu were to fly through the air every half-month, or every month, or every year, and display various miracles, all the people would become even more deeply confident. What if I were to request the Blessed One to perform a miracle?"
Having thought, "I should have one bhikkhu authorized [to go]," he approached the Blessed One and spoke thus.
In that context, "prosperous" (*iddhā*) means well-flourishing; "thriving" (*phītā*) means having reached growth due to being crowded with various goods.
"Crowded with people" (*ākiṇṇamanussā*) means filled with people moving about as if shoulder-to-shoulder. "Let him direct" (*samādisatu*) means let him command.

To establish [him] in a position. "Superhuman states" (*uttarimanussadhamma*) means: from the perspective of the states of supermen, or as being superior to the human states consisting of the ten wholesome courses of action.
"To an even greater degree" (*bhiyyosomattāya*): just as a lamp that is already burning naturally becomes even more radiant upon receiving oil, so too will he become exceedingly serene.
"Indeed, it was not I," said the Blessed One, in reference to the story of the merchant of Rājagaha.
He laid down a training rule; therefore, he said, "Indeed, I do not," and so forth.

482. "I do not destroy" means I do not destroy by way of destroying his virtues; having brought about a breach of morality, I do not place him in a low position by gradually causing him to fall from a high station.
Rather, it is because I am desiring the growth of the Buddha's dispensation.
He shows how this was so. "For a third time" means that up to three times there was no one capable of replying to the Buddhas' speech.
However, this [Māra], being a trusted friend to the Blessed One, having increased their mutual confidence and become a favorite, spoke three times, saying, "I am well-wishing."
Commentary on the Miracle of Psychic Power (Iddhipāṭihāriyavaṇṇanā) 483–484.
Then the Blessed One thought: “Even though I am warding him off, this lay follower continues to entreat me again and again.
Let me show him the disadvantage in performing a miracle. Having reflected thus, he said, “There are three...,” and so forth. In that context, *amāhaṃ*...
"Bhikkhunī" refers to that nun. "Gandhārī" is a science (vijjā) composed by the seer named Gandhāra, or it is a science that arose in the kingdom of Gandhāra.
The intended meaning is that many seers lived there, and it was composed by one among them.
"I am distressed" means I feel as if I am oppressed. "I am ashamed" means I feel shame. "I am loathsome" means I experience a sense of disgust, as if I had seen excrement.
Commentary on the Miracle of Declaration (Ādesanāpāṭihāriya) 485.
*Parasattānaṃ* means "of other beings. *Dutiyaṃ* is a synonym for that same term. *Ādisati* means "he declares" or "he speaks.
*Cetasikaṃ* refers here to mental joy (*somanassa*) and mental grief (*domanassa*). *Evampi te mano* means "in this way your mind is joyful."
Or [it is] dejected, or associated with sensual thought (*kāmavitakka*) and so forth. The second [term] is a synonym for that very same thing.
"Thus is your mind" (*iti te cittaṃ*): the meaning is that your mind proceeds while contemplating this and that object.
There is a certain science (*vijjā*) in the world known as the "Wish-fulfilling Gem" (*cintāmaṇi*). He illustrates that by means of it, one knows the minds of others.
Commentary on the Miracle of Instruction (Anusāsanīpāṭihāriyavaṇṇanā):
"Think thus": think by setting forth thoughts of renunciation and so forth in this manner. "Do not think thus":
do not set forth thoughts of sensual desire and so forth in this manner. "Attend thus": attend precisely to the perception of impermanence in this manner.
Or, attend to one of the perceptions such as that of suffering. Do not attend to it in this way—do not attend to it by way of [perceiving it as] "permanent" and so forth.
"This": abandon this lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure. "Having entered upon this":
having entered upon, attained, and accomplished this very supramundane state distinguished by the four paths and fruits, dwell therein.

Thus the Blessed One shows that the various kinds of supernormal power (*iddhividha*) are the miracle of supernormal power (*iddhipāṭihāriya*); speaking after having known another’s mind is the miracle of mind-reading (*ādesanāpāṭihāriya*);
and the constant teaching of the Dhamma by both disciples and Buddhas is the miracle of instruction (*anusāsanīpāṭihāriya*).
Among these, the miracle of instruction was the habitual practice of Mahāmoggallāna through the miracle of supernormal power, and [the miracle of mind-reading] through the miracle of mind-reading.

The miracle of instruction belongs to the General of the Dhamma. When Devadatta had split the Saṅgha and was teaching the Dhamma to five hundred bhikkhus at Gayāsīsa with the grace of a Buddha, the two chief disciples sent by the Blessed One—of whom the General of the Dhamma was one—understood the mental dispositions of those monks and taught them the Dhamma.
Having heard the Elder’s teaching of the Dhamma...
Five hundred bhikkhus were established in the fruit of stream-entry.
Then Mahāmoggallāna, repeatedly displaying his supernormal powers, taught them the Dhamma; having heard it, they all became established in the fruit of arhatship.
Then the two great Nāgas, taking those five hundred bhikkhus with them, rose into the air and returned to the Veḷuvana.
The miracle of instruction (*anusāsanī-pāṭihāriya*), however, is the Buddhas’ constant teaching of the Dhamma.

Among these, the miracles of psychic power (*iddhi-pāṭihāriya*) and of mind-reading (*ādesanā-pāṭihāriya*) involve provocation and possess faults; they do not endure for long, and because they do not endure for long, they do not lead to liberation.
The miracle of instruction, however, is free from provocation and faultless; it endures for long, and because it endures for long—

It leads out. Therefore, the Blessed One censures both the miracle of psychic power (*iddhipāṭihāriya*) and the miracle of mind-reading (*ādesanāpāṭihāriya*), and praises only the miracle of instruction (*anusāsanīpāṭihāriya*).
487. As for the phrase "In the past" (*bhūtapubba*):
why was this undertaken by the Blessed One? [It was] regarding the miracles of psychic power and the miracle of mind-reading.

It is for the purpose of showing that [the former] is not conducive to deliverance, and for the purpose of showing that the miracle of instruction (*anusāsanī-pāṭihāriya*) alone is conducive to deliverance.
Furthermore, there is always one monk among all Buddhas named Mahābhūtapariyesaka;

while searching for the great elements, he wandered as far as the Brahma-world, and having failed to find anyone who could answer him, he returned and questioned the Buddha alone, thereby becoming free from doubt.

It is so. Therefore, for the purpose of manifesting the greatness of the Buddhas, and because this reason was concealed, the Blessed One, even while teaching after having revealed it, said: "In the past... and so forth.
Therein, "Where indeed? means in what place; "having come to what, having attained what" refers to [the state] of those for whom [defilements] have ceased entirely through the mode of non-arising.
They cease. Furthermore, this discussion on the great primary elements has been explained in every aspect in the *Visuddhimagga*; therefore, it should be understood from that very source. 488.
As for the "divine path," there is no separate path called the way to the world of the devas; rather, this is a designation for the knowledge of the modes of supernormal power (*iddhividhañāṇa*).
For by means of that, one exercises mastery over the body even as far as the Brahma-world, [reaching] the world of the devas.

It goes. Therefore it is said, "That is the path leading to the gods. Thinking, "The deities possess great power," he approached [the Blessed One], even though the Blessed One was standing nearby in the realm of the Four Great Kings, having been prompted by the natural order of things without being asked.
"We too, monk, do not know"—thus the deities, having been questioned regarding a matter within the domain of a Buddha, do not know.
Therefore they spoke thus. Then that bhikkhu, thinking, "It is not right for me not to explain this question;
let us speak quickly," overwhelmed those deities and asked them again and again.
Thinking, "This bhikkhu is overwhelming us; come now, we shall release him from our hands," they said, "There are, bhikkhu, the four Great Kings," and so forth.
In this context, "more excellent" (*abhikkantatara*) means more desirable by surpassing [others]. "More sublime" (*paṇītatarā*) means superior in terms of complexion, fame, sovereignty, and so forth.
In this manner, the meaning should be understood in all sections. 491–493.
However, this is the distinction: it is said that Sakka, the king of the gods, thought, "This question is within the domain of the Buddha."

"It is not possible for anyone else to answer this; moreover, this bhikkhu wanders about abandoning the Supreme Person in the world, the Fully Enlightened One, asking questions of deities like one who discards a firefly to blow on a glowworm, or like one who abandons a drum to beat his belly.
I shall send him into the presence of the Teacher. Then he thought once more: "Even if it is very far..."
"Having gone into the presence of the Teacher, he will become free from doubt. There is indeed such a person as this;

let him wander about for a short while and grow weary, and afterwards he will know. Then he said to him, "I too," and so forth. The path leading to Brahmā (brahmayāniya) is similar to the path leading to the gods (devayāniya).
Whether it is called the path leading to the gods, the path leading to Brahmā, or the bridge of Dhamma, it is absorption lasting for a single moment of consciousness (ekacittakkhaṇika-appanā).
Whether it be "decisive volition," "lofty consciousness," or "knowledge of direct knowledge"—all these are merely names for the knowledge of the modes of psychic power (*iddhividha-ñāṇa*).
"Omen" (*pubbanimitta*) means a sign occurring prior to the arrival, like the dawn preceding the rising of the sun.
Therefore, they indicated: "Now Brahmā will surely come; thus do we know. "Pāturahosi" means he became manifest.
It happened thus. Then that Brahmā, being questioned by that bhikkhu, recognized his own lack of jurisdiction and thought:

"If I say, 'I do not know,' these people will despise me; yet if I say something as though I knew, this bhikkhu, displeased by my explanation, will launch a challenge against me. "I am here, bhikkhu..."
"But if I were to say 'I am Brahmā' and so forth, no one would believe my words.
What if I were to create a diversion and send this bhikkhu directly into the presence of the Teacher? Thinking thus, he said, "Bhikkhu, I am Brahmā," and so on.

495–496. Why did he act in this way by leading him aside? Because of his deceitfulness. He engaged in an external search as far as the Brahma-world, like one seeking oil who, when sand is being pressed, reaches out for something else entirely.

497. "They can catch a crow or a hawk. "This question, bhikkhu, should not be asked in this way"—the Blessed One said this because that question should have been asked with specific reference to a particular case, whereas this bhikkhu, taking even what is not clung-to (anupādinnaka), asks it without such specification;
therefore, he rejects it. Indeed, it is the custom of the Buddhas [to address one] who is confused about a question.
Having shown the fault in questioning by the public and having instructed them on how to question, [the Buddha] gave the answer to the question.
Why? Because one who asks questions without knowing how to do so becomes difficult to instruct. When instructing them on the inquiry, he said: "Where does water not find a footing? and so forth. 498.
In that context, "it does not find a footing" means it does not stand firm; having come to what, do these four great elements lack a foundation?
The meaning is "they exist. He asks this referring specifically to what is clung-to (*upādinna*).
"Long and short" refers to derived matter (*upādārūpa*) by way of its configuration. "Subtle and gross" means small or large;
by this too, only the color-aspect of derived matter is spoken of. "Beautiful and ugly" refers to both beautiful and ugly derived matter itself. But what, then, is derived matter?
"Are there beautiful things and ugly things? "No, there are not. However, what was spoken of were merely desirable and undesirable objects.
"Name-and-form": name and form divided into long and so forth. "Is ceased" means it ceases; "depending on what does all this cease to proceed?"—this is how the question should be asked.
Having thus shown the question, he now shows the answer by saying, "The explanation here is as follows," and then states, "Consciousness," and so forth.
499. Therein, "to be cognized" (*viññātabba*) refers to consciousness; this is a name for Nibbāna.
Because it lacks any visible manifestation, it is "invisible" (*anidassana*). Because it has no arising, no passing away, and no alteration while standing, it is "boundless" (*ananta*).
Furthermore, it is said that *pabha* is a name for a bathing place (*tittha*); for it is a "bathing place" (*papa*) because beings descend (*papanti*) into it. However, regarding the letter *pa*...
The letter *bh* has been changed [to *p*]. "Shining from all sides" means *sabbatopabhaṃ*.

It is said that for Nibbāna—just as for the great ocean, wherever people wish to descend, that very place is a landing-place (*tittha*), and there is no such thing as a non-landing-place (*atittha*)—even so, among the thirty-eight meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*), whichever door one wishes to use to descend into Nibbāna, that very door is a landing-place; for Nibbāna...
There is no such thing as a non-crossing place; therefore it is said, “radiant on all sides.

Here, in the phrase “and water,” it means that by coming to this *nibbāna*, the entire collection of conditioned phenomena (*upādinnaka-dhammajāta*) described in the manner beginning with “all this is water” ceases and comes to an end.
Now, showing the means for its cessation, he says: “By the cessation of consciousness, herein this is brought to an end.”

In this context, "consciousness" refers to both the final consciousness and the formative consciousness (*abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa*). For by the cessation of the final consciousness, this [stream of existence] is brought to an end here;
it passes into a state of non-designation (*apaṇṇattika-bhāva*), like the flame of an extinguished lamp.
By the non-arising and cessation of the formative consciousness, it is brought to an end through its non-arising. As it has been said: "By the knowledge of the path of stream-entry..."

"By the cessation of the consciousness of volitional formations, name-and-form—which would otherwise arise throughout the beginningless round of existence across the seven realms of being—cease right here.
All this is to be understood according to the method explained in the *Cūḷaniddesa*.
The rest is clear everywhere.
Thus ends the commentary on the Kevaṭṭa Sutta in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya. 12.
Commentary on the Lohicca Sutta.
The Exposition of the Story of the Brahmin Lohicca (Lohiccabrāhmaṇavatthuvaṇṇanā).
501. Thus have I heard... [pe] ...among the Kosalans: this is the Lohicca Sutta. Herein, this is the commentary on the words not already explained.
"Sālavatikā" is the name of that village; it is said that it was surrounded on all sides by a row of *sāla* trees as if by a fence (*vati*). Therefore—
It is called Sālavatikā. Lohicca is the name of that brahmin. 502–503.
"Evil" means base, because it is devoid of compassion for others; it does not refer to either annihilationism or eternalism.
"Has arisen" means it has been born, and it is not merely born in the mind alone. It is said that by its power...
He speaks exactly thus even in the midst of an assembly. For what can one person do for another?
That is to say, what will he who is being instructed do for his instructor? He says that one should dwell having honored and revered the wholesome state (dhamma) attained by oneself alone.
504–407. "He addressed the barber Rosika": he addressed the barber who had received the name Rosika by way of the feminine gender.
It is said that having heard of the Blessed One’s arrival, he thought: "It would be a burden to go to the monastery and see him;
however, if I send word to my home, I shall both see him and give alms to the visiting monks according to my means."
Therefore, he addressed the barber in this way:
"508. 'Following closely behind' means following right after him for the sake of conversational ease. 'Let him disentangle' means let him release;
he says this so that [the listener] may dispel that adherence to views. It is said that this lay follower [was formerly] of the brahmin Lohicca."
He was a companion in virtue. Therefore, out of a desire for his welfare, he spoke thus. Regarding the phrase "Perhaps it might be so":
with the first statement, the Blessed One roars; with the second statement, he roars in response. This, it is said, is the intended meaning here:
"O Rosika, it was for this very purpose that I, practicing various difficult austerities for four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons, fulfilled the perfections."
"This [wisdom] has been fulfilled; it was for this very purpose that omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) was penetrated.
It is not a burden for me to shatter the speculative view of Lohicca"—showing this meaning, the Blessed One roars with his first speech.
Whether there be merely the coming of the irritant Lohicca into my presence, or his sitting down, or even conversation and discussion, should there be those like Lohicca...

It should be understood that with his second statement, the Blessed One roars in response, demonstrating this meaning: "There is doubt regarding a hundred thousand [questions], yet I am capable of dispelling them; but what burden is it for me to dispel the view of a single Lohicca?
This concludes the commentary on the inquiry of the brahmin Lohicca.
509. *Samudayasañjāti*: the arising of the collection (*samudaya*), which is the production of wealth;
the meaning is that from this arise riches and grain. *Ye taṃ upajīvantīti*: those people—relatives, attendants, slaves, laborers, and so forth—who live depending upon that.
*Antarāyakaro*: one who creates an obstacle to gain. *Hitānukampī*: here, "benefit" (*hita*) means growth. *Anukampatīti*: he feels compassion for them.
"Compassionate" means he desires; it is said that he either desires growth or does not. "Either to hell or to the animal realm" means:
if that wrong view becomes established, it becomes fixed, and he is reborn in hell with certainty;
if not, he is reborn in the animal realm—this is the meaning.

510–512. Now, since beings are not as afflicted by obstacles to their own gain as they are by those of others, the Blessed One, desiring to bestow [the gift] upon the brahmin even more effectively, stated the second reason, beginning with "What do you think? Those who...
refers to those who, having heard the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma, were unable to enter the plane of the Noble Ones (ariyabhūmi).
“Noble sons, divine wombs” (*dibbā gabbhā*): this is the accusative case used in the sense of the locative; the meaning is “in the divine wombs.
Both “divine” (*dibbā*) and “wombs” (*gabbhā*) are designations for the six celestial worlds.

“They bring to maturity” means that those who fulfill the practice leading to the celestial worlds—by giving gifts, by observing moral discipline, by making offerings with perfumes, garlands, and so forth, and by practicing meditation—bring [beings] to maturity.
While being cultivated, they cook, ripen, bring to full maturity, and lead to transformation. "For the production of divine existences" (*dibbānaṃ bhavānaṃ abhinibbattiya*):

"divine existences" refers to the celestial mansions (*vimāna*) of the devas; the meaning is "for the sake of their production. Alternatively, "divine wombs" (*dibbā gabbhā*) refers to specific meritorious deeds such as giving and so forth.
"Divine existences" (*dibbā bhavā*) refers to the resultant aggregates (*vipākakkhandha*) in the world of the devas; [the phrase means] "for the sake of their production."

The meaning is: "They perform those meritorious deeds. "An obstacle-maker for them" means an obstacle-maker for their attainment of the path, their attainment of the fruit, and the distinctions of divine existence.

Thus, having by this much broken the Brahmin’s pride—which had risen as high as the peak of existence—by means of an unqualified method of illustration, the Blessed One now said, "There are three, Lohicca," and so forth, in order to show the three teachers who are worthy of censure.
The Commentary on the Three Worthy of Censure (Codanāraha) 513.
Therein, "that censure" refers to the censure of one who censures three types of teachers.

"They do not establish the mind for the sake of another" means they do not establish the mind for the purpose of understanding another [teaching]. "Transgressing" means [transgressing] his teaching continuously.

The meaning is that they proceed after having departed from there without having performed [the formal act]. "Or he might approach her while she is withdrawing" means he might approach her as she is retreating;
he might desire her though she does not desire it; what is meant is that a single man might desire union with a woman who does not desire it.
"Or he might embrace her when she has her back turned" means [he embraces] one who does not even wish to be seen and stands with her back turned.
"Having gone behind, one might embrace her. "In the same way, this" means:

even while these disciples of this Teacher have departed from the Dispensation—despite his saying, "These are my disciples"—and are conducting themselves [otherwise], I say that this very dhamma of greed with which he instructs them out of greed is "in the same way," that is, exactly like this. Thus, such is your dhamma of greed, by which you, while she is shrinking back, are reaching out toward her.
It is also worthy of that reproach to say, "He was as if embracing her while she stood with her back turned. For what can one person do for another?
One should first apply to oneself that same principle by which one instructs others; make yourself upright.
It is worthy of reproach to say, "For what can one person do for another?"
514. "It should be smoothed down" means that the grasses which have the appearance of blades should be pulled out and made perfectly clean.

515. Regarding the third admonition: "For what can one do for another?"—from the moment one does not accept the instruction, the other person should be instructed; for what will it avail the instructor of the other? Is there not, in that case, freedom from concern?
The meaning is that he "deserves admonition" because, having attained it, he should dwell having honored and worshipped the Dhamma penetrated by himself alone.
516. Regarding "he does not deserve admonition":
for this Teacher, having first established himself in what is appropriate, [then instructs] the disciples.
He teaches the Dhamma. His disciples, being obedient, practice according to his instructions and, through that practice, attain great distinction.
Therefore, he does not deserve censure. 517.
"Falling into the abyss of hell" means: "I am falling into the abyss of hell because of the view I have adopted."

"Having pulled out and established on dry land" means: having shattered that wrong view, he says, "With the hand of the Dhamma-teaching, I have pulled [the person] from the state of falling into the woeful states and established them on the dry land of the path to heaven. The rest here is self-evident.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, the commentary on the *Dīghanikāya*.
The commentary on the Lohicca Sutta is finished.
13. Commentary on the Tevijja Sutta:
518. “Thus have I heard... in the Kosalan country” refers to the Tevijja Sutta. Herein, this is the commentary on the words not [already] explained. “Manasākaṭa”: [text].
The name of that village was Manasākaṭa. "To the north of Manasākaṭa" means on the northern side, not far from Manasākaṭa. "In a mango grove" refers to a thicket of young mango trees;

it is said that the ground there was delightful, with sand scattered below like silver plates, and above, the mango grove had dense branches and leaves like a canopy of jewels. In that place, which was worthy of the Buddhas—
The meaning is that he dwells in the mango grove in the bliss of seclusion.
(519) "Renowned, renowned" means they are well-known here and there due to their perfection in family conduct and other qualities.
Caṅkī and the others are their names. Among them, Caṅkī was a resident of Opāsāda; Tārukkha was a resident of Icchānaṅgala; Pokkharasāti...
Ukkaṭṭhavāsika was a resident of Ukkaṭṭha; Jāṇusoṇī was a resident of Sāvatthī; Todeyya was a resident of the village of Tudigāma;
and "others" refers to many other people. Having come from their respective places of residence, they lived there for the purpose of reciting the mantras.
It is said that because of the beauty of Manasākaṭa, those brahmins built houses on the riverbank there and had them enclosed.
Having prevented many others from entering, they would go there and dwell there from time to time.
520–521. Regarding "Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja": these were the pupil of Pokkharasāti, who was of the Vāseṭṭha clan, and the pupil of Tārukkha, who was of the Bhāradvāja clan.
It is said that these two were of noble birth and had mastered the three Vedas.
"Strolling on foot" means walking about for the purpose of dispelling fatigue caused by sitting for too long.
It is said that after spending the day in recitation, they would rise in the evening, have their bathing requisites, perfumes, jasmine oil,
and washed clothes brought to them, and, surrounded by their attendants, go to the riverbank wishing to bathe upon a patch of sand with the color of a silver plate.
They paced back and forth. One paced while the other followed him; then the other followed the next one, and so on. Therefore it is said:
"as they were pacing back and forth, as they were wandering about. Regarding "on the path and off the path": both on the path and off the path. [Thinking:
"Having fulfilled which practice, by which path is it possible to go happily to the Brahma-world?"—thus...
The meaning is: they initiated a discussion concerning what is the path and what is not the path. "The direct way" (*añjasāyana*) is a synonym for the straight path;
alternatively, it is called the "direct way" because by means of it they come (*āyanti*) or arrive in a direct manner. It is "leading out" (*niyyānika*) because it leads out (*niyyāti*);
"it leads out" means that as one goes, one goes toward liberation. This is the meaning.

"For the sake of companionship with Brahmā for one who acts" means: for one who makes and practices that path, it goes toward companionship with Brahmā—that is, toward manifestation in the same place.
"Yvāyaṃ" means "this one. "Akkhāto" means declared, explained, and illuminated.
"By the Brahmin Pokkharasāti" refers to his own teacher. Thus spoke Vāseṭṭha.
He wanders about praising and upholding his own teacher’s doctrine alone; Bhāradvāja does likewise. Therefore it was said:
“Vāseṭṭha was not able,” and so forth. Then Vāseṭṭha thought:
“The discourse of both of us is indeed not leading to liberation, and in this world, [only he] is skilled in the path.”
"There is no one equal to Master Gotama by name; moreover, Master Gotama lives not far away.
He will cut through our doubt like a merchant sitting with a scale in hand.
Having reflected thus, they informed Bhāradvāja of this matter, and both went together and reported their own views to the Blessed One. Therefore it is said: "Then Vāseṭṭha... [and so on]."
“...that which has been declared by the brahmin Tārukkha.

522. “In this matter, Master Gotama”: regarding this path and non-path. In such terms as *viggaha* (dispute) and *vivāda* (contention), *viggaha* arises first; subsequently comes *vivāda*. Both of these constitute *nānāvāda* (diverse doctrines) because they are the assertions of various teachers. 523. Then, as for the phrase “But in what [matter]?”:
you too, having maintained your own teacher’s doctrine that “this alone is the path,”...
"Bhāradvāja also stands by his own teacher’s doctrine; not even a single person has any doubt.
This being so, he asks: 'In what, then, do you have this dispute?
[The others reply: 'In the path and the non-path, Master Gotama—in the right path and the wrong path.'"
This is the meaning. It is said that he would not say even of a single brahmin’s path, "This is not the path.

However, he does not concede that the path of others is as straight as the path of his own teacher; therefore, in order to illustrate this point, he spoke the words beginning with, "But though, Master Gotama... and so forth.
"Sabbāni tāni" (all those) is stated with a change of gender; it means "sabbe te" (all those). "Bahūni" (many) refers to eight or ten.

"Nānāmaggāni" (various paths) refers to various kinds of approaches—such as paths with large or small footpaths, cart tracks, and so forth—by which people come from the vicinity of villages, rivers, ponds, fields, and so on, to enter the village.
525–526. “‘They go forth,’ Vāseṭṭha, do you say? Thus the Blessed One made a verbal statement three times and caused him to give his assent.
Why? For when those of other sects have made a claim and are later being refuted, they tend to disregard the charge.
He would not be able to do so in that manner.
527–529. *Teva tevijjā* means "those [who are] possessed of the threefold knowledge. The letter *va* is merely for the purpose of euphonic junction (*āgama-sandhi*).

*Andhaveṇī* means a "blind procession": one blind man grasps the end of a staff held by a single sighted man; another blind man grasps that blind man, and yet another grasps him—thus, fifty or sixty blind men joined in succession are called a "blind procession. They are "clinging to one another in succession."
They were clinging to one another, meaning they were deprived even of a sighted person to hold their staffs.
It is said that a certain rogue, seeing a group of blind men, incited them by saying, "In such-and-such a village, food and provisions are easily obtained.
When they replied, "In that case, master, lead us there; we will give you this," he took a bribe, left the path midway, and [led them] off the road to a great...
Having gone and walked around them, he had the man in front take hold of the flank of the man behind with his hand, and saying, "There is some work to be done;
you must go on for now," he fled. They traveled for a whole day but could not find the path;
lamenting, "Where is our one with vision? Where is the way? and still failing to find the path, they died right there.
Referring to these, it was said: "mutually entangled. "Even one among the former" means even one among the ten brahmins mentioned previously.

"Even one among the middle" means even one among the teachers and their teachers mentioned in the middle section. "Even one among the latter" means even one among the present-day brahmins learned in the three Vedas.
"Merely laughable" means it is simply something to be laughed at. "Merely nominal" means it is merely contemptible. This is because of the absence of actual meaning.

It is empty; it is hollow precisely because of its emptiness. Now, let alone the Brahma-world which has never been seen before by those possessing the threefold knowledge—regarding even the moon and sun, which the possessors of the threefold knowledge do see, [the Buddha] said, "What do you think?
and so forth, in order to show that they are not even capable of teaching the path to companionship with them.
530. In this context, "from where the moon and sun rise" means at the time when they rise;
and "where they set" means at the time when they disappear. The meaning is that they behold [them] both at the time of rising and at the time of setting.
"They entreat" means they entreat thus: "May you, O Moon, arise! May you, O Sun, arise! "They praise" means: "The moon is beautiful..."
They praise [him] by saying, "The moon is perfectly round; the moon is radiant," and so forth. *Pañjalikā* means with hands raised in the gesture of reverence (*añjali*).
*Namassamānā* means uttering "Homage! Homage! (namo namo). Regarding the phrase *yaṃ passantī*:

here, *yaṃ* is merely a particle. As for *na kira*: what indeed needs to be said here? The meaning should be understood as follows: "Where, it is said, Brahmā has not been seen face-to-face even by the Brahmins who possess the threefold knowledge (*tevijja*)."
The Simile of the River Aciravatī (Aciravatīnadīupamākathā).
542. "Even with its surface level" means filled to the brim. "Drinkable by crows" means it is possible for a crow standing anywhere on the bank to drink from it;
thus it is "drinkable by crows. "Desiring to cross to the other side" means desiring to go beyond the river to the opposite shore. "He would call out" means...
"Let him summon": "Come, O Pāra, come to the further shore"—that is to say, "O Pāra, come to the other side; then you may take me by force and go, for I have urgent business.
(544) Regarding the phrase "those qualities that make one a brahmin":
here, the various qualities consisting of the five precepts and the ten courses of wholesome action are what make one a brahmin.
These are to be known; those who act contrary to them are non-Brahmins. "We invoke Indra" means we call upon or summon Indra.

Having thus shown the futility of the Brahmins' invocation, the Blessed One—blazing like the sun in the midst of the ocean, surrounded by five hundred bhikkhus and seated on the bank of the Aciravatī River—furthermore gave another simile concerning the river.
While bringing [the robes], he said, "Just as if," and so forth. 546.
*Kāmaguṇā* means "strands of sensual pleasure": they are called *kāmā* in the sense of being objects of desire, and *guṇā* in the sense of being bonds.
For in the passage, "I allow you, monks, a double-layered outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) made of unwashed cloth," the meaning of *guṇa* is that of a layer. "Times pass..."
In the passage, “The nights pass away, the qualities of youth are gradually abandoned,” the meaning of *guṇa* is that of a heap (*rāsa*).
In the passage, “A hundredfold reward for the offering is to be expected,” the meaning of *guṇa* is that of benefit (*ānisaṃsa*).

And in the passage, “One should make an end with the inner cord, though there be many flower-strings,” the meaning of *guṇa* is that of binding (*bandhana*). Here too, this very same meaning is intended. Therefore it was said:
“In the sense of binding, they are ‘strands’ (guṇa). “Cognizable by the eye” means they are to be seen by visual consciousness (*cakkhuviññāṇa*).

By this same method, the meaning should be understood for those cognizable by the ear and so forth as well. “Desirable” means whether they have been sought after or not, they have become desirable objects.
“Pleasant” means lovely. “Agreeable” means increasing the mind’s satisfaction. “Of a dear nature” means born of what is dear. “Connected with sensual desire” means...

They are "conjoined with desire" by means of the desire that arises having made them its object. "Lust-inducing" (*rajanīyā*) means "causing lust" (*rañjanīyā*); the meaning is that they are the causes for the arising of passion.
"Infatuated" (*gadhitā*) means being overcome by greed. "Intoxicated" (*mucchitā*) means being overcome by an excessive craving that has reached the state of a swoon.
"Adhered to" (*ajjhopannā*) means having descended deeply into them, having plunged in, and having reached a final conclusion, thinking, "This is the essence."
"Those who do not see the danger" means those who do not perceive the peril (*ādīnava*).
