"Lacking wisdom regarding the escape" means being devoid of the wisdom that fully understands, "This is the escape from this," which is to say, they are devoid of both reflective awareness and the enjoyment [of the object].

Regarding the terms "obstructions" (*āvaraṇa*) and so forth: they are called "obstructions" because they obstruct; "hindrances" (*nīvaraṇa*) because they hinder; "envelopments" (*onāhana*) because they envelop; and "complete envelopments" (*pariyonāhana*) because they completely envelop. A detailed explanation of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and the other hindrances should be taken from the *Visuddhimagga*.
549–550. The terms *āvutā*, *nivutā*, *onaddhā*, and *pariyonaddhā* are stated with reference to obstructions (*āvaraṇa*) and so forth.

"With a wife" (*sapariggaha*)—he asks this because of a wife as a possession (*itthipariggaha*). In such phrases as "without a wife, Master Gotama," there is no wife as a possession due to the absence of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*).
Due to the absence of ill will (*byāpāda*), [there is no wife] with anyone.
He is "without enmity" because of his truthful mind. He is "unafflicted" because, due to the absence of sloth and torpor, he is free from the affliction known as mental sickness.
Because of the absence of restlessness and remorse, his mind is undefiled by the corruptions such as restlessness and remorse; his heart is perfectly pure.
Because of the absence of doubt, he brings his mind under his own control. And just as the brahmins say, "The mind is the forerunner," [so it is].
They proceed under the influence of the mind; one who is not like them is "one who has mastery" (*vasavattī*).
"But here," however, means here on the path to the Brahma-world. "Having sat down" means having approached what is not a path, thinking it is a path.
"Sinking away" means they enter [the wrong path] as if descending into a swamp with the perception that it is level ground. Having sunk away, there is a spreading out...
“They reach [it]” means that, having sunk as if in mud, they reach a state of dispersal and the breaking apart of limb from limb.

“They cross thinking it is drier” means that, deceived by a mirage with the perception that it is a river “drinkable by crows,” they think, “We shall cross,” and while exerting themselves with hands and feet, they cross thinking it is drier. Therefore, just as with the hands, feet, and so forth—
Shattering and crushing; thus they undergo shattering and crushing in the states of misery.

And even here, they find neither happiness nor pleasure. Therefore, this "of the Brahmins who possess the threefold knowledge" means that this Threefold Knowledge tradition, which illuminates the path to companionship with Brahmā, belongs to those Brahmins who possess the threefold knowledge. [It is] the desert of the Threefold Knowledge.
For "the wilderness of the threefold knowledge" (*tevijjārañña*) refers to a great wilderness devoid of villages, called a wasteland (*iriṇa*).
"The forest of the threefold knowledge" (*tevijjāvivana*) is a waterless wilderness covered with trees that provide no enjoyment of flowers or fruit;

it is with reference to such a place where one cannot even turn back after straying from the path that he says, "it is also called the forest of the threefold knowledge. "The ruin of the threefold knowledge" (*tevijjābyasana*)...
This is like the fivefold ruin of those possessing the threefold knowledge (*tevijjā*).

For just as there is no happiness for one who has met with the ruin of relatives, disease, wealth, views, or virtue, so too it is shown that for those possessing the threefold knowledge, there is no happiness whatsoever by resorting to the tradition of the threefold knowledge (*tevijjaka-pāvacana*).
554. "Born and raised" means both born and raised; for one who is merely born there [but] elsewhere...
He was raised; for him, the village roads in every direction were not entirely unfamiliar. Therefore, he said, "raised from birth.

Even for one who has been ordained for a long time, if he is one who has grown up [in the world], those [roads] are not entirely familiar. Therefore, he said, "having entered [the path] at that very moment";
the meaning is that he departed at that very instant. "Dandhāyitatta" means: "Is this the path? or "Is this the way? [he wonders].
"This is not [the case]" refers to the state of lingering due to doubt.
"To be protracted" means that just as the body of someone who is asked about a subtle matter suddenly becomes rigid, so too is this grasping at rigidity.
By the words "but certainly not," he shows the unimpeded nature of the knowledge of omniscience. For that person...
Through the interference of Māra and other such factors, there might be an obstruction to knowledge; because of that, one might be slow or hesitant.
However, he demonstrates that the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) is unimpeded, and it is impossible for anyone to create an obstacle to it.
"May the venerable Gotama lift me up" means may the venerable Gotama rescue me. "They lead away the brahmin girl" means they lead away the young brahmin boy.
The meaning is: "May Master Gotama lift my son, who is a brahmin, out from the path to the lower realms (apāya) and establish him on the path to the Brahmā-world.

Then the Blessed One, having shown the arising of a Buddha, and desiring to teach him the path leading to the Brahmā-world—consisting of dwelling in loving-kindness (*mettā*) and so forth, together with its preliminary practice (*pubbabhāga-paṭipadā*)—said, "In that case, Vāseṭṭha," and so on.
Therein, the passage beginning with "Here, a Tathāgata" occurs in the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta*.

This has been explained in detail. Regarding the passage beginning with "accompanied by loving-kindness" (*mettāsahagatena*), everything that needs to be said has already been stated in the *Visuddhimagga* in the discourse on the divine abidings (*brahmavihāra*) as a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
However, the passage beginning with "Just as, Vāseṭṭha, a powerful conch-blower... is new here. In that context, "powerful" (*balavā*) means endowed with strength.
"Conch-blower" (*saṅkhadhamo*) means one who blows a conch. "Without difficulty" (*appakasirena*) means without hardship or suffering. "Weak" (*dubbalo*)...
For even when one blows a conch shell, though he is blowing it, he is not able to make himself understood in the four directions by means of its sound;
nor does the sound of his conch spread everywhere. But for one who is strong, it is far-reaching; therefore he said, "one who is strong," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "by the liberation of mind through loving-kindness" (*mettāya cetovimuttiyā*): here, when "loving-kindness" (*mettā*) is mentioned, both access concentration (*upacāra*) and absorption (*appanā*) are included; as for "liberation of mind" (*cetovimuttī*), [it refers to the state of being liberated].
But when it has been said, absorption itself is required. As for "action that is measured": action that is measured is said to be of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara).

"Action that is immeasurable" refers to the fine-material and immaterial spheres (rūpārūpāvacara). For that is called "immeasurable" because it is performed by extending it beyond measure, by means of specific, non-specific, or directional diffusion. "It will not remain there; it will not persist there."
That sense-sphere karma does not linger, nor does it remain, within that fine-material or immaterial-sphere karma.

What is meant? That sense-sphere karma cannot, in the interval of that fine-material or immaterial-sphere karma, either cling to it, stay within it, pervade it, exhaust it, or take up its own place and become established.

It is not able [to do so]. Rather, it is only the karma of the fine-material and immaterial spheres that, like a great flood, having overspread and exhausted the limited water of the sense-sphere, takes its own place and remains;
having warded off its result, it itself leads one to companionship with the Brahmās. "Abiding thus" means abiding thus in loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables].
559. “We are yours, venerable Gotama”—this was their second going for refuge.
Having already gone for refuge upon hearing the Vāseṭṭha Sutta in the *Majjhima Nikāya*, they went for refuge once more upon hearing this *Tevijja Sutta*.
After a few days had passed, having gone forth, they received full ordination (*upasampadā*) at the *Aggañña Sutta*.
And they attained arahantship. The rest is clear in every respect.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Tevijja Sutta* in the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, the commentary on the *Dīgha Nikāya*.
The commentary on the Chapter on the Aggregate of Virtue (Sīlakkhandhavagga),
adorned with thirteen suttas,
is completed. The word-commentary on the Chapter on the Aggregate of Virtue is finished.
